en: Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
Commentary on the Middle Fifty of the Majjhima Nikāya.
1. The Chapter on Householders (Gahapativagga) 1. Commentary on the Kandarakasutta "1.
In monasteries, lotus ponds, and so forth" means in monasteries, lotus ponds, parks, shrine sites, and the like. "Abundant" means numerous.

It should be understood that because it was interspersed with *asoka*, *kaṇikāra*, *koviḷāra*, and *kumbhīrāja* trees, that campaka grove was adorned with flowers of five colors, such as blue and others;

they say this is not because the campaka trees themselves possessed flowers of five colors like blue and so forth. By the statement, "The Blessed One dwelt in the campaka grove, fragrant with the scent of flowers," it is shown that [the city] was not [only] at the time of its measurement.
The *campaka* trees were in full bloom; this indicates that it was not only at that time, but also at a later period.

“By about five hundred and twelve and a half”—this expresses the limit of the number as it was not explicitly stated. One who trains and instructs elephants is an elephant trainer (*hatthācariya*), one who teaches elephants;
he is called “the son of an elephant trainer” because he is his son. At that time, the Blessed One, for the purpose of generating faith in them...
Showing that he sat there without concealing his own Buddha-power, he said, "The six-colored, dense rays of the Buddha," and so forth.
"Out of reverence for the Blessed One" means out of a sense of weightiness toward the Blessed One; alternatively, the reading is "out of reverence for the Blessed One.
"It does not occur constantly" means it does not occur frequently; the meaning is that it occurs only occasionally. For here, "constancy" refers to frequency.
This is what is intended, not the permanence of a fixed state. When people see something wonderful in the world, they make a gesture with their hands or snap their fingers;
it is with reference to this that it is said, "it is appropriate to clap one's hands.

This etymological method (*niruttinaya*)—that what was previously non-existent has now come into being—should be understood as generally stated by way of conventional usage (*ruḷhī*) based on a figurative application. Likewise...
For in the Pāli, it is said: “Those who, Master Gotama, existed in past time,” and so forth.

Whatever is done that ought not to be done becomes a source of wonder due to its difficulty; likewise, there is something that ought to be done. The former is a marvel of censure, while the latter is a marvel of praise.
To show both of these through the words of the Sutta, the passage beginning with “Therein” was stated.
“Sammāpaṭipādito” means established in the right way of practice (*sammāpaṭipadā*). “Esā paṭipadā paramā” means this is the supreme;
this is a neuter noun construction, as in the expression “the moon and sun revolve unevenly. This is the meaning here:

the Blessed One has had the community of monks (*bhikkhusaṅgha*) led by you in the right way of practice; even in the past, the Buddhas [led] the community of monks to no more than this supreme state.

The wanderer, by means of his grasp of the method, inferring the unseen from the seen, shows that just as they have practiced correctly in the past, so too in the future time they will practice correctly toward this very same supreme Saṅgha of bhikkhus;
thus, regarding the correct practice of the Saṅgha in the teachings of all Buddhas, he demonstrates it as being exactly equal, like gold broken in the middle. Demonstrating it in this way:

And it should be understood that he demonstrates their excellent nature (*sudhammatā*) in such a way; however, the state of being well-awakened by the Buddha (*buddhasubuddhatā*) regarding them is shown in its very form.

By the phrase "not beyond this," he shows that which is excluded by the restriction "only up to this much" in the text, because concentration has virtue as its foundation (*sīlapadaṭṭhāna*), and wisdom has concentration as its foundation (*samādhipadaṭṭhāna*).

And regarding virtue (*sīla*), because it is the preliminary practice (*pubbakaraṇa*) for the higher conduct (*abhisamācārika*) and is the beginning of the holy life (*brahmacariya*), it is said: "beginning with the duty of higher conduct. 2.
Because it is not included within the connections of the questions and so forth, it is called a "separate connection" (*pāṭiekko anusandhī*);

and in order to make that very meaning clear, the passage beginning with "The Blessed One, it is said... was stated. "The cause of being tranquil" (*upasantakāraṇaṃ*) means the cause for the state of being tranquil. For that belongs only to the Noble Ones (*ariya*).

The phrase beginning with "Not indeed you" (*na hi tvaṃ*) and so forth is spoken in order to demonstrate, both through negative and positive concomitance (*vyatireka* and *anvaya*), that this is the domain [of the Buddhas], and even therein, it is exclusively the domain of the Buddhas without exception.
In this context, the conduct for the sake of knowledge (*ñātatthacariyā*) is to be understood by way of the *Kākajātakādi*;

the conduct for the sake of the world (*lokatthacariyā*) by way of the fulfillment of the various perfections (*pāramī*); and the conduct for the sake of Buddhahood (*buddhatthacariyā*) by way of the *Mahābodhijātakādi*.
By the words "It is wonderful, Master Gotama," etc., he shows the expression of confidence made by Kandaraka.
By the words "And those who... and so forth, the Blessed One accepted what was stated by him, repeating the meaning back;

because this occurred as a natural course of events, it is said: "For there are [those called] Kandaraka"—this too is a separate connection (*pāṭiyekko anusandhi*). For that which was [stated] by Kandaraka to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus...

The state of being peaceful is praised; even while demonstrating that by analyzing it, the Blessed One, having been requested by him and according to his own inclination, began the teaching with the words "There are indeed...
and so forth. Therefore he said: "It is said that this thought occurred to the Blessed One," and so on.
"Having fashioned" means having represented oneself as something other than one actually is. "Having contrived" means by way of being visible.
Having taken [this], he said: “By way of deceitfulness,” and so forth. Regarding the phrase “fulfilling the practice”:

although those in training (sekkhā) are generally referred to without distinction, they cannot be called “fulfilling” by virtue of having attained the path, because their task has already been completed.
For the path lasts for only a single moment of consciousness; thus he said: “pacified by the insight of the higher path. “Released from this” means:

“Liberated through the subsiding [of defilements] attained by means of the path. This is said with reference to the noble worldlings (*kalyāṇaputhujjana*). Therefore he says, “peaceful by means of the four foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*).
"Of constant virtue" means those whose virtue is uninterrupted. For their state of virtue being unbroken and so forth is preeminent.

Because they possess a continuous course of conduct by way of the extreme purity of their virtue, they are called "those of constant conduct"; thus he says, "this is a synonym for that. In this way, by way of virtuous conduct...
Having explained the meaning of the phrase “of one who lives continuously,” he now says, “the meaning is ‘one whose livelihood is continuous,’” showing it by way of the livelihood for life.
Since the livelihood for life of the Dispensation is dependent solely upon virtue, he says “in that,” and so forth.
It dries up—that is, withers away—the defilements such as lust; or, it causes oneself to fall [into safety] from those [defilements], thus it is “nipaka,” meaning wise. Therefore he said:

“Possessing wisdom”: having established oneself in wisdom, one abandons wrong livelihood—which is censured by the Buddha—and lives by right livelihood; showing this, he said, “Just as some,” and so forth.
Whatever needs to be said regarding that should be understood according to the method already explained in the *Visuddhimagga* and its commentary. [The paths] beginning with the *Rathavinīta*...

They are to be understood according to the method stated in those various suttas. Since the supramundane foundations of mindfulness (*lokuttara-satipaṭṭhāna*) have been explained elsewhere, such as in the *Mahāgopālaka Sutta* and others, he says:
"But here, the foundations of mindfulness mixed with both the mundane and the supramundane are explained.
This is because even in the *Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta*, they are explained as being mixed. "By this much" means by this much teaching.
3. *Kārakabhāvaṃ*: the state of being one who practices in accordance with the practice.
By saying, "Even we householders, though burdened with many duties, dwell from time to time with our minds well-established in the foundations of mindfulness;
how much more so, then, those who live in seclusion," he proclaims his own status as a practitioner and thus extols the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. Therefore, he said: "This, indeed, here..."

The phrase beginning with “the intention” (*adhippāyo*) and so forth: the state of being a thicket of defilements (*kilesagahana*) refers to the occurrence of defilements such as lust, which arise repeatedly upon various objects in a manner described as dense and entangled.
Thus he said: “The tangle within, the tangle without; by the tangle, mankind is entangled.
By way of grasping the inclinations of human beings, he also shows that there is deceit (*sāṭheyya*); thus he said: “In the case of dregs and deceit, it is exactly the same.”
“Method”: Just as the state of dregs in ghee, honey, molasses, and so forth is called *kasaṭa*, so too the impure state of defilement within the continuum is called *kasaṭa*;
thus he says, “in the sense of being impure, it is *kasaṭatā*. *Kerāṭiya* is the concealing of qualities one does not possess in oneself.
He “knows” means he investigates: “This is harmful and should not be practiced; this is beneficial and should be practiced.”
He teaches. For the word *jānāti* (knows) also has the sense of investigating, as in the expression “the Venerable One knows.

All [these meanings] are intended here, as in the case of the term “cattle-herders” (*pasupālakā*) and so forth. Here, the word *antara* has the sense of a moment (*khaṇa*), as in expressions such as “in the interval between lightning flashes” (*vijjantarikāya*);
thus he says, “by whatever moment. “By that” means by the elephant. “Those” refers to deceitfulness (*sāṭheyya*) and the rest.
In terms of its meaning, these are specific modes of occurrence of a thought-moment accompanied by greed, which are the opposites of bodily and mental rectitude.
To show them by way of their mode of occurrence, the passage beginning with "Therein" (*tatthā*) was stated. Therein, "of whom" (*yassa*) refers to a living being, such as a horse or an elephant.
"I shall stand" (*ṭhassāmi*) means that there is no thought, "Having gone to that very place, even though it is dangerous, I shall stand."

The manifestation of his deceitfulness is due to his state of intent to deceive. For it is said in four instances, "having deceived," whereas if he were merely concealing [his tracks], he would simply go and stand right there. This same principle applies to the other cases as well.
"Wishing to mount the opposite path" means wishing to turn back and go along the very path by which he had come. Regarding the discharge of dung and so forth:
He concludes with the word "thus" (*tathā*) to indicate the absence of dependence on another time.
"Born within" means born from the womb of one's own female slave. "Bought with wealth" means taken as a slave by giving money.
"Brought by force" means seized by a military force to become a slave. "Slavery" means the state of being a slave. "O servant" (*pessa*).
"Being no longer slaves, they become servants. "Having released this" means having released what was in their own hands.

"Taking this" means taking what was in his hands. It should be understood that by showing a difference in their bodily and verbal conduct when face-to-face compared to when they are out of sight, the fact that their state of mind has changed is demonstrated.
4. "This too is a separate connection" (pāṭiyekko anusandhi): here too, the application of the connection should be understood according to the method stated immediately above.
For this reason, he said "for this," and so forth. The construction is: "the fourth one has entered upon the way of welfare" (hitapaṭipadaṃ paṭipanno).
Showing the practice of the person by means of the person's heading, he said "having abandoned the person. For it is the practice that is to be abandoned here, not [the person].

Regarding individuals: just as the cultivation of the faculty of faith and the other faculties succeeds by avoiding individuals who lack faith and so forth, so too, by avoiding individuals who have entered upon a wrong course of practice, the wrong course of practice itself must be avoided. Thus it is said: "Having abandoned the first three types of individuals.
As for the "fourth individual," this refers specifically to the practice of what is beneficial for the fourth individual mentioned in this tetrad.

He says, "I practice and I set in motion," showing this. Regarding the word *santa*, its meaning here is "attained to peace, destruction, and cessation"; thus he says, "They are called *santa* because they have ceased. Again, regarding *santa*, its meaning here is "peaceful due to the departure of the fever of the defilements through cultivation"; thus he says, "they are extinguished" (*nibbutā*). The construction is by bringing in the word *santa*. As for the phrase *santo hava*: [The commentary continues: ...here... [text fragment] ...the meaning is "having attained peace through the cessation of birth and so forth. He says, "It is said that they are *santa* because they have reached peace," referring to the state of having attained the cessation of suffering. Furthermore, he says, "They are *nibbuta*," meaning they are peaceful because the burning heat of the defilements has vanished through the power of meditation. The Noble Ones, endowed with wisdom—which acts as a cause for equanimity and serves as a specific condition for goodness—are called "the peaceful" (santo);
thus he said: "Truly, the peaceful... the wise.
That wherein the conceit of "I" (ahaṃmāna) is placed is the self (attā), that is, personal existence (attabhāva). But here, that which is not another is the self; [he refers to] that self.
"Other" means something different from oneself. "Craving" (*chāta*) is so called because it is the cause of hunger.
"Internal burning afflictions" refers to those defilements that generate internal fever and consume one within one's own continuum. "He gladdens the mind" means he inspires confidence in the mind;
the sense is that he encourages it. Furthermore, when one who has become thus perfects the mind and adopts a resolute intention...
Thus it is named; therefore it is said, "he perfects the mind," and so forth.

5. That which has suffering as its repulsive and loathsome quality is "repulsive-suffering" (*dukkhapaṭikkūla*). For the application of the qualifier and the qualified is according to one's preference.
However, in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), with reference to the fact that "suffering" is the qualified term, [the compound] is analyzed as a *bahubbīhi* (possessive) compound.
Without taking [the person] as a basis, the meaning stated is that “suffering is repulsive.
For by that aspect in which suffering is repulsive to a person, the person is likewise repulsive to suffering. Therefore he said: “standing in opposition. 6.
“By four reasons” means by the four reasons beginning with skill in the elements. “He performs an action” refers to the action of yoga (*yogakamma*).
He acts. Because the Fully Enlightened Ones have conceived the aspiration for others to attain the paths and fruits, they are constantly and uninterruptedly engaged in that very endeavor;
depending upon them, no obstacle whatsoever arises for those [seekers]. Thus he said, "But not depending on the Buddhas.
This is because, regarding the loss of practice, there is an absence of the specific application (tajja-yoga) either in the teacher or in that particular individual.

“Of one who is desirous” (desakassa): this should be understood with reference to the disciples. Regarding the phrase “by way of great benefit,” the word *attha* here is a synonym for *ānisaṃsa* (benefit);
thus he says, “by two benefits. One acquires confidence through the hearing of the well-practiced Saṅgha, as expressed by the words “the Arahants,” and so forth.
A new method has arisen by way of constant virtue and so on, and by way of not tormenting oneself and so forth.

Having heard that, he too—becoming especially modest, compassionate, and sympathetic toward his slaves and others—practiced the virtue of the trainee’s path and gradually cultivated the development of the foundations of mindfulness. Therefore the Blessed One said:
"He is endowed with great benefit."

8. He is *ludda* (cruel) because he causes others to weep by killing, slaughtering, and so forth; he is *dāruṇa* (terrible) because he tears apart body and mind through the state of causing affliction; he is *kakkhala* (harsh) due to his hostile speech; and he is a *bandhanāgārika* (jailer) because he is appointed to the prison. 9.

"By the consecration of a khattiya" means by the consecration to be performed for khattiyas. "Santhāgāra" refers to a hall constructed as a place of assembly, namely a sacrificial enclosure (*yaññāvāṭa*).
"With ghee-oil" means with oil made of ghee; for at that time there was a double-fat (*yamakasneha*) [consisting of both ghee and oil].
He anoints his body. Having passed beyond the state of a calf, he stands as a young bull (*vacchatara*).

"For the purpose of making an enclosure" means for the purpose of encircling the altar-platform with *dabba* grass together with forest garlands. "In the sacrificial ground" refers to the remaining place for sacrifice.
Furthermore, whatever is not explained here in terms of its meaning is indeed easy to understand.
The *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Obscure Meaning) for the commentary on the *Kandarakasutta* is completed.
2. Commentary on the *Aṭṭhakanāgarasutta* 17.

By the word "not far" (*avidūre*), it is shown that in the Pāḷi text, the term "at Vesālī" (*vesāliyam*) is a locative expression denoting proximity. Regarding the phrase "by counting the clans that have attained the essence" (*sārappattakulagaṇanāya*):
"In the reckoning of families that have attained great essence and greatness. "In the tenth place" means in the position of the number ten, where one thing follows another.
"A native of Aṭṭhakanagara" means one whose birth was in the city of Aṭṭhaka. "Kukkuṭārāma" refers to the Kukkuṭārāma at Pāṭaliputta, not the one at Kosambī. 18.
Regarding the demonstrative pronoun *ta* in the explanation of the established referent: it stands in grammatical apposition with the words "by the Blessed One" (*bhagavatā*) and so forth.

He said, "He who... has awakened," demonstrating by way of the meaning (atthabhāva) that state of full awakening by which the Blessed One is known, attained, and made manifest, together with the path leading thereto.
Although the words *ñāṇa* and *dassana* here are synonyms for wisdom (*paññā*), they refer to specific objects through their respective distinctions.
In order to demonstrate their manifestation, he spoke the passage beginning with “Of each of those,” showing that purpose by connecting it to the unique distinction of his knowledge,

to the threefold clear knowledge (*vijjā*), to the knowledge of the obstacles to clear knowledge and direct knowledge (*vijjā-abhiññā*), to the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutā-ñāṇa*), to the fleshly eye (*maṃsa-cakkhu*),

and to the knowledge of penetration and teaching. Therein, by knowing the underlying tendencies (*āsayānusaya*) through the knowledge of underlying tendencies, [he knows] every phenomenon to be known.
"By seeing with the knowledge of omniscience free from obscurations" means by the knowledges of past lives, the destruction of the taints, and so forth.

"By the wisdom of penetration" means by the wisdom of the Noble Path. "By seeing with the wisdom of teaching" means by the wisdom of teaching the Dhamma regarding the various aspects of the phenomena to be taught, as well as the inclinations, latent tendencies, temperaments, resolutions, and other distinctions of the persons to be enlightened.

"For one who sees according to reality": "of enemies" refers to the enemies that are the defilements (*kilesa*), or the fivefold Māras, or the adversaries of the Teaching, namely the followers of other sects.
Their "slaying," however, means overcoming them through the miracles (*pāṭihāriya*), rendering them speechless, or simply disregarding them;
the *Kesī-vinaya-sutta* is an illustration of this.

Likewise, by one who knows the distinction between the possible and the impossible (*ṭhānāṭṭhāna*) and so forth; by one who sees beings according to their karma (*yathākammūpaga*); by one who is an *arahant* due to the destruction of the taints (*āsava*) along with their latent tendencies (*savāsanā*);
and by one who is a *Sammāsambuddha* because of his unerring realization of the phenomena to be directly known (*abhiññeyya*) and so forth, as being "to be directly known" and so on.

Alternatively, he is "one who knows" by virtue of his unimpeded knowledge regarding the three times; and [he is the one] regarding the three types of kamma by way of bodily action (*kāyakamma*) and the rest...
One should also apply the analysis by way of the ten powers and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (āveṇika-buddhadhamma) as follows:

he is the "Arahat" because of his perfection in abandoning, which—due to acting with circumspection following upon knowledge—is the proof of the absence of negligence and the like; and he is the "Sammāsambuddha" because of his omniscience, which—being the cause for the non-decline of zeal and the other factors—is the proof of inexhaustible eloquence.
Thus, the application should be made according to these ten powers and eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
19. "Conditioned" (*abhisaṅkhata*) means made by coming together, having met, and being produced by one's own conditions.
Its state of being "made" is to be understood through its arising, not through the reconditioning of what has already arisen; thus he says "produced" (*uppādita*).
And to show that these conditions of his have volition as their primary factor, the text says: "conditioned and willed" (*abhisaṅkhataṃ abhisañcetayitaṃ*).

"Vuttaṃ" (said) expresses the meaning of "that which is willed and intended. By the phrases "constructed" and "volitionally produced," he indicates, by way of showing the manifestation of jhāna, the state of its being subject to destruction;

for whatever comes into being after not having been, that, having come to be, passes away. Therefore, it is said in the text: "constructed," and so forth. "Established in the states of serenity and insight."

Established in the states of serenity (*samatha*), he becomes concentrated; having initiated insight (*vipassanā*), he abandons perceptions of permanence and so forth by means of the contemplation of impermanence and the rest.
Gradually reaching that knowledge of conformity (*anuloma-ñāṇa*), he stands firm in the states of insight.
Regarding the states known as serenity and insight: in the sense of coloring, it is lust (*rāga*); in the sense of delighting, it is delight (*nandī*). Therein, subtle expectation is spoken of.
That which is called "craving" (*nikanti*).

"When this is so" means: when the meaning of this sutta passage is to be understood according to the literal expression (*yathāruta*), then desire and lust (*chandarāga*) must be applied toward serenity and insight;
for, having realized the fruit of a non-returner, one would not even have to realize serenity and insight for that purpose.
Only desire and lust for that [attainment] must be cultivated there. Why?

Because among those states known as serenity and insight, since the non-returner who has not yet attained the fruit of non-returning must attain it through mere desire and lust, when that is so, even the fruit of non-returning is indeed said to be "attained" by him.
Therefore he said: “The fruit of non-returning...”
"It will be penetrated. Because it is to be tasted by way of its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), the very meaning that is not perverted is the "taste of the meaning" (*attharasa*).
When he says, "any other happy destinies," he is referring to those in the states of ruin (*vinipātika*). When he says, "any other unhappy destinies," he is referring to the host of asuras.

The burden of serenity (*samatha*) alone is the burden, because the teaching has come down according to the vehicle of one for whom serenity is the primary practice. [This is stated] in the *Mahāmāluṅkyovāda*.

Having established the foundational jhāna by means of the words, “secluded from unwholesome states, with applied thought and sustained thought,” and having expanded upon insight (vipassanā) with the passage beginning, “Whatever there is therein belonging to form, belonging to feeling,” and so forth, it is stated that “standing upon that, he attains the destruction of the taints (āsava-kkhaya).
Therefore, it is said: “In the Mahāmāluṅkyovāda, insight alone is the burden.”
In the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta, because it is presented entirely with a more acute insight (vipassanā), it is said: "The supreme insight was taught.

In the Kāyagatāsati Sutta, because serenity and insight (samatha-vipassanā) are presented in a distinguished manner by way of the jhāna of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna) and so forth, it is said: "The supreme serenity was taught."
Just as a noble person, when asked for a little and giving much, might say "this too is one thing" when asked about a single quality,
so too these eleven qualities came to be called "one quality" by way of the question, according to the principle of completing the sentence with each individual term.
Furthermore, they are "one quality" by way of the practice, because the path to be realized through those twenty-one sections is of a single nature.

"Named as having arisen": here, in this *Aṭṭhakanāgara Sutta*. Because the phenomena of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception have reached a state of extreme subtlety through the remaining formations (*saṅkhārāvasesa*), it is difficult for disciples to practice there;
thus, the teaching does not come down here by way of the fourth immaterial attainment (*āruppa*).

Consequently, there are eleven [types of concentration] by way of the four divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*) and the three lower immaterial attainments. "By way of questions" refers to: "Is there, venerable sir..."
"Ānanda, by that... [omitted] ...Perfectly Enlightened One, one single dhamma has been proclaimed"—this is according to the manner of the question thus put forth.

"In the sense of being the source of the deathless" means: because it is the cause for the arising of the state of the deathless; the meaning is that all meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna), though having a single flavor, are the practice for attaining the deathless.
Thus, in this context, there are only two: the stage of the supreme fruit and the stage of the non-returning fruit.

The planes have been presented according to their formal characteristics; however, it should be understood that even the two lower planes have been presented according to their actual meaning by way of the immediate (ānantariya) offenses.
"Worth five hundred" means that its value is five hundred. The rest is self-evident.
The *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Hidden Meaning) for the commentary on the *Aṭṭhakanāgara-sutta* is complete.
3. Commentary on the Sekhasutta 22. *Santhāgāra*:
a hall for providing instruction on matters of practical utility. Therefore he says, "at times such as when preparing for a military expedition," and so forth. By the word "etc.
(*ādi*), the inclusion of festivals for great blessings (*maṅgala*) and the like should be understood. *Santhambhanti* means they rest; they dispel their fatigue.
The meaning is as follows. "Saha" means together, by way of being situated in one place.

In the sense of "a hall for the instruction of the meaning (atthānusāsana)," it should be understood that the word *santhāgāra* is used by changing the letter *ttha* to *ntha*. They "santharanti" (assemble) in the sense of standing together in agreement.

It should be understood that because the word of the Buddha (buddhavacana) consisting of the Three Piṭakas will indeed have arrived there, the noble fruits of the Dhamma (ariyaphaladhammā) are also included under the heading of the arrival of the word of the Buddha.
The arrival [of the Noble Path] has already been stated; for those dwelling there throughout the three watches of the night, there is the enjoyment of the fruition-attainment (*phalasamāpatti*).
And if it is asked whether, in that community of monks, virtuous worldlings (*kalyāṇaputhujjana*) are exerting themselves in insight (*vipassanā*), the answer is:
the Noble Path-dharmas indeed arrive there as well.
"With fresh cow dung" means with clear, fresh cow-dung juice. "Having smeared" means having plastered.
"With four kinds of scents" means with scents made by grinding together *tagara*, saffron, *yava* flowers, and *tamāla* leaves;

"of various colors" means of various colors such as blue and so forth, not by way of different types of walls. However, by way of different types of walls, there are indeed various shapes and forms. "In a large *piṭṭhika-kojava*" means...
They say that a *kojava* is so called because it is spread upon the backs of elephants and thus receives the conventional name "great back-cloth.
However, this was said with reference to a *kuttaka*; for elephant-spreads (*hatthattharaṇa*) are variegated with the forms of elephants.

Likewise, horse-spreads (*assatthara*), lion-spreads (*sīhatthara*), and so forth, are spreads variegated with the forms of horses, lions, and the like. A *cittattharaka* (patterned spread) is [variegated] both by means of various forms and by various kinds of floral designs (*mālākamma*) and the like.
And a variegated spreader-cloth.

"A pillow" (*upadhāna*) means having placed a support; that is, having set it down in a manner suitable for serving as a support. A "garland of fragrance" (*gandhadāma*) is one made with fragrant substances.
A "leaf-garland" (*pattadāma*) is one made with *tāla* leaves and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), [substances such as] vermilion, *takkola*, nutmeg, and jasmine flowers are included.

It includes what has been made with cords. A seat made in the shape of a cross-legged posture is a *pallaṅka-pīṭha*. A leaning-back chair with a support on three sides or on one side is an *apassaya-pīṭha*.
One without a support is a *muṇḍa-pīṭha*. "In a yojana" means within a yojana’s extent.
"Having arranged" means having made the corner portion and the other portion of the inner robe (*antaravāsaka*) even, having thus prepared it. Therefore he said:
Regarding the phrase, “As if cutting a lotus with a knife,” which means “concealing the three circles”:

since the Buddhas’ perfection of deportment (*ākappa-sampadā*) reaches the highest excellence just like their perfection of physical form (*rūpa-sampadā*), the Blessed One was thus resplendent at that time.
To demonstrate this, he said, “With a golden girdle,” and so forth; therein, by the words “with the peerless appearance of a Buddha,” and so on, the Blessed One [was described].
Because there was no reason to conceal the Buddha’s majesty, he entered Kapilavatthu by means of his own natural and inherent activity alone,
in order to inspire confidence in the gods, humans, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas,
and others who had assembled there. He said, "An area of eighty cubits," because the bodily radiance of Buddhas naturally pervades a space of only that extent.
“He took [them]”: by way of blue, yellow, red, white, madder-red, and crystal-clear, these are the six-colored rays of the Buddha.
“In full bloom with all its blossoms” means blooming and fully opened from the roots up to the tips. “As if placed in succession,” and so forth, is a metaphorical comparison (*parikappa-upamā*).
Just as another shines when that [tree] is thus adorned, even so did it shine; among the thirty-two...
The meaning is that it shone forth in this way precisely because it was conditioned by the perfections (*pāramitā*).
"Of the twenty-five rivers" refers to the twenty-five great rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā and ending with the Candabhāgā.
"It broke apart" means having reached a state of division—that is, a state of mingling—at the mouth, which is the place where they enter the ocean.

The phrase "the eyes of gods, humans, nāgas, supaṇṇas, gandhabbas, yakkhas, and so forth" is stated by way of metaphorical conception. "With a thousand" means with a thousand verses—that is, with a text measuring one *bhāṇavāra*.
"Shaking the earth" means causing an earthquake through the excellence of his own qualities; even while being thus, he does not harm living beings.
Because Buddhas are worthy of all offerings (*sabbadakkhiṇa*), he raised his first foot as an offering (*dakkhiṇa*).
He touches the ground evenly because of his well-placed feet. Even though he touches the ground evenly, he is not smeared by dust due to the extreme delicacy of his skin.
"The low places rise up," and so forth, is the natural result (*nissandaphala*) of the Buddhas' attainment of the mark of a Great Man known as well-placed feet.
"He does not lift [the foot] too far" means that he does not place it too far away.
He does not lift [the foot]. He departs without placing [the foot] too near, nor failing to place it when the spot is not too near.
"Delighting" means gladdening the world including the devas. "Moving with four feet" (catucārī) refers to one who moves with four steps.
This is said to be the time for praise, because he has gone forth by way of manifesting the majesty of the Buddha. Or, it refers to the praise of the physical form or the praise of his virtues.
Or, when it is being recited, it should not be said that "it is poorly recited. Why? Because the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, possess immeasurable qualities;
thus, a description of the Buddha’s virtues enters precisely into a description according to the true nature of things for one who understands them.
"With a *dukūla* pillow" means with a *dukūla* cloth taken and tied together. "With the stride of an elephant-king" means with a placement of the feet resembling that of a noble elephant.
"Satapuññalakkhaṇo" means one who possesses the marks of a Great Man produced by many hundreds of merits.
"Maṇiverocano yathā" means like a gem called *verocana*, which shines exceedingly; some say it is a particular kind of gem.
"Mahāsālo va" means like a great *sāla* tree, or like a great tree such as the *koviḷāra*. "Padumo kokanado yathā" refers to that which is known as the *kokanada* lotus.
Like a great lotus, or like a blooming lotus;

"as if causing the celestial Gaṅgā to descend," and so forth— this introductory narrative demonstrates both the difficulty of this task for others and its quality of bringing ultimate happiness to those who hear it, just as one drawing up water from the earth by means of a water-wheel.

Having joined it to the lower surface of the great earth and turned the *pappaṭaka* (creeper) juice upwards, as if pulling it up, [he gave] a "yojanika" honey-vessel, meaning a honey-comb measuring one *yojana*.
"Great" means sublime. "All giving has been given" means that every kind of requisite (*paccaya*) has been given by the donor of the dwelling.

It is indeed given. For instance, even for one who has wandered for alms through two or three villages and returned with nothing at all, once he has entered a monastery endowed with shade and water, bathed, and lain down for a short while in his lodging before rising and sitting up, strength is brought back to his body as if it had been injected.
Furthermore, the element of beauty in the body of one wandering outside suffers from wind and heat.

Having entered a shelter and closed the door, for one who sits for a moment, the dissimilar continuity (*visabhāga-santati*) subsides and the similar continuity (*sabhāga-santati*) becomes established;
it is as if the element of beauty (*vaṇṇa-dhātu*) has been brought in and placed there.
But for one wandering outside, a thorn pierces the foot, a stump strikes him, and dangers such as reptiles as well as the fear of thieves arise.
But for one who has entered a sheltered dwelling, closed the door, and lain down, all dangers cease; for one reciting the Dhamma, the bliss of the joy of the Dhamma arises;
and for one attending to the meditation subject, the bliss of tranquility arises due to the absence of external distraction.
However, for one wandering outside, sweat breaks out on the body, the eyes throb, and the lodging—

At the moment of entering, the beds, chairs, and so forth are not visible; however, for one who has sat there for a short while, it is as if the clarity of his eyes has been brought back and restored to him, and the doors, windows, beds, chairs, and so forth become visible.
Furthermore, seeing him dwelling in this residence, people attend upon him with due care by means of the four requisites. Therefore it was said:
—“When the gift of a dwelling place is given, every kind of gift has indeed been given. This meaning, beginning with the eight grounds...
and ending with “one is not able,” should be illustrated by the story of Mahāsudassana.
“Cold” refers to the cold that arises either through the disturbance of the internal elements or through the change of the external seasons.
"Hot" refers to the heat of fire; its occurrence, however, should be understood as occurring in forest fires and the like. "Wards off" means he repels it.
He acts in such a way that, by means of both [cold and heat], there is no affliction of body or mind.

For when the body is afflicted by cold or heat, a monk whose mind is distracted is unable to apply himself with wise attention (*yoniso padahati*). "Fierce beasts" refers to fierce beasts such as lions, tigers, and so forth.
For when you have entered a well-guarded dwelling and sat down after closing the door, there are no dangers for you.
"Reptiles" (*sarīsapa*) refers to any long-bodied creatures that move by crawling. "Gnats" (*makasa*) is an illustration;

by this term, the inclusion of gadflies and the like should be understood. "In the cold" (*sisire*) refers to the touch of cold arising due to the winter season or due to events such as a week-long rainstorm.
The construction is as follows: "He wards off the rains" means that whenever they arise, he repels the falling rains.
"Terrible wind and heat" refers to the wind—distinguished by its dustiness or lack thereof—which is terrible because it proceeds by uprooting and breaking trees, shrubs, and so forth;
and the solar heat, which is terrible because it arises during the seasons of summer and feverish distress. "Is warded off" means it is repelled.
"For the sake of a shelter" means for the purpose of delighting in seclusion by turning the mind away from various objects.

"For the sake of comfort" means for the purpose of living at ease through the absence of the aforementioned dangers. "To meditate" means to contemplate the mind upon any one among the thirty-eight meditation subjects.
"To practice insight" means to comprehend all conditioned phenomena as impermanent and so forth.
"Vihāra" means a dwelling or residence. "Kāraye" means he should have them built. "Ramma" means delightful and pleasant for the comfort of living.
"Vāsayettha bahussute" means that after having them built, he should cause those who are learned, virtuous, and of noble character to dwell there.
Furthermore, while causing them to dwell there, he should provide food and so forth in such a way that those learned ones do not experience exhaustion due to a lack of requisites.

One should give drinks, robes, and lodgings to those who have become upright and are endowed with noble aspiration, with a mind made serene through faith in the fruits of kamma and the qualities of the Triple Gem.
Now, in order to show the mutual assistance between householders and those gone forth, he spoke the verse beginning with “te tassa. Therein:
"Of him"—that is, of that lay follower (*upāsaka*). "Teaching the Dhamma": they teach the Dhamma that dispels the entire suffering of saṃsāra.

"Having understood that Dhamma here": that person, having understood the true Dhamma in this dispensation through right practice, becomes free from taints (*anāsava*) by attaining the supreme path and attains final Nibbāna.

The first watch was spent merely through the performance of worship and honor; since only a small portion remained of the Blessed One’s teaching by the time the middle watch had passed, it is said in the *Pāḷi* that "much of the night" had gone by. Therefore, he said, "more than one and a half watches.
"He instructed" means he showed the benefits (*ānisamsa*). After hearing the Dhamma talk connected with the gift of a dwelling place, [the King thought], "Great King..."
"Such is virtue, such is concentration, such is wisdom"—thus he correctly showed them the qualities of virtue and the rest;

as if taking them by the hand, he made them manifest to their direct experience. "He incited them" means he caused them to take up the qualities of virtue and the rest in such a way that they would adopt them, saying: "Virtue should be undertaken in this way;
for one established in virtue, concentration should be developed in this way, and wisdom in this way."

"Samuttejesi" means he inspired the mind so that the virtue (sīla) undertaken would become thoroughly purified, and so that serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā), when cultivated, would be well-cleansed and bring about higher distinctions;
thus he gladdened the mind by way of making it attentive and purified it through careful observation.

"Sampahaṃsesi" means he caused [the mind] to rejoice through the qualities of virtue and so forth as established according to the instruction, and through the benefits of the qualities presently attained.
He properly gladdened his mind with the special fruits to be obtained hereafter and thoroughly delighted it by means of the attainment of assurance (*assāsa*).
In this way, the meaning of these words is to be understood.

Furthermore, the term "eighty great elders" (*asīti-mahāthera*), though denoting a collective whole, is conventionally applied to a part thereof; thus he says, "while the eighty great elders were present. For the Elder Ānanda is also included therein. "In the Śākya territory" (*sākiyamaṇḍale*) means in the assembly of the Śākya kings.
Because he is engaged in the practice (*paṭipadā*), he is "one who practices" (*pāṭipada*). Therefore it was said: "one who has entered upon the way" (*paṭipannaka*).
He is a "learner" (*sekha*) by virtue of his habit of training and so forth; he is a "recluse" (*samaṇa*) because of having fully stilled evil through specific limits.

By defining the teaching on the practice through the person who is practicing—that is, by designating the person as the basis for the practice—it is said: "having defined the person by means of the practice, he shows [it]."
The way of practice for those in training (*sekha*) is the auspicious way of practice within the Dispensation;

it is a "progressing way of practice" because it brings about the fulfillment of the qualities of one beyond training (*asekha*) through the proper avoidance of what is not to be cultivated, the undertaking of what is to be cultivated, and the cultivation of the grounds for excellence.
The phrase "they will discern without weariness" was said because at that time they lacked the fitness to attain the stage of one beyond training.
"Without weariness": by this, he shows that even for one who has attained the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), the perception of a path not yet realized is a heavy burden.
"Entered" means having entered within. The entire *Vinaya Piṭaka* is indeed already included because of its abundance of discourse on virtue (*sīla*);
the same principle applies to the other two [piṭakas] as well. "By the three piṭakas": the instrumental case is used in the sense of an instrument. By that, [he indicates] those respective piṭakas...
This demonstrates the preeminent efficacy of each respective training.
Back pain arises because the body is composed of what is clung-to (*upādinnaka*) and because conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) are impermanent and bound up with suffering.
Or rather, "this is not the reason" refers to the intention with which it was stated; to clarify that very intention, [the text] says "it is capable," and so forth.
It has been stated. He wished to enjoy [the meal] through all four postures out of consideration for the inclination of the Sakyan kings;
for thus he will say: "The Teacher, with reference to that very thing, having spread his outer robe there, lay down.
If this is so, how is it that he said, "My back aches"? To this he replied: "And what is called the body composed of the clung-to (upādinnaka)," and so forth.
23. In such passages as “By this restraint of the Pātimokkha... endowed,” the word *sampanna* has the sense of being “possessed of.
However, here it is stated that “‘of perfected virtue’ is the meaning” in order to show that it carries the sense of completeness (*pāripūri*).
For one who is indeed possessed of virtue is one whose virtue is perfected; for virtue that is entirely pure is called “perfected,” not that which is mottled or flawed.

"By beautiful qualities" (*sundaradhammehi*) means by auspicious qualities. Because they bring about a state of beauty in the mental continuum (*santāna*) in which they have arisen, they are "qualities of true persons" (*sappurisadhammā*) because they accomplish the state of being a true person.
By this much—that is, from the passage beginning with "Here, Mahānāma, a noble disciple" up to "one who gains without difficulty"—[the first tetrad is completed].
Having established the matrix (mātikā) by this much of a summary heading (uddesapada), [the text says] "in sequence" (paṭipāṭiyā), meaning according to the sequence of the summary headings.
"Thus he said" means he spoke in the manner now being shown by the passage beginning, "And how, Mahānāma? and so forth.
25. "He feels shame" (hirīyati) means he is ashamed or oppressed [by conscience]. Since shame (hirī) has the characteristic of loathing evil, therefore [it is said] "he loathes."
"Meaning" (attha) has been stated. "Shame" (ottappa) means one is ashamed (uttappati). For shame is characterized by shrinking away from evil.
"With energy exerted" means with energy that has not fallen into contraction; therefore he said, "with a mind free from despondency. "For the sake of abandoning" means for the sake of cutting off.
Since the acquisition of wholesome states (kusala-dhamma) is indeed their attainment, he said, "for the sake of obtaining. "By mindfulness and discernment" (satinepakkena):

[This is] by means of mindfulness, by means of discernment (*nepakka*), and by means of a state that is sharp, clear, and courageous. In the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), however, with the intention that "discernment" (*nepakka*) is wisdom (*paññā*), the meaning is stated as "by means of mindfulness and by means of a state of being prudent (*nipaka*). If this were so, then [prudence] would be something distinct that has been specified.
By the very term "mindful" (*satimā*), mindfulness is already grasped as a specific quality; furthermore, [the text says]: "Even what was done long ago, even what was spoken long ago..."
In the phrase “well-remembered, recollected,” only the function of mindfulness (*sati*) is indicated, not the function of wisdom (*paññā*).

Therefore, it can be understood that “by mindfulness and discernment” (*satinepakkena*) means “by the state of mindfulness being discerning. For this very reason, the power of mindfulness is independent of other factors due to a specific condition;
thus, even with a consciousness dissociated from knowledge (*ñāṇa*), the processes of learning (*ajjhāyana*) and comprehension (*sammasana*) are possible.
Regarding "the observance of duties at the cetiya courtyard, etc.," the word "etc. includes the observance of duties at the Bodhi courtyard and so forth.

In the phrase "fulfilling the practice of the eighty great observances" (*asītimahāvattapaṭipattipūraṇaṃ*), the term *vattapaṭipattipūraṇa* (fulfillment of the practice of observances) should be applied to each individually: "fulfilling the practice of the eighty observances" and "fulfilling the practice of the great observances.
Among these, the "great observances" are those stated in the *Vattakkhandhaka*: the observance for incoming monks...

There are fourteen duties: those of a resident monk, a departing monk, one who expresses approval, the meal-distributor, the alms-collector, the forest-dweller, the lodgings-keeper, the bath-attendant, the latrine-attendant, the preceptor, the co-resident pupil, the teacher, and the pupil.

Beyond these, there are eighty minor duties that must occasionally be performed at times such as when a censure-act (*tajjanīya-kamma*) has been carried out, or during periods of probation (*pārivāsika*).
These are not to be practiced in all circumstances; therefore, they are not included among the major duties (*mahāvatta*).

Therein, beginning with “I shall prescribe the duty for monks who are on probation,” sixty-six duties are stated, ending with the duties to be practiced regarding prepared food, starting from “one must not confer full ordination...
[and so on] ...nor should one walk up and down on a walking-path while those walking on the path are on the ground.”

After that, [the Buddha said]: “Monks, a monk who is on probation (pārivāsika) should not dwell under one roof in a residence with a monk who is senior to him in the probationary status, nor with a monk who is subject to sending back to the beginning (mūlāyapaṭikassanāraha), nor with a monk who is subject to the trial period (mānattāraha), nor with a monk who is undergoing the trial period (mānattacārika), nor with a monk who is subject to rehabilitation (abbhānāraha);
and so forth—these rules are stated separately because those who are to undergo the penance as a regular (pakatatta) monk are not different from others.

Not counting them separately, because they must be observed among other classes of persons such as those on probation (*pārivāsika*) or those senior in ordination, they are to be counted by combining them and treating each as one;
thus there are seventy-one rules. Regarding the rules for those subjected to an act of suspension (*ukkhepaniya-kamma*), it is stated by way of prescribing the duties:
“One should not perform salutation or rising in respect toward a regular (*pakatatta*) bhikkhu... [and so forth].”
“Bathing and back-massage should be accepted”—this is one instance of not consenting to such acts as prostrations;
and there are ten others, such as “a regular bhikkhu must not be accused of a failure in virtue. Thus, these amount to eighty-two.

Furthermore, among these very rules, some are observances for those undergoing formal acts of censure (tajjanīya-kamma) and so forth, while others are observances for those on probation (pārivāsika) and so forth; this is stated by way of including what has not yet been mentioned.
“Eighty-two”: although there may be such slight deficiencies or excesses that they do not affect the count, here it is stated simply as “eighty.
However, in other places, according to the commentaries, it is said: “There are eighty-two duties of the Khandhaka.

The phrase “careful recitation” and “careful causing to recite” should each be construed with the word “carefully” (*sakkacca*). “Recitation” (*uddisana*) means the taking up of the recitation. “Recollection of the Dhamma” (*dhammosāraṇa*) means the vocalization of the Dhamma. “Teaching of the Dhamma” (*dhammadesanā*)—
“In the beginning one should teach virtue; in the middle, meditation and insight;
and at the conclusion, Nibbāna—this is the established method for a speaker.
Thus is the discourse on the Dhamma characterized. To any householder who has approached and sat down...

For one who has gone forth, a talk on the Dhamma appropriate to that occasion is an "upanisinnakathā" (a seated talk). A talk expressing gratitude for a meal is an "anumodaniyā" (a talk of thanksgiving).
Regarding the term "saritā" (recollection): here, what is intended is not merely the recollecting or remembering of things done long ago or spoken long ago;
rather, it is the practice of insight (*vipassanā*) as it occurs by way of discerning the mental and physical phenomena (*nāmarūpa-dhamma*) that have arisen in such a manner.
In order to show the arousing of the mindfulness factor of enlightenment (*satisambojjhaṅga*), it was said: "When that has been done for a long time by means of the body," and so forth.
"By remembering even once" means by remembering a single time. "By remembering again and again" means by remembering repeatedly.
And while remembering, one makes even the mindfulness factor of enlightenment dependent on seclusion, dependent on dispassion, dependent on cessation, and resulting in relinquishment. Therein—
In this context, it should be understood that she recollected by way of the access-javana and the limited-javana during the javana-phase.
Since the word *dhātu* has the sense of "going" (*gati*) as well as the sense of "understanding" (*buddhi*), he said: "capable of penetrating both arising and passing away.
He stated: "by way of suppression and by way of eradication," because this teaching is presented according to the mixed method (*missakanaya*).
Therefore he said, “And by means of insight-wisdom,” and so forth. This refers to insight-wisdom in its penetrating sense.
And since that [insight-wisdom] is partial, it was stated, “because it leads to the acquisition of path-wisdom,” in order to show it as being non-partial.
The same method applies to its being the state of leading to the destruction of suffering. “Sammā” means according to reality. By way of its unshakable nature...

For the wisdom of the path (maggapaññā) has already exhausted what was to be exhausted and there is nothing further to be done; thus he said, "by way of cause and method" (hetunā nayenā), meaning that its occurrence is precisely by means of skillful means and the correct principle. 26.

"Abhiceto" means superior mind (adhikaṃ ceto), which is to say, the exalted mind (mahaggatacitta). Its superiority, however, consists in the departure from the opposites such as sensual desire (kāmacchanda) and so forth.
The attainment of a distinguished state, and the higher mental states (*ābhicetasika*) dependent upon it. Therefore he said: "Of those things dependent on the higher mind, the excellent mind.

Regarding the phrase "of the dwellings in happiness in this very life" (*diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārānaṃ*): it refers to those which constitute a state of ease within this very personal existence (*attabhāva*).

Furthermore, at the moment of being endowed with them, there is the rapture and happiness born of seclusion (*vivekaja-pītisukha*), the rapture and happiness born of concentration (*samādhija-pītisukha*), and that which is not born of rapture (*apītija*).
He acquires and finds the happiness of knowledge through the purification of mindfulness; therefore, it says: "for the causes of obtaining happiness at every moment of absorption.
By the phrase "entering [jhāna] at whatever moment one wishes," the mastery of entering those jhānas is expressed;

furthermore, from the expression "one who obtains them at will," it should be understood that the masteries of adverting, resolving, and reviewing are also stated. "One who obtains them without difficulty" means:
By this, he shows that those jhānas possess a pleasant way of practice (*sukha-paṭipadā*) and quick direct knowledge (*khippābhiññā*);

by the phrase "one who gains them abundantly," he indicates their proficiency (*paguṇatā*), because it demonstrates that they have been brought to a state of mastery. Therefore, he says, "by way of proficiency," and so forth.
One is able to attain [them] because mastery over attainment has been accomplished. "Obstructive states to concentration" refers to those factors that are adverse to mastery.
Furthermore, the states that are adverse to the attainment of jhāna have already been suppressed; otherwise, the attainment of jhāna itself would not be possible.
Since one who is not weary is unable to suppress them, one suppresses and purifies them with difficulty.
Here, "suppression" refers to the removal from afar of sensual desire and other factors that obstruct concentration, by means of reflecting on the danger of sense-desires and so forth.
It should be understood as "purification.
Because it brings about successive distinctions for the sake of establishing insight (*vipassanā*), the preliminary practice consisting of virtue (*sīla*) and so forth increases.
That very preliminary practice, by virtue of being cultivated in accordance with its true nature, encompasses the distinction that will necessarily arise.
"Apucchaṇḍo" means one whose "aṇḍa" (egg/testicle) has departed; because it is not defiled by the *kilesas* (defilements), it is an "unputrid egg.

One who stands having exerted themselves in *vipassanā* is thus called *apuccaṇḍo*; the state of being such is *apuccaṇḍatā*. "For the differentiation of the knowledge of *vipassanā* and so forth" means for the differentiation of the various knowledges beginning with the knowledge of past lives (*pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa*).
"Therein" refers to the *Cetokhila Sutta*: "That person, bhikkhus, being thus endowed with the fifteen factors of exertion..."
Because it is stated that "a bhikkhu is capable of breaking out," the state of being endowed with fifteen factors including zeal (*ussoḷhi*) is what is meant;
thus, the connection is that this application of the simile which has been introduced should be understood here by applying it to this *sekha-sutta*.

28. It is "unsurpassed" (anuttara) because, by way of its loftiness (mahaggata) and other qualities, it stands having surpassed and transcended the lower jhānas, even those that are similar to it, by means of its own specific distinction.
Therefore, it is said: "It is incomparable and supreme compared to the first and subsequent jhānas. This applies also to the second and higher stages of penetration (abhinibbidā).
When the knowledge of past lives (pubbenivāsañāṇa) arises, it does so in such a way that it removes the veil obscuring its own objective domain.
It arises precisely while dispelling the darkness of the defilements; thus, it arises precisely while making some distinction within its own domain.
Therefore, he said: "First, it is born through the knowledge of past lives. This same method applies to the other two knowledges as well.

Regarding the phrase "in the case of conduct" (*caraṇasmiṃ*), this is the locative case used in the sense of the subject itself; thus he said: "The meaning is that it becomes what is called 'conduct'. The word is in the instrumental case in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇatthe*); for in the act of going to a direction not previously traversed, these [knowledges] function as the most effective means (*sādhakatamabhāvato*).

"Eight knowledges" refers to those included here as well as those not yet mentioned, taking into account those found in the Ambaṭṭha Sutta and others. "Having pierced through" means having broken and split open the darkness of the defilements that conceal past lives and so forth.
"By Sanaṅkumāra" means by Sanantana-kumāra. Indeed, it is precisely to show his state as Sanantana-kumāra that it is said, "from long ago.
"That personal existence" refers to the personal existence by which [he attained] jhāna on the path of men.
He manifested that state of a youth; therefore, although he has become a Brahmā, he moves about in such a form as a youth.
The word *janitasmiṃ* is spoken by changing the vowel *i* to *e*, thus becoming *janetasmiṃ*;

and its meaning should be understood as *janasmiṃ* (among people). Even though *janitasmiṃ* is used as a general term, it refers specifically to those places where the designation of the four castes (*cātuvaṇṇa*) applies.

"In that very world of humans" means: in order to show that even the worldly designation "the Kṣatriya is the best" applies only to the world of humans, and not to the host of gods or the host of Brahmas, it was said, "those who rely on their lineage.
"They rely" (paṭisaranti) means they each individually trace back and acknowledge their own lineage, saying, "I am a Gotama, I am a Kassapa," and so forth.
“By this much” means by the granting of applause with the words, “Excellent, excellent, Ānanda!
That which is called “spoken by the Conqueror” (jinabhāsita) has come to be so from beginning to end; that which was spoken by the Elder has indeed become spoken by the Buddha.
[One might ask: “Is this discourse ‘spoken by the Conqueror’ because it conforms to the Teacher’s instruction, or rather merely because of the granting of applause? Such [a doubt]...
In this context, there is no occasion for an objection, because the Elder’s teaching is based on following the teaching of the Blessed One;
thus, there is no reason to offer applause. Furthermore, whatever has not been analyzed here in terms of its meaning is indeed easy to understand.
The *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Hidden Meaning) of the commentary on the *Sekha-sutta* is completed.
4. Commentary on the Potaliya Sutta 31.
The "Aṅgas" were princes belonging to a particular region; because they resided there, that single region as well came to be called simply "Aṅga" by conventional usage.
Thus it is said: "That region was indeed Aṅga. To the north of this [region], however, lies the Mahī, which is the river Mahī.
The waters that lie to the north of that country are called "Uttarāpā" because they are not far from it.
However, since that Mahī river has broken apart and flowed away in various places here and there, he says, "the waters to the north of whichever Mahī [is meant].
The phrase "therein" (*tattha*) refers to this explanatory discourse beginning from the point where that Mahī arrived. Because it is worldly...

Regarding the passage beginning with "Jambudīpa, Himavā, and therein the oceans, lakes, mountains, and rivers": whatever among these is not within the range of human experience, there people become confused themselves and cause others to be confused as well;
therefore, for the purpose of dispelling confusion in each such case, the section beginning with "This, it is said, is Jambudīpa" was commenced.
It measures ten thousand yojanas in both length and breadth.
This is the intended meaning (*adhippāya*). Therefore, he said “therein,” and so forth. It is submerged by water due to the exhaustion of the merit of the beings who enjoy it.
Sudassanakūṭa means a peak of beautiful appearance; that which is called “Hemakūṭa” in the world. Root-fragrance refers to black cardamom (*kāḷānusāri*) and the like.
Heartwood-fragrance refers to sandalwood and the like. Inner-bark fragrance refers to *salala* and the like. Bark-fragrance refers to cloves (*lavaṅga*) and the like.
The scent of bark refers to *kapittha* and the like. The scent of sap refers to *sajja* and the like; the scent of leaves refers to *tamāla*, *hirivera*, and the like.
The scent of flowers refers to *nāga-kuṅkuma* and the like. The scent of fruit refers to *jāti-phala* and the like. The "scent of scents" is the fragrance of all fragrances.
For that tree which possesses the fragrance of all its parts, from the roots upward, it is here called "scent. Of that scent...
"Gandho gandhagandho" means "fragrance upon fragrance. They say that all [these mountains] are fifty yojanas in width, while in length they are like two hundred yojanas in height.
"Manohara-silātala" means delightful stone terraces for the purpose of descending. "Supaṭiyattāni" means well-prepared for the beings who enjoy them.
By the power of collective karma, they are well-prepared and function perfectly.

Because fish, turtles, and other creatures do not make the water turbid, the waters are as stainless as crystal. It is called the "mountain of the horizontal" (*tiracchānapabbata*) because it rises high and extends long across the horizontal plane.
He said, "thousands of market-fronts," because market-places are the very gateway to trade. "Distinguished" means demarcated, not intermingled with one another.
"Place of residence" means a place where one may dwell according to one's own convenience.
"Seat" (āsana) is so called because one sits there; it refers to places for sitting.
Because it conceals that which arises in dependence on what is unsuitable, it is "concealed" (*channa*);

because it is fitting for that very thing and manifests its excellence of aspiration, it is "suitable" (*patirūpa*). Therefore he said, "it is not suitable. "Synonyms for cause" means synonyms for a signifying cause;
for it is a signifying cause that is intended here. It is called a "mode" (*ākāra*) because it brings out or manifests the meaning; that very [meaning] is hidden and secret...
"It leads to the goal" is its characteristic (*liṅga*); it is called a "sign" (*nimitta*) because one is identified by means of it. Now, in order to explain that very meaning, he said:
"The long, the cloth, the cow... [etc. ...are called signs. "Those" refers to the vowels beginning with *ā*.
For instance, by the words "But I am... and so forth, the householder Potaliya thought: "I live according to the way of a wanderer; therefore, I am not a householder."
He speaks. "Admonishing" means instructing. "Reproaching" means censuring. 32.
"Greed is the state of being greedy" means greed has the nature of longing. That which has the characteristic of not longing is not greed.
"Non-reproach" means the absence of striking others, which is the opposite of reproach. "Reproach and striking" refers to [striking] by way of reproach.
“Provoking others” means reviling them. “Trade and commerce” refers to the characteristic of buying and selling; it is also called *vohāra* (transaction) because it consists of giving and taking.
It is also called *paññatti-vohāra* (conventional designation), because it is the designating or establishing [of things] through such expressions as “Datta” or “Tissa.

It is also called *vacana-vohāra* (verbal expression), because it is the expressing, speaking, or making known of a meaning according to one’s intention. One expresses [things] both as they truly are and as they are not.
“By this, ‘conventional expression’ (vohāra) means volition (cetanā). ‘This is intended here’ means that this conventional expression characterized by volition is intended here in this context;
moreover, it is precisely the blameworthy [volition] that is intended, because its total eradication is what is desired.
Now, in order to show the occurrence of all four kinds of conventional expression here, the passage beginning with ‘Because... was stated. ‘The householder has no volition’—”
There is no occurrence of the volition "I am a householder. There is no utterance of the word "householder" means there is no occurrence of the verbal expression "householder" for oneself or others.
There is no designation "householder" means there is no conventional name "householder. There is no usage "householder" means there is no customary behavior [based on that term].
33. Killing living beings (*pāṇātipāta*) itself is a fetter (*saṃyojana*). Why? Because it functions as a bond and because it does not allow for escape.
Since that person possesses killing living beings, they are called a "killer of living beings" (*pāṇātipātī*); thus he said: "Because of the existence of killing living beings...

[etc]... there is [the fetter]. For one is designated by that which one possesses. "Due to its multiplicity" means due to its manifold nature through the various divisions such as the lack of eyes and so forth.

The opposite of taking life is abstaining from taking life. In terms of its meaning, however, this is the restraint of virtue pertaining to the door of the body; thus he said, "by means of bodily restraint of virtue.
"One might censure me," and so forth, is the demonstration of the danger in taking life, for one who sees the danger will desist from it.
"By way of the teaching" refers to the ten fetters found elsewhere in the Suttas and the Abhidhamma.
Among the five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), even that which is not included [in the list of fetters] is here spoken of as both a fetter (*saṃyojana*) and a hindrance by way of its teaching.
Why? Because its purpose is the same. Therefore he said: "In the sense of being a bond for the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭabandhana*) and in the sense of concealing what is beneficial.
For killing living beings arises precisely while concealing the benefit that consists in the non-killing of living beings. One outflow (*āsava*) is ignorance (*avijjā*).

This has been stated by way of co-nascence (*sahajāta*); however, by way of decisive support (*upanissaya*), the arising of the other taints (*āsava*) should also be understood according to their respective cases.

For a person who takes life, thinking “I shall achieve wealth on that account,” longs for sensual pleasures, adopts wrong views, and looks forward to a particular state of existence (*bhava*). That which arises therein and strikes down or afflicts is called “affliction” (*vighāta*).
"Suffering" (dukkha) is the state of being afflicted; "fever" (pariḷāha) is the burning caused by the arising of harm—this is the distinction between them.
"In all instances" means in all sections. By the phrase "by this method," which is an elliptical reference (atidesa), it is indicated that the meaning will be understood from what follows.
34–40. Regarding the phrase "in this passage": by this, the passage as it has occurred in all seven sections is taken collectively.
Therefore he said, "By this," and so forth. Since irritation is both bodily and verbal, its opposite—non-irritation—is likewise twofold; thus he said, "by restraint of body and speech.
Just as covetousness is greed (*lobha*) and non-covetousness is non-greed (*alobha*), so too is ill-will (*abyāpāda*) the absence of anger and resentment;
it should be understood that "restraint" (*saṃvara*) means happiness in restraint. Furthermore, non-excessive greed pertains to the restraint of mindfulness, while non-excessive pride pertains to...

It should be understood that it is included within the restraint of knowledge (*ñāṇasaṃvara*). Furthermore, the connection [of the text] is that the application should be made in this manner across all sections in these locations.

Regarding the phrase "thus the arising of the taints (*āsava*) is to be known," although it was already stated there, because it is now being stated together in one place, it is said again: "Furthermore, this is the concise analysis."
It has been stated. For the sake of non-confusion regarding the object: in the first four sections, one should say "I am unable to desist.
In the commentary on the meaning of the phrase "my own self might censure me," it says "I am unable";
and in the commentary on the meaning of the phrase "wise investigators might condemn me," it says "he is unable."
It should be stated that, according to this method, the application should be understood accordingly for the final four [fetters] as well.
Regarding conceit (*atimāna*), it is said that there are the taints of existence (*bhavāsava*) and ignorance (*avijjāsava*), because conceit does not arise together with wrong view (*diṭṭhi*).

However, since conceit can indeed arise even through sensual lust (*kāmarāga*), one might have to say, "In conceit, there are the taints of sensual lust and ignorance. This principle follows the method already stated.
It was not shown as "easy to understand. The virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha was explained in the first four sections, or six, or five sections;
by the remaining three, the abandoning through reflection of a bhikkhu established in the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha was explained;
and by all [the sections], the cutting off of household affairs for one established in the state of a bhikkhu was explained. In all these instances:
Reflective abandoning (*paṭisaṅkhāpahāna*) is the abandoning [of unwholesome deeds] through reflection in the form: "It is not fitting for me to do this or that. 42.

Regarding the commentary on the discourse on the danger of sensual pleasures (*kāmādīnavakathā*): *Upasumbheyya*. Here, the prefix *upa-* has the sense of proximity; *sumbhanam* means throwing away or dispersing. For that very reason, [the text says] *tamenaṃ*.
He says, "one should throw it near it," meaning that one should throw the skeleton near that dog.

By the statement, "it is called a *kaṅkala* because it is devoid of flesh," he indicates that the word *kaṅkala* is conventionally established for a boneless skeleton, whether it be the breastbone, the spine, or the skull.
It shows [this]. "Well-scratched" means it has been written without distinction, having been completely scraped away.
Because of its occurrence through the mode of equanimity toward the manifestation of unity, he said: "equanimity of the fourth jhāna.
Furthermore, because its object also has a single nature, he said: "for that," and so forth. It is reckoned as a worldly bait.

The quality of being "sensual" (*kāma*) and the quality of being "worldly bait" (*āmisa*) belong to the strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*), because they are to be touched by a world that has not fully understood its true nature, or because they have attained the designation "bait" within the world.
That alone, in the primary sense, deserves to be called "bait.
"Sensual-bait" refers to desire and lust for the strands of sensual pleasure. It is so called in the sense of grasping and in the sense of seizing intensely.
43. "Flying" means traveling through the air; thus he said, "one would go by leaping up.
As for vultures and the like, they do not possess axes or hatchets; therefore he said, "biting with their beaks, they would carve [the flesh].

Regarding the word "would release" (*vissajjeyyuṃ*), here "releasing" (*vissajjana*) is intended in the sense of "pulling," because verbal roots have multiple meanings; and "pulling" implies following along and then causing to fall.
He said: "They would pull out a piece of flesh with their nails and cast it down.
47. That which is suitable for a man to mount is *poriseyya*. 48.
That which possesses excellent, beautiful fruit is *sampannaphala*. Regarding *phalūpapanna*, he said "abounding in fruit" (*bahuphala*), meaning it is endowed with fruits.

50. Regarding *suvidūravidūra*: in the discipline (*vinaya*) of the Noble One (*ariya*), because it involves the total cutting off of worldly discourse (*vohārasamuccheda*), [the path] has become truly very remote;

thus, "I stand far away. By showing that it is a karmic instrument (*kattusādhana*) in the sense of "not knowing" (*anājānīya*)—because one does not know even the meaning of anything whatsoever—he speaks of the conditions to be given to them under the heading of "food for the unknowing" (*ajānantabhojana*). The rest is easily understood.
The Exposition of the Meaning of the *Potaliya-sutta* is completed.
5. Commentary on the *Jīvaka-sutta*. 51.

One who is supported and nourished by a prince is a "prince-supporter" (*kumārabhata*); one who is a prince-supporter is precisely a "prince-nourisher" (*komārabhacca*), just as "medicine" is [called] "the physician's medicine" (*bhisakkabhesajja*).

Regarding the word *ārabhanti*: although the term *ārabha* appears here in the sense of accumulating sensual desires (*kāmāyūhana*), exertion (*yaññuṭṭhāpana*), incurring an offense (*āpattiāpajjana*), making known (*viññāpana*), and so forth, it should be understood here in the sense of harming;
thus he says, "‘They begin’ means they kill. Regarding "done by dedicating":

this means done or produced by way of killing while dedicating [the merit] to oneself. Regarding the term *kamma* in the phrase *paṭiccakamma*: [...]* *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly.*
Because it has action as its means of accomplishment and belongs to the past time, he said: "done in dependence upon oneself.

This is a designation for the *nimitta-kamma* (the causal or instrumental action), as in such passages as "it touches the action in dependence [upon it]. "Of the *nimitta-kamma*" means of the action that is to be obtained by way of being a cause (*nimittabhāva*), not by way of performing or causing to perform.
"Meat is *paṭiccakamma*" means that here there exists a dependent action (*paṭiccakamma*); just as in the case of "the Buddha... [is so called because the Buddha-action exists therein].
“He is a Buddha because he has this. “Of them” means of the Nigaṇṭhas. There are indeed others as well, such as Brahmins and so forth, who hold that same view.
Here, “reason” (kāraṇa) is intended in the sense of a logical justification; and since that very justification does not deviate from the Dhamma, it is called “Dhamma.
Thus he says: “The reason is the consumption of fish and meat that is pure in three respects. As for the “counter-reason,” it is for the sake of the common people...
Likewise, the explanation is that because it conforms to the Dhamma through reasoning, the eating of meat was permitted;

this is stated as such because it is spoken in that very manner. As for the phrase "he eats meat specifically prepared [for him]," the act of eating mentioned there is not the actual cause [of the offense], because it is entirely absent [in the case of the rule];
furthermore, if there were such a cause, it would be unrighteous (*adhamma*).

Having done so. Likewise, the "explanation" (*byākaraṇa*)—the statement that "one consumes meat specifically prepared for oneself"—is not a valid reason (*anukāraṇa*), because it is inconsistent with the Dhamma through lack of logical justification.
"Being accompanied by a reason" (*sakāraṇo*) means being accompanied by the reason stated by others;
that is, other sectarians (*titthiya*) speak and declare the Dhamma using such phrases as "knowing," etc., and thus [the Buddha's teaching] is accompanied by that which serves as a reason.
"Having offered. Having spoken in that manner, your own thesis or rejoinder—that "meat should be consumed"—is your discourse;
or the subsequent discussion by others regarding that same point is the counter-discourse. "A reason for censure by the wise" means:
let alone the sectarians (tīrthikas), it is a reason for censure by other wise men besides them.
"No one comes" means that he does not incur the state of being censurable.
"They speak having overcome" means they speak having overcome and crushed [the listener]; the meaning is that they revile him with words of victory.
