52. "By reasons" means by causes consisting in the impurity of the mind of enjoyment. The bhikkhus saw what was prepared specifically for them.
For such meat, being unfit for consumption, is a cause for the impurity of the mind because it brings about defilement of the mind.
Now, in order to show by way of their specific forms those things seen, heard, and suspected, the words beginning with “diṭṭhādīsu” were spoken.
Therein, “suspected [meat] free from both of these” means: without relying on either of these two—namely, “seen” or “heard”—[one wonders]: “What indeed...”
"He has killed this monk specifically for me and prepared it"—this was their sole suspicion.
"Comprehensive" (*sabbasaṅgāhaka*) means including all three types of suspicions.

By the word "etc. (*ādi*) in the phrase "auspicious occasions, etc.," [the author] includes offerings made to guests (*āhunapāhuna*) and so forth. "They became free from doubt" means by means of everything...
This expresses the absence of any suspicion regarding all [of the meat]. For those who do not know it is for them that it is permissible; for one who knows, there is an offense in this case.
"Those very ones" refers to those specifically intended when the meat was prepared.

To show the distinction between the consumption of unallowable meat (*akappiyamaṃsa*) and the consumption of meat prepared specifically for oneself (*uddissakatamaṃsa*), [the text says]: "Unallowable meat..."

The passage beginning with "panā" and so forth has been stated. In the former case, there is an offense involving intention (*sacittaka*); in the other, there is an offense without intention (*acittaka*). Therefore he said:
"Even for one who has eaten unallowable meat without knowing it, there is indeed an offense. "Consumption" (*paribhoga*) means "that which is to be consumed," such is the meaning.

Regarding "of such [meat]": this refers to the consumption of fish or meat that is pure in the three respects. By the word "even" (*api*) in "even for one dwelling in loving-kindness" (*mettāvihārinopī*),...

[This applies] even to one who dwells in loving-kindness (*mettāvihārin*). To show that for one dwelling in loving-kindness, there is a state of blamelessness (*anavajjatā*) reaching its peak in the enjoyment [of requisites], it was said:
"In this case, Jīvaka, monks... and so forth. "Without specifying" means without making a distinction, in a general sense.
For by the Blessed One—in the Mahāvacchagotta Sutta, with the words, "Vaccha, when a monk’s craving has been abandoned"—the self (*atta*)...
This was stated without making a definitive restriction. For instance, Vacchagotta said: "Let Master Gotama remain;

does Master Gotama have even a single bhikkhu disciple who, through the destruction of the taints... [and so on]... dwells having attained [that state]? To which [the Buddha replied] in the Caṅkī Sutta:
"In this case, Bhāradvāja, a bhikkhu dwells in dependence upon a certain village or town," and so forth.
The self (attā) is spoken of without being specifically defined. For in that regard, the teaching is introduced later as follows:
“Now, this Dhamma which this venerable one teaches is profound, hard to see, hard to understand, peaceful, sublime, beyond the sphere of mere reasoning, subtle, to be experienced by the wise;
that Dhamma cannot be easily taught by one who is greedy,” and so forth. Therefore it was said: “By the Blessed One...”
"In three places—the Mahāvacchagotta Sutta, the Caṅkī Sutta, and this very sutta—the teaching was given with reference to the self alone.
[Reply: "It is meat as a condiment that is intended, because it refers to the consumption of food consisting of fish and meat together, and because both fish and meat are intended here."
“Unagitated and unattached. Regarding “through the infatuation of craving”: it means through the attainment of infatuation by way of craving.
“Unswallowed” means not being overwhelmed by craving, not being submerged in it; the meaning is that one does not remain having swallowed and digested it.
Therefore he said: “Having devoured all,” and so forth. Here, the danger of nutriment is its repulsiveness; thus he said: “by staying for a single night,” and so forth.

This meaning is "the enjoyment of nutriment. One who possesses the wisdom that constitutes the escape from desire and lust bound to nutriment—which proceeds by way of the delimitation of the seven fetters through the passage beginning, "only for the maintenance of this body"—is "one possessed of the wisdom of escape" (*nissaraṇapañño*). "For this purpose" (*idamatthaṃ*) means for this reason.
"In such a case" (*evaṃ sante*) refers to not having stated [previously] that "the designation 'Brahmā' belongs to one who dwells in loving-kindness."
If what you have said refers to this— that Brahmā abandoned those states which are the opposites of dwelling in loving-kindness only partially,
whereas the Blessed One abandoned them without remainder— then, that being the case, I grant the validity of your aforementioned statement;
the meaning is that it does not refer merely to the commonality of dwelling in loving-kindness.
55. Having stated, “A separate connection,” the passage beginning with “In this [case], however,” was spoken in order to demonstrate the state of being a distinct connection.
“He closes the door” means that by permitting the consumption of fish and meat, he shuts the door of opportunity for others’ speech;
he blocks the path of censure. How does he show compassion for beings? By way of compassion for beings, [he addresses] the outsiders...
This prohibition against the consumption of fish and meat is incorrect;
for the Blessed One has permitted the consumption of fish and meat that is pure in three respects. Thus it was said:
"Jīvaka, I say that meat may be consumed on three grounds," and so forth. It is also stated in the Vinaya: "Devadatta, fish and meat that are pure in three respects..."
“...it has been permitted by me. For those who eat what is pure in three respects, compassion for beings is unshakable.
Expanding upon the meaning briefly stated as “he demonstrates compassion for beings,” he says, “If indeed,” and so forth.
“By the first reason” means by the first cause of harming others, both in terms of the teaching and in terms of the practical application. He was dragged away.

"Living being" (*pāṇa*). "By the throbbing of the neck" means by means of the cord around the neck, which is unable to endure [the pain]. "There is only much merit" is said because there is no expectation of causing harm, and because of the intention for welfare;
this is the intended meaning. Why was it said, "I go to you for refuge, O Blessed One," and so forth?

This was stated in response to the objection that one has already taken refuge by way of the formal act of going for refuge; thus he says, "This," and so on. "Plunging," etc. [is explained] from the beginning.
Recalling the discourse from beginning to end and reflecting upon its meaning. The remainder is easy to understand.
The elucidation of the hidden meaning in the commentary on the Jīvaka-sutta is complete.
6. Commentary on the Upāli-sutta.
56. One who wears a cloak (*pāvāra*) is a cloak-wearer (*pāvārika*); this is his name derived from his family lineage.

Furthermore, he was a man of great wealth and vast possessions, established in the position of a guild-leader (*seṭṭhi*) in the city. Therefore, it says, "of the guild-leader, the cloak-seller. Because of its length, it is "long" (*dīgha*).
It is said that in measurement, it stood exceeding one and a half *ratanas* when folded up. Thus he acquired that name.

“Dīghatapassī” is his acquired name. Regarding the phrase “in the external sense-spheres”: in the systems of the non-Buddhist sects (tīrthikas), there is no conventional usage for the term “alms-food” (piṇḍapāta);
therefore, the intention is that it is stated as “returned from alms-food” according to the terminology of the Buddha’s teaching (sāsana).
“He shows” means he teaches. “He establishes” means he defines [them] so as to prevent mutual confusion. “By action” means by the instrument.
"By way of occurrence" means by way of proceeding. Regarding the phrase "he prescribes punishments," why was it not asked by the Blessed One in that manner from the very beginning?
Because that is not the natural linguistic usage (*sabhāvanirutti*) for that meaning; such a conventional expression does not exist in the Dispensation, nor in the world, nor in other systems.
Rather, this [expression] belongs solely to that Nigaṇṭha, resembling a heap of refuse.
In order to show this meaning—that it is "manifest conduct" (samudācāra)—he said, “he prescribes actions.
“Without mind” (acittaka) means devoid of mind; the sense is that it is not originated by the mind. Anticipating the objection, “How can those two occur without the mind?
he provides an illustration for that, beginning with “As it is said, for instance... “Of those who have been distinguished” (paṭivibhattānaṃ) [is explained] by its meaning...
"Of those who are divided" means of those who are distinct, being different even in terms of their words by way of qualifying phrases.
"Desiring to establish the statement" means desiring to establish the statement as spoken by Dīgha Tapassin.
For when that has been established, the householder Upāli—who arrived in connection with that very context—will see the Dhamma in that place and gain deep confidence in the Teaching.
It is called *kathāvatthu* because it is the basis for raising further arguments; that is, it is the subject matter of the discussion.
"He established him in this discussion" means he established him either in the discussion itself or in its meaning.

Just as one would not disregard someone for fear of being subjected to an argument, so did he establish Dīgha Tapassī in that discussion or in that meaning, during the debate, up to the third time. *Vāda* here means fault.
57. Now, in order to show that even the states associated with volition (cetanā) are included under bodily action and so forth, the passage beginning with “Furthermore” (apicā) was stated.

Therein, the statement “The threefold misconduct of body is called bodily action,” etc., was spoken because unwholesome kamma was understood in the Pāḷi under the heading of “the performance of kamma”;
however, previously [it was stated] “the eight types of wholesome volition pertaining to the sense-sphere,” etc.
The blameworthy and the blameless have been shown together as one by way of their commonality. But why is volition (cetanā) not included here?

To this he says: "In this sutta, action (kamma) is the primary focus. Action—divided into bodily action and so forth—is itself the primary, the chief, and the precursor, and not merely volition alone.
"Even though they are mentioned thus" means even though they are mentioned under the name "actions."
Volition is the leader; the intention is that it is stated there having made volition the foremost, the chief, and the precursor.
But how is it that when "kamma" or "kamma-s" occurs there, volition has the status of being their leader?
To this he says: "In whatever [context]... it is found. Therein, "in whatever" means in whichever door. That has been explained.

That volition has already been explained; it is that volition which, by way of the "bodily formation" and so forth (i.e., the volition that sets in motion any kind of kamma through the doors of body, etc.), as well as the associated states, are—by virtue of that very fact—kamma itself, whether mundane or supramundane.
However, covetousness and the like should be understood as belonging to the side of volition.
"Great" means having bitter fruit. One does not grow weary because of the promise [of the teaching], owing to its quality of being accompanied by wonders (*sappāṭihāriya*).
Now, in order to demonstrate that quality of being accompanied by wonders for them, the passage beginning with "For thus" (*tathā hi*) was spoken.

If one who declares that bodily action and verbal action are great when encountering unwholesome states does not grow weary, then why did the Blessed One here state that unwholesome mental action is the most blameworthy?
He said, “But in this place,” and so forth. By merely establishing [the path] up to the third time, one proceeds along the path already traveled.
Therefore he said, “even though not seeing the accomplishment of any purpose. 58.
A *bālakinī* is a woman who has a child (*bālaka*) as her place of residence. He is called a *mahānigaṇṭha* because he is highly esteemed by the Nigaṇṭhas due to his being recognized as a teacher.
60. It is called *āvaṭṭanī* (the ensnaring) because it turns one back from a previous state, brings one under its own control, and by means of this, it is an illusion (*māyā*). Therefore he said:

"The illusion of seizing after having turned [one's mind]. It is the natural law (*dhammatā*) here that even the thought of seeing a Buddha does not arise in one who has made a promise to the Teacher.
However, if he were to approach the presence of the Buddhas without abandoning that promise, [he would see them].
His head might split into seven pieces; therefore, from the very beginning, the Blessed One acts in such a way that this fool does not obtain an audience, lest he perish.

This matter should be illustrated by the encounter with Pāṭikaputta. He states the necessity for the excellence of seeing [the Buddha] in the passage beginning with "For [to see] the Tathāgata... [and so on]. "Have you come here into our presence? [he asks].
61. "Standing firm in truthfulness of speech" means standing by one's word as it was originally pledged.
62. Living beings that are cold-blooded die at the time of drinking; they too are killed by that consumption of cold water.
Therefore, a true ascetic must not consume cold water in any way whatsoever. Thus [they say].
*Laḍḍhi*. The doctrine of the ancient Nigaṇṭhas was that water is a living being (*satta*). Therefore, it is said:
"They reject cold water because of the perception of a living being. This view of theirs contradicts the position of the modern Nigaṇṭhas;

for they maintain that the life-principle (*jīva*) is something entirely distinct from the categories of existence such as earth and so forth. [Thus,] one who desires to drink cold water with the mind...
Even when standing in the midst of illness, he does not have such an expansion of the mind toward the desire to consume [food].
Therefore it is said: “By that, his mental rod is broken right there. “By that” means by the desiring to drink and consume cold water.
“His” refers to the aforementioned Nigaṇṭha. “Right there” means at the very moment of such a thought arising. It is “broken” in terms of his restraint (*saṃvara*).
Because of being disturbed. Being in such a state, if that Nigaṇṭha were to obtain cold water, he might live for a short time;
but by not obtaining it, with his throat, lips, palate, tongue, and other parts completely parched and overwhelmed by burning heat, he would die.
Therefore he said: "Not obtaining cold water, he would pass away. Why? Because [his life] depends on the mind being supported by drinking cold water.
Death occurs; therefore it was said: "But the mental rod, even when broken, drags along death.
Furthermore, because the heretics hold the view that for a Nigaṇṭha whose mind has become thus, there is rebirth among the gods called Manosattas, it was said:
"But the mental rod, even when broken, drags along rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi). "Iti" means "thus."
"In this case, the Nigaṇṭha... and so forth. "Him" refers to the householder Upāli. "Great" means he caused [him] to say, "One passes away bound by the mind"—this is the intended meaning.

"Of the lay follower" refers to the householder Upāli. By the phrases beginning with "by way of fainting," etc., [the text demonstrates] the positive and negative concomitance of the mental rod (*manodaṇḍa*).
He manifests greatness. "Merely by the occurrence of a continuity of consciousness" means solely by the occurrence of a continuity of consciousness, without the rod of body or the rod of speech.
"Even having broken [the precepts]"—here, by changing the grammatical case of the word *api*, it also includes "even without having broken [them].
"Non-leading" means lacking a foundation (*appāṭihīra*); the sense is that they are improper. "The lay follower observed"—this is said by changing the grammatical case.
The *yojanā* (explanation): "Responses to questions" (*pañhapaṭibhānāni*) refers to the flashes of inspired insight that arise regarding a matter one wishes to know.
By saying, "One dies dependent on the mind," the speaker has effectively admitted, by implication, that the mental rod (*manodaṇḍa*) is superior to the others;
thus he says: "Now, this statement, 'The mental rod is great'... It is likewise stated: "The mental rod alone..."
"He made [him] say, 'I am strong, I am great. 63.
Restraint from killing living beings and so forth is *yāma*; fourfold restraint is *catuyāma*.

One who is restrained by the restraint designated as "fourfold restraint" is *cātuyāmasaṃvarasaṃvuta*. In the commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), however, the word *yāma* is used as a synonym for a constituent part (*koṭṭhāsa*).
“It is by this fourfold division,” it is said. Because it is to be cultivated by fools through passion toward objects such as forms that are dear, it is called “cultivated”;
thus he says, “‘Cultivated’ refers to the five strands of sensual pleasure.
That which wards off all evil and all taints is “all-warding” (*sabbavārī*); among its nine meanings, this is the seventh meaning.
Because he stands having warded off evil with every kind of warding-off, he is "warded-off-by-every-warding-off" (*sabbavārivārita*). Therefore it is said:

"one by whom evil has been warded off through every warding-off of evil. For that very reason, because he has shaken off all taints (*āsava*) that ought to be warded off, he is "shaken-off-by-every-warding-off" (*sabbavāridhuta*).

Because he has touched—that is, reached—the "every-warding-off" (*sabbavāri*) by way of warding off what ought to be warded off, he is "touched-by-every-warding-off" (*sabbavāriphuṭa*). The compound [is explained as follows]:...
"Killing suddenly" means killing unintentionally. "In which aggregate? means in which of the three aggregates of punishment. 64.
It is called *khala* because it is gathered (*khalīyati*) or accumulated; he says, "one *maṃsakhala*" means "one mass of flesh.

[He is] a possessor of psychic power (*iddhimā*) through the psychic power of a spell-holder (*vijjādhara*). Furthermore, that psychic power succeeds only for one endowed with majesty (*ānubhāva*), not otherwise.
Of anyone whatsoever. Therefore he said, "endowed with majesty. He is endowed with majesty precisely by means of the majesty of clear knowledge (*vijjā*).
Having attained mastery over the mind, he does so by bringing that very majesty—namely, clear knowledge—to a state of proficiency.

By this, the Blessed One, wishing to designate the householder Upāli as one who has attained mastery according to worldly convention, spoke thus. For worldly people [say] that through the psychic power (*iddhi*) consisting of meditation...
They think: “One possessed of psychic power who has attained mastery over the mind causes harm to others.
For in that way those seers praise others and extol the majesty of the seers. As for what should be said here, that will follow later.

65. “Having become forest itself”: having become entirely forest itself. It became forest by virtue of its state as forest, not merely by name. “For the sake of the seers”: for the purpose of providing a dwelling for the seers.
Not far from the banks of the Godhāvarī River. "Feeling envious" means feeling envy, thinking, "This person is surrounding me.

"Defiled" means his body is defiled by mud, dust on his teeth, dirt on his hair, and so forth. "Unanointed and unadorned" means his eyes are not anointed with collyrium and he is entirely without ornaments.
At that time, it was considered auspicious to apply collyrium to the eyes even at dawn.
This is the conviction of human beings; therefore, collyrium was mentioned separately.
"The king, having accepted his words" means that the king, thinking, "Such a thing must have come down in the Vedas," accepted the words of that domestic priest.
"With a heart born of heat" means with a heart that had become inflamed. "Not being able to breathe through the nostrils" means breathing through the mouth.
The place for the victorious army camp (*jayakhandhāvāra*) is where those who have come after achieving victory must sit while waiting for the conjunction of the auspicious stars.
The mention of "causing rain to fall" and so forth was included in order to encompass even those who were not personally involved in that evil deed, because they had consented to it.
"A shower of finished goods" refers to a rain of ornaments. The construction is: "the great multitude became consenting. "One who supports his mother" means... [rāma].
A man named Rāma was one who behaved rightly toward his mother. "Of those who have not attained equality" means of those who are not in agreement.

"Scattering" refers to [the act] on account of their refusal to listen. "Sparks" means sparks of fire. "They fall upon the body" means they fall here and there upon the body. It is said that these [beings], having opened up hell, show it to the great multitude.
"To a place that is comfortable" means: we do not go for the sake of any particular region; rather, wherever one dwells...
"It is comfortable for one who has gone forth; let us go to such a place that is comfortable"—this is the intended meaning. "The Saṅgha" means those who are gathered together (*saṃhatā*).
"The groups" (*gaṇā*) are so called because they are to be counted as various military units or divisions. "Having become groups" means having formed a mass with a common aspiration.

Regarding the phrases beginning with "taking what is not given," this should be connected by supplying the words: "by the remainder of the karmic result of one who, after being boiled in hell, has come to the human world."
"I shall take hold of him" means "I shall arouse his confidence. The construction is: "He thought, 'This is what must be done for them. What did he think?
He thought of a means to cause harm after having aroused resentment. Therefore he said, "At the conclusion of the Dhamma talk," and so forth.
"Of the mud consisting of *nāgabala*, mustard, *aṅkola* oil, *kaṇikāra* resin, etc. refers to the mud made of *nāgabala*, mustard, *aṅkola* oil, *kaṇikāra* resin, and other such substances.

They harassed him, provoking him with talk of the hells and other such things. Regarding "the objects of the six doors": this refers to the spheres of form and so forth, which serve as the objects for the six doors beginning with the eye.
"The nine rains" refers to: a rain of water, a rain of jasmine flowers, a rain of cowries, a rain of kahāpaṇa coins, and a rain of ornaments.
These are the nine kinds of rain: a rain of weapons, a rain of embers, a rain of stones, and a rain of sand.
"He deceived" means that while acting as if he were showing honor, he deceived by acting with dishonor through harmful conduct. "Innocent" means one who is without fault.
In the *Jātakaṭṭhakathā* and other texts, she is called "the brahmin girl Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā," but here she is called "the merchant's daughter."
"For the sake of marriage" means for the purpose of taking a wife; "for him" refers to the person sent [by the king].
Having obtained an opportunity through such karma conducive to birth in a low family, he was reborn in the womb of a *caṇḍāla*.
"In a leather-hut" means in a house covered with hides. His name was indeed Mātaṅga, derived from his birth. "Him"—
Sounding his bell and making a noise with his clapping, he set out upon the main road near the door of Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā’s house.

Her servants, attendants, and those addicted to liquor who were dependent on her, thinking him dead because he had fallen into a swoon from being so severely beaten—beaten until he was nearly reduced to a pulp—threw him away.
Then the Bodhisatta, because there was still life remaining in him and as a very gentle breeze blew, regained consciousness after a long time.
Therefore he said, “The Great Man,” and so forth. “In the courtyard of the house” means in the open space outside the main gate of the house.
“Fell” means having fallen down, having made his descent, and having entered by making the accomplishment of his desired goal his intermediate state.
“By Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā” means by reason of Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā.

They dwell in prosperity and in fame. "Candanti" means the moon’s orb; the sense is the celestial mansion of the moon (*candavimāna*). "Ucchiṭṭhagehe" means in a house used by others. "Maṇḍape" means in the great pavilion in the center of the city.
"Khīramaṇimūlaṃ" means the root of milk and the root of the jewel bound on the feet.
"Yāvatā vācuggatā pariyatti" means as much as has emerged, issued forth, and proceeded from the human door of speech; the sense is whatever consists of speech.

*Ākāsaṅgaṇe*: in an open courtyard. *Dummavāsī*: dusty with smoke; the intended meaning is "unadorned and unanointed. *Otallako*: one of base disposition; the meaning is "one of little power. *Paṭimuñca kaṇṭhe*:
having wrapped it around the neck, as far as the throat. *Ko re tuvaṃ*: "Who indeed are you?"—the sense being, "Are you someone? or "What is your name?"
“Prepared” (*pakata*) means made ready by being processed in various ways. “Standing alms” (*uttiṭṭhapiṇḍa*) refers to alms obtained by standing after approaching the interior of a house;
the meaning is “food obtained as alms. “May he receive” (*labhatu*) means may he obtain it.
“Sapāka” is how the Great Being reveals his true identity according to his birth.
"Believing in what exists" means believing in the existence of the welfare pertaining to future lives. "Go away" means depart. "From here" means from this place. "Foolish" means base.
"In a field that is not saline" means in a field that is not arid and is well-supplied with water, by those who expect a specific excellence of fruit.
"Give gifts with this faith" means: like a cloud filling both the lowlands and the highlands, give gifts to both the virtuous and the meritless.
"And giving thus, may you perhaps win over one worthy of offerings. "Worthy of offerings" means endowed with qualities such as virtue (*sīla*).
"Those" refers to those brahmins. "With a bamboo scraper" means with a bamboo tool.

"You dig a mountain with your fingernail" means he was like one who was digging at a mountain with his own fingernail. "Iron" means black iron. "You trample" means you overcome; he was like one who was overcoming [the earth] with his own body.
"Āvedhitaṃ" means moved or turned over and placed [in a different position]. "Piṭṭhito" means from behind.
"He stretches out his arm, which is incapable of action" means that he merely stretches out both arms, stiff like dry sticks, incapable of performing work;
he does not bend them. His eyes are white because, through their turning, the black circle [of the pupil] is no longer visible.
"Life" means living.
"In the air" means in the sky. "As on a journey" means as if on a journey along a path.
"He does not even form a perception" means he does not form even the mere perception that "these are people born of noble families. "A piece of tooth-stick refuse" means...

It was said because he had already chewed his tooth-stick. It will fall upon him alone, because he is free from malice and because at that time the Great Being was in the state of having reached the highest excellence.
The domain of psychic power (*iddhi*) is indeed inconceivable; therefore, one should not wonder how it was that the sun did not rise.
"The dawn-light was not seen" means that in that place, the radiance of the dawn...
Nothing is discernible; there is only darkness.
Is this a reversal of time caused by some demon? "Possessing great wisdom" means being the foundation for the wisdom of the great.
"Behold the face of the country" means behold the faces of the people living in this country, which have become dejected due to this calamity.

"The talk concerning this will fall back upon him alone": for those harsh words—termed a curse consisting in reviling the Noble Ones—which were uttered by him toward that Great Being (mahāsatta) who was well-composed in his continuum through the perfection of virtue and view, who had fulfilled various meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) through the excellence of his cultivation of the perfections (*pāramitā*), and who was the dwelling-place of great compassion;

those words, having been uttered, fell back upon him because of the specific nature of that [Great Being] as a field (*khetta*) and because of the harshness of his own underlying intention (*ajjhāsaya*).
If that action, having become karma to be experienced in the present life (*diṭṭhadhammavedanīya-kamma*), is not forgiven by the Great Being, it becomes destined to ripen on the seventh day;
however, once the Great Being has been forgiven, because its successful execution has been obstructed, it reaches a state of non-ripening through becoming "karma that has lapsed" (*ahosikamma*).
For this is the natural law regarding evil speech directed at a Noble One (*ariya*) that is to be experienced in the present life.
Therefore it was said: "The talk concerning this will fall upon this very person," and so forth.
But the Great Being did not allow that [curse] to fall upon him; rather, he released him through a skillful means. Therefore it is said in the *Cariyāpiṭaka*:
"That which he then cursed me with, being angry and of wicked mind..."
"It fell right upon his head; by means of a yoga, he released him.
For that which was performed there on the seventh day by the Bodhisatta to prevent the rising of the sun is what is intended here by "yoga.
Indeed, by means of this yoga, the assembly including the king, as well as the city-dwellers, the merchants, and the country-folk, were held back.
They brought the ascetic into the presence of the Bodhisatta and asked for his forgiveness. Having come to know the Bodhisatta’s virtues, he developed serene confidence in him.
As for the placing of the lump of clay upon his head and its subsequent splitting into seven pieces, that was done for the sake of protecting the minds of the people;
otherwise, [they might have thought], "These are renunciants..."
“They act under the control of the mind, but the mind does not act under their control.

Thinking thus, they might seize even a Great Being (mahāsatta) as being like that [ordinary person]; this would lead to their harm and suffering for a long time. Therefore he said, “Then to him,” and so forth.
“A rain of iron balls” means a rain of iron spheres; for at that time, [the balls] were as large as a cubit or even one and a half cubits, with sharp points.
Iron balls falling from this side and that reduced the bodies of people to pieces.
"Kalala-vassa" means a thin layer of mud or a coating of mire. "Upahacca" means having struck or collided with. That very same middle of the forest. 67. "Anuviccakāraṃ" means investigation.

In order to show the encouragement and restraint toward those who had entered his discipleship—despite remaining in a teaching that does not lead to liberation due to two reasons—the passage beginning with "Why? was spoken.
69. *Anupubbiṃ kathaṃ*: a discourse that should be told in successive order. What, then, is it? It is the discourse on giving and so forth.
First of all, the discourse on giving is taught because it is common to all people, including the general populace; because it is easy to practice;
and because it serves as the means for establishing oneself in virtue (*sīla*). For a person whose nature is one of renunciation is free from attachment toward the objects of possession.

One undertakes the precepts with ease and becomes well-established therein. Following the discourse on giving, the discourse on virtue (sīla) is presented because virtue purifies both the giver and the recipient;
because it speaks of benefiting others while avoiding causing harm to others; because it speaks of the nature of action (kiriya-dhamma) following the discussion of non-action (akiriya-dhamma);
and because it speaks of the cause for the attainment of existence (bhava-sampatti) following the discussion of the causes for the attainment of wealth and fame.
It has been explained. Furthermore, that virtue is dependent on the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*); this is for the purpose of showing that this prosperity of existence is its fruit.

And immediately after that, it is for the purpose of showing that through these bases of meritorious action consisting of giving and virtue—which are distinguished by various types of noble conduct—there arise immeasurable prosperities of existence and enjoyments, distinguished by various degrees of excellence, among the Cātumahārājika devas and the others.
The Discourse on Heaven. Now, this heaven is defiled by lust and the other [defilements], whereas the Noble Path is forever undefiled;
thus, after the discourse on heaven, the discourse on the Path is given for the purpose of showing this.

Furthermore, when speaking of the Path, in order to demonstrate the means for its attainment, it is said that all sensual pleasures—even those included within heaven, let alone others—are full of danger, impermanent, unstable, and subject to change.
"The danger of sensual pleasures" means that they are low, vulgar, worldly, ignoble, and not conducive to welfare; their "disgrace" (*okāra*) is their base nature.
Since all states of existence (*bhava*) serve as the basis for defilements (*kilesa*), there is "corruption" (*saṃkilesa*) therein.
And since Nibbāna is entirely free from defilements, the "benefit of renunciation" (*nekkhamme ānisaṃso*) must also be explained. This is the meaning of the word *iti* in the phrase *maggantīti*.
It should be understood that [this] is what has been shown.
"The source of all happiness" means the cause of all happiness—whether pertaining to the present life (*diṭṭhadhammika*), the future life (*samparāyika*), or associated with *nibbāna*.
For whatever is called the happiness of wealth in the world, all of that has giving as its source; this is well known.
This is the meaning. Furthermore, giving is indeed a decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*) even for that happiness associated with jhāna, insight, the path, the fruit, and nibbāna.

"The root of all attainments" refers to these various human prosperities—such as the sovereignty of a regional king, the glory of lordship, and the excellence of a wheel-turning monarch resplendent with the seven treasures—as well as the divine prosperities belonging to the Four Great Kings and so forth, or whatever else [there may be].

Furthermore, there are other prosperities as well, and this is the root cause of them all. "Of enjoyments" (*bhogānaṃ*) refers to agreeable forms and so forth, which have received the name "enjoyment" (*bhoga*) in the sense of being objects to be enjoyed;
or it refers to the pleasures of consumption that depend upon those [objects], [of which this generosity] is the foundation because of its quality as a stable basis.
"Of one who has fallen into adversity" (*visamagatassa*) means of one who has met with misfortune. "A refuge" (*tāṇaṃ*) means protection, because of its preserving one from that [misfortune].
A "refuge" (*leṇa*) is a place of shelter for one being overwhelmed by calamities. A "destination" (*gati*) is a place to be gone to. An "ultimate resort" (*parāyana*) is a support.
A "reliance" (*avassaya*) is a foundation that prevents one from falling into ruin. An "object" (*ārammaṇa*) is an object of clinging.
"Like a lion-throne made of jewels" means like a great seven-limbed lion-throne made of all kinds of jewels; it is of great value.
Because it prevents one from falling into the lower realms entirely; because, like the great earth, it provides a foundation wherever one goes;

and because, just as a supporting rope is a prop for a weak man who is rising up or standing firm, so too is giving a condition for the arising and the stability of beings in the realms of prosperity—thus he said, "in the sense of being a support."
"Like a rope for an object. "In the sense of crossing over suffering" means in the sense of crossing over the suffering of the miserable destinies (*duggati*).
"In the sense of providing consolation" means in the sense of properly consoling one from the danger posed by enemies such as greed and stinginess.

"In the sense of protection from fear" means in the sense of guarding against the fear of poverty. "By stinginess, defilements, etc. refers to stinginess, greed, hatred, envy, wrong view, doubt, and so forth.
"By the stains of the mind. "In the sense of being unstained" means by way of being undefiled. "Of these" refers to the stains of stinginess and so forth.
"In the sense of being difficult to assail" refers to these very same [stains]. "In the sense of being without fear" means by way of being a cause for the absence of fear;
for a donor, a master of giving, does not tremble from anyone even in the present, much less in the future. "In the sense of being powerful" means by way of great strength.
For the donor, as a master of giving, is powerful in the present through the strength of his faction, but in the future through bodily strength and so forth.

"In the sense of being esteemed as a supreme blessing" means by virtue of being universally recognized as a cause of prosperity. "Leading from misfortune to success" means bringing one to the attainment of the land of safety.
Now, in order to show the quality of giving even by way of the conduct for great enlightenment (*mahābodhicaryā*), it is said: "Giving, indeed," and so forth. Therein:
By the phrase "by surrendering oneself," he gives this instruction: "Great beings who correctly perceive the fruit of giving even sacrifice their own lives;
therefore, what wise person indeed would form an attachment to external objects?
Now, all those worldly and supramundane excellences that reach the highest peak proceed from giving alone.

Showing this, he said, "For giving," and so forth. Therein, the attainments of Sakka, Māra, and Brahmā are for one's own benefit alone, whereas the attainment of a Wheel-turning Monarch (cakkavatti) is for both one's own benefit and the benefit of others;
thus, it was mentioned after those [other attainments] to show this.

To show that those are mundane while these are supramundane, he said, "The knowledge of the disciple’s perfections," and so forth. Among those [perfections], there is indeed a gradation of superior, more superior, and most superior.
The three types of knowledge have been stated in order to demonstrate [this]. Furthermore, the fact that these serve as conditions for giving has already been explained above.
By this very [explanation], it should be understood that their status as a condition even for the attainment of Brahmā-hood is illuminated.
And what is called "giving" (dāna) is the relinquishing of one's own possessions to others, whether out of a desire for their welfare or by way of veneration.
Therefore, it was said: "It is impossible for a person who is a donor to steal the property of others," because one who gives a gift is able to undertake moral discipline (*sīla*).
There is no ornament like the ornament of moral discipline, because moral discipline brings about a particular excellence of beauty.
There is no flower like the flower of moral discipline; the same principle applies here as well. [There is no fragrance like] the fragrance of moral discipline...
Regarding the phrase "there is no fragrance," one should cite verses such as "Sandalwood or tagara...
and Jātaka verses beginning with "The fragrance of seers who have long been ordained departs from the body with the wind.
For virtue is indeed the ornament, the decoration, and the perfume of beings, and it brings about a state worthy of being seen. Therefore he said: "By the ornament of virtue," and so forth.
"This heaven is attained" is said with reference to the morality of undertaking [precepts] through middling levels of zeal and so forth. Therefore, Sakka, King of the Devas, said:
"By an inferior holy life one is reborn among the Khattiyas;
by a middling one, one attains the state of a deva; by the highest, one is purified."

*Ittha* means pleasant (*sukha*). *Kanta* means desirable (*kamanīya*). *Manāpa* means that which increases the mind’s delight. To demonstrate its state of being pleasant and so forth, it is said: "There is constant play here," and so on.
*Ādīnava* refers to the state of being defiled by impermanence and so forth, and by having little gratification and so forth, because of which they do not please the minds of the wise.

Alternatively, it is called *ādīnava* because it brings about (*vāti*) or produces (*pavatteti*) the beginning of faults; thus, it is extreme wretchedness. And so, sensual pleasures are [to be seen] as they truly are.
They stand ready for those who reflect upon them. "Baseness" means a state of inferiority that is practiced by the unworthy and not practiced by the noble.
"Corruption" means the quality of being oppressive and causing affliction.
"The advantage in renunciation" refers to the fact that in renunciation there are as many benefits as there are dangers in sensual pleasures, owing to their being the opposite of those dangers.
The advantages. Furthermore, he proclaimed the advantages of renunciation (*nekkhamma*) in such a manner as:

"This renunciation is indeed unconfined, undefiled, emerged from sensual desires, emerged from the perception of sensual desire, emerged from thoughts of sensual desire, emerged from the fever of sensual desire, and emerged from the perception of ill will," and so forth;
likewise, he proclaimed the advantages of going forth (*pabbajjā*) and of the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*), etc.

He analyzed and extolled the virtues. "A mind that is ready" means that because the defects of the mind—such as lack of faith (*assaddhiya*)—that had arisen during the preceding teaching have been removed, the mind has become a fit vessel for the subsequent teaching and is thus capable of performing the task.
In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, however, it says "a healthy mind" (*arogacitta*) because lack of faith and the other defects are like diseases of the mind, and at that time they have disappeared.
The mind is pliant through the departure of defilements such as views and conceit; it is free from hindrances through the departure of sensual desire and the like;
it is uplifted through the possession of sublime rapture and gladness in right practice; therein, it is serene through the perfection of faith.
"When the Blessed One knew"—this is the connection. Alternatively, "the fit mind" means a healthy mind through the departure of sensual desire.
"A mind that is gentle" means a mind that is not harsh due to the absence of ill will, by way of loving-kindness (*mettā*).
"A mind free from hindrances" means a mind that is not obstructed by agitation and remorse, because of the departure of distraction.

"An uplifted mind" means a mind that is not dejected, being sustained by the departure of sloth and torpor. "A serene mind" means a mind that is resolutely intent upon right practice due to the departure of doubt.
In this way, the meaning of the remaining phrases here should be understood.
With the words "Just as if," etc., he demonstrates, by means of a simile, Upāli’s abandonment of defilement and the accomplishment of the Noble Path.
*Apagatakāḷakaṃ* means free from blackness. *Sammadeva* means quite thoroughly. *Rajanaṃ* refers to the various kinds of dye, such as blue, yellow, and so forth.
"Should receive" means he would grasp it; it would become radiant. "On that very seat" means on that very sitting posture.

By this, his state of being one who possesses swift insight (*lahu-vipassaka*), his possession of sharp wisdom (*tikkha-paññatā*), his pleasant path of practice (*sukha-paṭipadā*), and his quick direct knowledge (*khippābhiññatā*) are demonstrated.

"Dustless" (*viraja*) means dustless through the disappearance of the dust of passion (*rāga*) and so forth that leads to rebirth in the states of misery (*apāya*). Through the removal of the stains of views and doubt without remainder...
“Free from stain. Regarding the phrase “of the three paths,” it refers to the three lower paths.
Why is it said, “the demonstration of the mode of its arising”? This is stated in response to the objection: “Is it not the case that path-knowledge has the unconditioned dhamma as its object?
To this, he says, “For that...,” and so forth. In that context, “penetrating” means penetrating by way of penetration through non-delusion. Therefore, he says, “by way of function.”
Herein, this is the correlation of the similes: the cloth is like the mind;

the state of the cloth being defiled by adventitious stains is like the state of the mind being thoroughly defiled by the stains of lust and so forth; the washing stone is like the progressive discourse;
the water is like faith; and [the process of] moistening the cloth with water and rubbing the dark spots with loads of wood-ash, cow-dung, and chaff is like...

Just as in the process of washing, one moistens a cloth with the moisture of faith, loosens its stains through mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom, and then applies effort in cleansing the mind by means of the method of hearing and so forth;

so too, by that application, the suppression of defilements occurs through the exertion of energy—just as the removal of blackness from a cloth occurs through that process—and the Noble Path is like the dye. By means of that, the state of radiant clarity arises for the cleansed cloth.
It is the purification by means of the Path of the mind whose defilements have been suppressed.

Having said "in this very life" (*diṭṭhadhammo*), the term "one who has attained the Dhamma" (*pattadhammo*) is stated in order to exclude the possibility that there might be some other kind of seeing besides that which consists in knowledge and vision (*ñāṇadassana*).
Furthermore, since there exists attainment other than the attainment of knowledge, the term [“pattadhammo”] is used for the sake of distinguishing it from that.

It is said, “one who has understood the Dhamma. However, since this state of having understood the Dhamma might apply to only a portion of the Dhammas, the phrase “one who has fathomed the Dhamma” is used to show that his understanding is exhaustive.

By this, it specifically illuminates his full awakening to the Truths. For path-knowledge, by accomplishing its functions such as full comprehension through a single clear vision, [fathoms] the Dhamma of the Four Truths exhaustively.
It is called "plunging all around. Therefore he said: "The Dhamma of the Noble Truths has been seen by this one; thus he is 'one who has seen the Dhamma' (diṭṭhadhammo).
"Crossed over doubt" means that they have crossed over doubt—doubt which resembles a perilous wilderness with sixteen bases and eight bases;
thus they are "those who have crossed over doubt" (tiṇṇavicikicchā). "Free from perplexity" means regarding the process of existence and so forth, [the thought]: "Is it thus? What indeed..."
"Kho" means that such wavering and doubt have been removed and cut off.

Because he has abandoned those evil qualities that cause agitation and because he is well-established in the opposing virtues such as morality (sīla), he has attained *vesārajja*—the state of being confident (*visāradabhāva*) and proficiency (*veyyattiya*).
Because he has seen this for himself through direct personal experience (*paccakkha*), there is no need for another to confirm it; thus, he is "not dependent on another" (*aparappaccaya*).
71. "Paṇḍito" means one possessed of wisdom (paññavā). 72.

"Tena hi samma" (then indeed, friend) is a conversation with the doorkeeper; even after hearing the words spoken by him, "Right here," he did not perceive their meaning. Why? Because of his lamentation. Therefore it is said:
"Overcome by intense sorrow. 73. "Teneva" (with that very same [robe]): wrapping around his belly with that very upper robe (uttarāsaṅga) with which he had swept the seat, [he thought], "May I..."
“Thinking, ‘The Teacher has touched me with his body,’ he made an interval by wrapping that [robe] around his belly with his upper robe (uttarāsaṅga), thus enclosing it.
Regarding the phrase “dattapaññattaṃ” and so forth, the word *datta* here is a synonym for a fool; thus he said, “You have been born dull-witted.
“Because of the change in the attendant” means because of the fact that his former attendant is now no longer an attendant.
75. "Inanimate" means made of wood, branches, and so forth. "Thickly coated with yellow pigment" refers to a type of dye that is exceedingly thick;
it is a coating and coloring with yellow, madder, and other such substances. "Having produced a surface by rubbing" means that which absorbs the dye.
"Hairless" means by repeatedly applying the ointment. "Fragmented" refers to the state of being broken into pieces.
“Colorable” means it is capable of being dyed; therefore he said, “it generates mere lust. “Anuyoga” means an inquiry or challenge.
“Vīmaṃsā” means investigation. The investigation for the core in the doctrine of the Nigaṇṭhas is like threshing chaff to seek rice, or like searching a plantain tree for its heartwood.
And for that very reason, one who investigates it finds it to be empty and hollow.
There is no word of the Buddha whatsoever that is not included within the Four Noble Truths;
and when investigated, it generates only joy and gladness for the wise, being insatiable because of its non-satiating nature. Thus he said, "The discourse on the Four Noble Truths," and so forth.
"In whatever way" means whether by way of the aggregates (*khandha*), or by way of one or another among the elements (*dhātu*), the bases (*āyatana*), and so on—the word of the Buddha.
It will be entered; for in whatever way it is entered, it remains profound precisely because it is the domain of those with profound knowledge.

And as for the wise, discerning person who has refuted the doctrines of others and applies himself to the challenge with all his might and resolve, that challenge is unable to move him even by the breadth of a hair.
Furthermore, it is because it can withstand scrutiny even when investigated for a very long time.
Thus, because the teaching of the Tathāgata possesses the quality of being well-expounded, it is said: "It is capable of withstanding inquiry and capable of withstanding scrutiny. 76.
One is called *dhīra* (wise) because one burns away [defilements] through the full understanding of the object-sphere and purifies its opposite;

since this state of wisdom (*dhīrabhāva*) consists in the total destruction of delusion, it is said: "The wisdom... [etc. ...of one who is endowed therewith. Of one whose moral restraint (*khīla*) has been shattered...

For one who has completely cut off all mental thorns, the Māras of the aggregates of volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhārakkhandhamāra*) are already conquered by the very conquest of the Māra of defilements and the Māra of death;
therefore, those two are not mentioned here. The word *igha* is a synonym for suffering; thus he said, "of one who is free from suffering.

In that regard, freedom from suffering through the attainment of *nibbāna* with residue remaining refers to freedom from the suffering of defilements, while [freedom from suffering] through the attainment of *nibbāna* without residue remaining...

“Freedom from suffering through the suffering of karmic result (vipākadukkha). Because he gazes upon [beings] in various ways (*vividham īsanato*) by means of passion, hatred, delusion, and so forth, he is *vīsaṃ*;
*vīsaṃ* itself is *vesaṃ*. Thus he says ‘of Vesantara,’ meaning ‘of one who stands having crossed over and transcended the *vīsaṃ*—passion and the rest.

‘Of Tusita’ means ‘of one who has gone to (*itassa*) and fared along (*saṃvattassa*) with contentment (*tusi*) by way of compassion. This being the case, the term “of Muditā” [is explained as follows].

It is indeed a repetition. "Of the man" (*manujassa*) indicates that the Blessed One, having been born as a human in his first birth, stands surpassing the world including the devas; it shows him to be the Blessed One, the marvelous one.
He is called a "man" (*naro*) because he leads (*narati*), that is, brings to attainment, the world including the devas from *saṃsāra* to the bliss of *nibbāna*; thus, the meaning is "leader."
For that person, therefore he said "repetition" (*punarutta*). Having stated "of the man" (*manujassa*), the word "of the person" (*narassa*) is a repeated phrase.
When expressed otherwise according to the meaning, ten qualities do not suffice for each individual verse;

the meaning is that they do not fulfill them. "He disciplines" (*vineti*) thus it is "discipline" (*vinaya*); discipline itself is the "guide" (*veneyika*), hence he said "of the guide of beings" (*sattānaṃ vināyakassa*). The inclination of the wise...
It is "radiant" (*rucira*) because it gladdens (*rāti*) or causes one to delight (*īreti*); its own state of radiance is due to skillfulness, which is why he says "of the pure Dhamma.
"Of the illuminator" means of that which makes things brilliant by the light of knowledge.
"Unattached" means detached from all eight assemblies, or from the entire world including the devas, through the relinquishing of grasping. "Of profound virtue" [means] of others...
Because of his knowledge, he possesses the quality of profundity that is without foundation. Therefore the Blessed One said:

"There are, monks, other things that are profound," and so forth. Or, it refers to one who has attained *mauna* (sagehood) through noble silence. "Established in the Dhamma" means well-established in the Dhamma-body (*dhammakāya*).
"One who is restrained" means one whose nature is restrained because his bodily conduct and so forth do not require guarding.
By the four reasons beginning with "He does not come," *pantasenāsanassa* means of a secluded lodging. *Paṭimantanapaññāya* means by the wisdom that turns back all the doctrines of others.
*Monaṃ* is said to be knowledge, because it shakes off all defilements from every side.
*Isisattamassa* means of the best among all seers (*isi*), the eldest. *Seṭṭhappattassa* means having attained the highest, the supreme.

[This refers to] one who has attained *sammāsambodhi*. "Letters and so forth" (*akkharādīni*) means the syllables, phrases, phonemes, forms, etymologies, explanations, indications, elucidations, clarifications, analyses, and manifestations;

these are the words that express the meaning of the phonemes. Because they are spoken and explained by bringing them together in accordance with the inclinations of those to be trained, they belong to the "one who possesses the words" (*padaka*).
The word *puri* has the same meaning as "previously" (*pubbe*); thus he says: "Of *Purindada*, [meaning] the giver of the gift of Dhamma for the very first time."
The Blessed One is capable of enduring what is unbearable; thus he said, "of the capable one. Therefore he said: "the Tathāgata, the Buddha, who endures the unbearable.

"Of those who have attained" means of those who have attained those qualities without exception. He is a "byākaraṇo" (an expounder) because he explains the phenomena of defilement and purification in detail;
a *byākaraṇo* itself is a *veyyākaraṇo*. A "textual passage" (*tantipada*) is a word established by being set down in the tradition (*tanti*).
Of one who is unbound by the bond of craving or by all the bonds of the defilements.
"With great wisdom" means with wisdom of great power, or with wisdom of great range. For all the Blessed One’s wisdom is of great power, and it is of great range within its respective domain;
moreover, because it is entirely without remainder through its singularity and so forth, it is called "of great range," which is none other than omniscience. "In the sense of demonstrating power":
In the sense of showing the world his own wondrous, inconceivable, and immeasurable power. Or, "of the yakkha" means of one worthy of worship by the world.

He said, "The analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) have come along with the path of stream-entry," because this lay follower has attained the analytical knowledges of a trainee (sekhapaṭisambhidā), just as the female lay follower Khujjuttarā did. When speaking in praise of the abandoning of defilements, [he refers to] the abandoning of defilements...
Making the object the sign, he speaks of its beauty.
77. "Sampiṇḍitā" means accumulated; the sense is that they are knotted together. "These beings"—whatever beings it may be that are wandering about.
"Thinking only of themselves"—because they have not transcended craving, they think only of their own purpose. For thus it is:
Even when grieving for their kinsmen who have died, they grieve only on account of their own purpose that must be accomplished by them.
"It was hot" means that the interior of the heart-region became heated by a powerful mental anguish, as if scorched by acacia charcoal;
therefore he said, "the blood melted. "Only a bowlful" means the measure of a single bowl.
Because the teaching on the Four Truths, which establishes clear realization, was taught in brief, it is said:
“The teaching of the Dhamma for the person who understands through a condensed summary is concluded.
The *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning) of the commentary on the *Upāli Sutta* is finished.
7. Commentary on the Kukkuravatika Sutta.
78. Regarding “Among the Koliyans”: this text is transmitted in the plural.
As for why the explanatory gloss “in the country of that name” was stated, he says “For he,” and so forth. It is not restricted means it is not specified as “in such-and-such a monastery.”

It is said: “Only in the lodging” means only in the monastery (*āvāsa*), not at the foot of a tree or elsewhere. The “cow-vow” (*govata*) is so called in the sense that it is to be undertaken by performing the duties of a cow, such as gathering fodder and so forth;
one who is engaged in that is a “cow-vower” (*govatika*). Thus he said: “one who has undertaken the cow-vow. With reference to this, those who know the Vedas say:
“While walking, he eats; while standing, he voids excrement; while drinking, he steams the water; he cuts the grass,” and so forth.
“This one is ‘naked’ (acela)” means he is naked by virtue of having gone forth as a naked ascetic;

however, the meaning should be stated here according to the method explained previously for the cow-vow follower and the dog-vow follower. “Crouching down” means having contracted both hands and both feet;
some also say it means “having become squatting. He said, “What is the destination? What is the result? because “destination” (gati) signifies the accomplishment or the outcome of going (gamana).
For the occurrence of resultant phenomena culminates in their actualization. It is called *abhisamparāya* because one goes (*sampareti*) to it after having performed and accumulated karma;
thus, it refers to the world beyond. He asks about its actualization therein, hence he says: "Where is there rebirth in the world beyond?
"The undertaking of the dog-vow" means the undertaking of the state of a dog, [beginning with] "From today..."
“I am a dog” is the resolve upon the state of being a dog. 79.
“Complete” means complete with as many canine transformations as there are. Therefore he said, “unimpaired. “Uninterrupted” means unmixed with those [other states].
By “the conduct of a dog,” he refers to the mind that resolves upon the state of being a dog through the conduct of dogs, such as their manner of walking, and so forth.

It is called *ākappa* because it must be assumed (*ākappetabba*) in such and such a way; it is the mode of conduct. In this context, however, that refers to walking and so forth; thus he said, "the mode of walking of dogs," and so on. "By conduct" means by the conduct of the dog's behavior.
"By the undertaking of a vow" means by the resolve upon the dog-vow (*kukkura-vata*). The very practice of the dog’s behavior is the performance of difficult asceticism.
The view is that which proceeds in the manner of such a reversal of one's natural state.
"For that dog-cooker there is no other destination" rejects any other destination; however, for others, there is simply no possibility [of such a destination].
"Lying down" means being established by way of guarding one's vows, moral conduct, and so forth.

Just as verbal roots that are transitive become intransitive through a specific shift in meaning—as in "the man has awakened" and "the cluster of lotuses has blossomed"—so too [is this] through a specific shift in meaning.
Showing that even intransitive verbs can become transitive, he said, “I do not lament, I do not wail,” and so forth.
The word *anutthuna* is used in the sense of a transitive verb, as in such passages as “wailing over old things.
By stating, “And this is the application here,” he shows that both wailing and weeping are intended in this verse.
80. By the phrase "in the same manner as stated," it refers to the undertaking of the cow-vow (*govata-samādāna*). "Cow-conduct" (*gosīla*) means the behavior of a cow.
"Cow-mind" (*gocitta*) refers to the thought that has arisen: "From today onwards, I shall do what is to be done by cows. This meaning is indicated by extension (*atidisa*).

Furthermore, whatever remains to be said regarding the ox-observance (*gvākappa*) is indicated by the very statement: "It is exactly like what was stated for the dog-observance (*kukkurākappa*)," and the specific distinctions are likewise indicated.

The meaning of "just as it was stated there" (*yathā pana tattha*) and so forth is exactly as previously explained. Furthermore, whatever remains to be said here follows the same method as that set forth regarding the dog-vow (*kukkuravata*) and other such practices.

81. "By way of the performance of certain actions" (*ekaccakammakiriyāvasena*) means by way of the undertaking of certain unwholesome or wholesome deeds. "Of these" (*imesaṃ*) refers to the cow-vow followers (*govatika*) and the dog-vow followers (*kukkuravatika*).
"Performance" (*kiriyā*) refers to the activity proceeding by way of the cultivation of the cow-vow and so forth.
"It will become manifest" means that it will become manifest as "this specific action is included within this fourfold classification of actions.

"Black" (*kāḷaka*) means soiled; the meaning is that it causes the mind's natural luminosity to become obscured. Furthermore, since only that which is fully accomplished as a course of action (*kammapatha*) is intended here, he says, "the ten unwholesome courses of action.
Or, it is "black" because it is a cause for rebirth in a black class of beings (*kaṇhābhijāti*).

Therefore he said, "black result" (*kaṇhavipāka*). Rebirth in the states of misery (*apāya*) and wretchedness among humans is the black result; this is stated according to its nature as darkness (*tama-bhāva*).
However, by way of a singular designation, it is said, "because of being produced in the states of misery," the meaning being "because of causing [rebirth] to be produced.
"White" (*sukka*) means bright; the meaning is that which makes the mind radiant, because it is the cause for a white birth (*sukkābhijāti*).
Or [it is] bright. Therefore he said, "bright result" (*sukkavipāka*). The bright result consists of rebirth in heaven and excellence in the human world;
and as for the state of radiance mentioned, it was stated by way of a singular designation as "because of being born in heaven," the meaning of which is "because of causing birth.
"Mixed karma" (*vomissakakamma*) is that action performed in a mixed manner, being dark at one time and bright at another.
Having stated, "The ripening of pleasure and pain," the passage beginning with "For mixed karma... was spoken in order to show the mode of occurrence of pleasure and pain.
The designation "black" and "white" for karma is due to its being the cause for birth in black and white classes [of beings].
Because it does not lead to the state beyond conditions, even the term "white" is not intended here for that karma which, being free from both, brings about the exhaustion of karma; thus he said.
—“Both... [as previously stated]... it is said that they do not flow. In this context, “of both results” means of the result already attained.
For here, the result included within the state of prosperity (*sampattibhava*) is intended by the term “bright result,” not that which is absolutely pure.
“Accompanied by suffering” means accompanied by the suffering that must be produced by oneself; the sense is that it leads to suffering.
“Volition is the burden in this sutta, while in the Upāli Sutta it is action”—this meaning, though stated below, is established here for the sake of understanding.
“Having formed” means having accumulated. Since that [formation] is achieved through the convergence of conditions, it is like a gathering or a massing together;
thus he says: “having gathered together, having made into a mass—this is the meaning. “The world with suffering...”
He speaks of the world of the woeful states (*apāyaloka*). By the term "contact as result" (*vipākaphassa*), he refers to the occurrence of karmic fruition there by way of the heading of contact.
"From past action" (*bhūtakamma*) means from the karma that has brought about rebirth, the karma accumulated by oneself. "As it really is" (*yathābhūta*) means of whatever kind [it may be].

"By way of similarity to the action" (*kammappabhāgavasena*) means by way of correspondence to the action. "Rebirth occurs" (*upapatti hoti*) refers to rebirth classified as being without feet and so forth. It is said to be "like the action."
"By whatever one does, by that one is reborn"—thus it is said that those various types of beings, such as the footless and so forth, seem to be born by means of a single action alone.
Furthermore, "rebirth" occurs through karmic ripening (*vipāka*); when ripening is possible, those specific modes of rebirth necessarily come to be.
If this is so, why is it stated that "by that one is reborn," implying they are caused by the karma of rebirth? To this he says: "But because... and so forth.
"By which kamma-result he is reborn" means: by which ripening kamma this being is said to be reborn.
"Contact as the result of that kamma" means: contacts that constitute the result of that respective kamma.
They are "heirs to kamma" because they take up the inheritance to be given by kamma, namely its result; [this refers to] contacts. The state of being an heir to kamma belongs to the fruit of kamma.
It is an inheritance; therefore it is said, "having karma as their inheritance. Thus he said: "Karma alone is their inheritance, their property.
And the three types of volition belonging to the lower jhānas—this establishes the causal status for the experience of non-afflictive feeling and the arising of absolute happiness.
If this is so, let the aforementioned jhāna-volitions suffice as the cause for the arising of absolute happiness.

Regarding the question, "What are the sense-sphere [states]?"—the opponent challenges: "But how is it that wholesome volition of the sense sphere, being devoid of that specific nature [of the fine-material sphere], has come to be called 'unafflicted mental formation' (abyābajjhā-manosaṅkhāra)? The other [the respondent], however, shows that not all wholesome volition of the sense sphere is taken in that way;
rather, certain types of volition are conducive to jhāna. He says: "At the time of establishing the kasiṇa, at the time of practicing the kasiṇa..."
"Are they obtained? he asked. In this context, the volition (*cetanā*) of practicing the *kasiṇa* is to be understood; that is what brings about access concentration (*upacāra-jjhāna*).
Therefore, because sense-sphere volition is joined with the volition of the first jhāna, the volition of preparing the *kasiṇa* is also included here, as it too can sometimes be of such a nature.
For the wholesome sense-sphere volitions consisting of development (*bhāvanā-maya*), which proceed by way of the preliminary stage (*parikamma*) and so forth, [are what is meant].

It is stated because of its proximity to the first jhāna. The volition of the fourth jhāna is connected with the volition of the third jhāna by virtue of the state of being a dwelling for beings who possess a single body and a single perception;
thus, in such instances, equanimity is similar to that [pleasure] in its peaceful nature and its association with knowledge. However, some say it is "conducive to the volition of the fourth jhāna."

They say that when illustrating [the third jhāna], it is stated that the volition of the third jhāna is "closely connected" because it is obtained at the time of preparing the kasiṇa, at the time of the kasiṇa-jhāna, and at the time of practicing the kasiṇa;
however, that is merely their own opinion. Their connection should be understood precisely according to the method already explained.
"By way of the mixture of both" refers to both the wholesome and unwholesome formations, as well as pleasure and pain.

By way of their mixed state. Regarding the phrase "hungry ghosts belonging to the intermediate realm" (*vemānika-peta*): this is stated by way of prevalence; for others who have fallen into states of misery (*vinipātika*) as well, suffering certainly occurs at times.
"For the abandoning of that" means for the purpose of establishing the state of non-arising (*anuppatti-dhammatā*) of that aforementioned karma. "That volition" (*yā cetanā*)...
"Volition leading to diminution. Regarding "having reached kamma":
when it is called "wholesome kamma," there is no other state more brilliant than the volition of the Path (magga-cetanā), because of its state of ultimate purity.

As for the statement "it is neither black nor white," the reason for negating its whiteness is exactly as explained in the method below. Therefore, he said: "But having reached this fourfold classification of kamma," and so forth.
82. "In a faction that does not lead to liberation" refers to the naked ascetic’s renunciation and the dog-vow. "In yoga" means in the practice of the Dhamma according to the proper method.
"By means of the *yona*" refers to that probation for heretics (*titthiyaparivāsa*) which was prescribed by the Blessed One.
The construction here is: "having undertaken that probation for heretics. "Having rubbed [it] like gold on a whetstone" means having ground it with the hand.
Like a potter’s vessel.

“Withdrawn” (*vūpakaṭṭho*) means secluded and solitary. “With mind directed toward” (*pesitatto*) means with the mind directed toward Nibbāna. By the words “...that unsurpassed consummation of the holy life...
he dwelt,” the teaching is brought to its conclusion by means of the pinnacle of Arahantship.

However, the statement beginning with “Now, as for a certain one... is primarily intended to praise the venerable Seniya’s practice and to demonstrate that he had attained the state of Arahantship directly; thus it says, “by way of the pinnacle of Arahantship.
The very attainment of Arahantship constitutes his being included among them. The rest is all easily understood.
The elucidation of the hidden meaning (*līnatthappakāsanā*) of the commentary on the *Kukkuravatika-sutta* is completed.
8. Commentary on the *Abhayarājakumāra-sutta* 83.
One who is not equal by birth, of low conduct, born from the womb of a mother who lives on the gifts of others, is a son of a slave-girl (*pādasikāputta*).
It is called *vāda* because one speaks by means of it; thus he says, "a fault (*aguṇa*) is a *vāda*," as in the phrase, "Lay the charge (*vādaṃ āropehi*), that is, lay the blame (*dosaṃ āropehi*).
One is destined for hell (*nerayika*) by virtue of being produced there, or because one is fixed in hell due to karma conducive to hell.
The same principle applies here to the term *āpāyika*. Having arisen in the Avīci hell, one remains there for an intermediate aeon (*antarakappa*), which is designated as a lifespan.
"He remains" means he is one who lasts for an eon (*kappaṭṭha*). "Curable" (*tekiccha*) means one who can be treated by way of avoiding rebirth in hell;

"not curable" (*atekiccha*) is the opposite. "Having released the two extremes" means: thinking "one might make it harsh or unpleasant," having let go of these two parts and not touching them, one "vomits forth" (*uggilati*) the matter asked about by placing it outside of those [two]. And that—
He said, "He is not able to do so," meaning, "he will not be able to vomit it up or bring it out.

In the same way, this question is not to be accepted; thinking, "This is the fault here," he swallows it—meaning he removes it by making it an invalid question—and failing to do so, he does not swallow it—meaning he establishes it as valid. But the Blessed One, regarding that matter, even a mere...
One who does not do so should be understood as failing in both respects. How so?
For when the Blessed One said, "In this matter, Prince, it is not one-sided," he overturned the Nigaṇṭha’s intention; having released him from both extremes, he answered the question.
Thus, for the time being, he succeeded in making him vomit it up. By saying, "In that regard, Prince, it is not one-sided," he...
And thus, pointing out the fault in the question by saying, "This is not a question that should be asked without such differentiation;

rather, it should be asked after making a distinction," he swallows it up, for even if one were able to swallow it, one would not be able to rise again due to the mind's altered state. Abhaya was one who had practiced the two paths.
Being clever and skilled, he wanders about as one habituated to debate. Therefore it was said:
“Because of his inclination toward debate, accepting his words, he said, ‘So be it, venerable sir.
(85) “Of such a kind” refers to speech that is unpleasant and disagreeable to others—speech of this sort, but not harsh speech.

For the destruction of the bridge [of trust] occurs for the Tathāgatas through harsh speech. Indeed, harsh speech is intended here as the state of being harsh in one's intention, not merely by causing displeasure to others.
The Nigaṇṭhas were ruined because their question—regarded as something to be swallowed whole (ogilika) and so forth—was shattered by a single word.
To show the reason for sitting on the lap of the child, the passage beginning with "lesavādino" was spoken. Therein:
"Quibblers" (*lesavādino*) means those who employ fallacies (*chala*), or those whose habit is to engage in debate merely by a slight pretext due to their incompleteness in the path of debate.

"One who has entered the fray of battle" (*osaṭasaṅgāmo*) means one who has descended into the battle of debate on many occasions by crushing the arguments of opponents. "Having pierced" means having pierced with a fingernail.
"This very one" refers to this boy who was made to sit on his lap for the purpose of avoiding the defeat of his own argument.
Thinking, "I shall break his argument by using the boy's horse as a supporting simile," he considered, "I shall shatter his argument because it has not been established.
"Apaneyyaṃ assa ahaṃ" means: "I shall remove that from the mouth of this boy. "Abhūtattho va abhūtaṃ" means: [it is] non-existent in its meaning, thus it is unreal.
By means of eliding the latter member of the compound, he says: “It is ‘unreal’ (abhūta), meaning it has the sense of being unreal.

“Untrue” (atacca) is a synonym for that very same thing; thus he says: “‘Untrue’ (atacca) means not true (na taccha). Alternatively, “unreal” (abhūta) means non-existent or non-occurrent. “Untrue” (atacca) means having an incorrect mode of being.
“Not connected with the goal” (anatthasaṃhita) means connected with what is harmful, whether pertaining to the present life or to future lives; [it is] harmful...
Or, "connected with harm" (*anatthasaṃhita*) means that which is connected with what is not beneficial; "not beneficial" (*anattha*) is the opposite of benefit, its very nature.
Thus, it is "connected with harm" because it is joined with that. The meaning is: malicious speech and frivolous talk.
In this way, it should be understood that all four kinds of verbal misconduct are included here.

"Badly practiced" means practicing wrongly. The Tathāgata does not speak that [first type of speech] because it is defiled by the fault of being untrue. The Tathāgata does not speak even that [second type of speech], although its meaning is true, because it is defiled by the fault of being unbeneficial.

"Possessing a ground" (*ṭhāniyā*) means having a basis or reason; by changing the letter *ka* to *ya*, it becomes *ṭhāniyā*. That which is not possessing a ground is "groundless" (*aṭṭhāniyā*), meaning without reason, improper, and unfitting.
Such speech is "groundless speech" (*aṭṭhāniyakathā*). "Let us speak from our own personal experience" means...
We speak this deceptive speech while acting as though we have personally witnessed it ourselves.

The village elder, thinking, "These people wish to deceive me; now I shall deceive them," said, "It shall be so," and so forth. Previously, they were unable even to say, "We are not slaves," because of the agreement that had been made.
"The third time, the very third time" means that on both sides, the third word was indeed the third. "Without exceeding the proper time for speaking" means...
Because he speaks exactly as, when, and for whom it ought to be spoken, he speaks without overstepping either the reason for speaking or the proper time for speaking. 87.
"By means of knowledge arising on the spot" (ṭhānuppattikañāṇena) means by means of knowledge that arises right at the occasion; [knowledge] regarding each respective cause.
The nature of phenomena (*dhammasabhāva*) is the state of understanding phenomena according to their true individual essence through the knowledge that arises regarding each respective state.

The "element of phenomena" (*dhammadhātu*) is the all-knowing wisdom (*sabbaññutā*), so called because it examines all phenomena—whether they be those possessing individual essences or otherwise—in accordance with reality.
Therefore, he said: "This is a designation for the knowledge of omniscience. It is "well-penetrated" (*suppaṭividdha*) in its entirety.

By way of thoroughly penetrating the state of one who is to be guided (*ñeyyadhamma*), the meaning is "it has been thoroughly penetrated. Therefore he said, "It has come into the hands of the Blessed One.

By means of this very teaching—which, through the analytical exposition of the discourse, concludes by way of the person to be guided—he directly realized *arahantship* while demonstrating the Four Noble Truths.
The *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Hidden Meaning) for the commentary on the *Abhayarājakumārasutta* is completed.
9. Commentary on the *Bahuvedaniyasutta* 88.

"Pañcakaṅga" means one who possesses a fivefold set of tools (*pañcakaṅga*)—such as an adze and so forth—which are the constituent parts (*aṅga*) or equipment (*saṃdhana*) for accomplishing the work of a carpenter. A "thapati" is one who establishes (*thapana*) pillars and other building materials; it refers here to the wise Elder Udāyī, not the Elder Kāḷudāyī.
