89. It is called a *pariyāya* because it proceeds (*pariyāyati*) and turns out its own fruit; thus, it is a cause. And the state of being bodily or mental is dependent upon feeling as its cause.
Therefore he said: "They should be understood as two by way of the bodily and the mental.

Therein, that which is dependent on the sensitive body is bodily, and that which is dependent on the mind is mental. Regarding the phrase "three by way of pleasure, etc.," these are pleasure, pain, and equanimity.
It is the cause for the feeling of pleasure and so forth. For it is by making those [objects] the basis for occurrence that the terms "pleasure" and so on are applied therein;
in this same manner, the cause should be determined and stated for the remaining cases as appropriate.
"By way of mental exploration" (upavicāra-vasena) means by way of occurring with distinction after having approached the object. For, in whatever object the feeling of joy (somanassa-vedanā) occurs—
Because it approaches that [object] by way of being its objective support (*ārammaṇatā*) and because it is distinguished from other feelings, it occurs there with a specific distinction.

Therefore he said: "It investigates the form that serves as the basis for joy. This same method applies to the remaining feelings. "House-based" (*gehassita*) means dependent on the household (*gehanissita*). 90.
"By way of a figurative expression" (*pariyāyena*) refers to what was stated in the passage: "I say this is suffering in this context."
"Showing that": although in this sutta two feelings were shown—beginning with the words, "Two feelings, Ānanda, have been taught"—nevertheless, even one feeling was indeed shown;

thus he shows it. "To support": thinking, "Even though only one feeling was stated by me by way of a method, since this is so, two should also be mentioned," he supports his opponent's argument. But how?
Is it said that there is only one feeling? "Whatever is felt—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—all this, I say, is suffering.
As for what ought to be said here, it should be understood according to the method explained in the *Paramatthadīpanī* commentary on the *Itivuttaka*.
But how is it that here—in the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere, in the immaterial attainments, and in the cessation of perception and feeling—pleasure is said to be "exalted"?
To this he says, "And here," and so forth. "In the sense of being peaceful" means by way of the subsiding of opposing states.

"In the sense of being sublime" means by way of its state of being unsurpassed and its state of excellence, distinguished by a specific development and by a specific condition, which constitutes its preeminence.
"Exquisite" (*paṇīta*) means "refined. What is called "bliss consisting in feeling" (*vedayita-sukha*) is so called because it is pleasure in the form of a feeling (*vedanā*).

What is called "bliss not consisting in feeling" (*avedayita-sukha*) is called "bliss" simply by virtue of the extent of its freedom from suffering (*niddukkhatā*). Alternatively, cessation (*nirodha*) is worthy of being called "it eats well" or "it digs away" physical and mental afflictions, because suffering ceases there even for as long as seven days.
Therefore he said: "In the sense of bliss, which is designated as the state of being free from suffering.

(91) In whatever existence, mental arising, or state there may be, the state of being free from suffering—the seclusion from suffering due to the non-apprehension of its opposite—is designated precisely as bliss. The rest is easy to understand.
The *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning) for the commentary on the *Bahuvedanīya-sutta* is completed.
10. Commentary on the Apaṇṇaka Sutta 93.
“Of various kinds” means those ascetics and brahmins who hold various views; they are called “ascetics” merely by virtue of their renunciation, and “brahmins” merely by virtue of their birth.
“Vision” means view. “Grasped” means grasped with dogmatic adherence. Thus, they [hold] their own vision...

They ask because they wish to grasp [the teaching]. "Without seeing, the world does not go forth" means that through the cultivation of liberation, the world does not emerge from the suffering of *saṃsāra* without a single instance of seeing.
They were unable to establish themselves even in a single view because of the absence of the mode of faith (*saddhākāra*).
For it was by means of this teaching that they established themselves in the Refuges (*saraṇa*). This is because, regarding a trustworthy object that is not perverted...

Faith that has arisen is intended here as "possessing a mode" (*ākāravatī*). Therefore, that which in the world is the teaching of the Dhamma without perversion—thinking "this alone is it"—is faith that proceeds by way of the means to the Path;
because it serves as the cause for that [faith], the faith supported by it is called "possessing a mode.
For faith without a basis is not "possessing a mode" due to its having an improper cause. In the word *ākāravatī*, the suffix *-vatī* [indicates possession].
It should be understood not merely as indicating existence, but rather as indicating excellence (*atisaya*) or as indicating praise (*pāsaṃsa*).

Therefore, "possessing modes" (*ākāravatī*) means here that it possesses the grounds for excellence, or that it possesses the grounds for being praiseworthy, by way of being a basis for trustworthiness.
Regarding the term "unfailing" (*apaṇṇaka*), just as the application of one who has begun to accomplish some purpose [is unfailing]...
When it is transgressed, one becomes as if a non-doer therein because it must be undertaken again. But when not transgressed, it is "infallible" (*apaṇṇaka*) because it accomplishes the goal;
likewise, this Dhamma is called "infallible" in an absolute sense because it proceeds by overcoming [all opposition].
Therefore he said: "It is untransgressed, leading to non-duality, and grasped with certainty."
94. *Tabbipaccanīkabhūtā* means those that are the opposites of that wrong view (*micchādiṭṭhi*).

95. *Nesaṃ* refers to wholesome states (*kusalā dhammā*). *Akusalato nikkhantabhāve* means in the state of being free from corruption (*asaṃkiliṭṭha*). *Ānisaṃso* means the quality of pure result (*suddhavipākatā*).
*Visuddhipakkho* means the side of purity, the state of purification, and luminosity (*pariyodātatā*). [This applies to] the state of view regarding phenomena that have not arisen.

It is the making known, the explaining, the making known of non-existent things. Regarding the grasping [of faults] among those things that are blameworthy, specifically the highest blame which is wrong view, he asks:
"From where does the grasping of good virtue come? He says: "For one who grasps at wrong view, good virtue is abandoned.
As for "wrong view and so forth," here wrong intention consists of the thought that there is no other world, and wrong speech consists of the doctrine that there is no other world.
False speech, hostility toward the noble ones, and so forth. "By way of arising again and again" means by way of arising repeatedly in the mind.
"Evil unwholesome states" refers to the unwholesome aggregates that arise and proceed in such a manner at times such as during reflection or making known one's intentions.
“Kaliggaha” means grasping at what is harmful. Since that leads to defeat both in this very life and in the future world, it is called “the grasp of defeat.
Regarding the term “dussamatta,” the prefix *du-* should be brought over and applied here as well from the word “samādinna”;
thus he says, “badly grasped. Just as it is badly grasped, so too is it wrongly undertaken; hence, “dussamatta.”

"Taken at the wrong time" is what was said. "Pervading only his own doctrine" means pervading by way of not allowing any room for another, while adhering strictly to his own doctrine of nihilism with the thought, "This alone is the truth; all else is vain. Therefore he said, "having resolved.
The passage beginning with "the Fully Enlightened One" is a demonstration of the manner of such resolution. "He leaves behind" means he separates or removes; therefore he said, "he avoids."
96. *Kaṭaggaho* means grasping after having made [the action] entirely successful. That, moreover, is the attainment of victory;
thus it is called "the seizing of victory" (*jayaggāho*). *Suggahito* means grasped by way of performing it well.
*Suparāmaṭṭho* means thoroughly touched by way of repeated practice. By both terms, he shows that the action has been performed and accumulated.
And it brings about a state of well-being because it leads to rebirth in heaven and because it abandons the nature of evil. 97.

"Doing with one's own hand" means doing by means of one's own hand alone. Herein, even things that are to be relinquished (*nissaggiya*) or those that are fixed (*thāvara*) are included under "doing with one's own hand.
By saying "cooking, burning, and afflicting," he means "one who oppresses with a staff. "One who personally causes grief" means...

"Causing grief for another" means either acting oneself as a cause of grief for another or producing grief in them. "By others who act according to one's word" refers to those who carry out one's instructions.
"Moving oneself as well" means moving oneself by means of an effort that afflicts another.

Regarding the term *atipātayato* ("causing to fall"), it functions both in the sense of the direct agent (*suddhakattuattha*) and the instrumental agent (*hetukattuattha*); thus he says: "both for one who kills and for one who causes another to kill."
The junction of a house (*gharasandhi*) refers to the joining of the walls both inside and outside that stand together. "Plunder" (*nillopa*) means to take away entirely, leaving nothing behind.

"Looting" (*vilopa*) is that which pertains to a single house; thus it is "single-house looting" (*ekāgārika*). "Obstruction" (*paripantha*) is the act of killing on a path in every way and completely.
Evil is not performed because it is impossible to produce what did not previously exist; therefore, there is no evil. If...
Thus, explaining how beings engage in evil, he said: "Beings, however, have the perception that 'we are doing [it]'" (sattā pana karomāti evaṃsaññino honti).
For it occurs to him thus: "Indeed, for these beings, the act of harming and so forth does not touch the self, because of its permanence and its changelessness;
but the body is insentient, like a wooden log or a clod of earth, and even when that is destroyed, nothing [of the self] is affected."
"Evil" means [the opposite]. "With wheel-rims of sharp hooves" means with rims made of sharpened hooves.

The statement beginning with "If [he goes] south" was spoken with the intention that the southern direction along the Ganges is an unsuitable location, whereas the northern direction is a suitable location; thus he said, "The people on the southern bank are harsh," and so forth.
"A great sacrifice" refers to a great offering similar to the Mahāvijita sacrifice. "By restraint of virtue" means by physical and verbal self-restraint.
“By truthful speech” means by true words. It is mentioned separately because it is regarded in the world as a merit more weighty than others.

For just as false speech is weighty among evil qualities, so is truthful speech among meritorious qualities. Therefore the Blessed One said: “For one who has transgressed even a single quality,” and so forth.
“In the manner already stated” means in the manner stated regarding the dark side (the side of demerit). For therein—
—“There is no evil, there is no result of evil”—this is what was stated there; here, “there is merit, there is a result of merit”—this is the only difference.
The rest is exactly as previously stated. He says this with reference to such passages as “this is to be expected for them,” which is similar to what was said above in the preceding section.

100. "By both" means by the statement that negates the condition of cause (*hetu-paccaya*). "Condition of defilement" (*saṃkilesa-paccaya*) refers to the cause for the state of being stained and soiled through wandering in *saṃsāra*.
By way of the opposite of what was stated, the literal meaning of "condition of purification" (*visuddhi-paccaya*) should be understood.
Regarding "power" (*bala*) and so forth, it refers to the power consisting of effort that brings about either the defilement or the purification of sentient beings.

Or else, there is no heroic effort—whether it be the energy reckoned as the state of a hero and a warrior, or the manly strength to be performed by a man—that leads to the attainment of ever higher stages;
nor is such manly exertion found or perceived.

They are called "beings" (*sattā*) because of their attachment (*satva-yoga*), and because of being stuck and fastened to form and the other aggregates. They are called "living beings" (*pāṇa*) because they proceed by way of inhalation and exhalation.
Regarding "living beings" (pāṇā): since he speaks of them by classifying them according to the single-facultied and so forth, he says "the single-facultied," and so on.

Since they are called "beings" (bhūtā) because of their existence within the egg-shell and so forth, he says "the egg-shell... they say. Because they sustain life as if bearing it, and because they grow, they are "living things" (jīvā).
Thus, the meaning of the terms for "beings," "living beings," "beings," and "living things" should be understood. There is no [self] in these...
"Powerless" (*avasā*) means they lack mastery over defilement and purification. "Weak and lacking vigor" (*abalā avīriyā*) means they possess neither strength nor energy.

"Fixed course" (*niyāma*) refers to the state of proceeding with necessity, like a gem strung on an unbreakable thread or woven into a seamless net; it is so called because it abandons the bonds of destiny, birth, and clan through its fixed progression.
"Going here and there" (*tatra tatra gamana*) refers to the approaching of the six classes of beings within their respective destinies by way of conjunction.

"Meeting. "It is simply its own nature (*sabhāva*)" means that just as there is sharpness in a thorn, roundness in wood-apple fruits, and variegated forms in animals and birds, so too, for the entire world, such-and-such a transformation occurs without a cause or condition;
this is simply its own nature, not something artificial. Therefore he said, "By which," and so forth.
One who kills birds is a fowler (*sākuṇika*); likewise one who kills pigs is a pig-trapper (*sūkarika*). A hunter (*ludda*) is anyone else who is a deer-stalker or a snare-setter.
Because of being intent upon evil deeds, they are called "black by birth" (*kaṇhābhijāti*). "Bhikkhus" refers to the Śākyan monks;

because of their eating fish and meat, they are said to be "blue by birth" (*nīlābhijāti*). Even while consuming requisites obtained through right means, because of their adherence to views contrary to the Ājīvaka system...
“They eat after having put thorns among their requisites,” so they say. Certain renunciants are those who are especially devoted to the practice of self-mortification;

for they act as if they were handling thorns, and thus they are called “those who live on thorns. Through their observance of vows such as eating while standing and refusing alms-food, they are exceedingly pure.
By the words “disciples of the naked ones,” he refers to the disciples of the Ājīvakas. It is said that because of the purity of mind resulting from the Ājīvaka tenets, they are so designated.
They are even whiter than the Nigaṇṭhas. For [the states] such as Nanda are to be attained through such a practice;
therefore, it is said that Nanda and the others are "whiter" than the Nigaṇṭhas and the disciples of the Ājīvakas, being thus called "of white birth.
This is their doctrine: that by entering into the state of bird-catchers and so forth, there is suffering and happiness among those of black birth and so on.

Experiencing [the results], they gradually exhaust eighty-four thousand great aeons (*mahākappa*), and by entering the state of an Ājīvaka, they abide in the supreme white birth-class (*paramasukkābhijāti*) and are purified from *saṃsāra*. This is their fixed destiny; such is the doctrine of the Ājīvakas.
Saying "there is no giving," one who denies it is a nihilist (*natthika*) because he rejects the fruit of giving; thus he said: "The view of nihilism (*natthikadiṭṭhi*)."
"...it obstructs the result. This has been explained below as well: "For the view of nihilism asserts that there is nothing.

The "view of no-cause" [obstructs] both; that is, both karma and its result. For by saying, "Beings become defiled and purified without cause and without condition," one asserts the absence of a causal condition for the defilement and purification of the result, just as one does for karma.
It is called "obstructing both. Resultant [kamma] is obstructed because, in the absence of [volitional] action, there can be no result.
Volitional action is obstructed because, in the absence of a result, action would become purposeless. "In its own nature" means by way of its specific characteristic.
Although they are stated individually according to their respective views, all those such as the nihilists and others are included under the heading of the nihilistic view and so forth.
Each of these three types of views exists because they both deny [the efficacy of action]. For the phrase "denying both" is a statement of the reason (*hetu*).
The phrase "those who maintain the doctrine of causelessness," and so forth, is the formal proposition (*paṭiññā*).

For one who is a nihilist (*natthikadiṭṭhika*) by denying the result of maturation (*vipāka*), is in fact a non-doerist (*akiriyadiṭṭhika*) by denying action (*kamma*) in its essential meaning, and is also a causelessist (*ahetukadiṭṭhika*) by denying both.
[The word] *hoti* [is used]. The same method applies to the remaining two [cases] as well.
"They recite" means they learn and chant that text which elucidates those views. "They investigate" means they examine its meaning.

The phrase beginning with "of them" (*tesam*) and so forth is a demonstration of the manner of investigation. "In that object" (*tasmiṃ ārammaṇe*) refers to that which elucidates the non-existence of the fruits of action as they have been imagined.
“Wrong mindfulness settles upon its object” means that through the habitual practice over a long period, one comes to accept [the view] as such— by way of reflection on the mode of that object—
once it has appeared to the mind in its own form, as if with a physical grasp, regarding the meaning obtained through hearsay by way of [the views] such as “there is no giving.
This occurs through the process of wrong mindfulness settling upon its object via the mode of the view beginning with “there is no giving.”

When that [state] has been grasped through reflective acceptance (*nijjhānakkhanti*), and as one repeatedly practices and cultivates it in that very same way, craving—associated with that particular adherence—comes to rest.

This craving, which is undertaken by wrong thought (*micchāvitakka*), supported by wrong effort (*micchāvāyāma*), and which grasps what lacks that nature as having "that nature," receives the name "wrong mindfulness" (*micchāsati*).
The mind becomes one-pointed (*ekagga*) through the acquisition of the aforementioned conditions such as thought and so forth.
By way of being fixed upon that object, having abandoned lack of one-pointedness, it becomes as if absorbed in one-pointedness.

For it should be understood that even wrong concentration (micchā-samādhi), through the power of cultivation obtained by specific conditions, can at times perform a function resembling that of true concentration, as in the case of piercing hair and so forth.
"The impulsions (javana) impel" means that many times in that manner, within the preliminary stages...
When the javana-moments have proceeded, in the very last of these seven javana-moments, seven javanas flow.
However, this is merely a demonstration of the intrinsic nature (*dhammasabhāva*) of phenomena—that they are "with-remedy" (*satekiccha*) in the first javana and likewise in the second and so on;
it is not possible for anyone to actually render them "with-remedy" at that specific moment.

"In that regard" means among those three wrong views. "Someone enters upon one view" means that for one whose insistence (*abhinivesa*) and habitual practice (*āsevanā*) proceed toward only one [view], he enters upon that very one view.
However, for one whose insistence proceeds toward two or even three, he enters upon two or three. By this, that which was previously [discussed] by way of the refutation of both...
It is said that all forms of wrong view are established as "settled" (niyata); this refers to their preliminary stage.

However, those which have actually entered the fixed course of falsehood (micchattaniyāma) are shown to be unmixed, because—due to being established through the convergence of their respective conditions—they do not converge together in a single instance, just as distinct attainments of specific qualities do not occur simultaneously.
This is indicated by the phrase beginning with "even when one has entered [the path]," and so forth.
This demonstrates that all three views possess equal strength and equal fruit;
therefore, even when these three arise in a single person, they are entirely contiguous with one another, and when the result of one is given, the others act as its supporting factors.
To show that the statement "it is called a 'stump of the cycle'" is of interpretable meaning (*neyyattha*) and not of direct meaning (*nītattha*), he explains it further.
But why was it said, beginning with "What then is this...? [The answer is: This unwholesome state is indeed weak and feeble, not possessing great power like the wholesome;
thus he said, "It is fixed within a single lifetime. Otherwise, the fixedness in wrongness (*micchattaniyāma*) would be as absolute as the fixedness in rightness (*sammattaniyāma*).
If that is so, how is the illustration of the "stump in the cycle of existence" explained? To this he said: "But by way of repetition," and so forth.
Therefore, just as it is said, "Once submerged, he remains submerged," so too is this illustration of the stump of the round (saṃsāra).

For when one has entered upon a particular mode of viewing in dependence on such-and-such conditions, it cannot be said that there will never again be for him a lifting of the head from that state by depending on conditions opposed to them. Thus it is said, "for the most part."
Therefore, because an unwholesome person is thus a condition even for the state of being a seed of *saṃsāra*, [the text says] "one who desires prosperity.
This means one who desires the increase of their own virtues by way of the present life, the future life, and the ultimate goal (*paramattha*).

Furthermore, regarding this point, some say: "Just as those skilled in the supporting conditions (*upanissaya-kusala*)—due to having acquired strength through reaching full maturity via long-term cultivation—"
“They completely cut off unwholesome states; thus, unwholesome phenomena, having gained strength through long-term cultivation, sometimes even cut off wholesome states.

And by doing so, they are capable of demonstrating the state of being a mere stump in the round of existence for one who possesses strong adherence to wrong views. This is as stated in the *Vassabhañña* [Sutta].
As for the statement "view," that is not so; it is not by the mere long-term cultivation of factors fixed in falsehood that one becomes capable of abandoning their opposite.

Rather, the state of being an abandoner occurs only through the nature of the abandoner itself—a capacity established by the very nature of things (dhammatā) and produced by specific conditions—and this is stated only for those skilled in cultivation regarding the abandoner, and only for the unwholesome regarding the state of being abandoned.
By the method beginning with “to be abandoned by vision,” the weakness of unwholesome states alone is established;
[this] is also to be understood either by name or by realization through the reasoning beginning with “the weak become strong.

Just as light is external and non-arisen, so too here, one should not suspect the existence of the state [of light] in what is not admitted, because the specific [quality] must be proven by the listener, and because the generality is already present for the listener.
Because the word *veda* is intended [in this sense], there is an elision [of the suffix];
it is established in its own nature as a means of proof, just as in the case of the existence of sound, and because there is no possibility of contradiction with pure inference and so forth.

For it cannot be said that, like external light, materiality can be established in the internal light by depending on a material body, such as being cognizable by the eye; thus it was stated, "not even..."

Since intermediate light, being unobstructed, is like feeling, it is established by the very fact that the darkness of ignorance is dispelled by the light of knowledge that all wholesome states (*kusaladhamma*) are susceptible to being cut off by some unwholesome state (*akusaladhamma*).

As for what ought to be said regarding the challenge concerning the "stump of the round of existence" (*vaṭṭakhāṇuka*), that has already been stated below; thus, let this prattle of foolish people rest.
103. *Jhānacittamayā* means produced by fine-material-sphere jhāna-consciousness. For it is because they are specifically produced by the mind of jhāna that they are called "mind-made" (*manomayā*);
yet, in a general sense, all beings are indeed mind-made because they are produced by the formative mental activity (*abhisaṅkhāra-manas*).

The same principle applies here to the term *saññāmayā*. Therefore, he said: "by means of the perception of immaterial jhāna. *Ayaṃ* refers to the person who proceeds toward the non-existence of the material.
"One who has not attained jhāna" means one who has not yet reached the fine-material (rūpa) jhānas. "Even for him" refers even to such a person as a mere reasoner (takkin).
For him, there is no doubt regarding the fine-material jhānas, because he has reached a conclusion based on hearsay.

"To the state of passion" means toward the condition of being possessed by passion. "In the vicinity" means nearby; they are not firmly established passions because they are not far removed from the view [of the teacher].
It is not because of association. For it is understood that she does not cling with firm attachment to phenomena included within the round of existence;
thus he said, "of clinging to the round by way of lust. Since all fetters arise precisely through craving, he said, "for the sake of fettering by way of craving.
However, as there is no doubt regarding the formless realm for her, [he speaks] by way of hearsay.

This was said with reference to that which has already reached a conclusion. Granted, it is evident that nihilistic views and the like are "unerring" (apaṇṇaka) because they invariably lead to the suffering of the miserable realms;
however, the objection is made by taking "unerring" in its primary sense as that which invariably accomplishes a blameless purpose.
The reply, meanwhile, takes the quality of being "one-sided" (ekaṃsika) even in the accomplishment of a blameworthy purpose. Therefore he said:
“By way of grasping,” and so forth. By this, he shows that through conventional usage (*ruḷhī*), the factors of the Infallible (*apaṇṇaka*)—such as “there is no gift” and so on—have arisen.
105. “Below there are only three persons”: in this tetrad consisting of the self-tormentor and the other-tormentor, there are three persons below.
All five persons mentioned above are indeed those who have practiced wrongly; following them are the five persons beginning with the proponent of existence (*atthikavāda*).
Because of practicing rightly, in this tetrad there is only one person, namely the fourth.

To show this meaning, the Blessed One began this teaching in order to demonstrate, by way of analysis, wrong practice and right practice, showing that the two sets of five persons mentioned below here are included within this very tetrad. As for the meaning herein:
It is undivided, and thus it is indeed easy to understand.
The exposition of the hidden meaning of the commentary on the Apaṇṇaka Sutta is completed.
And the commentary on the Gahapati Vagga is finished.
2. The Chapter on Bhikkhus. 1.
Commentary on the Ambalaṭṭhikārāhulovāda Sutta. 107.
Regarding the phrase "at Ambalaṭṭhikā": here, Ambalaṭṭhikā refers to a well-grown young mango tree; moreover, of that...
The palace not far away is what is intended here by “Ambalaṭṭhikā. Therefore he said, “of the Veḷuvana monastery,” and so forth.
“In the abbreviated term ‘meditation house’” means in the dwelling-place of yogis, which is of the nature of a house for cultivation. It is sharp indeed;
its sharpness need not be produced by anyone because it is established by its own intrinsic nature. In the same way, through one’s own action that ripens liberation...
Because he had become sharp and fierce in nature, this venerable one also... [as before] ...dwelt there.
"Established by nature" means established by nature; it was established by way of custom even prior to approaching the Buddhas. 108.
It is called a *udakādhāna* because water is held (*dhīyati*) or placed (*ṭhapīyati*) therein; it is also a small vessel for water.
Having stated, “He addressed [the monks] for the purpose of giving an exhortation,” [the commentator] explains that this giving of an exhortation by him did not occur only here,
but rather took place many times in many places; thus, after briefly indicating those various instances,
he says “by the Blessed One” and so forth for the sake of providing a commentary on this specific occasion.
In this context, by the phrase "not abandoned by all Buddhas," it is shown that these are known as the "Questions of the Youth" (Kumārapañha) within the dispensation of all Buddhas.
It is called "Ten Questions" (*dasapuccha*) because it contains ten questions proceeding from one [unit] up to ten units.
It contains fifty-five answers for the purpose of providing responses, proceeding by way of single increments from one up to ten units.

The connection is with the "Questions of the Novice. Whatever else needs to be said here should be understood according to the method already stated in the *Paramatthajotikā*, the Commentary on the Minor Works (*Khuddaka-aṭṭhakathā*).
Because he frequently utters falsehoods due to his failure to see the danger [in lying], he is called "one who speaks pleasant lies.

There are four similes regarding water-vessels, characterized by the discarding of remaining water, the overturning of a water-vessel, the righting of a water-vessel, and the perception of what is seen.
The two elephant similes are shown by way of both not performing and performing all the work of war.
Therein, the *Rāhulasutta* is the discourse found in the *Suttanipāta*.
By the phrase "spoken by way of repeated exhortation," it is shown that the Blessed One would instruct the Elder after having recited that discourse from time to time. And as for this...
This refers to the Blessed One’s giving of exhortation to himself, as described above, appropriate for each respective occasion.
"Seed" means an egg. In the phrase "Do you not see? (*passasi nū*), the particle *nu* expresses permission; the meaning is "Do you not see?
He said this because there is no evil whatsoever that one who stands having transgressed the true Dhamma should not commit: "In the case of intentional lying, for one devoid of restraint..."
“...were spoken for the purpose of providing an illustration. For it is said:
“For a person who has transgressed one principle, the liar, who has cast aside the world beyond, there is no evil that he would not do.”
"Uruḷhavāti" means having become broad, it has risen up. Furthermore, having been mounted according to the method of taming and having grown, it becomes fit for riding;
thus he said, "having grown, it is endowed with the capacity for mounting. "Āgatāgate" refers to those who have arrived at its own suitable place.
"The enemy's army's shields, watchtowers, bare walls, and so forth" refers to those things set up by the enemy army for the purpose of its own protection.
"In the gatehouse and in the high-roofed walls and so forth. "This location" means this position of the enemy army.
"By this much" means by the mere act of looking; it is shown precisely by the manner of his looking. Even an army of a hundred or a thousand soldiers splits in two;
like one who has fallen from a riverbank, being crushed, they split apart and flee on foot.

"Having struck with their ears" means: first of all, having discerned the sound of the arrows' approach and having raised them so that there would be no momentum, they strike and cause [the other] to fall.
In the phrase "striking an elephant, striking a horse," and so forth, the word *pati* should be applied to each term individually.
"With a long wooden staff" means: with a wooden staff made of a long creeper.

"Karaṇe" means in the performance of an action. "Maññati" refers to the elephant-driver. "Ayam uggaro" refers to the club taken up at such a time. "Oloketvā" means having seen with the eye of wisdom; the meaning is that he has established constant clear comprehension (*sampajañña*). 109.
"Sasakkam" means having made it fit to be seen and having generated effort, one should not do it;
since such an act is strictly forbidden, he says, "It must absolutely not be done. "Paṭisaṃhareyyāsi" means one should withdraw [the action] from its performance.
“You might fall into [that state]. Since one who is as he truly is—non-existent, desisting, and not acting—is said to be "one who does not act," he said, “you might desist;
you might not act. “You might assist” means you would become a provider of supporting power. Therefore he said, “you might sustain.
Furthermore, that providing of supporting power and sustaining is simply doing it again and again; thus he said, “you might do it repeatedly.”
"Sikkhamānā" means one who is training in, and fulfilling, that very training in higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*) along with its basis—the other two trainings.
Regarding the phrase "in how many places," it refers to how many points they occur.
Showing that they occur within a very short distance, he said, "They are to be purified within a single morning meal itself. For in this way, they become well-purified and thoroughly cleansed.

That which is disagreeable, heavy, and censurable to others— whether it be something other than the aforementioned objects or simply the attention directed toward the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*)—

is not included here because bodily actions and so forth have already been purified by that very attention. In the phrase "or aversion" (*paṭighaṃ vā*), the word "or" (*vā*) should be understood as including delusion (*moha*) when it is not being viewed with equanimity.
112. By the method already stated, the purification of bodily action and so forth occurs only here [in this dispensation] and not outside of it; thus he said, "The Buddhas...
or their disciples. For in actual fact, these are the recluses and brahmins.
Therefore—because the path ascended by all the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples has been declared to you by me, Rāhula—therefore, as you train yourself accordingly, in this way...
"One should train"—thus he gave the exhortation. The remainder is easily understood because it follows the method already explained.
The *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Hidden Meaning) of the commentary on the *Ambalaṭṭhikārāhulovādasutta* is completed.
2. Commentary on the Mahārāhulovāda Sutta 113.
"By following after his modes of deportment" means by following after his walking and other postures, not by following after his progress in the practice.
For the progress in the practice of the Buddhas is indeed one thing, and that of the disciples is another. "With graceful gait" means: "At a distance..."

By means of the graceful gait of the Buddhas, which is described as their natural virtue (*sabhāvasīla*)— namely, that they do not lift the foot too high, nor place the foot down too close [to the other], nor walk too fast, nor too slowly—
it is with reference to this very quality that it is said, "placing foot after foot. As for the Elder Rāhula, his feet were likewise perfected in their characteristics (*lakkhaṇapāripūri*).
"Gamanam" means that he began to go behind the Blessed One without leaving any space between them;
since he went everywhere following exactly in the footsteps of that [Blessed One], he is called "padānupadika.
This is the ground for the commentary, wherein the Blessed One and the Elder are praised with various kinds of similes. Therein—

He spoke the words beginning with “the Blessed One. The construction [of the sentence] is to supply the word “shone” (virocittha), as if [he were] a young elephant that has just emerged from its mother’s womb.

In the same way, this should be supplied and applied to the phrases “like a maned lion,” and so forth. “The King of Stars” means the moon. The phrase “of two moon-disks,” etc., is a figurative expression;
the splendor of the Buddhas’ deportment was like something belonging exclusively to the Buddhas—[think: “Oh, what a perfection of glory! This is the construction.
“Taking up” means they seize [the weapon]. One should not overlook it with the thought, “We shall deal with it later. Regarding the statement “this must not be done”:
when it is said that this taking of life must not be done, it means that this harming with a staff or a clod of earth must not be done;
and this giving of blows with the hand must certainly not be done, even if it is merely looking on in anger.
One penetrates [the meaning] by means of a hundred methods and even a thousand methods;

likewise, when it is said here, "first, the sweeping must be done," one penetrates it by a hundred methods and a thousand methods such as: preparing the floor, sweeping the monastery courtyard, clearing away refuse, and spreading sand. Therefore he said: "Even when it is said, 'This must be done'..."
“The same method applies,” he said. “They revile him” means they insult him. “I receive” means he expects to receive it.
“All this” refers to all this desire for training that is being received by me. “Having understood” means having known.
“Companion” is said with reference to the Elder Raṭṭhapāla; for he was placed by the Blessed One in the foremost position among those who went forth out of faith.
*Dhammārakkho* means the guardian of the Teacher’s jewel of the True Dhamma, the treasurer of the Dhamma. *Pettiyō* means the younger father.
*Sabbam me jinasāsanam* means the entire teaching of the Buddha belongs to me alone.
*Chandarāgam ñatvā* means having known that desire and lust had arisen in my mind. *Aññatarasmiṃ rukkhamūle* means at a certain suitable place at the foot of a tree on the outskirts of the monastery.
“At that time” means at the time when he was winning over the chief disciples through his inspiring manner.

He said, “This meditation subject is suitable for him during this particular sitting,” because other meditation subjects succeed even while walking on footpaths or stretching one’s back, whereas this one does not.
“Ānāpānassati” means the meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing.

"An equal-to-the-top" (*samasīsī*) means that if, having become equal-to-the-top, one does not attain final nibbāna, one realizes pratyekabodhi; if one does not realize pratyekabodhi, [one becomes an arahant]. "Of quick direct knowledge" (*khippābhiñña*) means one who quickly and very swiftly attains the six direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiññā*).
"Complete" (*paripuṇṇā*) means entirely full because there is no deficiency in any of the sixteen aspects.

"Well-developed" (*subhāvitā*) means well-developed through the successive accomplishment of both serenity meditation (*samatha-bhāvanā*) and insight meditation (*vipassanā-bhāvanā*). "Gradually accumulated" means accumulated step-by-step through the practice of the sequence of counting and application.

“Or conceit” means pride consisting of such things as despising or looking down upon others. “Or overweening pride” means: how could one give rise to overweening pride, thinking, “What is the use of these? I shall live by my own power alone”? “Having dismantled” means having made them dissociated;
the meaning is that one has analyzed them so that they no longer undergo grasping in the manner of a composite whole.
One should first expand upon the great primary elements (*mahābhūtāni*), because they are suitable for comprehension (*sammasanūpaga*); [the derived matter] is not suitable for comprehension.
To the question, "Then why did you expand upon the space element? he replied, "For the purpose of showing derived matter (upādārūpa). The water element is subtle matter.
Since the distinction between gross and subtle is also found among the others, he said, "For the purpose of showing derived matter.
Previously, only the four great elements were discussed, not derived matter; however, here, by way of the method of characteristic-removal (lakkhaṇahāra-naya), through the demonstration of space—

It should be understood as having been shown. Therefore he said, "in order to show that by means of this door. He spoke the words beginning with "Furthermore" (*apica*) in order to demonstrate that the space element was not expanded merely for the purpose of showing the inclusion of derived matter (*upādārūpa*), but also for the sake of ease in discernment (*pariggahasukhatā*).
In that context, he used the qualification "by the internal" (*ajjhattikena*) in order to exhaustively include all matter that is to be delimited.

"By space" means by the space element being apprehended. "Determinate form" (paricchinnarūpa) means that even the portion belonging to the group delimited by that [space] becomes manifest and appears clearly.

Now, he shows this very meaning already stated by means of a verse for the sake of easy comprehension. "Of that" refers to derived form (upādāyarūpa). "Thus for the purpose of manifestation" means for the purpose of its becoming manifest by way of the space that is thus delimited. "That" refers to the space element.

118. *Ākāsabhāvaṃ gataṃ*: it has attained the state of space; that is, it has become something to be grasped as "space" by way of delimiting those [forms] which are not touched by the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
Alternatively, *ākāsagataṃ* means "gone to space," just as in the expressions *diṭṭhigataṃ* (gone to views) and *atthaṅgataṃ* (gone to destruction).
*Ādinnam*: this is seized by craving and views. Therefore he said, "grasped, adhered to. Elsewhere...
That which is born of karma is called "clung-to" (*upādinna*); since it is not so here, he says, "the meaning is 'abiding in the body'.
"In the same manner as stated regarding the earth element and so forth" refers to his speaking with reference to the demonstration of the method taught in the *Mahāhatthipadopama Sutta*.
119. The state of being "such-like" (*tādibhāva*) belongs to one whose task is finished; yet this person is still applying himself to insight meditation (*vipassanā*). Therefore, for what purpose?

Is it stated that they possess such a nature? It is because the characteristics of the earth-like quality and so forth are explained for the purpose of facilitating the smooth progress of insight meditation (vipassanā).

Therefore, he said: "In regard to the desirable and the undesirable," and so on. "Having grasped" means having encompassed them by way of providing an opening for the occurrence of the wholesome state.
"Not established" means not dependent, not clinging.

120. The development of the divine abidings (brahmavihāra), the development of the foul (asubha), and the development of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānassati)—whether they induce access concentration (upacāra) or absorption (appanā)—serve as the foundation for insight (vipassanā).
By striving through the perception of impermanence and so forth in the mode of insight, they lead to the attainment of Arahantship according to the sequence of the paths;
thus it is said: "But [they lead] by means of the development of loving-kindness and the rest. Where...
In some instances, it refers to the state of resentment (*āghāta*) itself as a defilement that strikes out against beings and formations;

this is because it is a state contrary to the True Way (*ñāya*), as is the case with others as well. "The conceit 'I am' (*asmimāna*)" is that which occurs by grasping form and so forth either individually or collectively, thinking, "I am this. 121.

Regarding the phrase "this is the meditation subject" (*kammaṭṭhāna*): here, the inhalations and exhalations, when practiced by way of counting and so forth, constitute the work of yoga (*yogakamma*).
The meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) is so called because it serves as a foundation. Furthermore, the attention (*manasikāra*) proceeding in that manner therein is "development" (*bhāvanā*).

In this context, since many meditation subjects were taught by the Blessed One to that same elder, the point is established that meditation subjects are suitable for all types of persons regardless of their temperament; however, among the meditation subjects, [one should choose] according to what is most suitable.
It should be understood that the discourse on analysis has been told.
The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning in the Commentary on the Mahā-Rāhulovāda Sutta is completed.
3. Commentary on the Cūḷa-Māluṅkyaputta Sutta.

122. “Thus set aside” means that the various types of views proceeding in the manner of “the world is eternal,” and so forth, are not to be declared nor to be spoken of because they do not lead to liberation;
thus they are placed on the side of those things to be set aside (*ṭhapanīya*) and rejected because they must be discarded from the liberating teaching.
However, in this context, it is the very rejection of them that is to be declared. Just as:
"One being has come to this state of existence through the influence of karma and defilements; likewise another, and yet another.
Thus, because a "being" (satto) is what is called a "Tathāgata," he said: "A Tathāgata is a being. "That non-explanation does not please me":
if the world were eternal, one should simply have explained, "The world is eternal," or if it were non-eternal, "The world is non-eternal"; however, that which...
There is no declaration in either way; that does not satisfy my mind because the non-declaration is due to a lack of knowledge.
Therefore he said: “But for one who does not know and does not see, this alone is straightforward: namely, ‘I do not know, I do not see.
Regarding the terms beginning with “eternal,” “eternal” means existing at all times; the meaning is that it is permanent, stable, and of an unchanging nature. For that...
It is intended as "the world" (*loka*) because merit and demerit, along with their respective results, are perceived therein by those who hold views;

or, it is called the world because it is perceived by those who themselves are inseparable from the state of producing such results and so forth. By this, all four types of eternalist views (*sassatavāda*) are shown.

"Non-eternal" (*asassata*) means not eternal; the meaning is that it is impermanent, unstable, and subject to disintegration. Furthermore, "non-eternal" is expressed by way of the negation of the state of being eternal.
"Annihilation is explained" means that the seven types of annihilationist views are shown. "Finite" means having a boundary, being limited in extent;
the meaning is "not all-pervading. By this, views such as "the self is the size of the body, the size of a thumb, the size of a barley grain, or the size of an atom" are shown.
“The Tathāgata exists after death”: the meaning is that the Tathāgata—the life-principle (*jīva*), the self—exists, is found, and persists beyond death, following the breakup of this body.

By way of this door of eternalism (*sassatavāda*), sixteen views of those who hold the soul to be conscious (*saññīvāda*), eight views of those who hold it to be unconscious (*asaññīvāda*), and eight views of those who hold it to be neither-conscious-nor-unconscious (*nevasaññīnāsaññīvāda*) are shown. “He does not exist” means he is not; there is none.
"It is perceived. By this, the doctrine of annihilationism (ucchedavāda) is shown. Furthermore, "it both exists and does not exist" means "it both is and is not.

By this, the doctrine of partial eternalism (ekaccasassatavāda) is shown. However, it should be understood that by the statement "neither exists nor does not exist," the doctrine of the Eel-Wriggler (amarāvikkhepavāda) is shown.
For the Blessed One [declared] that these views are unbeneficial because they do not lead to emancipation.
Those [questions] were not explained; it was with reference to that non-explanation that this Elder said, "This does not please me.
Having rejected the training means having abandoned the training as it had been undertaken.

"You are not even a petitioner" refers to such statements as, "Venerable sir, I shall lead the holy life under the Blessed One. "You are not one who has requested [instruction]" refers to such statements as, "Māluṅkyaputta, you do not lead the holy life under me."
126. By a man standing in the enemy army. "With thick ointment" means with a thick application [of oil].
All the soft bamboo varieties, such as *mahāsupiya* and others, are delicate. "Maruva" is *makaci*.
"Milk-leaved" refers to the *khīrapaṇṇī*, from which milk flows at the mere cutting of its leaves. "Gaccha" is that which is produced from a thicket growing spontaneously (*sayaṃjātagumbato*).
The intended meaning is "grasped. A "drooping jaw" (*sithilahanu*) refers to a *dattākaṇṇo pataṅgo*. When this view exists, there is no [practice];
that is, when the view "the world is eternal" exists, there is no dwelling in the holy life of the path (*maggabrahmacariyavāsa*), because that [state] is to be attained only by abandoning it.

By the passage beginning "Is there birth? and so forth, he shows that these views, even individually, nourish the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), increase the funeral pyre (*kaṭasi*), and obstruct Nibbāna.

128. Therefore, the phrase "tasmātihā" (therefore, in this case) has been extracted out of place; rather, it should be commented upon by placing it after the words "but it should be understood by the method of the opposite of what was stated," which occurs at the appropriate place.

Since a cause is also called "attha" (meaning/purpose) because it is to be sought after or followed for its own fruit, he said "dependent on the cause. Thus he said: "even the very beginning of the holy life."
"Foundation in the preceding" means the initial commencement. The rest is easy to understand.
The elucidation of the hidden meaning in the commentary on the Cūḷamāluṅkyasutta is completed.
4. Commentary on the Mahāmāluṅkyasutta.
129. "Ora" refers to the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*). Because they lead to wandering therein, they are called *orambhāgiyāni* (lower-fettering), meaning they "belong to the lower part.
Alternatively, because they are to be abandoned by the lower paths, they belong to the lower portion—the lower section—thus they are *orambhāgiyāni*, with the letter *ka* changed to *ya*.
Therefore, it is said: "those belonging to the lower section," and so forth. For they yoke one to suffering through both kamma and the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*).
The fetters—specifically those known as the lower-fettering fetters—for one who has not abandoned them, there is indeed the suffering of the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).

But for one by whom they have been abandoned, that [suffering] does not exist. "It underlies due to non-abandonment" means that when the causal conditions are met, it arises because it has not been eradicated by the Noble Path; it underlies by way of its state of being unabandoned. While underlying...
"Is called a fetter (saṃyojana)" means that a defilement (pāpadhamma) which occurs by pervading the state of underlying tendency (anusaya) is, in the sense already stated,
"called a fetter. By this, he shows that although a fetter may exist as an underlying tendency during its occurrence, nevertheless,
those very things such as sensual lust (kāmarāga) and so forth which are called "underlying tendencies" are themselves "fetters" in the sense of being a bond.

"Even though this is so": although the very same lower fetter (*orambhāgiya-saṃyojana*) that was asked about by the Blessed One was answered by the Elder as well, nevertheless, this [particular] tenet has its basis [in a specific interpretation].

To demonstrate the attribution of fault therein, it is said, "In his doctrine," and so forth. "Only at the moment of manifestation" means only at the moment of occurrence. For not all [factors] are present...
The intention is that the defilements spread for the purpose of fettering. "By that" means by that reason; the meaning is: because he had acquired such a disposition.
The construction is: "He thought, 'I shall teach the Dhamma. "By his own nature alone" means by his internal inclination alone.
"Deceived" means set aside by the failure to satisfy the Teacher's mind. "He did thus" means he taught the Dhamma in this manner.
130. "Obsessed by the view of individuality" (sakkāyadiṭṭhipariyuṭṭhitena) means by one possessing a view of individuality capable of manifesting as obsession.
And such a mind is said to be "plunged" and "overwhelmed" by that view; thus he says, "by what is grasped and overcome.
The escape from views is the path of seeing, because it is by that path that they must be eradicated; and that [path] comes about by resorting to Nibbāna.

It cuts that off; therefore it is said, “Nirvana is the escape from views. By the two phrases “not dispelled” (*avinodita*) and “not removed” (*anīhaṭa*), he speaks precisely of its state of not being abandoned by way of complete eradication (*samuccheda*).
They say that the fetter (*saṃyojana*) is one thing and the underlying tendency (*anusaya*) is another, for co-existence (*sahabhāva*) occurs with something other than itself.
For it is not said that the very same thing co-exists with itself—such is their intention.
"By another" means by something other in its actual meaning (*attha*).

Although from the standpoint of mere state (*avatthāmatta*) there is no whole (*samudāya*) separate from its parts (*avayava*), nevertheless, since a part is not the whole, it can be said that the part is "other than" the whole.
Suspecting that the aforementioned resolution lacks decisiveness, he introduces an alternative position with the words "But it might be... and so forth.

The refutations are provided by way of alternative positions; according to the method already stated, it might be another person [who speaks], yet here there is this further fault, which is why he says, "If that very same [thing]," and so forth.
Furthermore, if such were your reflection: "If that very same thing is the fetter," and so on.
It is with reference to this meaning that he says: "In the ultimate sense, that very defilement is both the fetter and the underlying tendency."
And it is with reference to this point—that there is indeed a distinction between the state of having abandoned the purpose of bondage and the state of not having abandoned it—that [this is said].

(132) Meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) is like cutting through the bark, because by suppressing the defilements (*kilesa*) through attainment, one cuts through the core of the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*), which are thereby rendered distant.

Insight (*vipassanā*) is like cutting through the sapwood, because it is close to those [tendencies]. "Persons of such a kind" refers to those whose powers, such as faith (*saddhā*), have not been cultivated.
There are persons of weak mental constituents who, regarding the cessation of identity (*sakkāyanirodha*)... [as before] ...do not resolve.

"It should be seen thus" means that this person should be seen just like that weak man, because he is incapable of going to the further shore of identity, just as that man was incapable of going to the further shore of the Ganges.
The meaning of the bright side (*sukkapaṅkha*) should be understood by way of the opposite of what has been stated.
133. By the phrase "by seclusion from the substrata" (*upadhivivekena*), he shows that *upadhiviveka* is used in the ablative sense (*nissakkavacana*).

Alternatively, in the expression "seclusion from the substrata" (*upadhivivekā*), the ablative form is used in the sense of a cause (*hetu*); thus, by using the instrumental case (*karaṇavacana*) in "by seclusion from the substrata," the seclusion from the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañcakāmaguṇa*) is indicated.

For the strands of sensual pleasure are called "substrata" (*upadhi*) because suffering is attached (*upadhīyati*) therein. [The following refers to] the conditions for sloth and torpor (*thinamiddha*).
Physical languor is distinguished by such things as bodily stretching. "Therein" means within the attainment (*samāpatti*), that is, born inside the attainment.
To show that this [languor] is both included within the attainment and not included within it, it is said: "At the very moment of the attainment," and so forth.
"Phenomena such as form" refers to the phenomena of the five aggregates, beginning with form and feeling. By the phrase "not permanent,"...

He states their impermanence by way of the negation of permanence. For that very reason, it is illuminated that they are impermanent because of arising and passing away, because of change, and because of being temporary.

For whatever is not permanent is delimited by arising and passing away, is transformed in two ways—by aging and by death—and exists for only a brief moment. By the phrase "not as pleasure," he indicates the negation of pleasure.
He said they are the most painful; therefore, because they constantly oppress and because they are the basis of suffering, it is made clear that they are suffering.
For, by virtue of possessing arising and passing away, they constantly oppress, and due to their state of uninterrupted suffering, they are the very foundation of suffering.
They are sickness because they must be maintained by conditions and because they are the root of disease. They are like a thorn because they are associated with the sting of suffering.
It is a boil because it drips with the impurities of the defilements (*kilesa*), and because it swells, ripens, and bursts due to arising, aging, and dissolution.

It is an affliction because it produces oppression, because it pierces within, because it is difficult to remove, because it brings about non-prosperity, because it is a basis for misfortune, because it causes loss of mastery, and because it is the foundation of disease.
It is subject to others because it does not function according to one's will and lacks independence. It is subject to decay through illness, aging, and death.
As perishable. As empty, because it is devoid of a master, an inhabitant, an agent, an experiencer, and a controller.
As non-self, in the sense of the negation of a self; for even phenomena such as form do not constitute a self here, thus this [body] also is not a self, and so it is "non-self.
By this, it is shown that it is non-self because it is inactive, effortless, and void. This is precisely the three characteristics.
The phrase beginning with “Therein” is stated to show that [the meaning] has been grasped by analyzing it through eleven terms for the sake of clear understanding.
“Within the attainments” means within the attainments due to their co-nascence (*sahajāta*).
“He withdraws the mind” means he withdraws the insight-mind by suppressing the defilements such as desire and lust (*chandarāga*) bound up with it.
Therefore he said, “He liberates. “By way of hearing” means by way of hearing [the teaching] such as, “The stilling of all formations,” and so forth.
“By way of praise” means by way of extolling it in that same manner, that is, by way of proclaiming its qualities.
“By way of mastery” means by way of thoroughly mastering that Dhamma. “By way of description” means by way of describing its meaning. It is also by way of making it an object of mind.
It brings the path-consciousness (maggacitta) into focus. The passage beginning with "This is peaceful" (etaṃ santaṃ), however, demonstrates the meaning by way of exclusion through emphasis.

Just as insight (vipassanā) brings the mind into focus upon the unconditioned element (asaṅkhata-dhātu) by means of such phrases as "This is peaceful, this is sublime," so too the Path, while realizing Nibbāna through the clear realization of direct experience (sacchikiriyābhisamaya), [brings the mind] to all [qualities] obtainable therein.
Understanding through non-delusion regarding the specific distinctions, he applies his mind to that [object]. Therefore, he said: "But by this mode," and so forth.

"He is established therein" means that the yogi, possessing unobstructed insight (*adandhavipassana*), is established therein by means of that insight (*vipassanā*) which has the three characteristics—impermanence and so forth—as its object.
"In all" refers to the serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*) produced for the attainment of that path.
"Being unable [to do so], he becomes a non-returner (anāgāmī)" means that, having abandoned desire and lust for the serenity and insight that carry one through the lower paths,
yet being unable to exhaust his attachment to those [higher stages] that carry one through the supreme path, he settles precisely at the stage of non-returning.
"Because of having transcended" means because of having transcended form in every respect, both by way of serenity and by way of insight.

Therefore he said, “For this,” and so forth. “By him” means by the yogi. “Having transcended that” refers to one who, having first correctly contemplated the phenomena included within the five-aggregate existence (*pañcavokārabhava*) and having avoided them, subsequently enters the formless attainments (*arūpasamāpatti*) and contemplates the formless phenomena;
it is with reference to such a person that this was said. Hence he said, “Now he contemplates the formless.”
"One who proceeds by way of serenity" refers to one who devotes himself to the preliminary practice in which serenity is predominant.

"One-pointedness of mind is the primary factor" means that because his development of insight proceeded in such a manner previously, the insight leading to emergence has concentration as its predominant factor;
on the path as well, one-pointedness of mind is the primary factor, and the faculty of concentration is the precursor.
"He is powerful. "He is called one liberated in mind" means that this noble one is called liberated in mind.
Regarding the phrase "proceeding by way of insight," the meaning should be understood according to the method explained previously under the heading "proceeding by way of serenity.

Furthermore, this classification of persons stated here according to the method of the Suttas is called a "pariyāya" (a figurative or discursive exposition); [the definitive exposition] according to the method of the Abhidhamma follows later.
We shall demonstrate this in the commentary on the Kīṭāgiri Sutta. As for the statement "this is merely a phenomenon possessing its own intrinsic nature (dhammasabhāva)":
whether the primary focus of the preliminary practice is concentration (samādhi) or wisdom (paññā), this is simply the inherent nature of phenomena;
herein, nothing at all is to be clung to.
The knowledge of the higher and lower degrees of the faculties is the diversity of the faculties. Therefore he said, “I speak of the diversity of the faculties.

This shows that the cause is the diversity of the faculties: just as there is a fixed application to insight by way of impermanence and so forth, so too the preliminary progress by way of serenity and insight is immeasurable; that is the insight leading to emergence, for which concentration [is the basis].
When concentration (*samādhi*) is the leader, the precursor, and powerful, that noble one is called "liberated by mind" (*cetovimutta*).
When wisdom (*paññā*) is the leader, the precursor, and powerful, that noble one is called "liberated by wisdom" (*paññāvimutta*).
Now, demonstrating this matter through an illustration of distinguished intelligence, he said, "The two chief disciples," and so forth; that is indeed easy to understand.
The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning (*Līnatthappakāsanā*) of the Commentary on the Mahāmāluṅkyasutta is completed.
5. Commentary on the Bhaddālisutta:
134. *Asiyati* means eating; *bhuñjanaṃ* is food (*bhojana*). The eating of food is *asanabhojana*, which is the consumption of nutriment.

“Eating at one sitting” (*ekāsanabhojana*) means eating a meal at a single time. That time, however, is intended here as the forenoon alone, according to the established practice of all Buddhas and all Paccekabuddhas;
thus he says, “eating a meal at one time before midday. “Remorse and scruple” (*vippaṭisārakukkucca*) refers to [the thought]:
“Alas, what has been done by me is improper, since I, not knowing the natural constitution of my own body...”
"If I were to eat at a single sitting, this body of mine would become emaciated and it would not be a support for the holy life"—thinking thus, there might arise remorse and anxiety.
It was with reference to this that the Teacher spoke, not as one permitting such an action as Bhaddāli did.
"Otherwise" means if one were to divide a single meal into two parts and [eat from] one of those portions...
"Eating" here refers to eating only a portion [of the meal]. "Who is able? means who is able to subsist in such a manner.
He said "in the past," etc., because even the familiarity with past births follows only these very beings.
"Of one who merely groans" is a genitive used in a sense of disregard. "Having trampled that" means: "This training has been practiced by all Buddhas in their dispensations, and this..."
Having said, "A bhikkhu trains in this," the Blessed One—having overcome that Bhaddāli and his proclamation of non-exhortation—did not go to the Vitakkamaḷaka for the purpose of wandering for alms;
rather, while walking on a tour of the monastery, the Blessed One went to the place where he resided.
135. That by which they corrupt and censure is *dosa* (fault); it is an offense. That very thing, by virtue of its blameworthy nature, is *dosaka*. It is [used] for the sake of censure.
"Space" refers to the locus of occurrence. Thus he said: "This is the space; this is the offense. "More difficult to remedy" means it is exceedingly difficult to remedy by way of making amends.
For an offense is difficult to remedy for one who does not ask for forgiveness, as it becomes extensive according to the circumstances.
Thus he said: "For a year," and so forth.

"Having prodded" (*alaggittvā*) means having failed to guide him by saying, "He has indeed removed this as well"; the meaning is that one has obstructed his various practices conducive to his welfare.
An *accaya* is a transgression; it is so called because it goes beyond (*aticca*) or proceeds against the practice of the right method (*ñāyapaṭipatti*).
In its essential sense, it is a fault set in motion by being trampled upon by a person; it proceeds having gone beyond (*aticca*) and overcome the person.
Thus it is called [an offense]. Therefore he said, "Venerable sir, a transgression has overcome me. Regarding the remaining conditions:
that from which the fruit comes, approaches, arises, or occurs is a *samaya* (occasion/cause); as in the term "assemblage" (*samudāya*), he says "one cause" (*ekaṃ kāraṇaṃ*).
Furthermore, as for the Bhikkhus and others being known here through the fact that the Elder Bhaddāli did not fulfill his duties—
It shows that by making even this a reason, one should say, "Venerable sir, I am indeed not able," and so forth.
(136) "Occurring in a single moment of consciousness" means occurring in the same moment of consciousness as the first path-consciousness.

"It is not proper to command thus" means it is not proper to command for the purpose of stepping across, because there is no necessity for it; furthermore, this is not the established practice of the Buddhas.
That is to say, treading with the feet. For it was said:
“Having stepped upon me, may the Buddha go together with his disciples;
let him not step on the mud, for that will be for my benefit.”
The wise Sumedha did not do what he had expected. As it is said:
“Dīpaṅkara, the knower of the world, the receiver of offerings, standing at my head, spoke these words.”
When the Blessed One has given his command, it is likewise not proper for them to act otherwise; the same principle applies here as well.
The statement that "it is proper to prevent them" is made by way of a hypothetical impossibility (*aṭṭhānaparikappana*).

For there is no task whatsoever undertaken by the Buddhas that can properly be prevented by anyone, since they simply do not perform what is to be prevented. Of the certainty of rightness (*sammattaniyāma*)...
Because it has not entered [the stream], it is called "external" (*bāhiraka*). 137.
"The meditation subject does not adhere" means that the mind does not descend into the meditation subject.
140. "Performing again and again" means performing the causes for punishment, such as striking with a rod, again and again. Regarding "proper conduct" (*sammāvatta*):

"He does not conduct himself properly" means he does not conduct himself according to the right conduct (sammāvatta) prescribed by the Blessed One for the purpose of emerging from each respective offense.

"He does not conduct himself according to the conformable conduct" means that whatever conduct makes the Saṅgha conformable, he does not conduct himself according to that respective conformable conduct;
rather, he adopts the contrary, he acts in opposition. "In the conduct for deliverance" means...
Regarding the practice by which the Saṅgha becomes compliant and has emerged from the state of being guilty of an offense—one does not engage in that practice of deliverance.
Therefore he said, “an offense,” and so forth. Regarding “the act of one who is difficult to speak with”: it means the act of a bhikkhu who is difficult to speak with.

144. “He sustains himself” means he conducts himself; the meaning is that he stands within the Dispensation. “Attained to renown” means having reached the state of being well-known through such expressions as, “So-and-so and so-and-so elder are virtuous, of beautiful character, and learned,” thus having attained renown.
145. "When beings are declining" means when those beings who are practicing [the path] are falling away due to an abundance of defilements (*kilesa*), and when contrary paths are arising.

It is said that [the teaching] "disappears" because it is dependent upon them [as its support]. "Censure by others and so forth" refers to things pertaining to the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma*). "Specific sufferings in the states of woe" refers to things pertaining to future lives (*samparāya*).
They are called "taints" (*āsava*) because they flow (*āsavanti*) and proceed by way of various conditions. "Of these" refers to the taints such as censure by others and so forth.
These are the states of transgression.

"Having shown the improper time" means having shown the improper time for the proclamation of a training rule (*sikkhāpada*). "The arising" refers to the arising of those states that are the basis for the taints (*āsava*).
[He thought: "This is the time for the proclamation of a training rule; for as long as the dwellings are sufficient, by reason of that—such as stinginess regarding one's residence—"
In the Dispensation, certain things that are the basis for the taints do not arise.
By this method—and by this reason—the inclusion of the training rules (sikkhāpada) concerning the recitation of the words should be understood.
"Fame" (yasa) refers to reputation and retinue. Due to the fame of his subduing the Naga, the Elder Sāgata experienced the phenomenon that is the basis for the taints, namely, the drinking of liquor.
“Having blended taste with taste” means having blended the taste of the physical (upādinnaka) phlegm with the taste of the non-physical (anupādinnaka) phlegm.

146. Showing that this is not the only reason, but that there is another as well, the Blessed One said, “Moreover,” and so forth. By this, he urges the Elder to listen to the Dhamma with due care. 147.

“The practice of taming” (*visevanācāra*) refers to the act of subduing. “He attains final Nibbāna” means he becomes fully pacified. In that regard, by abandoning the act of taming, he becomes tamed. “Of the yoke” means of the chariot-pole.
*Anukkama* means a corresponding progression. It refers to the lifting and placing of the feet in accordance with that particular state.
Therefore, he said, "the four feet," and so forth. *Rajjubandhanavidhānena* means by the method of releasing [the horse] from the ground by its feet.
*Evaṃ karaṇatthaṃ* means in such a way that while the horse remains seated [on the rider], it is possible for him to grasp the ground; thus, the four feet are [positioned] accordingly.
Having done this for the purpose of making oneself immovable. "In the circle" means in the circular pit.
"In the earth-treading" means in the act of walking by merely touching the ground; thus he said, "with the tips of the hooves.
"In the causing of entry" means in the crushing of the enemy army after having caused them to enter. "In one place" means in any one of the four feet.
The meaning is that they urge him toward movement in the proper place; moreover, in this context, a particularly swift movement is intended.

"In distress" (*davatte*) means for various purposes involving the transgression of boundaries, such as capturing the great shouts raised by an enemy army; thus he said, "at the time of battle," and so forth.
"Qualities to be known by the king" means the reason for those qualities which the king ought to know regarding the horse, just as the king comes to know the horse's virtues.

He causes [the king] to act. Regarding "in the royal lineage of horses": even when encountering unbearable suffering, he trains [the king] so that he will not abandon conduct befitting his royal lineage.
Indeed, it is with reference specifically to this training that it is stated everywhere, "he causes him to act," because the terms "acting" and "causing to act" are synonymous.
"Just as he possesses supreme speed" means that in the place for demonstrating speed, he trains him so that the horse does not lose its supreme speed.

"In the state of being a supreme horse" means that at the time of performing work, he trains him with the highest speed so that his own supreme nature is neither concealed nor neglected, and thus the purpose is accomplished. Just as...
To show that action cannot exist without substance, nor can substance exist without action, it is said:
"In that regard, by nature," and so forth.
Therein, "by nature" refers to the state of being fit for the causes of a supreme horse, specifically in the undertaking of supreme speed.
“Like horses that eat their own dung” means like those defective, stubborn mules that have eaten their own excrement.
“The king’s staff” refers to the golden staff to be held by the king. “Supported by his own elements” means being propped up by the very elements produced within himself.
“In the highest gentleness” means in the state of supreme amiability, because he must be tamed by gentle speech alone. Therefore, he said: “By soft words,” and so forth.
"Right view of the fruit of arahantship" refers to the right knowledge that occurs at the time of the attainment of the fruit.
As for the statement that "right knowledge is the same as the right view mentioned previously," this is said because of the commonality of being the state of right view of the fruit.

Some, however, say it is "reviewing-knowledge" (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*), but that is not tenable because it is specified as "by one beyond training" (*asekkhena*). That too is knowledge of one beyond training.
Why is this? Even if one takes "the trainee" (sekha) in its primary sense, it is not at all appropriate to take "the trainee" here in a figurative sense;

rather, it should be understood as being stated according to the difference in function. For that same single wisdom is called "right view" (sammā-diṭṭhi) with reference to its function of seeing correctly for the purpose of directly realizing Nibbāna, and it is called "right knowledge" (sammā-ñāṇa) with reference to its function of knowing correctly. By way of the faculty of one who has already known (aññātāvindriya)...
Or, it is right view; by way of the faculty of wisdom, it is right knowledge—thus the meaning should be understood here.
It is said, "by way of the person who gains knowledge through a condensed teaching," because this teaching was presented in brief as a means for bringing about the path and its fruit.
The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning of the Commentary on the Bhaddāli Sutta is complete.
6. Commentary on the Laṭukikopama Sutta 148.
"The Elder Mahā-Udāyī": He is a distinct elder from the elders Kāḷudāyī and Lāḷudāyī, known in the Teaching as Mahā-Udāyī because of his large physical stature.
"One who carries away" (*apahattā*): he has carried away, he carries away, and he will carry away; for this term refers to all three periods of time.
“Upahatta” (brought near)—here too the method is the same. “Apahārako” means one who removes; “upahārako” means one who brings near. 149.

“Yaṃ” is the nominative singular used in the sense of the locative; by this, the time just mentioned is referred back, hence he says “yasmiṃ samaye” (at which time). “Na bhagavantaṃ paṭicca” means not having made the Blessed One the object.

“Kammanipphannatthaṃ” means for the sake of accomplishing the task requested by herself. “Bhavati” is *bhū*; “na bhū” is *abhū*. However, out of fear, that woman said “abhu. Regarding “ātu mātū,” here, as for example—
“From limb by limb you are produced, from the heart you are born;

you are indeed one’s own self (attā), O son, so live for a hundred autumns”—in such passages as these, the son is called “one’s own self” because he continues the lineage through the family line. In the same way, the father [is also called the son].

It is called “self. Because [the Buddha] said, “The mother is the self of the bhikkhu,” referring to sense-desires as objects (*vatthukāmā*) out of fear, he therefore said, “*Ātu* means father,” and so forth. 150.
“In this very way” (*evamevaṃ*)—this is stated to be a particle (*nipātapada*) indicating censure; thus it is said, “he spoke while censuring. Likewise...
Indeed, showing this by means of the word *vācaka* (speaker), he said: "Here, certain foolish persons.
He said "they said" (*āhaṃsu*) to indicate the continuous occurrence of their speaking in that manner; thus he said "they speak" (*vadanti*). But what [is the point] of this trivial thing?
