This was said by those who despise the matter that ought to be abandoned. Therefore he said: "But what [of it]? This is used when the reason (*hetu*) is to be illuminated.

The word *sāmī* (master/owner) is used as in the expressions “for the sake of tradition” (*anussavassa hetu*) and “for the sake of study” (*ajjhenassa hetu*). Therefore, he said, “for the sake of a trifling thing” (*appamattakassa hetū*).

[Objection: Should it not be that one must act as if not seeing and as if not hearing? [Response: This is an explanation according to their intention, namely, that the Teacher must indeed act as if not seeing and as if not hearing even regarding minor faults.

"Among them" (*tesu*) means among those who desire training (*sikkhākāmesu*). He shows that the phrase "causing [the offense] to arise without a condition" (*appaccayaṃ upaṭṭhāpentī*) must be supplied and connected [to the sentence].

"Of them" (*tesaṃ*) refers to those persons who were called "foolish men" (*moghapurisā*). "A large wooden block tied to the neck" (*gale baddhaṃ mahākaṭṭhaṃ*) refers to a tree-stick tied and suspended around the neck.
"By a rotten creeper" (*pūtilatāya*) means by a *galocī* plant. It is as difficult to abandon as the basis for a *pārājika* offense.
"It happens" means that one is unable to abandon it by way of abandoning desire (*chanda*). 151.
"Free from longing" (*anussukka*) means being devoid of striving for the abandonment of that which is to be abandoned. "In the state of not looking back" (*apaccāsīsanapakkha*):
because of living on what is given by others, standing in the position of not looking back for any requisite from anywhere, one abandons well.
It exists; there is no difficulty in abandoning it.
152. *Daliddo* means poor. *Duggato* means miserable. *Assako* means one who possesses no property. *Gehayaṭṭhiyo* means the supports for the roof of the house;
these are the beams that must be placed straight across. Those beams that are to be placed all around the walls and foundations are called *maṇḍala*.
*Kākātidāyinti*: It should be scattered here and there by crows due to their extreme impetuosity. Therefore, he said, "Wherever anything at all," and so forth. *Sūrakākāti*:
This refers to the manner in which crows scatter [the contents]. *Naparamarūpan* means inferior form. *Vilīvamañcako*: A bed woven with palm-leaf strips and the like.
Its state of being dilapidated and broken down is due to the threads being cut and torn; such being the case, that—
Because it becomes uneven in form, he said, "bent," and so forth. Because that person eats coarse food, he said, "grain means *kudrūsaka* (millet).
It is called "sown at the right time" (*samavāpaka*) because it is to be sown at the proper season; it refers to seed that is to be sown according to the appropriate climate.
A "wicked wife" (*jāyikā*) is a contemptible wife; in all instances, the word *ka* denotes censure. "I would indeed go forth"—that is, I would shave off my hair and beard.
"Having discarded [the world], I would go forth, thinking, 'May I indeed be a man!'"—by means of this going forth, one awakens to oneself as a man.
For one established in that true nature, awakening is not difficult;
it is like a bedspread, or like a cooking pot, or like the twelve hundred and fifty storehouses of the merchant Meṇḍaka.

153. "Of hundreds of gold coins" (*suvaṇṇanikkhasatānaṃ*) means of many hundreds of gold coins. "A hoard" (*caya*) is an accumulation through a continuous series; it is an uninterrupted, constant accumulation. Therefore he said: "An accumulation made by way of a series. 154.
Although those who do not abandon [defilements] were shown first below, those who abandon them are primary;

and it is by way of them that the fourfold classification of persons (*puggalacatukka*) is shown here. Those who abandon both that [defilement] and [the object] are taken first as "those who abandon. "By way of a heap" (*rāsivasena*)...
“By the phrase ‘here, Udāyi, a certain person’ and so forth, [the text] was spoken in the common idiom ‘this or that,’ without referring to the distinctions presented in the tetrad.

Therefore he said, ‘they are not analyzed separately. To show that it is a worldly convention to grasp what has been grasped without distinction by way of its divisions, he said, ‘Just as, for example,’ and so forth. ‘Persons who abandon’ means ‘those very ones...’”
"Abandoning"—thus, these are indeed persons who abandon.

"Those who run after acquisitions" means those who pursue after acquisitions, those whose mental states proceed by taking acquisitions as their object. "Only thoughts" refers specifically to thoughts such as sensual intention (*kāmasaṅkappa*) and so forth.
"The diversity of faculties" refers to the comparative degree (superiority or inferiority) of the faculties that bring about the maturation of liberation.
Indeed, it is by virtue of that [defilement] alone that those four types of persons come into being.

As long as they have not yet eradicated it through the path—having exerted themselves in insight (vipassanā) for the sake of the supreme path—they are said to "not abandon" it. Thus, even the three lower noble ones (ariyas) are described as "not abandoning" due to the presence of defilements that have not been abandoned;
how much more so the worldlings (puthujjanas)? This is according to the method already stated.
However, those four persons who unite insight with the path are said to abandon [the defilements] at the moment of the supreme path (*aggamagga*).
They alone are called "swift-acting" there because they abandon them quickly; therefore he says, "there," and so forth.
It is like a man who, having felt a sense of urgency (*saṃvega*), steps into a fire. "By the path" means by the supreme path that has arrived in due succession. In the *Mahāhatthipadopama-sutta*...

In the Mahāhatthipadopama-sutta, three sections are set forth in the commentary according to the types of persons who are very sharp, not very sharp, very dull, and not very dull—based on the passage: "His mind leaps forward toward the element as its object, becomes confident, settles, and resolves.
Among these, the question is stated by way of the middling type. [The phrase] "development of the faculties" (indriyabhāvanā) refers to this.
In the *Indriyabhāvanā-sutta*, the question there too was stated according to the method of the *Majjhima Nikāya*.

Therefore he said, "Of these," and so forth. "That" refers to the pentad of aggregates (khandhas) spoken of as "acquisitions" (*upadhī*). "The root of suffering" means the cause of all the suffering of saṃsāra. "Without grasping" (*niggahaṇo*) means free from clinging (*nirupādāno*).
Therefore he said, "free from craving" (*nittaṇho*). 155. "Those who abandon" refers to the persons mentioned thus: "They abandon that very [clinging]. They are indeed this many.

"They abandon defilements" means that those worldlings who possess the five strands of sensual pleasure abandon only so many defilements as are delimited by the fact that they are to be abandoned by their respective paths, based on the respective objects such as the various jhānas.

"Those who do not abandon them"—the meaning here should be understood according to the method explained previously. "Impure pleasure" is so called because it is dependent upon the impurity of the body. "By the ignoble ones" means...
Because they are impure. One should fear them in terms of acquisition because they lead to the suffering of the defilements;

one should fear them in terms of their result because they lead to the suffering of the states of deprivation. "The bliss of seclusion from both groups and defilements" means the bliss of being secluded from both association with groups and association with defilements.
"For the sake of the subsiding of lust and so forth" means the bliss that brings about the subsiding of lust and so forth. One should not fear it.
Because it is of absolute benefit both now and in the future.

(156) Regarding the phrase "in the moving" (*iñjite*), he says "moving" (*iñjana*) and so forth; this is a locative case used in the sense of the object itself. It is "moved" (*iñjita*) by that [factor];
thus, it refers to the coarse factor of jhāna that causes agitation in each respective jhāna. The fourth jhāna is "unmoving" (*aniñjana*) because of the absence of agitation.
For it has been said: “When it is established and has attained imperturbability.

The word *alaṃ* also carries the sense of fitness—as in such passages as “it is enough to become disenchanted, it is enough to be liberated”—therefore, the meaning is that it is not fit to form a secondary attachment (*anusaṅga*).
Thus he said: “I say it is a clinging that should not be made. This is the definitive conclusion (*sanniṭṭhāna*).
The construction is as follows: one should not form a final conclusion by way of relaxing one's effort, thinking, "This much is sufficient for right practice.

Whether it be subtle, termed "higher-fettering," or gross, termed "lower-fettering"—such as subtle lust for the fine-material realm (*rūparāga*), or gross outflow of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*), or gross aversion (*paṭigha*)—or whether it is slightly blameworthy due to a mild mode of manifestation; [all such states must be abandoned].
Alternatively, it should be understood as "less blameworthy" in the sense of being a bond of kamma, and its opposite as "more blameworthy.
It is said to be "for the sake of the person who needs guidance" because the teaching proceeds by way of one whose wisdom is not exceedingly sharp.

Indeed, because the cessation of perception and feeling is presented for the sake of the noble person whose inclinations are entirely exhausted, it is concluded "by means of the pinnacle of Arahantship" alone.
Thus it was said. Furthermore, that which has not been analyzed here according to its meaning is indeed easy to understand.
The elucidation of the hidden meaning (*līnatthappakāsanā*) for the commentary on the *Laṭukikopama-sutta* is completed.
7. Commentary on the *Cātuma-sutta*.

157. "According to their respective supports" (*yathāupanissayena*) means by whatever support (*upanissaya*) they have, that is, by that respective support; [it refers to] through right application (*sammāpayoga*).
"They will be established in the Dispensation" (*patiṭṭhahissanti sāsane*) means they will obtain a firm footing in the Teaching.

"Residences" (*vasanaṭṭhānāni*) means places for dwelling according to the rainy-season retreat (*vassa*) and so forth. "Arranging them" (*saṇṭhāpayamānā*) means establishing them in a well-ordered state.
"Indivisible sound" (*avinibbhoga-sadda*) means a sound that cannot be grasped by separating its components.
For even the resonance of speech, when produced by many people at once and from a great distance, reaches the range of hearing merely as a single great noise.
"In the catching of fish" (*maccha-vilopa*) refers to seizing them as if plundering fish, or to the leading away of fish.
158. *Vavassaggattha* means in the sense of resolution. The intention is: "First, this speech being spoken by us must be heard exclusively;
afterwards, perform what is to be done by you. *Vacanaparihāra* means the response to the speech uttered by those Śākya kings.
*Lesakappa* means a semblance of what is allowable (*kappiya*). *Dhuravaha* means those who bear the burden; the meaning is *dhorayha*. *Pādamūla* means...

He speaks figuratively. "It will vanish" means it will diminish. "He opposes" means he does not merely oppose the Blessed One face-to-face, but even in the presence of the Sakyans, he acts as one who opposes.
"May he rejoice" means may he be glad, facing [the truth]. "May he speak" means may he speak by way of its beauty.
“Change of confidence” (*pasādaññathatta*) refers to the transformation of lack of confidence, which is a turning away characterized by a lapse [from the faith];
thus he said, “for those who are disrobing. Change through transformation” (*vipariṇāmaññathatta*). By way of figurative usage regarding the cause, the term “seed” is applied to the crops;
thus he said, “of young seeds,” meaning “of young crops. It is a transformation due to the absence of that future fruit because of its state of being merely young.
160. Performing what ought to be done by one’s own power alone is according to the mind’s inclination; it is not so through the instigation of another. Thus he said:

“For those being summoned, going [to them] is not comfortable. This indicates that they too, like the Blessed One, will dwell in the blissful abiding of the present life (diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra), because they have naturally possessed a disposition toward seclusion (vivekajjhāsaya) and have merely failed to carry the burden that had come to them.
Therefore he said, "He did not know his own state of being a burden.

(161) Why did he begin [this teaching]? Because it was appropriate. For there were five hundred newly ordained bhikkhus; therefore, for the sake of giving them instruction, the Blessed One began this teaching.

(162) Regarding the phrase "of anger and distress": here, "anger" (*kodha*) is so called in the sense of being angry; that very same [state] [is characterized] by the excessive crushing and churning of both mind and body.

Despair (*upāyāsa*) is so called in the sense of intense exertion. Having occurred many times, it overwhelms the being associated with it and, like a wave, should be seen as resembling the despair of anger because it does not allow the head to be raised and leads to ruin and calamity.
Therefore he said, "In the despair of anger," and so forth.

163. "Devoured by gluttony" means that because his qualities such as virtue have been destroyed through gluttony—that is, through greed for material things and a livelihood maintained by wrong living—his body of Dhamma has been devoured. 164.

"Having submerged oneself in the whirlpool of the five strands of sensual pleasure": here, beings overcome by sensual lust are made to wander in saṃsāra within this whirlpool consisting of agreeable objects such as forms, thinking "from here to there, and from there back here," until they emerge from it.

One does not even arouse the mind toward renunciation (*nekkhamma*); having thus enticed [beings] and brought about their ruin, the similarity of the strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*) to a snare is to be understood.
Therefore he said, "Just as," and so forth.
165. *Rāgānuddhaṃsitenā* means by one who has been agitated by lust. *Caṇḍamacchaṃ āgamma* means having encountered a fierce fish, such as a shark (*susuka*).

"Having approached. Regarding "having approached a woman": for a woman, by means of her own gestures, expressions, and charms—which are like the arts of a courtesan—overcomes and seizes a man lacking wise attention and lacking steadfastness;

and even one of a steadfast nature she renders incapable of fully accomplishing the qualities conducive to his welfare, such as virtue (*sīla*) and so forth, through the power of seduction by her beauty and other traits, leading him to ruin and disaster.
It brings about [this result]. Therefore he said: “Sensual lust arising in dependence upon women departs.
What is called fear exists only for one who enters into that which is to be feared, not for one who does not enter;
having entered into it, one must dispel the fear and accomplish what needs to be done there. Otherwise, the attainment of one’s goal will not occur.
The phrase beginning with "Just as" (*yathā*) was stated in order to demonstrate the meaning of "there is" (*hoti*) by way of the similarity between the simile and that which is to be illustrated.
Therein, the benefits dependent upon water are such as the quelling of thirst, the purification of the body, the subsiding of feverish heat, and the refreshing of the physical frame.
However, the benefit dependent upon the Teaching (*sāsana*), in brief, is the subsiding of the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭa-dukkha*); in detail, however—
It is manifold, by way of the benefits of virtue (*sīla*) and so forth; it should be understood according to the method explained in the *Visuddhimagga*.
The intention is that such benefits accrue to one who proceeds having overcome those fears.
"Without fearing these" means having proceeded by overcoming these fears, such as anger and distress, and thus not fearing them. For it is from anger, distress, and the like that one fears.
"From this they fear" is what was said. "The Elder" refers to the Elder Mahādhammarakkhita.

Granted that the very moment of the realization of abandonment (*pahānābhisamaya*) is also the moment of the realization of verification (*sacchikiriyābhisamaya*), yet—in order to demonstrate that the function of right view (*sammādiṭṭhi*) regarding the phenomena of defilement and purification is performed without confusion—it is stated as if it were not simultaneous, even though it is simultaneous: "Having cut the stream of craving, [he crossed] to the further shore of Nibbāna."
“He is not able to see [it]. The remainder is easy to understand.
The *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning) for the commentary on the *Cātumamā-sutta* is completed.
8. Commentary on the *Naḷakapāna-sutta*.
166. Where the monkey, led by the Bodhisatta, drank water from a reed, that lotus pond, the surrounding area of land, and the village settled there were known simply as “Naḷakapāna.
However, since it is the village that is intended here, he says, “in the village named Naḷakapāna. Now, regarding this matter, starting from its origin:
In order to demonstrate this, he began with the words, "It is said that in the past... He was called "wise" (paññavā) because of his wisdom regarding what ought to be done.
He was called "large-toothed" (mahādāṭhika) because he was endowed with large fangs due to their being thick, long, and numerous.
Having declared, "I am a water-demon," and without releasing any of the monkeys, he showed them, "You are all now in my hands."
"But I shall eat you all," he said. [The text continues: "...they drank.
Regarding "the reed taken by the Bodhisatta was entirely without residue, becoming a single hole due to the pressure within all its joints":
[this means] even though you, O water-demon, desire to kill me, you will not kill me by means of human strength.
Having spoken thus, the Great Being, feeling compassion and thinking, "May this wicked creature not harm other beings while drinking water here," made a resolution:
"May all the reeds growing here be without knots and have only a single opening. Having thus resolved, he departed.
Therefore, it is said: "From that time onwards," and so forth.
167. When the Blessed One asked the monks headed by Anuruddha, "Is it true, Anuruddhas? the Elder replied, "Indeed it is, Bhante.
"Raja-abhinīta" means those who have been led to go forth by a king, [thinking], "If he goes forth, he will save his life; otherwise, he will not.
The same principle applies here to "cora-abhinīta" (those led by thieves). [The phrase] "cutting off the root of the thieves" means "I shall perform the clearing of the thorns."
“By means of livelihood” (ājīvikāya) means by means of one’s way of life. Now, regarding these [monks] such as the Elder Anuruddha and others:
he said “having secluded oneself” (viviccā) to indicate the exertion in practice belonging to the earlier period, as in the passages beginning with “endowed with non-affliction” (abyāpajjaṃ upetaṃ);

the meaning is having secluded oneself, having become secluded, having become detached. “The duty of one who has gone forth” (pabbajitakiccaṃ) refers to the appropriate task for one who has gone forth.

“Monk’s duty” (*samaṇakicca*) means the duty that produces the state of a monk. For at the very point where one is unable to perform the duties of one who has gone forth, at that same point one is also unable to perform the duties that produce the state of a monk. Therefore he said, “He himself,” and so forth. 168.

First, in explaining [the case] regarding those without rebirth-linking (*appaṭisandhika*), he explains it with respect to their future births—taking into account that they have passed beyond the state of existence (*pavatti*)—because he describes the absence of rebirth-linking therein. “Great joy” (*mahantatuṭṭhi*) means abundant gladness.
169. *Imassa* is an explanation of the meaning of the word *assā*. The construction is: "Of this venerable one who is established, [the Dhamma] is either seen by himself or heard by tradition.
The "states" (*dhammā*) intended here are those belonging to the side of concentration;

however, concentration itself is included by the word "abiding" (*vihāra*) in the phrase "one who abides thus. In the phrase "thus liberated," it is by the word "liberation" (*vimutti*) that [concentration is meant].
"Freedom through fruition" (*phalavimutti*) is included. "Even while walking" means even while walking or dwelling in the practice of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*).

It should be understood that although Arahantship is found among the ranks of male and female lay followers (*upāsaka-upāsikā*), it is not mentioned in the text because of its rarity. The rest is easily understood.
The *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Hidden Meaning) for the commentary on the *Naḷakapāna Sutta* is completed.
9. Commentary on the Goliyāni Sutta 173.
“Padasamācāra” means a conduct characterized by poverty in various ways, because of the absence [of wealth] shown through the distinction of various conditions;
it means a lax conduct. However, since such a conduct is not called stable or firm, therefore—
It is said, “one of weak conduct. Alternatively, the reading is “sākhasamācāro”;
in that case, the meaning is that his virtue is like a branch in the sense of clinging here and there. Therefore he says, “one of coarse conduct.
His conduct is to be understood as coarse precisely because of his dependence on the requisites. When something is said by a superior, listening with respect out of a sense of reverence—
"Patissa" means respect; the meaning is that it refers to anything respectful, including the words of respect and what is similar to them.
"Sappatissena" means with respect, that is, with the acceptance of instruction accompanied by respect. Alternatively, "patissa" is that which is respected (*patissīyati*);
thus, "saha patissenā" (with respect) is explained in its entirety as before. Therefore he said, "together with the eldest. This is called "dwelling with respect."
This is the dwelling characterized by self-exertion. Therefore he said, “by living without restraint.

“Without encroaching” means without having dragged [someone] in. To show the meaning of “entering among those worthy of respect without asking permission,” it was said, beginning with “therein, whoever...”.
“Pertaining to right conduct” (ābhisamācārika) means existing in right conduct. But what is that? He said: “even the mere performance of duties.”
It was intended that one should enter before the Saṅgha and withdraw after them;
thus, entering the village too early and withdrawing too late were prohibited. To demonstrate this, it is said: “not too early,” and so forth.
“Of a restless nature” means one whose mind is distracted. “By fickleness” means by a state of restlessness resembling a leaf struck by a strong wind.

By the term "possessing wisdom" (*paññavata*), the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-paññā*) regarding those duties appropriate for a bhikkhu is intended, not the wisdom consisting of learning (*suta-mayā-paññā*).

By the phrase "application to the Abhidhamma and the Abhivinaya," application (*yoga*) to the superhuman states (*uttari-manussa-dhamma*) through the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanā-paññā*) is clarified.
Furthermore, "application" (*yoga*) refers to proficiency by way of thorough mastery.
By the term "formless" (*ārūppa*), all four formless attainments (*arūpasamāpatti*) are included.
However, since these do not succeed without the four form attainments (*rūpasamāpatti*), he said: "By this much, 'the formless,' the eight attainments have been stated.

Regarding "the kasiṇas," it refers to the tenfold kasiṇa. "One preparatory meditation subject" (*parikamma-kammaṭṭhāna*) refers to any single meditation subject that illustrates the preparation for development.

This refers to the meditation subject consisting of the aggregates (*khandha-kammaṭṭhāna*). Therefore, he said, "having made it proficient. However, the preliminary work for the *kasiṇas* is already included by that very mention;
since mundane superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhamma*) were mentioned below, he said, "By the phrase 'superhuman states,' he shows all supramundane states as well.
"By way of a person who is to be guided" means having understood and having explained in detail.
"By way of the person to be known.
This concludes the *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Hidden Meaning) for the commentary on the *Goliyāni Sutta*.
10. Commentary on the *Kīṭāgiri Sutta*.

174. “Five benefits” refers to the five qualities beginning with being free from illness. In this context, *appābādhatā* (freedom from illness) is the absence of eye diseases, stomach diseases, and so forth.
*Appātaṅkaṃ* (freedom from affliction) is the absence of the suffering caused by the disturbance of those [humors] within the body.

*Lahuṭṭhānaṃ* (lightness) is the ease with which the body rises. *Balaṃ* (strength) refers to physical strength. *Phāsuvihāro* (comfortable living) is the state of having pleasant postures (*iriyāpatha*). “Not overwhelmed” means...
They have entered into beings by way of being difficult to abandon. Regarding the phrase "you will perceive," the word *iti* here has the sense of "beginning";
therefore, the meaning is "thus, with such benefits. 175.

Those who are connected to a residence are called *āvāsika* (resident monks) because they do not overstep that [residence]. Hence he said, "those who dwell permanently," meaning those who dwell in a fixed manner.

The meaning is as follows. "Tannibandhā" means that *nibandha* is said to be activity (*byāpāra*). Those who are bound (*bandhā*) to that, being intent (*pasutā*) or eager (*ussukā*), are "tannibandhā.
To explain how they are bound to that, he says: "the lodging has not yet been prepared," and so forth.
That which is to be obtained at the time of arising is "kālika"; however, since that time has not yet arrived, he says: "to be obtained at a future time."
178. “So many feelings are to be cultivated”: all eighteen kinds of feelings based on renunciation are to be cultivated; those based on the household life are not to be cultivated. 181.
“That has been done” because the sixteenfold duty has been completed. “Conducive” means suitable by way of being pleasant according to the season.
Therefore he said, “conducive to the meditation subject. “Making them equal” means [balancing] the slightness and the intensity.
"Having abandoned, they accomplish their common duty.
(182) "Those two" refers to the two mentioned at the beginning.

"One liberated in both ways" (*ubhatobhāgavimutta*) means liberated from both parts; this is according to the grammatical rule of *ekadesasarūpeka-sesa* (retaining one member of a group that shares a common form).
For it is said in the Abhidhamma-ṭṭhakathā: “He is ‘liberated in both ways’ (ubhatobhāgavimutto) because he is liberated in two parts or on two occasions.

Regarding this, some elders say: “He is liberated in both ways because he is liberated through the suppression-liberation by means of meditative attainment (samāpatti) and through the eradication-liberation by means of the Path (magga).
Other elders say: “This one liberated in both ways [is so called] because of form...”
Having said, "One who stands having been liberated by means of a name, yet is still being liberated from that, is 'dependent on a name,'" he stated the proof for this:
"Just as a flame cast by the force of the wind, Upasīva, goes out and can no longer be reckoned as such; (Thus spoke the Blessed One.)"
"Thus the sage, liberated from the group of mental aggregates (nāmakāya), goes to his end and does not enter into reckoning.

Having spoken this passage from the Sutta, [the Buddha] said: "Because he is well-liberated both from the group of mental aggregates and from the group of material form (rūpakāya), he is one who is liberated in both ways (ubhatobhāgavimutta)."
They say this because, in the Sutta, the Blessed One declared that the brahmin Upasīva, who had attained the base of nothingness, was "liberated from the group of names" and thus "doubly liberated.
Others, however, maintain: "He is doubly liberated in the sense that he is liberated once by suppression through meditative attainment, and liberated once by eradication through the Path."
They say: "In this context, according to the first statement, one who is liberated by way of two parts is 'liberated in both ways' (*ubhatobhāgavimutto*).

According to the second statement, one who is liberated from both parts is 'liberated in both ways. But in the third statement, one who is liberated by way of two parts on two occasions—this is the distinction between them.
One who is liberated from defilements, or [one for whom] defilements have been suppressed or eradicated..."
The meaning should be understood as: "one who is liberated from both parts. Therefore, he said, "by means of two portions," and so forth.

"He" refers to the one liberated in both ways (*ubhatobhāgavimutta*). Although here the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*)—just like the immaterial-sphere jhāna—is said to possess two factors and to have reached imperturbability (*āneñjappatta*), yet it is by taking that [fine-material jhāna] as its proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) that one attains Arahantship.

One is not called "liberated both ways" because of not being liberated from the material body (*rūpakāya*). For that [person] is liberated only from the defilement-body (*kilesakāya*), not from the material body;
therefore, having emerged from that [attainment], one who reaches Arahantship is not "liberated both ways.

Thus it is said: "Of the four formless... [there are] five kinds. Regarding the section beginning with "Possessing form, he sees forms," up to the end of the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*):
Although it is stated in the Mahānidāna Sutta after explaining the eight liberations: “But when, Ānanda, a bhikkhu dwells having personally realized these eight liberations with the body,
and having seen with wisdom, his taints are utterly destroyed— this, Ānanda,
is called a bhikkhu liberated both ways,” that was said with reference to the foremost type of one liberated both ways.
Regarding the word "stated": here, in order to include all those liberated both ways (*ubhatobhāgavimutta*), it was said, "it is fivefold," and then he said, "But as for the textual tradition here...
[etc. ...it is presented in the Abhidhamma by way of those who have attained the eight liberations. For here too, in the Kīṭāgiri Sutta, it says: "Here, monks, a certain person... [etc.
...is one liberated both ways," and thus four are mentioned by way of the formless attainments (*arūpasamāpatti*).
The one liberated both ways (*ubhatobhāgavimutta*) is said to be the best because he possesses the characteristics described.
For among the five types mentioned, the first four are called "liberated both ways" only in a figurative sense, as they do not attain cessation (*nirodha*).

However, the non-returner (*anāgāmī*) who has attained the eight meditative attainments (*aṭṭhasamāpatti*), and having entered that [cessation], emerged from it, and then developed insight (*vipassanā*) to reach Arahantship, is so called in the literal sense.
The one called "the best among those liberated in both ways" (ubhatobhāgavimutta-seṭṭha).

Regarding the phrases "What kind of person? and so forth: "what kind" (katama) is the interrogative statement; "person" (puggala) is the statement indicating that which is to be inquired about in its specific, non-common sense.
"Here" (idha) means in this teaching (sāsana). "A certain one" (ekacca) means one. "Having touched the eight liberations with the body, he dwells therein" refers to the eight...

Having attained the meditative absorptions (samāpattiyo) by means of the co-nascent mental body (nāmakāya), he dwells therein. Regarding the phrase "having seen with wisdom, his taints (āsava) are utterly destroyed":

this should be understood as follows—the taints are destroyed through insight-wisdom (vipassanā-paññā) regarding the conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāragata), and through path-wisdom (magga-paññā), having seen the four truths, all four taints are utterly destroyed.

"Released by wisdom" (*paññāvimutta*) means released specifically by wisdom alone, not by the preeminent concentration known as the eight liberations (*aṭṭhavimokkha*), which serves as its foundation;
thus he is "released by wisdom. This is a designation for the noble one who, without having attained the eight liberations, is entirely freed from the taints (*āsava*).
For even when the liberations consisting of form-sphere jhānas have been attained, he does not rely on that preeminent concentration.

It has already been stated that one does not become "liberated in both ways" (*ubhatobhāgavimutta*) by virtue of that [the formless attainment alone]. However, when even one of the formless jhānas is present, one is indeed called "liberated in both ways.
For that reason, because it possesses the capacity to bestow that name through its status as a single part of the eight liberations, one is said to be a "possessor of the eight liberations.
Indeed, a designation applied to a whole is also seen to apply to a part, just as...
“*Sattisayo*”: “The *Pāḷi*” refers to the Abhidhamma *Pāḷi*. “In this” means in this discussion on liberation through wisdom (*paññāvimutti*).

By the restrictive phrase “only by way of rejecting the eight liberations,” he shows that here too it has come down [in the tradition] precisely by way of rejection. Therefore he said: “He dwells having touched [them] with the body.
“The limit of what is touched” (*phuṭṭhanta*) means the end (*anta*) of what is touched (*phuṭṭha*); that is, the limit of the immaterial jhānas (*arūpajjhāna*).
The intended meaning is "the immediately subsequent time. This is the accusative case used to express immediate succession (*accantasaṃyoga*);

thus it is said that one realizes precisely the moment immediately following contact by means of the method to be realized. Alternatively, this is a neuter abstract noun, as in such phrases as "he sat to one side" (*ekamantaṃ nisīdi*).
For he who, through formless jhāna, [attains] liberation by suppression from the material body and from a portion of the mental body...
Being liberated, by that [liberation] the release designated as cessation becomes as if observed and manifested; yet it has not been realized by means of the body.
However, when some of the taints have been exhausted by taking cessation as the object, it is realized by him through that [body];
therefore, because he realizes the cessation to be realized exactly as it was observed by means of the mental body (*nāmakāya*), he is called a "body-witness" (*kāyasakkhī*).
It is said [to be "liberated"], but not "completely liberated" because some taints (*āsava*) have not yet been exhausted. Therefore he said:
"First one touches the contact of jhāna; afterwards one realizes cessation, Nibbāna.

This refers to the four who, having emerged from each of the four formless attainments (*arūpasamāpatti*), contemplated formations (*saṅkhāra*) and attained the state of a body-witness (*kāyasakkhi*), and [who emerge] from cessation...
Having emerged [from the fruit], there are five types, including those liberated in both ways (ubhatobhāgavimutta) by way of non-returners who have attained the highest path.
Therefore, it is said in the Abhidhamma-ṭīkā: "The same method applies to the body-witness (kāyasakkhin) as well.
"One who has reached the conclusion" (diṭṭhantaṃ patto) means one who has reached immediately after the knowledge of the path of stream-entry, which is designated as "seeing."

“Because it has been seen, it has been attained”—this is also a reading. By this, he illustrates that through the vision consisting of the seeing of the Four Noble Truths, cessation (nirodha) has been attained.
Therefore he said: “It is known that formations are suffering and cessation is bliss. In that context, “by means of wisdom” (paññāya) refers to the wisdom of the Path.
One is “attained to vision” (diṭṭhippatto) from the stage of the first fruit up to the stage of the supreme path. Therefore he said: “He too...”

"...is sixfold, like the body-witness (kāyasakkhi). Just as the one liberated by wisdom (paññāvimutta) was said to be fivefold, so too this dry-insight practitioner (sukkha-vipassaka) should be understood as fivefold:
namely, himself, and the four who have attained the state of "one who has reached vision" (diṭṭhippatto) after emerging from the four fine-material jhānas.
The same method applies to the one liberated by faith (saddhāvimutta). This much is "this is suffering."

“He understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering; there is no suffering beyond this. This means that, setting craving aside, he understands the five aggregates of clinging as the truth of suffering exactly as they are.
Furthermore, because craving gives rise to and produces suffering, and from that [craving] suffering originates, he understands it as it really is: “This is the origin of suffering. Because...
However, this suffering and its origin cease upon reaching Nibbāna and go to non-occurrence;
therefore, one understands "this is the cessation of suffering" as it truly is. Furthermore, the Noble Eightfold Path goes toward that cessation of suffering;
therefore, one understands "this is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering" as it truly is. Up to this point—

The determination of the truths at different moments has been shown. Now, in order to show that same determination at a single moment, the passage beginning with “proclaimed by the Tathāgata” was spoken;
its meaning will follow.
By the phrase “liberated through faith,” even for one who is not liberated in every respect, the state of being liberated by mere faith is illuminated.

It exists. Alternatively, *saddhāvimutto* means one who is intent upon faith (*saddhāya adhimutto*). "In the manner already stated" refers to the manner stated as "the fruit of stream-entry," and so forth. "Of one who has faith" means of one who has faith in this way:
"This practice certainly brings about the destruction of the defilements because it was spoken by the Fully Enlightened One.
Furthermore, because for him, through the contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*) and so forth, the perception of permanence (*niccasaññā*) has been abandoned...

In the cultivation [of the path], one perceives a distinction between what precedes and what follows; thus, there is direct personal realization (paccakkhatā) in each respective stage. Therefore, it is said:
"as if for one who has faith. The remaining two phrases are synonyms for that same state.

And here, by the expression "cultivation of the preliminary path," it is shown that through the diversity of the paths leading thereto, there is a diversity of wisdom among those liberated by faith, those attained through vision, and so forth.

This has been shown. In the *Abhidhammaṭṭhakathā* as well, after stating, “There is no difference between them regarding the abandoning of defilements, but there is indeed a difference in their wisdom,” it is said:
“The conclusion was reached that the one liberated by faith does not reach the level of the one who has attained vision solely because of the difference in their progress.”
One is a *dhammānusārī* (a follower of the Dhamma) because one recollects the Dhamma—comprising wisdom—which functions as the pre-eminent forerunner due to its excellence.

Therefore, he says "the Dhamma," and so forth. By saying "the same method applies," he extends this principle to the sense that one recollects faith and develops the path with faith as its forerunner.
One is a *paññāvāhī* (one who carries wisdom) because one conveys wisdom; that is, one causes wisdom to proceed with particular intensity.

This is the meaning. Therefore he said: "He develops the Noble Path preceded by wisdom. Regarding the phrase "carrying along with faith," the meaning should be understood according to the method stated here.
"The discussion beginning with those liberated in both ways" refers to the discourse that should be told starting from the arrival [of those] among those liberated in both ways and so forth.
"Of these" refers to those aforementioned individuals, such as the liberated in both ways. "Here" means in this Kīṭāgiri Sutta.

But surely, the "liberated in both ways" (ubhatobhāgavimutta), the "body-witness" (kāyasakkhī), and others who have attained the eight meditative attainments (aṭṭhasamāpatti) are mentioned in the Abhidhamma;
how then are they excluded here by reference only to those who have attained the formless jhānas? With this objection in mind, he says "Because," and so forth.
"Having touched" means having reached. Regarding the statement, "And having seen with wisdom, his taints (āsava) are utterly destroyed," it is not that the taints are seen by means of wisdom.
"Completely destroyed by vision through wisdom" means they are said to be "completely destroyed by having seen with wisdom.
For it is precisely because their destruction depends upon vision that vision is the preliminary action for the destruction of the taints (*āsava*).

"Proclaimed by the Tathāgata" means that while sitting at the seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), the Tathāgata realized and understood them, and subsequently made them manifest to others. "The Dhamma of the Four Truths."
Having stated this, because virtue (*sīla*) and the other factors are included therein, it was said: "In this place, virtue is explained," and so forth.
"By way of purpose" means by way of the aim, such as non-regret (*avippaṭisāra*), or by way of the respective purposes such as rapture (*pīti*).

"By way of cause" means that virtue and the rest are the causes because they serve as the proximate bases (*padaṭṭhāna*) for concentration (*samādhi*) and the other factors, through causes such as reliance upon true persons (*sappurisūpanissaya*). "Because of habitual practice" means by way of the state of having practiced faith (*saddhā*).

In the state conducive to full enlightenment (*sambodhāvaha-bhāve*). Having wandered here and there, having especially practiced; the meaning is that by means of that [wisdom], his wisdom was made to proceed well.
It becomes firmly established because it has come via the Path (*magga*). "By measure" means by a limited amount. They are able to look upon it;
they come within the range of being grasped by wisdom.

"Three" refers to those who are body-witnesses (*kāyasakkhī*), those who have attained through vision (*diṭṭhippatto*), and those liberated by faith (*saddhāvimutto*). The meaning of the text remains exactly as it stands; there is nothing further to be determined or stated therein.
Thus, he speaks what was not explicitly stated according to the method of the Suttantas.
"Of that path" means because of the attainment of that which was to be done regarding the path of stream-entry (*sotāpattimagga*). However, for the sake of the three higher paths...
By attending to lodgings in a manner that is favorable, by associating with virtuous friends, and by bringing the faculties into harmony,
they will gradually reach Arahantship through the sequence of the path of development, because the path consists of many moments of consciousness;
such is the meaning of the Pāḷi in this passage of the Sutta.
"Taking this very passage" means that after stating "And what kind of person is a follower by faith?
regarding a person standing on the path, [the Buddha] spoke of the practice of sitting in accordance with seniority and so forth by way of those individuals, beginning with "Of this one, monks...
It is by taking this very passage as stated that he says, "The supramundane dhamma lasts for many moments of consciousness."

"He should be addressed thus": that sophist should be addressed as follows. "If, having spoken of persons established on the path, it is stated in the Canon that they practice such things as using lodgings in accordance with the Dhamma, and that they proceed in that manner only while being possessors of the path—this being the case, then according to your view, those who grasp insight into the form and other phenomena associated with lodgings would necessarily have to be possessors of the path;
yet this is not so. Therefore, I have found the Sutta [to be against you]."
He should be stopped with the words, "Do not say anything at all. Therefore he said, "If [it is] with another mind," and so forth.
In that context, "this being so" means when the use of lodgings and so on occurs precisely with a different mind. Therein, regarding the text:

if you accept that even at the time one possesses the fivefold sense-consciousness, one still possesses supramundane states—provided one is indeed possessed of supramundane states—then [you would have to agree] with the Teacher.
"You contradict [the teaching]" because you point out a contradiction with the Suttas. Therefore he said, "By the Teacher," and so forth.
"Investigation of the Dhamma" is not within your domain; therefore, one should be urged: "Drink the gruel.
(183) "By the very first" means by the very first [instruction]. "Gradual training" refers to training that proceeds in a gradual sequence. Therefore he said:
“The nominative case [is used] in the sense of the instrument. One in whom faith has arisen is “one whose faith has arisen” (*saddhājāto*);

the word *jāta* follows [the noun] because of its exclusion by the alternative form *agyāhita*. “Thus it is” is the resolution that constitutes resolute faith (*okappaniya-saddhā*). He sits near [the teacher] for the purpose of attending upon him.
“He retains it well” means he brings the Dhamma as it was heard into his verbal mastery.

Having made that proficient, one retains it by way of its essential core. "Zeal arises" means that regarding those phenomena capable of being scrutinized, the wholesome zeal of the desire-to-act arises, thinking:

"I shall directly master these phenomena through the wisdom of development. "Exerts himself" means that he does not remain at the mere arising of zeal, but exerts himself from there by way of commencing the development. "Weighs" means by way of comprehension (*sammasana*).

Regarding formations (*saṅkhāre*): "weighing by means of scrutinizing insight" means knowing through the full understanding of scrutiny (*tīraṇapariññā*) and then weighing and acknowledging them by way of the subsequent full understanding of abandonment (*pahānapariññā*).

"Exerts himself in the striving for the path" means he exerts himself in the path that has the characteristics of the path as its primary quality. "With a mind directed toward" means with a mind directed toward *nibbāna*. "By means of the mental body" refers to the sequence of the path.
By means of the mental body associated with each respective path. However, he did not say anything at all because of their distance;
the Blessed One said nothing at all in order to restrain them more firmly.
184. *Paṇaviyā* is an explanation by means of a low form of speech; *opaṇaviyā* is due to the absence of such low speech. It does not apply.
It is not appropriate. The word "this" (*taṃ*) is used here to indicate that which is intended as the wager and the thing staked.
All of this, the Blessed One says, referring to the statement made by Assaji and Punabbasuka—“Friends, we eat both in the evening”—which illustrates their failure to conform to the training.
"Having taken up" means having undertaken it as if grasping it with the head. "In accordance with the Dhamma" (*anudhammo*) means a corresponding nature, [the nature] of being a disciple.
“Appropriate practice” (anucchavikā paṭipatti). “Rohanīyaṃ” means the state of growth. “Sineha” is that in which one clings, or by which one clings; it is the cause.

Because that [cause] exists therein, it is “possessing moisture” (sinehavantaṃ); the meaning is “the foundation” (pādaka). “The skin is one limb” means that the skin is one constituent part in the state of being a hero.
For even when the skin of one who is devoted to the supreme effort (padhāna) is wasting away, for the sake of that [effort]—
Not falling into despondency is one factor, one cause of energy. The same should be stated for the remaining [factors].
Therefore he said: “He practices thus: ‘I will not emerge until I have attained arahantship. The rest is easy to understand.
The exposition of the hidden meaning of the Kīṭāgiri Sutta commentary is complete.
The commentary on the Bhikkhu-vagga is completed.
3. Paribbājaka-vagga 1.
Commentary on the Tevijja-Vacchagotta Sutta.
185. "There" means in the wandering ascetics' park known as Ekapuṇḍarīka.
[The phrase] "It has been a long time, venerable sir," and so forth, is spoken by way of worldly convention for those who have not previously come;

however, this was said here with reference to the fact that he had indeed come before. For the Blessed One [came] for the sake of producing liberation in some, for the sake of maturing the faculties in some, and for the sake of some...
Sometimes he goes to the monastery of a sectarian for the sake of attaining a specific distinction. "Standing where it is not permitted" means standing where one should not be allowed to stay.
There may be something that ought to be permitted, because there is nothing knowable that has not been known [by him].

For as far as the knowable extends, so far extends the Blessed One’s knowledge; and as far as the Blessed One’s knowledge extends, so far extends the knowable. Therefore he said: "There is nothing for him..."
“There is nothing here that is unseen, nor anything unperceived or unknown,” and so forth.

For it is by means of omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) that the Blessed One, having adverted his mind, understands. Indeed, this has been said: “The knowledge of the Buddha, the Blessed One, is bound up with adverting.
If this is so, how is one to explain this passage from the Sutta: “The Naga walks concentrated, the Naga stands concentrated”?
This phrase illustrates the absence of distraction; it does not illustrate the occurrence of knowledges even without an act of adverting.
Whatever else needs to be said on this matter has already been explained in detail below.

186. Regarding the phrase "only so far": since it might be thought that, as with occurrence according to one's preference, there could also be successive arising [of knowledges], this phrase is used to show the absence of such.
Showing this, he said: "Because there is no further need to exhaust the taints (āsava) that have already been exhausted.

Regarding the phrase "the quality of knowing the present," this is stated without including the knowledge of the future (anāgataṃsañāṇa), which is an ancillary knowledge (paribhaṇḍañāṇa) of the divine eye-knowledge (dibbacakkhuñāṇa);
however, it may be said that by means of that [ancillary knowledge], the quality of the knowledge of the future is also demonstrated.
“Among the requisites of a householder” means among the requisites of a householder such as clothing, ornaments, wealth, grain, and so forth.
However, the mark of a householder is not the measure; therefore, having severed the bonds of a householder, they indeed become those who make an end of suffering.

Showing that when there is the making of an end of suffering, they do not remain at all in the mark of a householder, he said, “And those who...,” etc. “Having dried up” means having completely eradicated.
The method of either going forth or attaining final nibbāna on the very day one reaches arahantship is not common to all;
thus he said, "But the earth deities remain. Therein, the reason for this is stated as "because there is a place for them to hide.
A secluded place such as a forest or a mountain is a place for hiding. "In the rest of the sensual realm" means in the world of sense-desire (*kāmaloka*). "Of playful people" means...
[It is] for people possessed of luxury by means of ornaments, decorations, dancing, singing, and so forth.
"He too" refers to "he too [is said to be] other than one. "Evil is not done by the doer"—in this way, he does not deny the action.
If he speaks while grasping only the self, then why did the Great Being at that time take up the asceticism of the Ājīvakas?
"He approached," he said, [referring to] "At that time indeed," and so forth. "Of him too" means not only of other heretics, but of him as well.
"He did not let his energy decline" means that having undertaken the practice of asceticism and self-mortification, he did not abandon the observance he had taken up for the sake of dispassion;
he did not cast aside the Teacher’s instruction. Therefore he said: "Having been a proponent of action, he was reborn in heaven."
The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning (*Līnatthappakāsanā*) of the Commentary on the *Tevijja-Vacchagotta Sutta* is completed.
2. Commentary on the *Aggivacchagotta Sutta*. 187.
A doctrine that proceeds by way of rejecting the eternity of the world results in nihilism (*ucchedavāda*).
Since the view of annihilationism exists in the absence of the view of eternalism, the wanderer, by asserting "the world is not eternal," was questioned regarding the view of annihilationism;
and the Blessed One likewise rejected that very same [view]. Thus he said, "In the second [case], I am not one who holds the view of annihilation.
Regarding the phrase "by way of the views concerning the finite and infinite," here, by the inclusion of the term "finite and infinite," [it refers to] the world as finite or the world as infinite.
He states two positions. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), he includes the tetrad of views beginning with "That which is the soul is the body," while the other two are included by their actual form.
"The rejection is to be understood" means that the rejection is to be understood through such statements as, "In the third [view] I am not one who holds the view of finitude;
in the fourth, I am not one who holds the view of infinity. "Does the Tathāgata exist..."

“Does not exist after death”—this too is an eternalist view (sassatavāda), but it is by way of speculation concerning the future limit (*aparantakappika*); whereas “the world is eternal” is by way of speculation concerning the past limit (*pubbantakappika*)—this is the distinction between them.
“The Tathāgata does not exist after death”—this too is an annihilationist view (ucchedavāda), but it is by way of the sentient being (*satta*);
whereas “the world is non-eternal” is, they say, by way of both the sentient being and conditioned formations (*saṅkhāra*).
189. It is "accompanied by suffering" (*sadukkha*) because it arises together with fear. Thus he said, "by the suffering of the defilements," and so forth.
"Of those very [two]" means of the suffering of the defilements and the suffering of their result. "With affliction" (*saupaghātaka*) means with distress.
"With despair" (*saupāyāsa*) means with turmoil, with burning heat, and with oppression. "With fever" (*sapariḷāha*) means with longing.
"Any kind of speculative view (*diṭṭhigata*)": let us set aside these eight views for now; however, Master Gotama, is there any kind of speculative view that has been adopted?
He asks with the intention that it is not possible to maintain any system of thought without such a view.
"Cast away" (*apaviddha*): discarded by means of abandonment through eradication. "Seen with wisdom" (*paññāya diṭṭha*).
The Blessed One has realized the wisdom of the path accompanied by insight-wisdom (*vipassanā-paññā*). Regarding the term "shaken" (*mathita*):
it is said that they are "shaken" because they agitate and crush the being in whom [defilements] arise; thus, "of those shaken" is a synonym for that very same thing.
"Any phenomenon" (*kañci dhammaṃ*) refers to either a material phenomenon (*rūpa-dhamma*) or an immaterial phenomenon (*arūpa-dhamma*). "Without clinging" (*anupādiyitvā*) means without grasping.
190. "It does not approach" means it does not go to a designation; thus he said, "it is not applicable.

One might grant that for one liberated through non-clinging there is no arising whatsoever. And while it is indeed the case that "one whose mind is thus liberated does not re-arise" is a description of the nature of final Nibbāna, some who hold the doctrine of annihilationism say: "We too [say] 'a being...'"
“We say that one does not re-arise in the future, and the ascetic Gotama says the same,” they would think, and thus they would settle into the very state of annihilationism.
Therefore, the Blessed One said, “Vaccha, ‘one does not re-arise’ does not imply [annihilation]. However, if it were said, “one re-arises,” one would grasp at eternalism;
such is the application [of the logic]. The same principle applies to the other two positions as well. “Without a foundation” means by way of annihilationism and so forth.
“Lacking a foundation”: it is without a foundation because of the absence of a supporting object for those very same doctrines.
“A place for easy entry”: [the phrase] “may he not find a place for the easy entry of those very same doctrines. “Standing without having assented”:

because of the reason for standing, which is the refusal to give an assent that ought to be given, such as “he is not reborn,” and so forth. “Even though it should be assented to”: even though it ought to be assented to.

He rejected the second question. However, since the Dhamma as study is, in its actual meaning, the principle of conditionality (*paccayākāra*), he said: "Dhamma means the Dhamma of the principle of conditionality.

Regarding the phrase "by application elsewhere": the meaning is by means of an application occurring in another wrong system apart from this liberating teaching (*niyyānika-sāsana*), that is, by one who practices various forms of wrong practice that do not lead to liberation. It is also [read] as "by one who speaks otherwise."
The meaning is: "by one who stands having adopted the teacher’s doctrine which demonstrates a mode other than the mode of conditions (*paccayākāra*)";
this refers to the recitation (*pāṭha*). 191. "Without condition" (*appaccaya*) means without fuel for clinging (*anupādāna*); the meaning is "without fuel" (*nirindhana*). 192.

"By whatever form" (*yena rūpena*) means by whatever material phenomenon (*rūpadhamma*) distinguished as the primary elements (*bhūta*), derived matter (*upādā*), and so forth. That form [is abandoned] through the abandoning of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) bound to it.
In the case of the Tathāgata whose taints are exhausted, [these qualities] have been abandoned and have reached the state of non-arising. Therefore it is said in the Pāḷi:

“having the nature of non-arising,” and so forth. Because he possesses the quality of the absence of knowledge in others, he is profound in virtue. He cannot be grasped by a measure such as “there are only this many virtues.
Because his virtues cannot be fathomed by determining that “his virtues are like this,” he is difficult to fathom.

“Hard to fathom” means that, being profound due to its unfathomable depth, it cannot be measured by such expressions as “there are so many hundreds of water-pots”; for this very reason, it is hard to fathom.
“In the same way” means that just as the great ocean is profound, immeasurable, and hard to fathom, so too is the one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) in terms of his qualities.
Therefore, having taken up form and the rest, there might be the conventional designation (vohāra) of him as “possessed of form” and so forth.

However, because that [state of being led] no longer exists for one who has attained final Nibbāna (parinibbuta), it is impossible to designate him in such a way; consequently, it would be illogical to say that he "arises" with reference to that [state], and so forth.

To show that even one whose taints are exhausted (khīṇāsava) is like a fire that still exists—such that when it is being led by a skilled man, it may be said to have gone to the eastern or other directions, but not because it is extinguished (nibbuto)—he says, "In the same way," and so on.
Regarding the term "impermanence" (*aniccatā*): here, the mention of impermanence is an indication of the lack of essence (*asāra*).

By this, he shows that just as that *sāla* tree was purified by the removal of its non-essential parts such as branches and foliage and established in its essence, so too this Dhamma and Discipline is established in the essence of the supramundane Dhamma through the departure from the non-essence known as the conditioned phenomena associated with taints (*sāsavasaṅkhāta*). The rest is easy to understand.
The explanation of the *Aggivacchasutta*, which clarifies the hidden meaning, is completed.
3. Explanation of the *Mahāvacchasutta*. 193.
One who has discourse with another is a "discourse-companion" (*sahakathī*); [this refers to] "we by way of questioning and you by way of answering."
Thus, the meaning is "discourse delivered together. Regarding these very discourses: in the first, the threefold knowledge (*tevijjā*) was taught;
in the second, it was shown by means of fire. Therefore, they are stated with their specific names distinguished as the *Tevijja-Vacchagotta Sutta* and the *Aggivacchagotta Sutta*.
They do not quickly relinquish their [wrong] views because this destruction of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhārā*) is fixed and does not arise from anything else.
Even though they have arisen from causes, they do not endure long under reflection, nor are they swift; therefore he said, “They are purified by ghee-oil... etc.
The final movement occurs because knowledge has reached maturity.

A man who is descending into water while leaning on a staff is described as “one who has descended with the staff and fallen into the water. This is a detailed teaching by way of the paths of action (kamma-patha).
This was said with reference to the concise teaching. Therefore he said, "And here, by way of the roots," and so forth.

"Similar to the detailed [teaching]" means that the teaching taught here by way of the courses of action (*kammappatha*) is similar to the detailed teaching when compared to the teaching taught by way of the roots.
There is no such thing as a "detailed teaching" in an absolute sense; for not only this one, but indeed all teachings of the Buddhas are, in the ultimate sense, [detailed].
There is no detailed teaching that is entirely exhaustive by means of a straightforward approach,

because of the vast scope of the knowledge of teaching (*desanāñāṇa*) and because of the great power of omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) due to its specific causal perfection. For, through its possession of omniscient knowledge— which is empowered by the remaining analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*),
which has arisen from a mass of accumulated knowledge gathered over immeasurable time, and which is never subject to exhaustion— it is not shared by anyone else.

How could the Blessed One’s teaching—being expanded through the analytical knowledge of ready wit (*paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā*) and the perfection of a vast tongue and a corresponding physical form—ever be limited or circumscribed?

However, out of great compassion, the Blessed One brings it to a conclusion by making it limited and circumscribed here and there in accordance with the inclinations of those to be trained (*veneyya*). And this...
The meaning should be illustrated by the Mahāsīhanāda Sutta. This is because everything has been condensed;
rather than being taught according to one's own personal inclination, the teaching was brought to its conclusion according to the inclination of the person to be enlightened.

Furthermore, there is no contradiction with the Dhamma or the Dispensation here, because the teachings have been made known in accordance with the Dhamma itself, without relying on mere figurative methods, and because they are all-encompassing.
194. Seven factors belong to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), because here it is the volitions of undertaking and abstention that are intended.

"Without specifying" means without making a specific determination such as "the Perfectly Enlightened One" or "a disciple. "One should understand oneself alone... [and so forth]... for thus the wanderer said, "May the venerable Gotama remain. 195.

Only the Teacher is an *arahant*, because of the state of having brought the practice to its full completion. "When this was declared" means when this question had been well-stated, beginning with, "Is there even a single disciple... and so forth.
196. *Sampādaka*: one who accomplishes the practice. 197.

Regarding the phrase "by means of the knowledge of the trainee" (*sekhiyā vijjāya*): this is stated by way of the instrument (*karaṇa*), emphasizing the path-wisdom (*magga-paññā*) that has attained the characteristics of a trainee;

however, the fruition-wisdom (*phala-paññā*) is stated by way of the object of action (*kamma-bhāva*), because it is what is to be attained by that [path-wisdom]. Therefore he said: "The three lower fruits..."

"to be attained. Now, because they do not penetrate this unerring meaning which is evident from the text itself, the caviller—seizing upon the mere phrasing of the statement, "Whatever is to be attained by one in training has been attained by me"—claims, "He must have attained even the path of arahantship.
"Thus" refers to the verse that is now being spoken.
"Having abandoned the five defilements" means having abandoned or relinquished the fivefold corruption known as the lower fetters (*orambhāgiya-saṃyojana*), or else, by reason of such abandonment.

"One whose training is fulfilled" means one in whom the qualities of training (*sekhadhamma*) have increased in every respect. "One whose nature is not subject to decline" means one whose essential character does not fall away;
for there is no falling away from those qualities such as virtue (*sīla*) that have been attained, due to the fulfillment of his practice in concentration (*samādhi*).
He has attained mastery over his mind; therefore, it is said, “one whose faculties are concentrated. Because he is of a nature not subject to decline, he is “steadfast in self.
For a non-returner must fulfill those qualities that bring about the state of one beyond training (*asekha*), not those that bring about the state of one still in training (*sekha*);

thus, he is called a trainee who is entirely perfected. As for the claim that this is not the word of the Buddha, the statement that “the path consists of many moments of consciousness” is not [the word of the Buddha].
The word of the Buddha is supramundane wholesome [kamma] because it yields its result immediately and because there is no purpose in its repeated occurrence.
Sutta passages such as, "They call this concentration immediate; they do not go to the further shore by means of a double [practice]," establish this meaning.
Through the abandoning of the lower fetters, there is the fulfillment of the state of the qualities of one in training (sekha).
"The meaning [of what you said] contradicts your own statement," said the Venerable Vaccha. 198.

"Or else, higher knowledge (*abhiññā*) is the cause": for that which consists of the various kinds of supernormal power (*iddhividha*), such as the experience of psychic powers described as the capacity to bear witness in various instances, has higher knowledge as its cause.

Alternatively, if the experience of the various kinds of supernormal power and so forth is itself higher knowledge, then in that case, the jhāna that serves as the basis for higher knowledge (*abhiññāpādaka-jjhāna*) [is the cause].
The cause [is the path]. At the conclusion, however, through the sixth direct knowledge, there is Arahantship.

And here, because the destruction of the taints (*āsava-kkhaya*) was intended in the first sutta—where the taints have already been destroyed and are not to be destroyed again—the phrase "only as long as" (*yāvadeva*) was not stated there.
Here, however, the attainment of fruition (*phala-samāpatti*) is intended, and since that is entered into again and again, the phrase "only as long as" is used.
Thus it was said. For that very reason, it is stated: "Or arahantship is the cause.

This is indeed the cause for one who, having established a longing for the unsurpassed liberations, develops direct knowledge [with the thought]: "When indeed shall I enter and dwell in that sphere which the Noble Ones now enter and dwell in? And this is not common to all.
Showing this by way of what is common [to all], he said: “Or insight into arahantship.
(200) They are called “those who have attended upon” because they have lived the holy life without interruption.

A disciple is said to have “attended upon” the Teacher because he has properly completed all the services that ought to be performed for the Teacher’s Dhamma. Therefore he said: “Thus... the Elder...”
"Thus he spoke. "Of their qualities" means of those qualities of one beyond training (*asekkha-guṇa*). The rest is easily understood.
The *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Hidden Meaning) for the commentary on the *Mahāvaccha-sutta* is completed.
4. Commentary on the *Dīghanakha-sutta*.
201. *Khānaṇaṃ*: that which has been dug. *Sūkarakhatā*: because a pig has dug here, it is "dug by a pig" (*sūkarakhatā*);
or, taking into account that this was first dug by a pig in this era of a Buddha's appearance, it is "dug by a pig. *Evaṃnāmike*: having such a name acquired according to the feminine gender.
*Paṃsudhote*: with the dust washed away. *Otaritvā abhiruhitabbaṃ*: having descended from the natural ground...
Having descended by means of many steps, one must then ascend to the entrance of the cave by a few.
"Standing" means that because his maternal uncle was standing there, he remained standing out of reverence and deference toward him.
Although the word *sabba* (all) generally denotes a complete inclusion without exception, the application of a term depends upon the intended subject matter.
With reference to this meaning, the wanderer said, "Nothing is acceptable to me.
Those rebirths in the world as human beings and so forth are "arisen for no purpose" because, in each case, sentient beings are cut off right there;
therefore, all future rebirths spoken of by those who propound doctrines [of non-existence] do not occur. For these sentient beings are like bubbles on the water.
Having arisen at various times and places, they break up; his intention is that there is no rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) for them there.

Therefore he said, "rebirth-linkings," and so forth. "Releasing his intention" means that even though [the Buddha] knew the intention with which the wanderer said, "Nothing is acceptable to me," he acted as if not knowing it.
This was stated by him with reference to a partial totality (*padesasabba*), meaning that he points out a fault in its syllables as if they were [the whole];
it does not, however, take the fault in that regard by making it a total-totality (*sabbasabbavisaya*).
Just as in the world, when someone says, "Everything you have said is false," the falsity would apply because that statement itself is included within "everything," so too is it here.
When one says, “Nothing is acceptable to me,” it follows by implication that even the view occurring in that manner is not acceptable.
Therefore the Blessed One said: “This view of yours is also not acceptable.

Just as when someone says, “Everything spoken is false,” the application of the words conforms to the underlying intention—setting aside his specific statement and applying it to other things—so too here.
The falsity [of the opponent's position] is established by logic; likewise here, from the statement "Nothing is acceptable to me," the meaning established by logic is this:
having abandoned that view by virtue of which one says "Nothing is acceptable to me," one does not accept everything else as intended.
However, the Blessed One, the supreme among speakers, [uses] a thick [axle] with a subtle pin...
As if pulling out a pin, he spoke the passage beginning with "But as for that which... in order to extract that person's wrong view through a skillful means;
rather than stating it according to the person's own intention, he first pointed out the fault obtainable by way of the literal sound of the words. Therefore it was said:
"Setting aside his intention, he first pointed out the fault in the syllables."
However, the wanderer, thinking, "This is that [person] regarding whom I said, 'Nothing is acceptable to me,'" spoke the words beginning with "This is mine" (*esā me*)—

desiring to avoid the aforementioned fault while concealing his own underlying intention that, when that meaning is stated for the sake of avoiding the faults already mentioned, all those faults would no longer apply, yet even so, the ascetic Gotama would merely be attributing a fault to his own doctrine.
In that regard, "that too would be exactly like this for him" means that even the matter grasped by the thought,
"Nothing is acceptable to me," would be exactly like that. Furthermore, this view which is included within everything— namely,
"May this ground of my own view be acceptable to you"— is the very view which was stated by you, Gotama, when you said, "This view of yours is not acceptable to me."
“That too is not acceptable to me; therefore, everything is simply not acceptable to me”—this is the intention of the wanderer.
Thus he said: “He speaks with the perception that ‘I am maintaining this. And so he will say later: “Therefore, even the view of annihilation is not acceptable to me. “This is my view”:
by means of that view which has become established, [he says] “everything is not acceptable to me.”
Since this is included here by the inclusion of the term "all," he says: "In its meaning, however, this view results in the admission:
'This does not please me. Showing that this is a fault, he says: "But for one who... and so forth. "This" refers to the view.
"Accepted" means grasped after having adhered to it through the presentation of the view and having found it pleasing. Therefore, because the view is unacceptable and not pleasing—
"‘It must be so’ means that when there is an inability to endure a view, one might then endure or find it agreeable because of what has been grasped by that [view];
thus, while initially there is an inability to endure everything, later on one arrives at the position that everything is endured and found agreeable.
But he does not accept that; for this annihilationist, who says ‘nothing is agreeable to me,’ [does not accept it] in the manner described."
He does not accept or approve of the forbearance toward everything. To the question, "How is it that he does not accept the matter as stated according to the proper method?
he says: "He grasps only the annihilation of even that [forbearance], due to his view of annihilation.
For, disapproving of the future arising of all phenomena, it is with reference to this that he says, "Nothing is acceptable to me," among those who hold the view of annihilation.
And when [the aggregates] are cut off, how could there be the nature of the annihilationist view?
"By that" means by that reason; it is said: because here some beings remain having adopted such a view, therefore [it is so].
Or, having grasped them together as a whole with the mind that abandons [them], one distinguishes those who abandon from those who do not abandon.

The Blessed One said, “Therefore... [as above] ...they are more numerous,” which he stated as “among those who abandon, [the former are] in the ablative case,” just as in the expression, “those developed by means of the five precepts are wiser.
Having said “many,” he used the term “more numerous” to show that they are not merely many, but indeed exceedingly many.
As for the phrase “for they are many,” this is not an ablative expression, but rather a nominative expression.

Regarding the word "hi," he says: "The syllable *hi* is merely a particle. First, as for the non-derivative expression (*anissakkavacana*), because those who abandon it are numerous, they too are subsequently called "more numerous" (*bahutarā*). "Showing the root" (*mūladassana*) refers to those who first adopt such a view;
the subsequently adopted view is of the same nature. For a view first adopted regarding something of a different kind—
Without abandoning the apprehension of one thing, the apprehension of another of a different kind is not possible, because two contradictory determinations cannot coexist simultaneously.
However, it is possible to apprehend another view—distinguished by differences such as its object—without relinquishing the fundamental view.
Therefore, he said, "And here," and so forth.

In this context, although the doctrine of partial eternalism is, respectively, of a nature that grasps at both eternalism and annihilationism by way of its adherence to eternalism and annihilationism, it is nevertheless stated that in both cases "it is impossible to grasp [anything] as partially eternal.

This is because the adherence to eternalism is contradicted by the grasping at annihilationism, and the adherence to non-eternalism is contradicted by the grasping at that [eternalism]. Likewise, "either eternalism or annihilationism..."
“Or it cannot be grasped. For the eternalism of the root (mūla-sassata) was grasped first. It should also be applied to the sense bases (āyatana):

having first grasped that the eye base (cakkhāyatana) is eternal, one subsequently grasps that not only the eye base but also the ear base (sotāyatana) is eternal, and that the nose base (ghānāyatana), etc., are also eternal; it should be applied in this manner.
By the word "also" (*pi*) in the phrase "in the sense-bases (*āyatana*) also," it should be understood that the elements (*dhātu*) and the faculties (*indriya*) are likewise included.
"With reference to this" means with reference to a subsequent apprehension of the same class as the first apprehension stated by the words "eternality in the root" and so forth.
In the second section, what was stated in the first section should be understood in exactly the same manner. Therein, "having seen the danger" means:
“If form were eternal, it would not lead to affliction.
But because this form is non-eternal, therefore—by way of constant oppression and by virtue of its nature of arising and passing away—form is impermanent, conditioned, and dependently originated;
thus, the adherence to the view of eternity is wrong. In this manner, he [describes] the disadvantage and fault therein regarding the doctrine of eternalism.
Having seen [it]. "Coarse" (*oḷārika*): therefore, in the sense of being oppressive and because it is grasped as not being as it truly is, form is not subtle;

it is indeed coarse. The demonstration of the impermanent nature and so forth of feeling and the rest is due to the fact that form, feeling, and the others share a common destiny (*samānayogakkhema*).
