"He relinquishes" means he abandons. "Three tenets" refers to the views of eternalism, annihilationism, and partial-eternalism. Because those with the view of eternalism [remain] in the cycle of existence...

They are close to lust; for it is said that they "cling" (olīyanti). Because of their views of becoming and non-becoming, these beings have no lifting up of the head from saṃsāra—this much should be understood as the specific distinction of these three.
By stating, "He knows that this world and the other world exist," he expresses the reason why the view of eternalism is less blameworthy.
“He relishes and delights in the round” indicates slow fading away (dandhavirāgatā). Therefore he said, “Therefore,” and so forth.
By the statement “he knows that this world and the other world exist,” he shows that he rejects the wandering of beings through various destinies.
By the statement “he knows that there is a fruit for well-done and ill-done deeds,” he [shows] the fruit of karma. Wholesome...

By the phrase "he does not act," [the text] shows that karma is [the cause]; by the phrase "he does not fear while performing unwholesome deeds," it shows that merit and demerit arise from their own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).
He relishes and delights in the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) because he is inclined toward it.

He is unable to quickly abandon his wrong view because he does not approve of the cutting off of the cycle of existence. For the proponent of annihilationism (*ucchedavādī*) conceives of annihilation within that very existence.
Beyond that, he knows that this world and the other world exist; he knows that there is a fruit for good and evil deeds because he is one who proclaims the efficacy of kamma.
For generally, among those who hold views of annihilationism, or who are intent upon inherent nature, destiny, or chance, his adherence is directed elsewhere.
He quickly abandons [wrong] views due to the absence of delight in the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*). The Perfections (*pāramiyo*).
The construction is as follows: being able to fulfill [the requirements], he becomes a Paccekabuddha; merely by way of worldly convention, he becomes a Sammāsambuddha and attains Parinibbāna.
"Unable" means unable to become a Buddha. "Having made an aspiration" means having accomplished the aspiration for the state of being the Chief Disciples (Aggasāvaka) and so forth.
"Having become a disciple" means having become a Chief Disciple or a Great Disciple (Mahāsāvaka), and therein also a possessor of the three knowledges (tevijja).

Having become a disciple of the Buddha, one who possesses the six direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiñña*) and has attained the analytical insights (*paṭisambhidā*), or even one who is a practitioner of bare insight (*sukkha-vipassaka*), attains final Nibbāna.

All of this is presented for the purpose of showing how, by relying on a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitta*), one enters the certainty of rightness (*sammatta-niyāma*) and quickly achieves dispassion (*virāga*).
Therefore, he said, "Therefore," and so forth.
"202. With sour gruel (kañjiya) alone": with fermented rice water (āranāḷa). "With a view similar to sour gruel": with a nihilistic view (ucchedadassana). "Filled":
one whose underlying intention (ajjhāsaya) is full. "He": that wanderer (paribbājaka). "Without abandoning": without breaking [the bonds]. "Strife (viggaha)": conflict;
taking it as a mutual contradictory grasping, thinking, "This alone is the truth, the other is false. "Dispute (vivāda)": a contradictory argument. "Affliction (vighāta)": caused by opposition.
"Cittavighātaṃ" means they cause vexation; they inflict physical and mental exhaustion by means of quarrels and disputes. "Disvā ādīnavaṃ" means having seen the disadvantage, thinking:
"Such is the disadvantage of these views; moreover, because they do not lead to liberation, they are a great disadvantage both now and in the future.
Thus, having seen the disadvantage.
205. “It follows after the body” (*kāyanvaya*) in such phrases as “This am I, this is my self”; that itself, or the collection thereof, is *kāyanvayatā*, which is a defilement bound to the body.

Therefore he said: “The body... [the meaning]. “The state of being unmixed” means the state of being established through non-confusion. By this, he shows their arising and passing away according to their respective conditions;
for in this way, there is never any confusion among them. Therefore he said: “In this regard, this is the summarized meaning,” and so forth.
Since it was stated without specification as "another feeling" without grasping its specific nature, he said, "they are either unarisen or have disappeared," in order to show that very disappearance.
If it were stated by specifying its specific nature, one might think that some [feelings] are unarisen while others have disappeared.
It is for the purpose of showing their state of being pulverized and scattered—that is, for the purpose of showing their state of breaking up moment by moment.
"He does not agree with anyone" means that he does not speak with any person while his mind is defiled by attachment to views.
Therefore, he said, "Having grasped eternalism," and so forth. "He does not dispute" means that he does not dispute by being in a state of opposition.
"Having turned it over" means having grasped annihilationism or having grasped partial eternalism; thus, according to the method stated, there are three positions.

[The words] should be rearranged and connected. "He expresses by means of that" means that, without overstepping worldly convention (*lokavohāra*) or worldly designation (*lokasamaññā*), he expresses [beings] as a "sentient being," a "person," an "individual," and so forth;
however, unlike those outside this [teaching], he does not adhere [to them with dogmatic clinging]. Therefore, he said, "without misapprehending.
"Any phenomenon whatsoever" means even a single phenomenon among form and the rest. "Not grasping through the grip of misapprehension" means...

"Not grasping" means not grasping by touching upon and apprehending [the object] from the outside, thereby overstepping the true nature (*dhammasabhāva*) of phenomena through such notions as "permanent," etc., or "this is mine," etc.

"One who has done" (*katāvī*) means one who has completed what was to be done. "He would speak" refers to a monk whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*), even though both the conceits of "I-making" (*ahaṅkāra*) and "mine-making" (*mamaṅkāra*) have been utterly eradicated.
One might say, "I say. In this context, "I" refers to one's own internal continuum (*niyakajjhattasantāne*).

"Mine" refers to the objects belonging to that [continuum], as established by worldly convention (*lokaniruḷhe*). "Common usage" (*samañña*) refers to being skilled in that regard; having understood it as "skillful" according to worldly convention, [one uses it].

"By way of mere conventional expression" (*vohāramattena*) means that, having become a *paccekabuddha*, one who is unable to fulfill the perfections for Great Enlightenment becomes a disciple (*sāvaka*).
Having offered [the sacrifice], one does not—like the blind worldling whose craving is not abandoned—cling by way of dogmatic adherence merely through conventional worldly usage.

206. "Regarding eternalism and so forth" means regarding the dogmatic adherence to eternalism and the rest. "Of those various phenomena" is the genitive case used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*).
"Having directly known eternalism" means having directly known the view of eternalism by way of its origin, its passing away, its gratification, and its escape.
Having penetrated by means of distinguished wisdom. "Abandonment" (*pahāna*) means absolute abandonment, total eradication.
"The abandonment of form" (*rūpassa pahāna*) means the abandonment of form through the abandonment of the fetters bound to it.

By means of non-arising and cessation, the mind was liberated without even grasping at the taints (*āsava*) that had already ceased. Regarding the phrase "the mind was liberated from the taints," here [it means] without grasping at anything whatsoever.
"Without omitting": the sixteen kinds of wisdom refer to the sixteen types of wisdom beginning with "great wisdom. "Endowed with four factors" means: being on a full Uposatha day;
the gathering together of many hundreds or many thousands of monks even without being invited by anyone; the fact that all have received full ordination by the "Come, monk" formula (*ehibhikkhu*);
and the possession of the six direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiññā*). Therefore he said, "In this regard, these are the factors," and so forth.
Whatever herein has not been analyzed according to its meaning is indeed easy to understand.
The *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Hidden Meaning) for the commentary on the *Dīghanakhasutta* is completed.
5. Commentary on the *Māgaṇḍiyasutta*.
“Two Māgaṇḍiyas” means two named Māgaṇḍiya. “Resembling the womb of a deity” means resembling the dwelling place of deities.
“This was said” refers to what was said: “on the grass mat in the fire-chamber of the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan.
“Not only on that day” refers to the day on which the wandering ascetic Māgaṇḍiya had a grass mat prepared.
The construction is: "It was not only on that day that the Blessed One approached a certain grove.
"In the vicinity of the village" means near the village. "Having made a sign" means as if having made a sign; for there was no purpose for the Blessed One in making such a sign.
“Suitable for the recluse’s bed” (*samaṇaseyyānurūpa*) means a bed appropriate for a recluse. For this word *rūpa* has the sense of praise.
Therefore he said, “this grass mat,” and so forth. “Uncluttered” (*anākiṇṇa*) means not disordered or jumbled.
It is not shaken or broken by being struck here and there with hands, feet, or head; precisely because it is unshaken, the covering is unbroken. Having demarcated [the area],...
"As if fashioned" means like a painted bed made by a skilled painter, having first conceived it in his mind and then delineated it with lines drawn using a stylus.
"Bhūna" is said to mean "increased"; one who destroys that is a "bhūnahano. Therefore he says, "one who has destroyed growth.
Furthermore, this person considers the practice of restraint regarding the eye and so forth to be the destruction of growth. Therefore he says:
“Of one who establishes a boundary”: “to be expanded” means it should be increased and nourished by the presentation of sublime objects.
Since that occurs through experiencing what has not yet been experienced, he says, “the unseen is to be seen.

But since what has already been experienced becomes redundant, it is said, “the seen is to be transcended. The same method applies to the remaining sections. [He is] one who proclaims the supreme Nibbāna in this very life.
This wanderer is thus; therefore, he proclaims growth in regard to these six doors.

Since he, by rejecting the respective apprehension of objects by each of the six—beginning with the eye—proclaims for the world not growth but rather destruction, he himself is one whose growth has been destroyed and who is devoid of growth.
Because it is remote from defilement, it is noble (*ariya*); because it is a state of the Dhamma that leads to liberation, it is the method (*ñāya*);

and because it is free even from the slightest stain, it is wholesome (*kusala*). Therefore he said: "In the pure, blameless causal factors. "Of one who is exalted" means of one who is sublime by virtue of high birth and so forth.
"Having established a guard over the mouth" means being restrained by means of the mouth. Having taken hold of mangoes, rose-apples, and so forth...

"Without filling [the gaps] as it were" means not mentioning anything whatsoever according to the method of filling out [the discourse], which would otherwise be like mangoes, rose-apples, and so forth, being mutually dissimilar.
Therefore he said: "In the manner I have related.
(208) "Emerging from the attainment of fruition" means emerging from the midday rest (*divāvihāra*). For even the midday rest is called "seclusion" (*paṭisallāna*).
It is said [in such passages] as: "To one who had gone into seclusion and was dwelling in private, this reflection arose in the mind.
For the Blessed One, having heard their conversation after emerging from the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*), rose from his midday rest and went there.
"A sense of urgency" (*saṃvega*) is knowledge accompanied by moral dread; it also arises by way of disenchantment (*nibbidā*), and it is based upon that sense of urgency.
He spoke with intentional meaning, saying: "Agitated by the agitation of rapture. Furthermore, because there is a movement of the mind from its previous state, he said:
"Shaken and trembling. By the phrase "by a man with a sharp intellect," he refers to the Blessed One.
He began the teaching of the Dhamma in the sense that he is skilled in training those to be disciplined, as a place of dwelling; this refers to the state of what ought to be resorted to.

This is an expression denoting a state or characteristic. It is called an *ārāma* (pleasure grove) because one delights (*āramati*) therein; that which has form as its pleasure grove is "form-pleasure-grove" (*rūpārāma*).

For that very reason, because of being inclined toward it, they delight in form, thus it is "delighting in form" (*rūparata*). Because of that, one is intoxicated by form through a wrong attainment, thus it is "intoxicated with form" (*rūpasammudita*).
This is stated having attributed to it the function of impulsion (*javana*) that was struck by that [object]. The same applies to the terms "tamed" (*danta*) and so forth.

The same method applies here. "Tamed" (*danta*) means tamed (*damita*). "Free from wickedness" (*nibbisevana*) means devoid of the nature of deceit. "Guarded" (*gutta*) means guarded by mindfulness; "protected" (*rakkhita*) is a synonym for that.
"Restrained" (*saṃvuta*) means removed by the prevention of entry; hence he said "shut off" (*pihita*). 210.
"The fever of arising" (*uppajjanapariḷāha*) means the fever of the defilements that arise. What statement should be made?

Having experienced the object of form, having grasped the abandonment of its origination and so forth, and having become disenchanted and dispassionate toward it, one who is liberated—does such a person necessarily undergo the designation "one whose growth has been destroyed"? He asks this question.
The wanderer thought that regarding one liberated through attachment to such an essence, one should not say they are "one whose growth has been destroyed," and thus he said, "Nothing, Master Gotama."

211. *Teti tayā*: this is the reading, or else *ayameva* [is the reading]. *Vassa-vāso* means "the rainy-season dwelling," with the middle term elided; one who is fit for the rains is called *vassiko*, meaning suitable for residence during the rainy season.
"Neither too high nor too low" means it is not as high as a summer [dwelling] nor as low as a winter [dwelling];
rather, by having the characteristics of the middle between those two, it is neither too high nor too low. "Neither too thin" refers to [the wall], like that of the winter season...
"Not small" means not too many, as in the case of a summer dwelling (*gimhika*). "Mixed" means having characteristics combined from those described for winter (*hemantika*) and summer dwellings.

"For the purpose of letting in heat" means for the purpose of allowing heat to enter inside through the windows (*niyūha*) by means of the sunlight falling before and after the meal. "The walls and windows are being removed" means...
On the right side, niches are made by projecting them out from the walls. "Large lattices" means wide openings.
"Water-courses" means channels for carrying water.
"Having made bower-groves of blue lotuses" means having made groves of reeds with blooming blue lotuses. "A paste of perfumes."
"Mud mixed with fragrance. "A double wall" means a pair of walls; between them is a pipe through which the water rises up.
"Iron pipe" means a pipe made of iron for the machine. "Net" means a net made of copper or bronze.
"Turning the machine below" means they direct the water-machine at the lower part. "Because of being moistened by the spray of water, there is discoloration."
“Māhosī” means he puts on a blue cloth. “At daybreak” (divākāle) means at the time of day.
Regarding the phrase “I dwell with a mind inwardly calmed,” it is said that by this the Blessed One has shown his own dwelling in the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti); thus he says:
“‘Delighting in that delight’—this was spoken with reference to the delight of the fruition-attainment belonging to the fourth jhāna.”
212. "And their proliferation (papañca) is great" means that for these kings, there is a "great proliferation" consisting of the sphere of success through royal power at all times;
the intention is that they do not obtain [the opportunity] to experience it. They wander about seeking mantras, not the pleasure of wealth.
"Counting" (gaṇanā) refers to counting by uninterrupted units, not counting by groups (vigaṇa) or counting by coins (paṇa). "Turning back" (āvaṭṭa) refers to what has been thus acquired.
Having abandoned divine sensual pleasures, one might turn back, turn around, and be drawn away for the sake of human sensual pleasures. Thus are human sensual pleasures:
just as if someone were to take water with the tip of a blade of *kusa* grass and measure it against the water of the great ocean.
In that case, the water of the great ocean alone is vast, abundant, and sublime; even so, when compared with divine sensual pleasures, human sensual pleasures—
Sensual pleasures are trifling, insignificant, and base; divine pleasures alone are great, abundant, sublime, and exquisite.
"Having attained" means having firmly grasped by way of right attainment, he remains having rendered even divine pleasure inferior.
213. One who possesses happiness caused by health is "happy"; since that happiness belongs to him precisely through the departure of disease, it is said: "First..."
“Suffering first, happy afterwards. One who is *serī* is called one whose life is dependent on themselves; thus he said, “One should be *serī*, alone.

*Sayaṃvaso* means having mastery over oneself; one who possesses that is *sayaṃvasī*. Because it is the cause of the feverish burning of the objects of sensual desire, it is like a pan of glowing coals.
“Having scraped” means having rubbed, that is to say, having scratched.
214. That by which the body becomes sweet-smelling is said to destroy the skin; the hide becomes as if perforated.
For this very reason it is said, "one whose bodily sensitivities are impaired. "Obtained" means acquired.

Because the faculty of wisdom (*paññindriya*) has been impaired due to being overcome by ignorance and through conjunction with opposing conditions, [it leads] to the fruit of suffering in the future. At present...
And because of the abundance of the suffering of the defilements and the painful contact inherent in sensual pleasures, one who— regarding those things associated with both—

fails to perceive them as such and instead adheres to them as being exclusively pleasant, possesses a perception based on perversion; he does not merely perceive what is pleasant as "pleasant" due to a pleasant feeling alone.
215. “Those” refers to the openings of wounds on the body of one afflicted with leprosy. “Impure” means unattractive (*asubha*). “Foul-smelling” means having a stench of putrefaction.
“Putrid” means consisting of corpses. “Now” means at this present time. When [the body] is excessively tormented by scratching with the nails or by being scorched with fire, the worms...
[etc. ...ooze out; thereby the sensation becomes slight. “Thus” means because of the attenuation of the sensation in the manner described.
Health is the supreme gain because the acquisition of wealth and other benefits arises when health exists, whereas in the absence of health, such gain is rendered useless;
and because health serves as the basis for all attainments, both pertaining to the present life and otherwise.
Nibbāna is the supreme bliss because bliss arises from it, and because such bliss is unattainable in its absence; furthermore, it is so because it is secluded from all conditioned phenomena.

And because of the total absence of the suffering of *saṃsāra*, and because once that [Nibbāna] is attained there is an absence of all the suffering of the round (*vaṭṭa*), Nibbāna is the supreme happiness. "Of the preliminary paths" refers to those paths belonging to the prior stage of the Noble Path, which are distinguished by the divisions of body-contemplation (*kāyānupassanā*) and so forth.
And their quality of "leading to the Deathless" consists precisely in their being inclined toward it and in their being realized as such.

He said: "By the very path of the prior stage, it leads to the Deathless. The Noble Eightfold Path is secure because it is free from affliction through the eradication of all perils, and because it is the cause of total security for those who possess it, owing to their being entirely free from affliction.
"Taken by way of their respective tenets" means that they were grasped as such solely by way of the tenets of the eternalists and others.
Regarding the phrase *khemam-atagāminam*: this is an expression formed by the elision of a case ending (*vibhattilopa*), namely *khemam-angatagāminam*.
It shows that the meaning, however, should be understood through the elision of the case ending.
216. *Anomajjati* means he immerses himself repeatedly; he bathes while lowering his hand further and further downward.

217. It is "thick" (*ghana*) because it is dense; it is "excellent" (*sampanna*) because it is beautiful due to its glossy quality. It is called *sāhuḷi* because it is taken up by those who are good—those who are supremely desireless and contented. A "rags from a dustheap" (*saṅkāracoḷaka*) is always black. 218.

It is "like a disease" (*rogabhūta*) in the sense of causing pain and in the sense of being an affliction here and there. Even with insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*) that has reached its peak, one sees health only partially; and since Nibbāna is the opposite of the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*), he said, "and also insight-knowledge."
219. "In the interval" means in the midst of the first arising of aging and death. "Impaired" is said in the sense of being corrupted by the humors such as bile and phlegm.
One who removes the humors of bile and so forth through the use of medicine, restoring what was impaired to its natural state, is said to "produce eyes.
"Ruined" means having fallen into a state where they are incapable of arising again.

220. Regarding the previously mentioned *sāhuḷiya* robes: "with a mind following the cycle" means with a conforming mind due to not seeing the danger in the beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra-vatta*).
221. "Of the Dhamma" means of Nibbāna. "In accordance with the Dhamma" means a suitable method leading to liberation. Therefore he said, "the appropriate practice.
"In the five aggregates" indicates the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcupādānakkhandhā*). By the words "Alas, for a long time indeed... and so forth...
In the Pāli text, the turning away (*vivaṭṭa*) is shown. Therefore he said: "By saying 'the cessation of clinging,' he shows the turning away. The rest is easy to understand.
The *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Hidden Meaning) for the commentary on the *Māgaṇḍiya-sutta* is completed.
6. Commentary on the *Sandaka-sutta*.
223. A pool made by rain from the sky is a "sky-made pool. Therefore he said: "rain... [and] a lake. As for "caves," there are three types of caves:
sand caves, stone caves, and mixed caves. Among these, the sand cave was located in a place where water had seeped through;
however, the low-lying area was completely submerged by water. "Having made a hollow" means having made a very deep depression below.

"Having reflected on the 'beginningless' (anamatagga)" means: having reflected on the beginninglessness [of saṃsāra] by way of such passages as, "That abode of beings is not easily found which has not been inhabited by me throughout this long stretch of time," and likewise, "This pond must have been inhabited by me before;
even that place and that personal existence (attabhāva) have reached the state of non-designation (apaññattikabhāva). Thus, one reflects on the beginningless.
It is proper to go to such a place. By this same method, the procedure for reflection regarding the sight of the ocean, mountains, and so forth, should also be understood.

Regarding the phrase "to her crying out loudly": she makes a loud sound; [the contemplation is] on the basis for the gratification of sensual desires (*kāmassāda*) and the gratification of existence (*bhavassāda*), etc., thinking:
"This and that sensual pleasure is desirable, lovely, and agreeable; such-and-such an existence is desirable, lovely, and agreeable; thus this world, through those things dear..."

"More dear"—thus [he speaks] regarding the object known as the gratification of sensual pleasures (*kāmasāda*), the gratification of existence (*bhavassāda*), the gratification of the world (*lokassāda*), and so forth.

It is called "leading out" (*niyyāna*) because by means of it one goes out from an unhappy rebirth and from *saṃsāra*. It is "leading out" because it deserves that leading out, or because it is connected with leading out;
or else, it is "leading out" because it has leading out as its fruit. [It is so called] in contrast to the defilement of verbal misconduct and the like.
It is called "leading out" (*niyyānīyā*) because it leads out; by shortening the vowel *ī* and changing the letter *y* to *k*, it becomes "leading forth" (*niyyānikā*).

This refers to the abstention from idle chatter together with volition. Its opposite is "not leading forth" (*aniyyānikā*); the state of being that is "the quality of not leading forth" (*aniyyānikatta*);
therefore, it is "because of the quality of not leading forth. "Become horizontal" (*tiracchānabhūtā*) means having become a barrier (*tirokaraṇabhūtā*). "Household talk" (*gehassitakathā*)...

Discourse connected with sensual desire (*kāmapaṭisaṃyuttakathā*). "Cultivating the meditation subject" means cultivating the meditation subject of the Four Noble Truths connected with impermanence (*aniccatā*).
"Together with the goal" means *sātthaka*; the meaning is that it is connected with welfare (*hita*). "Street" (*visikhā*) refers to a residential area;
by the mention of the street, the inhabitants thereof are included, just as in expressions such as "a village has arrived. For this very reason, he said: "brave and capable," and "faithful..."

And [the phrase] “faithful” is used. Since the word *kumbhadāsī* (water-carrier slave-girls) is spoken by way of their place of residence (*kumbhaṭṭhāna*), he says: “or the discourse on the water-carrier slave-girls.
Just as with common usage, having taken up their mere conventional designation (*vohāramatta*), it is said:

“in the practice of the holy life (*brahmacariyavāsa*)”; they are “unmade,” meaning not made or fashioned by any cause, whether even or uneven. There is no method of making (*katavidha-karaṇavidhi*) that exists.
"These are unconditioned" (*akaṭavidhā*). By these two phrases, he shows that in the world they are not produced by any cause or condition whatsoever.
"Not even fashioned by supernormal power" (*iddhiyāpi na nimmitā*): they are not created even by the supernormal power of anyone who has attained mastery over the mind, such as a deity or a lord.

"Unfashioned" (*animmātā*): not caused to be fashioned by anyone. "The state of being a producer of form and so forth" (*rūpādijanakabhāva*): [the state of being a producer] of visible forms, sounds, and so on.
His intention is that even visible forms and so forth have an existence that is not dependent on earth and the other elements.
Just as a mountain peak is not produced by anyone and does not produce anything else, so too are these [elements];

thus he said, "They are called 'fixed-peaks' (kūṭaṭṭhā) because they stand like mountain peaks. That which is spoken of as the sprout and so forth being born from the seed exists already [at the time of the seed].
It departs from there without being perceived; the intention is that otherwise, there would be the apprehension of one thing by means of another.
"Thus standing" means thus standing without modification. "By both ways as well" means they say it is by both meanings: also by the two phrases, "standing firm like a peak, standing like a pillar.
"Of those seven bodies" refers to their state of standing, which is due to the absence of modification.

Because they are established. "They do not move" means they do not undergo change (*vikāra*). For it is due to the absence of change that those seven bodies possess the stability of a pillar firmly fixed in its base.
And to show that "immovability" in actual meaning is simply remaining in one's natural state (*pakati*), it is said: "they do not transform.
Precisely because they are of a nature not subject to transformation, they do not obstruct one another. For if there were change...
There might be harmfulness due to the need for something to be produced, and likewise there might be helpfulness due to the need for something to be assisted;
therefore, in order to show the absence of such [agency], the text says "it is not capable," and so forth.
Earth itself is called the "earth-body" because it is a part of the body. There is no one indeed who is capable of killing or causing to be killed.

Because the seven bodies are permanent and unchanging, it should be understood that by this very fact their indestructibility and inviolability are stated in substance. For it is said: "Of the seven bodies," and so forth.
There is no one capable of hearing or making them hear, because each of them individually lacks the capacity for hearing, even with respect to a single part thereof.
This demonstrates its lack of efficacy. If there is no killer at all, how can there be the striking of a weapon? To this he says: "Just as in the case of a heap of beans," and so forth.
The intention is that it is merely a matter of perception; for in the ultimate sense, killing, slaughtering, and so on do not exist at all, because the bodies cannot be disintegrated.
By saying "he demonstrates a useless view through mere reasoning," he indicates that because of such logicians...

Because they imagine whatever they have conceived out of unrestrained imagination to be essential, and thus adhere to it while grasping at speculative views, he shows that wise people should not engage in investigation regarding the basis of their views.
"Some" refers to the teachers of the *Sārasamāsa*. "By way of the five faculties" means by way of the five physical faculties (*rūpindriya*).
"Kamma" is their tenet because it is well-known as the nature of kamma. The sixty-two paths of practice include crooked speech, evasion, and so forth.
"In one eon" means in one great eon (*mahākappa*).
"The plane of men" is a designation by way of the preeminent individual; indeed, women also desire these planes. "Bhikkhu."
And terms such as *pannaka* and so forth are found in the scriptures themselves. Regarding these, they say that a *pannaka* is one who wanders about for alms;
or else, he is one who has entered upon their mode of practice (*paṭipanna*). A *jina* is "worn out" (*jiṇṇa*);

they say it means one whose constituent elements have become debased due to old age, or one who stands having conquered the opposite of his own practice. It is said that when he has become such, he does not teach the Dhamma to anyone.
He does not speak; therefore he says, "he said nothing. Regarding "one who does not obtain" (alābhin):

he is one who does not obtain due to being endowed with the causes of non-obtainment as described in the passage beginning, "He does not accept from the mouth of a jar," and so forth. For that very reason, because the ascetic is overcome by weakness from hunger and is intent on lying down, he calls him "pannabhūmi" (the fallen ground).
“Hundreds of livelihoods” means hundreds of ways of making a living that constitute the livelihoods of beings. By the mention of cattle (*pasu*), the species of sheep is included;

by the mention of deer (*miga*), the entire species of wild animals such as the *ruru* and the *gavaya* is included. “Many gods” refers to the many gods categorized according to their internal divisions, such as those belonging to the realm of the Four Great Kings (*cātumahārājika*) and those belonging to the Brahmā-world (*brahmakāyika*).
Among these, a certain internal division of the gods of the Four Great Kings is [described] in the *Mahāsamaya Sutta*.
It should be illustrated. Humans are also infinite: humans are of infinite divisions according to the distinctions of continent, country, clan, lineage, livelihood, and so forth.
*Pesācā* are simply *pisācā*; they should be understood as the great [spirits] such as the *aparapeta*s and others.

He refers to the Chaddanta Lake and the Mandākinī by the names Kuḷīra and Mucalinda. "Knots" (*gaṇṭhikā*) means knots on tree trunks. Even a wise person... [etc. ...does not go upward; why? Because the duration of the wandering of sentient beings is fixed.
That which is unripened, being the cause for wandering in *saṃsāra*, is said to be "ripened" by means of virtue (*sīla*) and so forth, in order that purity may be attained very swiftly.
That which is ripened is said to be "cleansed" by bringing it to a state of complete exhaustion through repeated contact and attainment.
"In a ball of thread" means in a coil of thread. "It runs away even as it is being unwound" is the simile for the gradual nature of the *saṃsāra* of sentient beings.
It shows that [the view] merely diminishes and does not increase, because its nature is limited. 229.

"Including it within the doctrine of necessity" means that even though he has claimed omniscience, being unable to achieve it through partial knowledge and unable to avoid the manifestation of his own ignorance in that regard, he includes it within the doctrine of necessity, saying, "Such is this necessity. 230.
One who possesses oral tradition (*anussava*) which serves as a support for his discourse on the Dhamma is called an *anussavī*; therefore, this is his "supporting doctrine" (*apassayavāda*).

To show this, he said, "dependent on hearsay" (*anussavanissita*). "Taking what is heard as truth" means that one stands by accepting whatever has been heard as the truth. "By way of mastery of the Piṭakas" means by way of the accomplishment of the texts;
having made such a text proficient and mastered through recitation, one expounds the Dhamma based upon it. Therefore, he said, "from the Vaggas, Paṇṇāsakas," and so forth.

232. "Of dull wisdom" means of limited wisdom. "Deluded" means utterly confused. "Verbal evasion" (vācāvikkhepa) refers to the various and manifold ways of evading through speech—the rejection (*khepa*) of the arguments of opponents—such as saying, "It is not thus for me," and so forth.

It is called *amarā* because the aforementioned verbal evasion does not die (*na marati*) nor is it cut off (*na pacchijjati*) by means of this [view]. The view that operates therein is the *amarā-vikkhepikā-diṭṭhi*.
Evasive proliferation (*amarāvikkhepa*): that is evasive proliferation. "Endless proliferation" (*apariyantavikkhepa*) refers to the evasion of one who is questioned with "Is it thus for me?
and so forth, by not reaching a conclusion. It "runs hither and thither" because it does not settle upon a single nature.
"It does not arrive at a grasp" means that, due to its state of false grasping, it sets aside the previous position in order to formulate a reply, and thus fails to reach a firm conclusion.
He does not approach [the truth]. *Amarāvikkhepa* is the "evasion by the immortal" (or the "immortal evasion") in the direction of the immortal.
In the phrase "this is wholesome," the word *iti* has the sense of a manner; the meaning is "in this manner.

An evasive person (*amarāvikkhepika*), because he finds nothing to his own liking, [responds] to whatever matter is asked of him by anyone—just as he would with what is wholesome—in the same way [with anything else].
By saying, “It is not so for me either,” and so forth, he falls into mere equivocation in each instance;
therefore, the statement beginning with “It is not so for me either” is a demonstration of the mode of equivocation by way of negating the various modes of questioning encountered therein.
But is it not appropriate here that one who speaks with equivocation should remain steadfast in the position of equivocation by not conceding the side of equivocation?
No; for even there, because that confused person’s evasive doctrine proceeds precisely by way of denial.

Therefore it was said, "No. For instance, when Sañjaya Belaṭṭhaputta was questioned by King Ajātasattu regarding the visible fruits of the ascetic life, he gave an evasive answer by means of denying the existence of the threefold world beyond and so forth.

Here it is asked: "But surely this Eel-Wriggler, not understanding as they really are any phenomena such as the wholesome and so forth, nor the triad of the next world and so on, merely resorts to evasion whenever he is questioned on various points;
how then can he be considered one who holds a speculative view? For he does not [evoke] the matter asked about like one who is unwilling to speak."
“Is it not logical that one who does not know [the answer] becomes a holder of a wrong view merely by resorting to equivocation? It is replied:
It is not merely by resorting to equivocation in response to a question that one becomes a holder of a wrong view; rather, it is through the influence of a false adherence (*micchābhinivesa*).

For it is precisely the person who has falsely adhered through the adherence to eternalism (*sassatābhinivesa*) who, due to dullness of intellect, [fails to understand] wholesome and other such phenomena.
Furthermore, by failing to practice correctly according to reality regarding the triad of the afterlife and so forth,
one falls into evasive equivocation because of the inability to make another understand a matter that one has not understood oneself, and out of fear of speaking falsehood. Alternatively,
due to a lack of comprehension and a lack of conviction concerning merit and demerit and their respective results, one merely employs evasive equivocation when questioned on those subjects.
"Beautiful" (*sundara*) should be understood as a distinct view that arises for one who, having generated liking and preference, becomes attached;
it is like the "sevenfold negation" (*sattabhaṅga*) view. Furthermore, because it is bound to the faculties, it is shown to exist in the third position. 234.
Regarding the phrase "one who makes a store" (*sannidhikāraka*), here those things not bound to the faculties are intended; thus, there is the mention of sesame, rice, and so forth.

It was said, "Sesame, rice, and so forth are recognized," with reference to the occasional practice of collecting a measure of rice and other items for the sake of avoiding the world's loss of confidence. 236.
"The Ājīvakas are dead" means that these Ājīvakas are entirely devoid of right practice and are practicing only wrongly.
They are called "dead" because of the absence of that life of virtue (sīla-jīvita) which is designated as "higher virtue" (adhisīla). "Those whose sons are dead" means those whose sons have died.

Regarding the phrase "there is a dwelling in the holy life under the ascetic Gotama": there is indeed for the practitioner a dwelling in the holy life that is pure, complete, and brings about the total destruction of suffering for one who practices it.
By this, the excellence of the Dhamma (dhammasudhammatā) and so forth is illustrated here.
It illuminates the state of being a perfectly awakened Buddha, and by the phrase "it does not exist elsewhere," it shows its absence among the outsiders (*bāhiraka*). The rest is easy to understand.
The *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Hidden Meaning) for the commentary on the *Sandaka-sutta* is completed.
7. Commentary on the *Mahāsakuludāyi-sutta*.
237. *Abhiññāta* means known by way of specific characteristics as being "such-and-such" or "of such-and-such a kind.

When it is said *appasaddavinīta*, this can mean either "disciplined in making little noise" or "disciplined through the state of making little noise and speaking softly"; however, in these cases, the state of being disciplined by another is indicated.
But the Blessed One was disciplined by his own self-existent knowledge (*sayambhuñāṇa*) all by himself. Therefore, in the Pāḷi it says: "*Appasaddavinīto*."
It was not stated. Therefore he said: "For the Blessed One was not disciplined by another.
238. Starting from yesterday, the few days immediately preceding that are called "prior";
"prior" means earlier, which is to say, past. "After that" means immediately following the aforementioned past day.
*Paraṃ* means "further" because it is exceedingly prior (*atisayena purimattā*).

Thus, although there is a state of being prior and further among these two as they occur respectively, nevertheless, starting from that which is called "further" (*purimatara*) here, whatever is proximal to it is "further," and whatever is further is called "further. A hall associated with curiosity is a "curiosity-hall" (*kutūhalasālā*).
As in the expression “a chariot drawn by thoroughbreds. These are seeing and so forth.

“By means of qualities that are not according to reality” means: it is proclaimed, resounded, and raised up by means of qualities that are falsely illuminated—that is, by the mere object [of those qualities] as it has been wrongly described.

A “ford” (tittha) is that by which one crosses over or transcends; it refers to the supreme path. However, the path of those who hold wrong views, though not according to reality, is also [called a ford].

Because they cause those [beings] to cross over in such a manner, they are called "founders" (*titthakara*) by way of that verbal designation. "Enters" (*osarati*) means "penetrates. (239) "Coherent" (*sahita*) means not contradictory in its preceding and succeeding parts.

"Nothing has arisen" (*na kiñci jātaṃ*): because it is corrupted by the fault of the thesis (*paṭiññā-dosa*), the fault of the reason (*hetu-dosa*), the fault of the example (*udāharaṇa-dosa*), and the fault of the conclusion (*upasaṃhāra-dosa*), nothing at all has arisen.
Therefore he said: "Your proposition has been refuted. A "proposition" (*vāda*) is a fault, for they revile one another by means of it.
“By way of its own nature” means by way of the portion as it occurs in its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).

240. “One should press” means one should press it in a vessel together with honey-syrup and give it. “Having associated with fellow celibates” means having employed a means of harassment toward those who share the same Dhamma; therefore he said, “having engaged in dispute. 241.
“By this or that” means by something inferior compared to what is excellent. Therefore he said, “by the base and the basest.”

242. *Bhattakosakena* means by one who eats from a bowl; the meaning is "one who eats from a small saucer. *Beluvamattabhattāhārā* means those whose food intake consists of a meal the size of a *billā* fruit. *Oṭṭhavaṭṭiyā* means by the rim of the mouth. *Sabbākāreneva* means in every single way.

*Anappāhāro* (one of non-meager food) should not be called "meager" even occasionally, considering that he never takes little food. In this regard, it is something exceedingly difficult for others to master.
In order to show the Blessed One’s moderation in food, the words “on the ground for striving,” and so forth, were spoken. “Mayā” (by me) is an ablative expression.
“Visesatarā” means more distinguished by that quality.
Because they wear rag-robes solely by way of undertaking a vow, they are called “paṃsukūlikā”; thus he said, “those who have undertaken the practice of wearing rag-robes.”
The meaning of the word, however, should be understood according to the method explained in the *Visuddhimagga*.

The same principle applies to such terms as "alms-food eaters" (*piṇḍapātika*) and "those who go from house to house" (*sapadānacārin*). Because they are cut with a knife at various places, they are "knife-harvested" (*satthalūkha*). They gather only whatever is suitable;
thus it is said: "having gathered... pe... having taken only a firm place. [Regarding] "alābu-roma-sāni":
"Alābuloma" refers to those whose robe-cloth threads are even finer than the fibers of a bottle-gourd.
"Pātitasāṇa-paṃsukūla" means rag-robes discarded along with a corpse, such as the one made of *sāṇa* cloth which the Teacher took after shaking out the chaff from a mere gourd-sized bundle.
The practice of the honey-bee-like alms-round, described in the verse beginning "Just as a bee [from a flower]," is the "eating of scraps of alms-food" (*piṇḍiyālopabhojana*).
Because of the statement, "Renunciation depends on [this]," it is said that they delight in the "alms-gathering vow" (*uñchāsaka-vata*), which is the natural state (*pakati*) of the monks.
Here, the word *vata* refers to their own vow known as the "natural vow. Therefore, he says:
"In the natural vow of the monks, known as the practice of alms-gathering. "Standing at the doors of high and low houses" means standing outside the gate-porches of large and small dwellings.
"Having gathered together the rice mixed with *kabara*" means having collected the rice mixed with *kaṇājaka* (bran).
"Starting from the threshold" means starting from the door-sill of the house.
"For the purpose of supporting the robe" means for the purpose of protecting the robe. And here, because the Buddhas, in this world including the devas...
It is an unsurpassed field of merit, and its status as a field of merit has reached the highest excellence; therefore,
having described such assistance to sentient beings and accepting the householder’s robe while not neglecting them,
it should be understood that they have indeed reached the highest excellence in contentment with the four requisites.
244. "With a cause" (*sappaccaya*) means that he teaches the Dhamma by way of having a root-cause (*sa-hetuka*) and a reason (*sa-kāraṇa*); this is the meaning here.

However, the questioner, not understanding the underlying intention (*adhippāya*), said, "But what... and so forth. The other [the teacher] clarifies the intention with the words, "It is not that he does not teach," and so on.
And here, "source" (*nidāna*) is intended in the sense of an indicative cause of origin (*uppatti-kāraṇa*); and that refers to each respective thing that is appropriate for its non-arising.
It is called "possessing a demonstration" (*sappāṭihāriya*) because it removes that which is opposed to the goal; thus he says, "This is a synonym for the former [term].
Alternatively, the warding off of lust and so forth is *paṭihāriya*; that itself is *pāṭihāriya*. Together with this *pāṭihāriya*, it is "possessing a demonstration.
For the Teacher teaches the Dhamma precisely by way of the prohibition of lust and the other defilements.
“Of each and every question” means: whatever question another person, having prepared, approaches the Blessed One and asks—of each and every such question.
“The path of discourse that comes further on” means: when the answer has been given, the path of discourse that proceeds further than that.
“Speaking with distinction” is what is meant; [as in the phrase] “Venerable Gotama, it is fit to be spoken.”
By means of a striking statement, he speaks with distinction, as if pointing out a weapon brought for his own destruction or a reason brought for the purpose of shattering his own position.
"In between" (antarantare) means within the sequence of discourse being spoken by me.
"He should give" (dadeyya) means he should speak. "In such places" (evarūpesu ṭhānesu) refers to occasions of debate and counter-debate with opponents.
Having brought forward the words of the Sutta taught by me in order to restrain them, they expect my very own instruction and advice.
246. "I fulfill" means I fulfill their wish; "I complete" means I complete their aspiration.
Regarding "higher virtue" (*adhisīla*): the virtue of the Buddhas is superior to the virtue of the disciples and the virtue of the Paccekabuddhas.
"Exalted" (*ukkaṭṭha*) means supreme, because it is not shared by others. Therefore he said: "It is called the Buddha’s virtue.
"Situation-arisen wisdom" (*ṭhānuppattikapaññā*) is wisdom that arises spontaneously in various situations. Therefore he said: "In that regard," and so forth.
"The remaining wisdom" refers to the wisdom—both that which has been mentioned in this text and that which has not—which is distinct from the two types of knowledge already described.

"247. Of the special attainments": this refers to the special qualities to be attained, such as the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*). "Higher knowledge" (*abhiññā*) means the six higher knowledges;

among these, according to the description of the highest level, it is the wisdom of the supreme path (*aggamagga-paññā*)—possessing the six higher knowledges—that is intended here by the term "higher knowledge.
Its "consummation," "termination," "perfection," "culmination," and "pinnacle" is the fruit of the summit (*aggaphala*).
He says, "It is called... having attained the superknowledges (*abhiññā*) ...

up to arahantship. Regarding "exertion as a means" (*upāyapadhāna*): it refers to the exertion that serves as the means for the attainment of the noble fruits (*ariyaphala*). The phrase "for the purpose of the non-arising of unarisen evil states, etc.
is included; these [purposes] remain exactly as they are, and the word *sammā* (right) is an illuminator of this meaning, signifying that it accomplishes that very purpose.
It means that which serves as the means for the non-arising of unarisen evil and so forth regarding the intended goal;
the sense is "the means for striving. Alternatively, with reference to the word *sammā* (rightly) indicating the sense of "properly" (*yoniso*), it is said: "in proper striving.
"He generates desire" means he arouses or sets in motion wholesome desire characterized by the wish to act. "He exerts effort" means [he applies] the exertion of application.
"He exerts": he performs physical and mental energy (*vīriya*). "He rouses the mind": by means of that very co-nascent energy, he rouses the mind from the side of indolence.

"He strives": he sets in motion energy that constitutes the right exertion (*sammappadhāna*). Furthermore, these four terms [exertion, rousing, striving, and endeavoring] correspond respectively to cultivation through repetition (*āsevana*), development (*bhāvanā*), frequent practice (*bahulīkamma*), and steadfast performance (*sātaccakiriyā*).
They should be joined together. Or rather, by the term "exerts" (*padahati*), the energy that has reached its culmination through repeated practice and so forth should be joined with it.
"For the sake of fulfilling growth" means for the sake of fulfilling [it] as far as the completion of cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
"That which is stability" is the firm establishment of wholesome states (*kusaladhamma*) through the departure of their opposites. That is non-forgetfulness.
Non-destruction (*avināsa*). "Expansion" (*vepulla*) means that which is entirely vastness and greatness. "Fulfillment of development" (*bhāvanāpāripūrī*) means the completion of development.
It should also be understood as having the same meaning [as "non-destruction"], because the preceding and following terms share an identical sense.
The preliminary practice (*pubbabhāgapaṭipadā*) has been described, since it was undertaken for the purpose of elucidating the path to the attainment of various specific distinctions.
It is said that there is no lack of harmfulness in unwholesome states through their non-arising;
thus, the expression "arising" is used because those already arisen are grasped as being in the interval between aggregates. Likewise, it is said regarding wholesome states through their arising:
the expression "not arising" is used because those already arisen are grasped as being in the interval between aggregates. "Ceasing"...
"Perishing through conjunction with their opposites," not ceasing by way of momentary cessation.

Greed and the rest are to be understood as those [defilements] liable to arise in those who have commenced insight meditation (*vipassanā*). "Having arisen once" is merely a statement regarding their intrinsic nature;
for the Path arises only a single time. "Ceasing" means ceasing by its own inherent power (*sarasena*); for it does not [persist].
There is indeed what is called "the conjunction with opposites. "Of the fruit" means of the fruit that arises immediately in the subsequent moment.
By the phrase "it ceases only after having given its condition," he shows that the Path brings benefit exclusively both now and in the future.
"In the former case as well" refers to the thought: "If unarisen wholesome states do not arise in me, they would lead to my harm."
Regarding this third instance as well, it is stated in the Commentary that "serenity and insight must be taken up.

However, he rejects this as inappropriate because, since the Path has not yet arisen, those two [serenity and insight] still exist; and even if the Path does not arise, the existence of the round of existence (vaṭṭa) and its disadvantages remains.
Thus, he rejects it on the grounds that serenity and insight are common to both states. If [it is argued that] even for serenity and insight...
Non-attainment brings about harm; however, regarding the non-attainment of the Path, nothing need be said.

There is great reverence [due to the Saṅgha]; therefore, thinking, "Because of my reverence for the Saṅgha, I am not permitted to pay homage according to my own wish," he did not go out together with the Saṅgha.
There is no such treasury of relics elsewhere as this great treasury of relics.
For indeed, after being brought out, only a few relics were taken to various cetiyas;

however, here, when the Rāmagāma stūpa had collapsed, a measure (doṇa) of relics was brought and entered into the Nāga abode. "Not too weak" means: are they not indeed exceedingly weak? "Having become stirred" means:

having generated a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), thinking, "How indeed could one such as I come to such misfortune? "Not accepting that statement," meaning: what does he say who refuses to accept the words, "Such a thing as this should be spoken concerning one such as me"?
"There is no other powerful cause for stabilization more potent than the attainment of peace (santasamāpatti)"; therefore, he said, "one who has fallen away from that...
cannot," meaning: how can one who has lapsed from it become established in right practice? For when a great rope is cut, strands of thread are not able to provide support.
Having thus shown this with respect to serenity (samatha), [the same principle applies] to this subject as being of the same nature as that.
With this intention regarding *vipassanā-pīti* (insight-rapture), he said: “Thus, when serenity and insight have arisen... they lead [to the goal].

“Wearing the saffron robe” means possessing the saffron-colored garment. “Having pressed the waist and wrapped it around” is to be construed as: they saw him wrapped firmly, as if pressing down the lower fold (*ovaṭṭika*) from behind. “In the manner stated” refers to [the passage] beginning with:
“These sensual pleasures are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change,” concerning both sensual objects (*vatthu-kāma*) and defilements of sensuality (*kilesa-kāma*).

For one who suppresses and eradicates desire and lust through the practice of renunciation preceded by the vision of danger, [the taints are abandoned] according to the method explained below in the commentary on the *Sabbāsava Sutta* and other texts, beginning with: "The unarisen taint of sensual desire does not arise.
It is called "having that as its object" (*tad-ārammaṇa*) because the resultant consciousness has ceased after having experienced the flavor of that object. Having experienced it, having existed...

And it is "vanished" (*vigata*), meaning it has become vanished. For that which has been experienced (*anubhūta*) is expressed by the word *bhūta* (become) through its commonality with the state of having become;

indeed, the commonality itself is specified by the prefix. Furthermore, because there is no desire for it to denote the object (*kamma-vacana*), the word *anubhūta* should be understood as signifying the experiencer (*anubhavaka*).
Having arisen and ceased with respect to the object, the ripening (*vipāka*) deserves to be called "having become and vanished."

By way of grasping through conceptualization (*vikappa*), unwholesome and wholesome karma—due to lust and its opposites respectively—experiences the flavor of the object and thus deserves to be called "vanished" after having experienced it.

However, since the aforementioned result (*vipāka*) proceeds solely by way of experiencing the flavor of the object, it is described as "vanished" in the primary sense (*nippariyāya*) precisely because it has experienced [the object]; and because it is described in that manner, [it is so designated].

Having become [a latent tendency] through the process of transformation (*bhavita*), by way of its disappearance; and having taken the term "arisen" (*uppanna*) from the passage, "for the abandoning of arisen unwholesome states and for the maintenance of arisen wholesome states," the abandoning and increase of things similar to that [arisen state] were taught.
Furthermore, past karma has "arisen" (*uppatita*) in the sense of making an opportunity for maturation (*vipaccituṃ*). And from that...
Future resultant [kamma] that has begun to arise is called "arisen by way of making room" (*okāsakatuppanna*).
With reference to that which is understood as "arisen" even without the word *uppanna*, it was said: "I do not, O monks, [declare a result] for volitional actions," and so forth.
"In those" refers to the aggregates that have become the ground for insight (*vipassanā*). "Latent defilements" (*anusayita-kilesa*) are those that proceed by way of latent tendency (*anusaya*).
The defilements to be abandoned by the path that have not yet been abandoned are intended here. Therefore he said: “The past... [etc.

...should not be so called. For it cannot be said that those [defilements] which are to be abandoned by the path possess a state of being present and so forth, according to the simile of the mango tree, because no such distinction arises for them.
By the phrase “they remain unabandoned,” he shows that the sense of a latent tendency (*anusaya*) is the sense of being unabandoned. This...

Regarding the phrase "arisen by way of having acquired a plane" (*bhūmiladdhuppanna*): among those aggregates, that class of defilements capable of arising is called "arisen by way of having acquired a plane" precisely because of that capacity for arising;
the meaning is that they are said to have "acquired the planes" consisting of the three realms (*tebhūmaka*).

"In those respective planes" refers to the aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandha*) comprised within the personal existences (*attabhāva*) of humans, devas, and so forth. This is because [the defilements] have not been produced or brought about within this or that particular continuum (*santāna*).
"Not eradicated. And here, "attained to the plane" (*bhūmiladdha*) is said in the sense of having acquired the plane, just like one who has taken hold of fire.

Furthermore, regarding the two meanings of the words *okāsakata* and *uppanna*—namely, "by whom space was made" (*okāso kato etena*) and "for whom space was made" (*okāso kato etassa*)—the inversion of the word *kata* (placed after the noun) should be understood.
It is "grasped" by way of seizing the sign (*nimittaggāha*), like a milk-tree that has been tapped.
The object is like an uncut milk-tree; because it has not been suppressed, the defilements are contained within it.
Alternatively, persons who grasp at signs while their defilements are unsuppressed are like the cut and uncut milk-trees.
"In the same manner as before" means that, just as with those [defilements] that have arisen without being suppressed, one cannot say, "They will not arise in this particular place. Why?
Having joined [the phrase] with “because they have not been eradicated,” it should be explained in detail.

This was stated in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*. And therein, in order to make clearly manifest the threefold state of not being subject to relapse—which applies specifically to those defilements abandoned by the Path—the simile of a tree that has not yet borne fruit is introduced. [This illustrates] the non-abandonment of past [defilements] and so forth.
For the sake of illustration, it is said: "It should be illustrated by means of a tree that has already borne fruit.

In this regard, just as fruits that were capable of arising on a tree when it was uncut do not arise once the tree is cut—and thus they have never been, are not, and will never be possessed of their own intrinsic nature (sasabhāva)—and therefore cannot be described in terms of past existence and so forth; even so are the defilements abandoned by the Path.

They are to be seen thus: just as the purposefulness of pruning is established by the fact that fruits will arise when there is no pruning, but will not arise when there is, so too should the purposefulness of the cultivation of the path be applied.
He abandons even those [formations] through the very abandoning of the defilements, because he brings about their state of non-arising. Regarding "of the volitional-formative consciousness":

Of rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhiviññāṇa*). Regarding "clung-to and not clung-to" (*upādinnaanupādinnato*): this refers to both the aggregates that are clung-to and the defilements (*kilesa*).
To show emergence by way of rebirth, he said: "But by way of existence," and so forth.

Of the seven existences (*bhava*) remaining for a stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*) that have not yet been abandoned, setting aside five, the other two are intended here as "a portion of the happy destinies' existence. [This refers to] from the existence of the happy destinies' sense-sphere realm (*sugatikāmabhava*).

From sense-sphere existence (*kāma-bhava*), which constitutes a portion of the fortunate states of existence (*sugati-bhava*). The path of Arahantship emerges from fine-material and immaterial existence (*rūpa-ārūpa-bhava*) because it effects the total eradication of the higher fetters (*uddhambhāgiya-saṃyojana*).
If the path of Arahantship alone were the noble path (*ariya-magga*), it would abandon all defilements (*kilesa*) and emerge from all forms of existence.
However, since defilements are abandoned only gradually, [the lower stages are reached] by means of the progressively lower paths.
He abandons the defilements that remain after those already abandoned; it is with reference to this capacity that it is said, "He indeed emerges from all states of existence.
For it is he alone who is described as "like a thunderbolt.
Let it be granted, then, that according to the stated method, there is the non-arising of unarisen unwholesome states and the non-arising of those that have arisen or are similar to what has arisen.

The development of the path is for the purpose of abandoning [the defilements] and for establishing the state of non-arising. Now, one raises an objection: "At the moment of the path, how can there be a development for the arising of wholesome states that have not yet arisen and for the stability of those already arisen, since that [moment of the path] lasts for only a single thought-moment?
The other replies with the solution: "Precisely by means of the occurrence of the path. For although the path indeed lasts for only a single thought-moment, [it effects these results].

Yet there is a particular excellence in its activity such that wholesome states (*kusaladhammā*) that have not yet arisen arise with great intensity, and those already arisen reach a state of distinguished fulfillment.

Therefore he said, "The path," and so forth. Although the Noble Path is not called "unarisen" at the moment it is actually occurring, it is designated as such by way of figurative usage (*upacāra*), based on its having previously been unarisen.

In order to show what is meant by "is said," the passage beginning with "never before occurred" was stated. "This very same" means that this very occurrence of the path according to its conditions is what is called "stability";
thus, it is appropriate to say that when a person possessing the path develops the path itself, they are developing its stability.

"Proceeding toward pacification" refers to the defilements being pacified either by way of suppression or by way of eradication. Alternatively, the faculties belonging to the preliminary stage are intended; for this reason, he says, "or it proceeds toward the pacification of the defilements."
248. "In the sense of resolving" (*adhimuccanaṭṭhena*) means in the sense of releasing more intensely or with distinction; hence he says, "the sense of releasing thoroughly.

By this, although all fine-material-sphere jhāna is liberated from its opposites by way of suppression, that specific mode of development by which that jhāna proceeds after being especially liberated from its opposites—this specific mode of development [is what is meant].
It has been explained. For even among those belonging to the same class, there are distinctions in the mode of occurrence due to differences in cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

Just as it is for one who has attained vision (*diṭṭhippatta*) compared to one liberated through faith (*saddhāvimutta*), so too is it "liberation" (*vimokkha*) in the sense of being well-resolved, by way of delighting in an unreserved state and freedom from apprehension, precisely because of being thoroughly liberated from opposing states (*paccanīkadhamma*). Therefore he said: "In the object..."
"...and so forth. However, this meaning—namely, the sense of "resolving"—is absent in the final liberation, which is cessation (*nirodha*).
There, only the sense of "liberation" alone is found; he himself will explain that later.
"Possessing form" (*rūpī*) means that by whatever form included within one's own continuity (*sasantati*) one is endowed, that [form] serves as the cause for the meditative absorption (*jhāna*).

The form is distinguished. That distinguished form by which one might be called "possessed of form" (rūpī)—because the word *rūpī* indicates a sense of excellence—should be understood as the very sign of the form included within one's own continuity (*sasantatipariyāpanna*), which, like jhāna, establishes the state of being possessed of form in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*).
Therefore he said, "internally," and so forth. "Form-jhāna" is "form" with the elision of the latter member of the compound. "Forms" (plural)...
In this context, the elision of the first member of the compound should be understood. Therefore it was said: "the blue kasiṇa and so forth are forms.
By the statement, "In the internal absorption there is no mental engagement (*ābhoga*) as 'beautiful,'" he shows that the resolve (*adhimutti*) might arise by way of prior mental engagement.
For in this way, the objection regarding the possibility of being described in such a manner here is rendered groundless. This is because, in the case of well-purified blues and so forth—
In the case of the color-kasiṇas, there may be a firm resolve (*adhimutti*) due to the delight of those who have previously practiced them;

therefore, the third liberation is described in that way in the Commentary. However, because meditation proceeding by way of loving-kindness (*mettā*) and so forth perceives beings as non-repulsive and proceeds only after resolving upon them as beautiful (*subha*), it is [described] thus in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*.
The development of the divine abodes (brahmavihāra) is called the "beautiful liberation" (subhavimokkha);
it should be understood that these two [designations] do not contradict each other because they have been stated by various methods.
"In its entirety" means without remainder; for not even a single portion of the four formless aggregates remains there.
"Relaxed" (*vissaṭṭhattā*) means because it has been ceased within the time limit as determined.

It is called "the supreme liberation" (*uttamo vimokkho*) because it must be attained by the Noble Ones (*ariya*) alone, because it culminates in the fruit of the Noble Ones, and because it constitutes the attainment of Nibbāna in this very life (*diṭṭheva dhamme*). 249.

"It overcomes" (*abhibhavati*); thus, "overcomer" (*abhibhu*) refers either to the preliminary work (*parikamma*) or to knowledge (*ñāṇa*). That which has an overcomer as its sphere (*āyatana*) is a "sphere of mastery" (*abhibhāyatana*).
Jhāna. Or, it is "sphere of mastery" (*abhibhāyatana*) because the sphere (*āyatana*), which is reckoned as the object, is to be mastered by this; thus it is jhāna.

Because of its mastery over the object, and because it serves as the basis for the yogi’s specific kinds of happiness, and because it consists of the mind-base (*manāyatana*) and the mental-object-base (*dhammāyatana*), jhāna together with its associated states is also called a "sphere of mastery. Therefore he said:
“‘The bases of mastery’ (abhibhavana-kāraṇāni), etc.”: “Those” refers to the meditative absorptions (jhāna) known as the bases of mastery.

It should be understood that for one who has emerged from attainment, the mental application (ābhoga) occurs by way of preliminary development (pubbabhāga-bhāvanā), taking hold of the mode of mastery that occurred at the moment of the absorption.

By way of the preliminary work (parikamma), one is percipient of forms internally, not by way of absorption (appanā); for [the bases of mastery] do not have the counterpart sign (paṭibhāga-nimitta) as their object.
Absorption (appanā) occurs with an internal object. However, that kasiṇa sign obtained through internal preliminary work (parikamma) is not yet perfectly purified;
it is not as pure as that obtained through external preliminary work.
"Limited" (parittāni) means they are just as they were obtained, having the size of a small water-jar. Therefore he said, "unextended. "Only by way of the limited" means...
Even though there is mental application (*ābhoga*) by way of color, this base of mastery (*abhibhāyatana*) is described specifically by way of the limited (*paritta*).
For here, limitation is the cause of mastery. Whether there is mental application to the color or not, the cultivation of the bases of mastery occurs only for one of sharp wisdom, not for another;
thus, [the Buddha] said, "The person who has knowledge as supreme. Having mastered...

Regarding the phrase "he enters upon" (*samāpajjati*): here, both "overcoming" and "entering upon" refer to the arising of absorption concentration (*appanā-jhāna*) immediately after the attainment of access concentration (*upacāra-jhāna*).
Therefore, it is said: "Right at the moment the sign arises, he reaches absorption here.

The expression "right at the moment the sign arises" is a characteristic statement indicating the absence of a preparatory period for absorption (*appanā-parivāsa*). This applies even to one who is called "one of quick direct knowledge" (*khippābhiñño*).

The development of the bases of mastery (*abhibhāyatana*) belongs specifically to the highest knowledge (*ñāṇuttara*). "In this" means in this sign (*nimitta*). "It brings it to absorption" means that the development leads to absorption (*appanā*).

And here, some say: "When access concentration (*upacāra-jjhāna*) has arisen, the two or three impulsion-moments (*javana-vāra*) that occur taking that as their object belong to the side of access concentration;
and immediately after that, through the dwelling of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga-parivāsa*), by the practice of access..."
And they say that absorption occurs without [the preliminary work], reaching absorption at the very moment the sign arises; but that is merely their own opinion.

For the procedure for absorption is not intended to be like the probationary rite (*pārivāsika-parikamma*), nor is retrospective reflection absolutely required in access concentration as it is in the sublime and measureless jhānas. Therefore, after the attainment of access concentration—
Reaching absorption at the conclusion of a few bhavaṅga consciousnesses, it is said that "one attains absorption here simultaneously with the arising of the sign.
This statement, "simultaneously with the arising of the sign," is intentional (adhippāyika) and not of direct meaning (nītattha);
the intention should be understood in the manner already explained.
This is because such an act of attention (*ābhoga*) is impossible while one is actually within the attainment;

rather, it should be understood that for one who has emerged from the attainment, the attention occurs by way of the preliminary development (*pubbabhāga-bhāvanā*), taking up the mode of mastery that occurred at the moment of the jhāna.
In the *Abhidhamma-aṭṭhakathā*, however, it is stated: "By this, his preliminary stage is explained."
If there is likewise an absence of mental application (*ābhoga*) in the attainment of the base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana-samāpatti*), why is it said, "even by the perception of jhāna"?

To this he says: "Because of mastery... there is. "Increased in measure" means "vast in measure"; it does not mean increased in measure by one or two finger-breadths and so forth, because such an increase is impossible here.

Therefore he says, "great. Perception of form is *rūpa-saññā*; one who possesses that is "possessing the perception of form" (*rūpasaññī*); one who does not possess the perception of form is "possessing the perception of the formless" (*arūpasaññī*). By way of the term "perception" (*saññā*)—
He speaks of jhāna. Here, "non-attainment" refers precisely to the non-arising of the perception of form. "Arising only externally" means arising only with respect to an external object.

However, in the Abhidhamma, regarding the four bases of mastery (*abhibhāyatana*), it is stated: "Not perceiving forms internally, one sees forms externally—limited, beautiful or ugly; or immeasurable, beautiful or ugly. Thus [are the four].
Because it has been handed down in the *Abhidhamma-ṭṭhakathā*, a challenge is raised:

"Why is it that, whereas in the Suttanta it is stated—'Possessing the perception of internal forms, one sees external forms that are limited,' and so on—here, in all four bases of mastery (*abhibhāyatana*), only the state of being 'without the perception of internal form' is mentioned? To this, it is replied: "Because internal forms are not to be mastered."
Having stated the reason, it was said: "Whether there or here, only external forms are to be mastered;

therefore, since they must necessarily be mentioned, they are spoken of both there and here. However, the phrase 'perceiving no internal form' is merely an elegant stylistic device in the Teacher’s teaching."
And here, all [objects]—both those devoid of attention to color and those accompanied by it—are called "limited, whether beautiful or ugly.
Likewise, they should be understood as "immeasurable. For there is this method of explanation:
"Having mastered the limited, and if at any time they are attended to by way of color, having mastered them as beautiful or ugly. This is an explanatory discourse (*pariyāyakathā*).

For this is a teaching given according to the discourses (suttanta). In the Abhidhamma, however, because it is a teaching according to the definitive method (nippariyāya), they are stated separately—both those devoid of the mental application of color (vaṇṇa) and those accompanied by it. Indeed, there is a figurative way of speaking (abhibhavana-pariyāya) in both cases:

thus, the first liberation occurs in the first and second bases of mastery (abhibhāyatana) through the formula "perceiving forms internally," and the second liberation occurs in the third and fourth bases of mastery.
The third liberation is included among the bases of mastery because it functions as a mastery;

however, since the Abhidhamma teaches according to the definitive method (*nippariyāya*), in order to show the liberations and the bases of mastery without confusion, the bases of mastery are explained while omitting the liberations.
Furthermore, all meditative absorptions that perform the function of liberation are stated in the teaching on the liberations.

Thus, it is understood that a specific determination has been made: because the two *abhibhāyatana*s (bases of mastery) introduced as "perceiving forms internally" are not mentioned among the *abhibhāyatana*s in the Abhidhamma,
and because [the formulas] such as "possessing form, he sees forms" are expressions common to the functions of all the liberations (*vimokkha*).

“Because internal forms are not to be overcome”—this is the statement of the reason for the fact that, although nowhere in the Abhidhamma is it said "one sees internal forms," it is everywhere stated "one sees external forms.
By this, whatever [teaching] has another cause is stated by that cause; however, that which is due to the elegance of the teaching (*desanāvilāsa*) regarding the internal—
This shows that the statement in the Abhidhamma is made solely because they are designated as "formless" (arūpa), and no other reason for it need be sought.
Furthermore, the fact that internal forms cannot be overcome is due to their lack of distinct manifestation (*avibhūtatā*), unlike external forms;

and the elegance of the teaching (*desanāvilāsa*) should be understood by way of the aforementioned analysis, since it consists in speaking by means of available synonyms according to the inclinations of those to be trained (*veneyyajjhāsaya*).
If it is argued that the bases of mastery over blue and so forth need not be mentioned because they are already established by the phrase "gold and ugly colors," we say no.
This is because for those who have practiced with respect to blue and so forth, it is precisely the state of being blue and so forth that is the cause of mastery.
For it is neither the limitedness nor the immeasurability of those pure or impure colors that is the cause of mastery; rather, it is simply their state as blue and so forth. Regarding these:
And in order to show for which temperament these bases of mastery (*abhibhāyatana*) succeed among the limited and other kasiṇa-forms, it was said:
“But in these...,” and so forth.
“By way of including everything” means by way of the commonality of all blue color, blue appearance, and blue luster.
"By way of color" means by way of its natural color. "By way of appearance" means by way of being visible.
"By way of radiance" means by way of shining with a luster. "Umā flower" means an *atasī* flower; it is blue only because there is no mixture of colors.
"Produced in Bārāṇasī" means arisen in Bārāṇasī.
