"Those states" refers both to those states such as the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) and to the states of the eight liberations (*aṭṭhavimokkha*). Having attained mastery over them, they have reached the ultimate perfection through highly distinguished wisdom; they have attained the finality of direct knowledge (*abhiññā*) and the perfection of its culmination.

"In the sense of being complete" means by way of their entirety. The meaning is that they are to be grasped without remainder, not remaining merely in part as is the case with the sign of foulness (*asubhanimitta*) and so forth. Just as a field is the place for the arising of crops and the place for their growth, even so...
He says, "in the sense of a field," referring to those various associated states. "Having delimited" should be connected with "above, below, and across.
For it is only after delimiting that the kasiṇa should be expanded everywhere.
"By this or that cause" means by this or that kasiṇa in the upper [directions] and so forth. To the question "How? he says: "like one desiring to see forms [seeks] light."

Just as one who wishes to see forms above with the divine eye extends light upwards, or downwards if they wish to see below, or all around if they wish to see forms all around—in this way, it refers to all the kasiṇas.

"Of one" means of each individual one among the earth-kasiṇa and the rest. "For the purpose of not passing into the state of another" means for the purpose of demonstrating that it does not pass into the state of being any other kasiṇa.

Or rather, it is for the purpose of illustrating that they do not attain the state of being another *kasiṇa*. For a *kasiṇa* extended by one person does not attain the state of being a *kasiṇa* extended by another;
in this way, too, the absence of intermingling with other *kasiṇas* should be understood.

It is not "another," such as earth and so forth. For where water stands, there is no earth together with its constituent parts (*sasambhāra-pathavī*). This is what is meant by "intermingling with other *kasiṇas*."
There is a confusion with the water-kasiṇa and others. "In all places" means in all the remaining kasiṇas.

Because it does not remain in one part but pervades without remainder, and because no limit is grasped, it is called "immeasurable" (appamāṇa). For that very reason they have the designation "kasiṇa. Thus he says, "For there," and so forth.
In that context, "pervading with the mind" means making the object of the mind through the mind of meditation (bhāvanācitta); for the mind of meditation [takes] the kasiṇa as its object.
One attends to it in its entirety, whether it be limited or vast.
The consciousness that occurs in the space where the kasiṇa has been removed is called the "consciousness-kasiṇa" by way of its pervasiveness and immeasurability.
For it is indeed called "consciousness. By way of the kasiṇa means by way of the kasiṇa that has been removed, [namely] in the space where the kasiṇa has been removed.
The upward, downward, and horizontal extent should be understood. For as much space as the *kasiṇa* is extended, so much becomes space by way of the meditation on space.

Thus, because consciousness proceeds by way of its arrival, becoming space itself for as long as that space has appeared, the upward, downward, and horizontal extent is also stated in the case of the consciousness-*kasiṇa*. "By way of the space revealed by the removal of the *kasiṇa*"...
"In that regard, the upward, downward, and horizontal movement of the consciousness occurring therein should be understood," he said.
This has already been stated in the *Vammika Sutta*. It is "dependent" because insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*) depends upon the six bases.
It is "bound" because it does not occur without that [consciousness], and because it takes as its object those material phenomena (*rūpa-dhamma*) designated as the body. Well...
It is called *subho* because it shines (*bhāti*) or illuminates (*obhāsati*). Even specific types of gems, such as those from Kuruvinda, are rooted in the purity of their source;
therefore, it says, "arisen from a perfectly pure mine. The accomplishment of the preliminary work consists in the removal of defects;
thus it says, "well-prepared through the removal of stones and gravel. [The phrase] "by means of washing, piercing, and so forth" refers to the four stones.
By washing, for the purpose of removing black spots and the like; and by piercing with thread, for the purpose of threading it.
The word "etc. includes processes such as heating and smoothing. "Perfection of color" refers to the perfection of the thread's color.

Because the body composed of the four primary elements (karajakāya) must be reflected upon like a gem; and because insight-knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa), having entered [the mind], is like the thread that has been threaded through.
Because it is established. A monk who has attained insight (vipassanā) sees that [object] correctly, just like a man with sight.

"Having that as their object" means having material phenomena (rūpa-dhamma) as their object. It should be understood that even those factors included by the mention of the "contact-fifth" (i.e., the consciousness and mental factors associated with contact) are themselves comprised within the arising of the insight-consciousness;
for in this way, they fall under the category of insight-knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa).
The statement, “insight-knowledge is like a thread that has been spun,” is thus not contradicted.
“Of knowledge” means of reviewing-knowledge (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*). If it must be stated in this way by way of knowledge and not by way of the person, he said, “But for him,” and so forth.
It occurs immediately after the path; therefore, it follows after the mundane direct knowledges (*lokīyābhiññā*) and precedes the sixth direct knowledge.
The knowledge of insight (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*) should be stated first.

Even though this is so—that is, even if this is the sequential order of knowledges—nevertheless, there is no opportunity for it in between; thus, when the five mundane higher knowledges (*lokīyābhiññā*) have been discussed, as in the *Ākaṅkheyya Sutta* and other such texts, the sixth higher knowledge must be explained.
This is because that knowledge of insight, which lacks the characteristic of a higher knowledge (*anabhiññā-lakkhaṇa*), [belongs] to them...

There is no intermediate turn; therefore, because there is no opportunity for it there, the knowledge of insight (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*) is shown here alone, immediately after the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*).
And as for the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "because... and," it has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*).
By this, it illuminates the meaning that not only that [reason], but also this reason is why the knowledge of insight is shown here alone. By means of the divine...

Regarding the phrase "seeing a terrifying form with the eye," it should be stated that one sees the terrifying form with the eye after having fashioned it by means of the knowledge of supernormal powers (*iddhividhañāṇa*).

Even so, fear and terror arise in one who has attained the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) but lacks full understanding of the basis [of phenomena], just as in the case of the Venerable Mahānāga Thera, who lived at Uccavālika. "In this too" means even in this knowledge of insight (*vipassanāñāṇa*).
The intention is that it is not only in the case of the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) and so forth.

253. The construction is as follows: "In the case of mind-made psychic power (manomayiddhi), one should understand that the higher knowledge (abhiññā) has reached the perfection of mastery through having practiced it.
It is produced by the mind; it is produced by the mind of higher knowledge. It is precisely for the purpose of showing its similarity [to the original] even in terms of its shape (saṇṭhāna).

This is for the purpose of showing similarity both in terms of color and in terms of specific parts. He stands in his own class (*sajātiya*), not appearing in the form of another class through the power of a Naga’s psychic potency (*iddhi*).
This is because the knowledge of the modes of psychic potency (*iddhividhañāṇa*) serves as the basis for the act of transformation, just like well-prepared clay and so forth.
"Without difficulty" means without hardship.
256. Even a dull-witted infant lying on its back is called "young" (*dahara*); therefore, to distinguish him from such, the word "youth" (*yuvā*) is used.
Since even some youths, due to a lack of desire, may not have a habit for adornment, the word "of a naturally ornamental disposition" (*maṇḍanakajātiko*) is used to distinguish him from them.
Thus it is said: "Even though he is a youth," and so forth. Black spots the size of black sesame seeds are *kāḷatilakāni*. [Those] not exceeding the size of a half-sesame seed...
Bindus are forehead marks (*tilakas*). *Vaṅka* is the name for *piyaṅgu*. Pimples of youth and so forth are pimples that defile the face.

"Fault of the face" (*mukhadoṣa*) refers to a fault located on the face; this is a term of definition (*lakkhaṇavacana*), because even the manifestation of what is not a fault on the face is intended here.

Or, just as a fault on the face is a "fault of the face," so too the absence of a fault on the face is a "fault of the face" by means of the elision of the vowel *a* (*saralopa*); thus, both the presence and the absence of a fault on the face are termed "faults of the face."

And here, the meaning should be understood by means of the grammatical principle of "single remainder" (*ekasesanaya*), namely, that there is both [defilement] and the "fault of the mouth" (*mukhadosa*).
For in this way, the statement that "the sixteenfold consciousness of others becomes manifest" is justified.

259. "By way of the path of practice" (*paṭipadāvasena*) means by way of the paths of practice of serenity (*samatha*), insight (*vipassanā*), and the [supramundane] path (*magga*), as appropriate. "In the eight sections" (*aṭṭhasu koṭṭhāsesu*)...

"In the sections on the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyadhamma) such as the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), and in the sections on the liberations (vimokkha)" refers to these eight sections.
"In the remaining ones" refers to the remaining sections mentioned, such as the bases of mastery (abhibhāyatana). The rest is easy to understand.
The elucidation of the hidden meaning of the commentary on the Mahāsakuludāyisutta is completed.
8. Commentary on the Samaṇamuṇḍikāputta Sutta 260.
*Uggahitaṃ* means to learn. *Uggāhetuṃ* means to cause others to learn;

the meaning is to cause others to grasp [the doctrine] by means of recitation, for the purpose of clarifying the matter exactly as it was learned by oneself from the text. *Samayaṃ* means a view (*diṭṭhi*). That...
Indeed, it is called *samaya* because, through the state of being a fetter (*saṃyojana*), beings come together (*sameti*) and proceed (*eti*) in connection with it;
or, because beings proceed (*ayanti*) and move about (*pavattanti*) bound (*saṃyuttā*) by it according to their respective inclinations (*abhinivesa*).

For by the fetter of views (*diṭṭhi-saṃyojana*), beings are exceedingly bound. From the rising of the sun until its setting, this duration of time is [defined] by the dispelling of the darkness of night.
"By day" means that the time known as the "middle stroke," characterized by the blazing radiance of the dawn's heat, is called "day.
Therefore he said: "when it has become day even of the day. "Having withdrawn" means having turned back. Thus, the withdrawal of the mind is the placing [of it] within the field of its own range;
therefore he said: "by way of cultivating the delight of jhāna, [bringing about] a state of oneness..."
"Has gone. By this, he speaks of mental seclusion preceded by physical seclusion. Because they possess distinguished qualities such as virtue (*sīla*), they are worthy of esteem by the mind;

and since they are pleasing to the wise through their own qualities of virtue (because the non-suppression of the defilements depends upon the fivefold serene confidence), he says "those who increase the mind," and so forth. In that context, "it rises up" means *udagga* (exultant).
"It increases": it increases by way of faith (*saddhā*). Therefore the Blessed One said:
"Monks, I say that even mere recollection is of great benefit to those bhikkhus.
"I describe" (*paññapemi*): I make known by way of the state of understanding (*pajānana*), and likewise I define it. Therefore he said: "I show, I establish."

“Complete in wholesome states” means possessing wholesome qualities in their entirety. “Supreme in wholesome states” means possessing wholesome qualities that have attained the highest state, the most excellent state.
Or, “invincible” (ayojjha) means not to be overcome by a battle of words; he shows that even if there were a battle of words, there would be no defeat thereby.
Thus he says, “by a battle of words,” and so forth. “Restraint and abandonment” refers to the fivefold restraint.
By means of any restraint whatsoever, there is the characteristic of restraint, which is abandonment.

By the word "or" (*vā*) in the phrase "or abandonment by avoidance" (*paṭisevanappahānaṃ vā*), it includes abandonment by shunning (*parivajjanappahānaṃ*) and so forth. "In the remaining passages" refers to the passages such as "he does not speak.
By the phrase "this same method," it extends [the rule] to cases such as "he speaks only what is not [false]."
"He did not rejoice" means he did not accept it. The avoidance of the three types of misconduct and wrong livelihood is praised in the Dispensation;
yet this person speaks thus, so [the Buddha] thought he was speaking in conformity with the Dispensation.
Furthermore, while speaking, he did not show lack of confidence in the Fully Enlightened One or in the Dhamma; therefore, thinking that he was even expressing a sign of faith, [the Buddha spoke].
He does not refute his argument.
"As his word says, so it is" means that while such a state of being a recluse (samaṇabhāva) exists as described by that wanderer's words, we do not say it is so;
by this, he means that what is called the state of a recluse is not like that.

He shows this: for whatever a phenomenon is like, in that very way the Buddhas illuminate it. "There is no knowledge of distinction" means that at that time he lacks the knowledge regarding the specific qualities of the body by which he might perform an intervention upon another's body; thus he shows that he possesses no such knowledge of distinction there either.
Since bodily action is bound to the body, therefore, in order to preclude it, he says: "except for mere movement."
"By a mind accompanied by defilements" means by a mind accompanied by grief, which is the cause for not enduring painful contact.
The same method applies to the second section as well; it refers specifically to the grief that is the cause for not enduring the suffering of hunger and thirst.
"Merely crying out" (*vikūjitamattā*): here, *vikūjita* is an improper wailing, a lamentation based on past lives. That—
In this context, it should be understood that "accompanied by the mind which arouses weeping or laughter" refers to [the mind] accompanied by hatred (*dosa*) and accompanied by greed (*lobha*).
"Mind" (*citta*) here refers to a wholesome mind (*kusala-citta*); indeed, it cannot even be said that an unwholesome mind (*akusala-citta*) occurs with a past object.
"Having remembered" means [remembering] what was experienced in a dream until such time as the mental states (*dhammā*) for establishing mindfulness arise.
They weep, remembering suffering as if it were present. The same principle applies here to the phrase "they laugh.
This method should be understood as being stated with reference to those who, having obtained a pleasant object [of rebirth], take conception and even emerge from the mother’s womb in comfort.
"To one who suckles" means to one who suckles according to her own native country and appearance. "This too" refers to the livelihood of the mother.
And at times other than those [of formal practice], it occurs precisely with a mind accompanied by defilements (*kilesa*) due to worldly delight (*lokassāda*).
"Having attained" (*samadhigayha*) means having grasped by way of right attainment, having overcome, having distinguished, and thus being distinguished.
"With reference to one whose taints are destroyed" (*khīṇāsavaṃ sandhāya*) is said by way of contrast (*byatireka*); this is the meaning here.

Even one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) describes wholesome [states] pertaining to a stream-enterer because he stands upon the plane of training (sekkhabhūmi). The same method applies to the remaining phrases as well.

"Relying on three phrases" means: relying on these three phrases—“he does not perform an evil deed with the body, he does not utter evil speech, and he does not lead an evil livelihood”—there are both roots of wholesome virtue and roots of unwholesome virtue.

Thus, two initial tetrads have been established. "Based on one word" means that based on this single word, "he does not conceive an evil intention," these two final tetrads—those rooted in wholesome intention and those rooted in unwholesome intention—have been established. 264.

Even the two types of consciousness accompanied by doubt and restlessness are included because they are possessed of powerful delusion; for it is said of them that they are "muddled states of consciousness."
"For what purpose" (*kiṃnimittaṃ*) means for what cause. "Having reached which place" (*kataraṃ ṭhānaṃ pāpuṇitvā*) means by resorting to what reason.
"In this [regard]" (*ettha ete*): "in this" refers to the accomplishment of the cultivation of good conduct of body, speech, and mind, as well as right livelihood.

Since that [accomplishment] should be illustrated by the fruit of stream-entry at its lowest limit, he said, "the locative case in 'stream-entry-fruit'. Because the eightfold livelihood and the remaining virtue...
And because the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha is established through the attainment of the pure Pātimokkha and the realization of the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti), it is said:

“The Pātimokkha... ceases. Expressions such as “unwholesome virtue” (akusala-sīla) are stated by taking the word *sīla* in its sense of natural disposition (*pakati*), as in the cases of “one of pleasant disposition” (*sukha-sīla*) or “one of painful disposition” (*dukkha-sīla*).

265. Only wholesome sense-sphere consciousness (*kāmāvacara-kusala-citta*) is mentioned here, because it is this that is intended as the virtue (*sīla*) preceded by the undertaking of abstinence when conditions are favorable. Therefore he said: "For by this, wholesome virtue (*kusala-sīla*) arises.
Regarding the phrase "one who is virtuous" (*sīlavā*), the particle *vā* should be understood here in the sense of praise; thus he said: "He is endowed with virtue.

One who is established merely in virtue, but not in concentration and wisdom, is "made of virtue" (*sīlamaya*) due to being filled with the qualities consisting of virtue. Therefore he said: "That much is enough," and so forth.
“In which”: in that liberation of mind (cetovimutti) and liberation by wisdom (paññāvimutti).

Since both of these are included within the fruit of arahantship, it is said: “the locative case [is used] for the fruit of arahantship. It ceases without remainder because the state of having a pleasant result is entirely stilled.
266. Perception associated with sensual desire is "perception of sensual desire. The same method applies to the remaining [terms] as well. The other two are the perceptions of ill will and cruelty.
"The first jhāna together with the fruit of non-returning" means the first jhāna accompanied by the fruit of non-returning. "In this" refers to the first jhāna as described above.
And here, the mention of the first jhāna is because the abandonment of the opposing factor through its direct opposite is particularly prominent.

Therefore he said, "They cease without remainder. The fact that the perceptions of renunciation are accompanied by sense-sphere consciousness, as well as the fact that they are the source of that virtue, should be understood according to the method of association (*sampayutta-naya*). 267.

By the mention of the fruit of Arahantship associated with the second jhāna through the cessation of wholesome intentions, and the fruit of Non-returning associated with the first jhāna through the cessation of unwholesome intentions, the recluse (*samaṇa*) is demonstrated. The rest is easy to understand.
The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning of the Commentary on the Samaṇamuṇḍikāputta Sutta is completed.
9. Commentary on the Cūḷasakuludāyi Sutta 271.

"Question" (pañha) refers to the matter desired to be known; that very thing is the cause (kāraṇa), because it serves as the basis for the teaching of the Dhamma. "Let him attend" (upaṭṭhātu): [this means] let him be present.
"May it come within the range of knowledge. As for the phrase "by which reason":
that reason by which the teaching of the Dhamma might be established for you has been stated thus according to the inclination of the wanderer (paribbājaka).
Therefore he said: "By this... [etc. ...he illustrates. "Level ground" means they are like level ground due to the absence of any covering. Therefore he said: "manifest."
“Knowing” means knowing his own state for himself. “He listens attentively” means he listens with reverence, thinking, “He has spoken to me exactly as one who is truly such.
“Therefore” refers to the fact that one who possesses the divine eye also possesses knowledge of the future.
“Thus he said” begins with the words, “Udāyi, whoever with the divine eye... and continues, “or he [speaks] concerning the future limit regarding me...”
"one should ask a question"—thus he spoke.

"The other" refers to what remains to be said in this context. "In the same manner as stated" means precisely in the manner stated beginning with "he who is a possessor [of supernormal powers]," and so forth.

"In the past" refers to objects that have become the domain of the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pubbenivāsānussati-ñāṇa*). "In the future" refers to the knowledge of future states (*anāgataṃsa-ñāṇa*).
Regarding a future object that has become a sensory domain:
it is called a "dust-demon" (*paṃsupisācaka*) because it is produced in a patch of dust and because its body is smeared with dust.
"Taking one root" means taking a length of four finger-breadths from the bottom end and one span (*vidatthi*) from the top end, [from among] trees, shrubs, creepers, and so forth.
Whosoever takes one root [of this plant], their body becomes invisible to those of other species.

This, it is said, is the natural law established by their birth (*jātisiddhadhammatā*). "Therein" means: by virtue of that root, through the state of being invisible. "Is not seen" means: it is not perceived by knowledge; it is not beheld.
"And it would not illuminate the meaning" means: that speech would not illuminate the intended meaning in its own form (*sarūpato*), but only...

The intended meaning is "exceeding the measure of speech. In the sense of being repelled and in the sense of being led into another continuum, the essential meaning is to be understood through the verbal root *paṭihāriya*.

By way of etymological derivation (*niruttinaya*), that very thing is *pāṭihīraka*. Through the method of negative formation (*na-vigata*), there is no *pāṭihīraka* in this, which is *appāṭihīrakata*;
by extending the word with the suffix *-ta*, it is stated thus as "non-issuance" (*aniyyāna*). Therefore he said: "meaningless."
“It is accomplished. By the phrase “it shines like the aggregates in the Subhakiṇha deva-world,” he demonstrates this meaning:
“The self is divine, material, mind-made, complete in all its limbs and parts, and not deficient in its faculties.
(273) Since the meaning of a word with a prefix can be understood even without the prefix, he says: “‘Viddha’ means ‘erected’ (*ubbiddhe*).”
And because that state of being cloudless appears through the removal of defilements and by way of its purity, he said, "when [the sky] has become clear due to the departure of clouds.
It shines and illuminates like an indranīla gem; thus it is called *devo*, meaning the sky.

Although one might have said "at the time of midnight" (*aḍḍharattasamaye*), the accusative case is to be understood here because the forms used are prescribed for the locative sense in the absence of absolute conjunction (*accantasaṃyoga*).
For on the full-moon day, when the moon stands in front of or behind the middle of the sky, at midnight it is said that the time is "divided" (bhinna);
however, when it stands exactly in the middle, it is said to be "undivided" (abhinna). Therefore he said, "at the undivided time of midnight.
"Those who experience" means those deities who experience, enjoy, and utilize the radiance of the moon and sun.
Those devas do not experience even a fraction, let alone a greater portion, of the radiance of the moon and sun. Therefore it is said:
"They dwell having pervaded the space with the light of their own bodies.
274. But he became confused by the question, because of the removal of the phrase grasped [by him] as "this is the supreme beauty. The *Acelaka-pāḷi*...

He speaks of those doctrines revealed by that very title through the heading "the text" (*gantha*), which sets forth the practice of the naked ascetic (*acelaka*) in such passages as "he is naked, he is one who has abandoned the use of clothing.

For a person devoted to the drinking of fermented liquor and spirits, abstinence from drinking such liquor leads to the warming of their body and mind; thus it is called "abstinence from drinking liquor" (*surāpānavirati*). [This is] austerity (*tapo*); it is that very quality. Therefore he said: "The meaning is 'abstinence from drinking liquor'."
275. "Entirely and absolutely blissful" means *ekantasukha*. "In the five things" refers to the five factors of virtue and conduct, beginning with "abstaining from taking life.
"They did not know" means that through confusion they failed to attend to them and did not understand their meaning.
It is said that by the arising of a Buddha, the mantra-words of great power have had their splendor eclipsed.
Just as the practice of the yogāvacaras perishes along with the manuals of the outsiders (bāhiraka), so too [the teaching] would perish.
"They learned" means they merely learned the mere words of the statement beginning with "five pre-accessory factors" (pañca pubbabhāgadhammā).
"From the third jhāna" refers to the fruit by way of a metaphorical designation for its cause; that is, from the third jhāna which has become the fruit.
276. The realization through attainment is the arising there for the sake of obtaining the world of absolute happiness.

The realization through direct perception is the seeing, by means of psychic power (*iddhi*), of that world of sentient beings and the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*) directly, without having been reborn in that world of absolute happiness. Therefore he said, "Therein," and so forth.
277. *Udañcanikā* means a water-drawing machine. Because the villages were not settled on the slopes of the Vindhya mountains, an area measuring about thirty *yojanas* was called a forest (*aṭavī*).
Therein was a lodging; because many monks engaged in the practice of striving (*padhāna*) resided there at that forest lodging, there came to be one striving-hall (*padhānaghara*).
The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning (*Līnatthappakāsanā*) for the Commentary on the *Cūḷasakuludāyisutta* is completed.
10. Commentary on the *Vekhanasasutta* 280.

One who has "desire for sense-pleasures as their burden" (*kāmagaru*) is so called because they hold the desire for defilements (*kilesakāma*)—along with the objects of that desire—as something heavy and worthy of being honored. Regarding those very same sense-pleasures...
"One whose inclination, tendency, and disposition are directed downwards" means one who is intent upon sensual pleasures (*kāmādhimutta*).
"One who values renunciation" (*nekkhammagaru*) refers to one for whom renunciation—such as the going-forth and the first *jhāna*—is held dear and worthy of esteem.

In this context, the fact that one whose inclination, tendency, and disposition are directed downwards is intent upon renunciation (*nekkhammādhimutta*) applies not only to some householders but also to some who have gone forth; thus he says, "even one who has gone forth," and so on.
But this wanderer Vekhanasa— having entered the ascetic life of the Vekhanasa recluses and remaining there having adopted and undertaken this particular view—
is called "Vekhanasa. Just as the world, though itself burning with eleven fires,

does not perceive the heat of the fire from the fire-sticks being experienced directly before its eyes, so too it fails to perceive the heat of the mass of evil conduct that has followed it since beginningless time.

One does not perceive it as burning; however, when the Fully Enlightened One, his mind impelled by great compassion, teaches the Discourse on Burning, saying, "Bhikkhus, everything is burning," then one perceives it.

In the same way, this person—failing to investigate with their own wisdom that which has been cultivated since beginningless time, established in self-interest, and intent upon sensual pleasures—is addressed by the Teacher: "Indeed, there are five..."

When the sensual pleasures (*kāmaguṇa*) and the happiness of sense-desires (*kāmasukha*) were being described in the passage beginning with, “These, Kaccāna, are the strands of sensual pleasure,” [the Blessed One] said,

“By this discourse being told, he will perceive his own devotion to sense-desires (*kāmādhimuttatā*), thinking, ‘Alas, the mind of one who has gone forth is indeed intent upon sense-desires (*kāmādhimutta*).
“The supreme happiness of sense-desires (*kāmaggasukha*)” means the happiness that is the highest among the things to be desired.
For all phenomena belonging to the three planes are "sensual pleasures" (kāma) in the sense of being desirable;

and among the happinesses that arise dependent upon them, the happiness of Nibbāna alone is the supreme happiness. As it is said: “Bhikkhus, to whatever extent there are phenomena, whether conditioned or unconditioned, dispassion (virāga) is declared to be the foremost among them”; and: “Nibbāna is the supreme happiness. Therefore it is stated: “Nibbāna is intended.”
281. Discourse concerning the past given by one who has attained knowledge of former births (*pubbenivāsañāṇa*) is appropriate because that matter is directly perceived;
it is inappropriate for a Vekhanasa because he lacks that [knowledge]. Thus it was said: "Because... there is not.
The same principle applies here to the discourse concerning the future, where it is said "...there is not. "For the sake of protection" means by means of deities and mantra-words.

It remained there for the purpose of protection. "By ignorance" (*avijjāya*) is a statement of its defining characteristic; or rather, because all defiled phenomena have ignorance as their root, it is ignorance alone that is mentioned.
"Knowing" refers to the knowledge of reviewing the defilements that have been abandoned. The rest is easily understood.
The *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Hidden Meaning) of the commentary on the *Vekhanasa-sutta* is completed.
The commentary on the Paribbājaka-vagga is completed.
4. The Rāja-vagga: 1.
The Commentary on the Ghaṭīkāra Sutta.
282. "Cariyā" means the practice of a bodhisatta, which is to say, the conduct set forth for the purpose of accumulating the requisites of enlightenment (*bodhisambhāra*).
"A good cause" refers to the excellent and certain cause for the maturation of enlightenment; he says this with reference to his attendance upon the Blessed One Kassapa and other such acts.
For it can be said that those [deeds] were performed by me here together with him.
He obtains [it]. "A gentle smile" (*mandahasita*) means a slight smile. "Kuhaṃ kuhanti" is an imitation of the sound of laughter.

"Merely the appearance of being overjoyed" (*haṭṭhapahaṭṭhākāramattaṃ*) means merely the state of being overjoyed. Just as those who have grasped the convention recognize [the Buddha] as "the Blessed One is overjoyed," so too it is merely the manifestation of that appearance.
Now, in this context, in order to show their origin by way of classification, the passage beginning with “And what is called laughter” is commenced.
Therein, since laughter does not even occur by way of equanimity, let alone by way of mental distress, he says:
“by thirteen types of consciousness accompanied by joy. But is it not the case that some laugh even by way of anger?
No; for even in their case, laughter arises with a mind of joy that is difficult to discern, accompanied by the thought: "Now we shall act as we please regarding that object of anger.
"Among those" refers to the five types of consciousness accompanied by joy (*somanassa-sahagata-citta*).
"With a powerful object" means with a sublime object, such as the Twin Miracle (*yamaka-mahāpāṭihāriya*). "With a weak object" means with one that is not sublime.
Regarding the object: in this context, however, the statement "he produced [the smile]" is stated because it is so recorded in the *Porāṇa-aṭṭhakathā*.
It is for the purpose of showing that the Blessed One’s smile does not occur with a mind accompanied by rootless joy (*ahetuka-somanassa-sahagata-citta*).
In the *Abhidhammaṭīkā*, however, after stating that his knowledge is unimpeded regarding the past and so forth, [it says]: "By these three factors..."

It is said: "Because of such statements as, 'For the Buddha, the Blessed One, who is thus endowed, all bodily action is preceded by knowledge and follows after knowledge,' one must examine the statement that 'this thought arises in the Blessed One.

In this regard, even though the Blessed One’s act of smiling occurs through this thought that gives rise to a smile, it is [an expression] of his knowledge of past lives, of future states, and of omniscience.

Because it functions as a follower, it is indeed a concomitant of knowledge (*ñāṇānuparivatti*). When there is thus a state of being a concomitant of knowledge, there is no contradiction whatsoever with the Canon (*pāḷi*) or the Commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*). For instance, it is stated in the *Abhidhamma-aṭṭhakathā*:

"When those knowledges have reached their limit through practice, this consciousness arises. And this must necessarily be accepted as such; otherwise, even for adverting (*āvajjana*), [the same would follow].
The Blessed One’s statement would not be consistent with such a time, for even that [mental consciousness] is intended to possess the quality of originating intimation (*viññatti*);
thus it has been said: "And by doing so, it is established that even the adverting of the mind-door (*manodvārāvajjana*) possesses the quality of originating intimation.
Nor does the fact of originating intimation imply that the intimation originated by it constitutes bodily action (*kāyakamma*) and so forth.
He speaks with reference to that very state, saying "the state of falling away acts as an obstruction. Therefore he says, "even one who is thus slightly negligent.

A flash of lightning that flickers is called a "flickering lightning-flash" (*sateratāvijjulatā*). For unlike other lightning-flashes, it does not have a momentary duration nor is it subject to rapid cessation;
rather, its cessation is slow, and this occurs only during the time of the great clouds over the four continents.
Therefore, it is said: "from the mouth of the great cloud that covers the four continents.

This, it is said, is the natural law (*dhammatā*) of those circles of rays: namely, that after circumambulating the noble head three times from left to right, they vanish right at the tips of the fangs.
Even though [the Bodhisatta] had cultivated the perfection of wisdom for four incalculable eons and a hundred thousand aeons, [he did not attain Buddhahood until this final birth].
Nevertheless, because that interval between Buddhas must now be explained to her, it is said:
"Because of the immaturity of her knowledge. Granted that there is still a need to explain this for the sake of her knowledge even now;

yet, even so, should she not have developed confidence and esteem toward the Perfectly Enlightened Ones due to having cultivated them over such a long period? How, then, could there be contempt for them?

He said, “In a brahmin family,” and so forth. For even the cultivation of virtues, though long practiced, undergoes transformation and reaches a state of alteration through even a slight association with unwholesome friends.
Therefore, the Great Being, standing upon this view established by birth and with pride born of that birth, spoke thus: “But what is the use of seeing that shaven-headed little ascetic? Likewise:
For it is said in the Aṭṭhakathā:
“Therefore, one who desires prosperity and possesses discernment should avoid an unwholesome person from afar, just as one would avoid a venomous serpent.”

A *sotti* is a cloth made from bathing powder and thread; it is a *kuruvinda* pill. It is called a *sināna* (bath) because by means of it they bathe and cleanse the body. Therefore he said: "The *sotti-sināna* is a cloth made for the purpose of bathing.

(284) "By the avoidance of the noble ones" (*ariyaparihārena*) means by the avoidance of the noble ones; the meaning is: by the rule of avoiding one's own body at the time of bathing for non-returners (*anāgāmin*).
He will be able to show his appreciation through his own attainment of knowledge and his attainment of wealth. "For this purpose" (*etadatthaṃ*).
“Preventing what is harmful, enjoining one toward what is beneficial, and avoiding calamity”—this is the purpose for which they are called friends.
Some read “yāvettha ahupī,” for them the meaning is: “As far as there was here, even unto the grasping of a hair-tip, this connection existed.”

285. "For the sake of attaining mindfulness" (*satipaṭilābhatthāya*) means for the sake of attaining mindfulness in the fulfillment of the practice of the requisites for enlightenment (*bodhisambhāra*), having made the great resolve (*mahābhinīhāra*) for enlightenment.
Now, in order to show briefly the manner in which the discourse that arouses mindfulness proceeded for him, it was said: "To him, indeed...
(*tassa hi*). Therein, by the phrase "a being who has not descended into a lowly state," [the author] refers to the Great Being.
Having demonstrated his inclination toward the sublime, and showing that for one so inclined toward the sublime it is not fitting to engage in negligence, he said:
"For one such as this, a state of negligence is not appropriate. At that time, the Bodhisatta’s aspiration for renunciation arose with particular intensity, like a lamp fed with oil;
seeing this, the Blessed One delivered a discourse on the Dhamma suited to that occasion.
“...to such a person... he spoke. The elders dwelling beyond the sea speak otherwise. However, in the Commentary, it is said:

“This is not a burden for the Buddhas; namely, that the Bodhisattvas who have fulfilled the perfections teach the Dhamma in such a manner, because even immediately after their great aspiration (mahābhinīhāra), they have personally realized through their own self-originated knowledge (sayambhuñāṇa) the requisites for enlightenment. Therefore...”
In order to show that the Blessed One indeed performed the proclamation of the state of a bodhisattva for him, it was said:

“for the sake of the attainment of mindfulness,” and so forth. “For the sake of the attainment of mindfulness” means for the attainment of that mindfulness which makes right practice radiant and manifest.

(286) For knowledge (*ñāṇa*) is called a “horn” (*siṅga*) because, by tearing asunder and crushing the defiled phenomena (*kilesadhamma*), it is like a horn. Indeed, that [knowledge] belongs to right practice...
When it is supported, it is called "uplifted"; in its absence, it is called "fallen. Some, however, say that energy is called "the horn.

When that [energy] proceeds by way of the right exertions (*sammappadhāna*), even those Great Beings who have entered the external renunciation—being pure in aspiration and endowed with qualities such as fewness of desires—dwell cultivating, as appropriate, either the burden of study (*ganthadhura*) or the burden of meditation (*vāsadhura*).

He said, "In the Buddha’s teaching, [they progress] by means of fewness of wishes and so forth," beginning with the words, "But regarding the fourfold purification of virtue. It was stated that those who develop insight reach the culmination of insight;
this means they proceed as far as, and stop at, the knowledge of conformity (*anuloma-ñāṇa*). Or, they do not exert effort for the sake of the paths and fruits.
Because the womb of omniscient knowledge has not been fulfilled and has not reached maturity through the perfection of wisdom (paññāpāramitā).
287. "There" means among those who are more senior. "While residing" means while staying in that very place where one went forth.
"At the time of sowing" means at the time when the crops are being sown. As before, after that, by means of the sharp heat of the sun...
It is said that there is no purpose [in this], as it is stated: “having tied a cloth or a mat above like a canopy at the time of sowing.

“In a bundle” means in a cluster. 288. Since the attainment of the Dhamma has the completeness of requisites as its cause, even Noble Ones—who possess the basis of full understanding in part—take up whatever is not excessively blameworthy when a condition for mental distress arises; such is the nature of things (dhammatā) in this case.
He said: "A change of mind concerning non-gain," and so forth. "He" refers to Kikī, the King of Kāsi. "Devoted to brahmins" means one who is devoted to brahmins.
"O God," he says referring to the brahmins. "Earth-gods" is their conventional designation; at that time, the world was held in high esteem for brahmins.
For even the Blessed One Kassapa was born into a brahmin family at that time. Having spoken dispraise of his daughter: "Great King..."

Having spoken thus of the princess's faults, beginning with, "Your daughter has abandoned the doctrine of the Brahmins and has taken up the doctrine of the shaven heretics," the kinsmen chose the boon.
He handed over the kingdom, thinking, "Let my word not be false;
on the eighth day I shall restrain her."

Because they have been properly purified by means of winnowing and washing, they are pure grains. In the text, "taṇḍulapaṭibhastāni" refers to fragments of rice. The same method applies to the "muggapaṭibhastaka" (bean-pouch) and "kalāyapaṭibhastaka" (pea-pouch).
Regarding the phrase "Ko nu kho," he says that it is a nominative singular used in the sense of the locative;

thus, "Kuhiṃ nu kho" (Where indeed? completes the sense. It is called "pariyoga" because the condiments and food are contained therein (*pariyujjanti*); hence, "from the pariyoga. Therefore, he said, "from the soup-bowl. [He gave] the signal.
Having said "having given," and having explained everything that was stated, he gave the instruction: "Inform the Blessed One that an attendant has been prepared for your sake and set aside.
"Excessively trusted" (*ativissattha*) means one who is placed in very high confidence.
"Fivefold" (*pañcavaṇṇā*) means of five types, by way of the *khuddika* and so forth.
290. Why is there a nominative case in the sense of the ablative (*nissakka*)? The meaning is "why? By the word *dhammiko*, he demonstrates purity of lineage.
By the phrase "like rice in the bowls of the bhikkhus," he demonstrates that the Teacher had been relinquished by the lay follower and that the Teacher had no suspicion regarding it.
[The phrase] "there is no such thing as a time for training rules" is because of his status as the Lord of the Dhamma.

In the case of an offense against the formal rule (*paṇṇattivajja*), there is no such thing as the "boundary of the training" (*sikkhāpadamariyādā*); however, in the case of a natural offense (*pakativajja*), there is indeed the "destruction of the bridge" (*setughāta*).
291. That which is space in the place of covering is itself the roof of that house; thus it is called "space-roof. By nature, it is simply the pervasion of the weather;
therefore, whatever kind of weather there is when it is covered, even if the covering is made of grass, in that house the weather remains exactly the same.
There was an overflow of the weather. "Of those very people" means of Ghaṭīkāra’s parents themselves.
292. "Four handfuls make one *kuḍuva*; four *kuḍuvas* make one *pattha*;
four *patthas* make one *āḷhaka*; four *āḷhakas* make one *doṇa*; four *doṇas* make one *mānikā*; four *mānikās* make one..."
In the *Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā* and other works, it is stated that twenty *khārī*s make one *vāha*, which is the same as one cart;

however, here it is stated that "two carts make one *vāha*. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "oil, molasses, etc.," one includes ghee and so forth, as well as pungent spices such as black pepper.
"I have never been seen by the king; how then could there be physical contact?"—this is the intended meaning.
"Having danced" means having performed a dance.
The exposition of the hidden meaning of the *Ghaṭikāra-sutta* is completed.
2. The Exposition of the *Raṭṭhapāla-sutta*.
293. *Thūlameva thullaṃ*; that which has become large, abundant, and great in its sections (*koṭṭha*) is called *thullakoṭṭhika*.
This is the name of a town obtained because of the abundance of boiled rice and cakes (*pūpa*). In the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), however, the meaning given is *thullakoṭṭha*.
By this, he shows that in the Canon (*Pāḷi*) the word was extended by the addition of the suffix *-ika*.
294. *Raṭṭhapāla* is the name of that clansman. To show, starting from his origin, how he followed the lineage of the family descended through tradition, it was said: "Why *Raṭṭhapāla*? and so forth.
*Sandhāretuṃ* means capable of maintaining [it] correctly, exactly as it was before its destruction. *Saddhā* means endowed with faith in the results of kamma.
"Seeing the novice" means seeing him being placed at the very head [of the community] due to his desire for training.
"Together with the king" (*sarājika*) means the royal assembly together with the king. "The four castes" (*cātuvaṇṇa*) refers to the collection of the four castes beginning with the brahmins.
"To nourish" means to cause to grow and to sustain through the bases of sympathy such as giving. "Whatever family" refers to whichever family. "Will be able" (*pahossati*) means will be capable.

"In whatever way I have investigated them": I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One—explaining through various modes how sensual pleasures are impermanent, suffering, subject to change, and like a skeleton, and so forth;
and how, by contrast, renunciation possesses benefits and virtues—in that very manner.
As I investigate and examine it, this occurs to me and appears thus to me:

"The holy life of the three trainings" refers to the supreme conduct comprised by the three trainings, beginning with higher virtue (*adhisīla*). It is "unbroken" because it has been brought to a state of being unimpaired;

for this is a term expressing its characteristic. It is "absolutely fulfilled" because it must be fulfilled in its entirety, without leaving out even a single portion of the training. Even a mere arising of thought...
It is "absolutely pure" because it must be maintained by not producing the stain of defilement and by making it utterly pure.
For that very reason, it is "scratched like a coin" (*saṅkhalikhita*), meaning it is as if engraved like a coin. Therefore he said, "resembling a scratched coin.
By the mention of "beard," the whiskers are also included; thus it is stated simply as "beard," meaning the upper and lower beard.

“Kāsāya” means dyed with *kasāya* (astringent dye); thus they are called *kāsāya*. He does not ordain a son who has not been permitted [by his parents], thinking, “May there be no change of heart in the minds of the parents or the worldly public.
For such was the boon granted to the Great King Suddhodana.

Because he is to be loved, he is called “dear” (*piya*); hence he says, “one who generates joy” (*pītijanaka*). Because he refreshes the mind, he is called “pleasing” (*manāpa*); hence he says, “one who increases the mind” (*manavaḍḍhanaka*).

He was nurtured in happiness during his childhood as a young boy. Thereafter, he was brought up in comfort through an abundance of agreeable food and drink, such as ghee and milk, which were rich in flavor.

Alternatively, he was nurtured in happiness by the excellence of his retinue—consisting of kinsmen and others who were firm in their devotion—as well as by the excellence of his possessions, and by the presentation of superior and refined requisites for pleasure; thus, the removal of conditions for suffering occurred for him without any difficulty.
"Accustomed to pleasure. This means either nurtured by pleasure through the attainment of internal factors, or accustomed to pleasure through the attainment of external factors.
"Of anyone" (*kassaci*) is a genitive used in the sense of the accusative; thus, it means "anything," or this is simply the reading itself. For indeed, the meaning stated is:
"You do not know even a tiny fraction, even a minute part, of suffering. "This being so" (*evaṃ sante*)—is it not?
“Raṭṭhapāla, by some means or other—whether it be death itself or something else that cannot be remedied—we shall be separated from you even against our will;

such being the case. Regarding the word *yenā* (by which): [it means] “for what reason. To show that here *kiṃ* is used in the sense of a reason with a nominative case ending, he says: “For what reason (*kena pana kāraṇena*)?”
296. *Paricārehī* means: cause [them] to move about here and there among their respective objects. Therefore he said, "Lead them hither and thither. Alternatively, *paricārehī* means:
cause yourself to be served by means of articles of pleasure; cause your own attendance to be performed.
And because one who is thus situated is said to be "sporting" (*laḷanto*) or "playing" (*kīḷanto*), the words beginning with "sport" (*laḷā*) were spoken.
"Constant giving" (*niccadāna*) refers to regular alms-giving; "extraordinary giving" (*padāna*) refers to additional gifts to be given on occasions such as the Uposatha days.
Alternatively, giving performed for the sake of preserving family tradition is called *dāna*, while giving initiated and performed by oneself alone is called *padāna*.

Or, giving that is common among the general populace and not particularly magnificent is called *dāna*, whereas giving that is uncommon to others and exceptionally magnificent is called *padāna*. [The phrase] "should be shown" (*uddassetabbā*)...
[The parents] must be shown above. From what point upward must they be shown? From the time of his going forth (pabbajitā), the parents must be shown as themselves;
therefore he said, "Just as," and so forth. 299.
Regarding the phrase "having taken hold of strength": here, "taking hold of strength" means precisely the production of bodily strength (kāyabala); thus he said, "bodily strength."
"Having generated [it]" means: dwelling thus, as stated in the Pāḷi, dwelling alone, secluded, and diligent.

"Therefore" means: because he was one who had to be guided (neyya), neither one who understands by a brief indication (ugghaṭitaññū) nor one who understands through detailed exposition (vipañcitaññū);
therefore, having gone forth late, in the twelfth year, he attained Arahatship. As for what was said in the Pāḷi, "not long after," that refers to sixty [days].
This is stated with reference to those who dwell in the retreat of insight (vipassanā-parivāsa) for more than that many years.
"Of the seven-gated courtyard" refers to the interior rooms by way of the courtyard gateways of the seven inner chambers.
"Has her adorned" means she has had her decorated with appropriate dress and ornaments suitable for her youth and age. She is like a kinswoman because she was born within [the household].
A female slave or a slave-girl. Fault is to be characterized by its state of putrefaction;

or "abhidoso" means that very [fault], and "ābhidosiko" refers to what has reached or exceeded the time of *abhidosa*—that is, the dawn (*paccūsakāla*). Therefore he said, "of that which has exceeded one night," and so forth.
It is unworthy of use because it has become putrid. "By noble expression" means by noble conduct (*ariyasamudācāra*). For the Noble Ones [regard] a woman...
They address her with the term "sister. "Relinquished possession" means that which has been abandoned as a dwelling-place.
It is said that "it is proper to speak [of it]" because of the state of being free from expectation; however, in this context, it is specifically because the object is not fit for use.
It is called a "sign" (*nimitta*) because it is marked or recognized; thus he says, "he took up the appearance," meaning the form as it was observed.
300. “Having entered the house” means having entered the interior of the house, which is the place where the mistress of the household is to sit.
“Addressing” refers to addressing the class of female servants. “Going out from outside” refers to those going out from the aforementioned interior of the house.
“There are halls in the houses” means that in the houses there are dining halls situated in a secluded spot, enclosed by walls and provided with well-secured door-fastenings.
The courtyard has its sand well-swept.
Non-acceptance is lack of conviction. Non-endurance is intolerance. A future statement is the employment of a word referring to the future;

however, the meaning [of the verb] pertains only to the present time. Therefore he said, “even though it is directly perceived. Regarding “noble psychic power”: “perceiving the repulsive in the non-repulsive...”
"In the noble psychic power (ariyiddhi) spoken of as 'he dwells'":
although putrid rice is of a nature to be discarded, even if obtained from that house, it is not fit to be given because it was given by a servant;
thus he said, "We did not receive a gift by way of the object to be given. By the words of contempt, "By these shavelings," and so forth...
In its actual meaning, the refusal was indeed obtained; however, because it was not obtained through upright and pleasant conduct, it is said, "not by way of refusal.
Therefore he said: "We did not obtain even a refusal by way of hospitality.
As for the phrase "neither a gift," and so forth, the common folk might imagine it was spoken out of expectation or impatience; therefore, this was said in order to preclude that notion.
In order to clarify his intention, the passage beginning with “But why? was stated. “Covered with a cloth” means covered with a small cloth (*sippikā*).
“Because of being a strict *ekāsanika*” (one who eats in one sitting) is merely a statement of fact, intended to show that the Elder was indeed such;
for even for a mild *ekāsanika*, once he has risen from whatever seat he used while eating even a small amount of food, [he does not sit again].
It is not permissible to eat again. Therefore, the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷābhaya said: "One should guard either the seat or the food.
Regarding the term *ukkaṭṭhasapadānacārika*: this refers to one who, without accepting even alms brought from the front or the back, stands outside the door and merely offers his bowl [to the donor].
By this very description, the elder’s status as an *ukkaṭṭhapiṇḍapātika* (one who follows the strict practice of alms-gathering) is illustrated.
Therefore he said: "He did not consent to alms for his own sake. Then, as to why he did consent, he said:

"Out of favor toward his mother," and so forth. For wise men do not become purifiers of ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) by neglecting the favor that ought to be shown to their parents or to their teachers and preceptors.
301. *Payuttaṃ* means employed by way of increase; it should be understood as being stated after the elision of a *taddhita* suffix, just as in other instances such as:
"Having obtained ancestral wealth, Sañcaya lives happily. *Jeṭṭhakitthiyo* means principal women.
*Itaḥ* means from the abundance of wealth to be enjoyed in this family. *Aññato* means from another [family], because it has been given to this one.
Because of the prosperity to be experienced within the family.
302. *Cittavicittaṃ*: variegated both by way of its design and by way of ornaments such as jewelry, which serve as a fitting adornment.
*Vaṇakāyaṃ*: a body that has become like a wound. *Samantato ussitaṃ*: raised up all around, from the lower part of the body upwards.
And it is dependent [on others]. It is constantly afflicted by the four [elements], or always suffering.

It is "full of many intentions" because it is to be intended for by many—by kinsmen through gestures, expressions, and charms due to its being an object of passion, and by dogs, jackals, and the like, due to its being a source of food.
As for "stability," there is no persistence or non-transformation. Therefore he said: "The very nature of being subject to breaking."
“Fixed” means that the attainment of the state of being a leak (*parissava*) and the attainment of destruction are absolute.
“Even painted” means even when painted with perfumes and so forth. “Form” means the body.
“Made with lac” means made beautiful with lump-lac; hence he said, “colored with lac. “Smeared with powder” means...
It was smeared with illuminating powders such as *gorocanā*, which had been processed through methods of heating and burning to remove impurities;
therefore, he said, "with mustard-paste," and so forth.
"With juice-water" means with water mixed with the sap of pine resin (*sarala*). "Having performed the turning and rolling" means by way of turning and rolling [the clay].

"Having paid homage. "By means of the arrangement of the eightfold grid" means by means of the arrangement of the eightfold grid for the purpose of distinguishing between the walls, the corners, the half-moons, and so forth.
"While crying out" means while crying out, "He is fleeing! Seize him! Seize him! "Gold, silver, and women" should be stated [as the objects of theft]. 303.
"To each one who was exalted" means to each one who was elevated by the excellence of noble lineage, wealth, great learning, and wisdom. "Distinguished" means by way of his sublime nature.

304. *Parijuññāni* means states of decline. He says "worn out by old age" (*jarājiṇṇo*) referring to those beings who, overcome by disease, are like those whose youth has decayed and who are in a state of senility;
he speaks thus to turn them away from that [state]. It is one grown old in years, not one grown old in virtue and so forth.
One who takes or acquires greatness is a *mahallaka*; it is one grown old by birth, not one grown old by wealth and so forth. This refers to what is reckoned as three or two royal cycles...

“Addhagata” means one who has gone through the course of time and has passed beyond it. And since he has thus transcended both the first and middle stages of life, it is said, “he has surpassed the course of time.

Because the first and middle stages of life are understood by the terms *jiṇṇa* (aged) and so forth, the word *vaya* (stage of life), distinguished by its state of having been reached, refers specifically to the final stage; hence it is said, “he has arrived at the last stage of life.”
With the intention that in such passages as “one who has few desires, one who is not touched by gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, heat, and creeping things,” the word *appa-* signifies absence, he said:
“‘Free from illness’ means healthy; ‘free from affliction’ means without suffering. Or rather, the sense of “little” (*appa*) is intended here;
in that case too, the word *appa-* should be understood [in its primary sense]. For thus it is said: “Householder, whoever, while maintaining this putrid body...”
The scriptural passage, “Who else but a fool would claim health even for a moment? is thus established. *Vipāka* means ripening; that itself is *vepāka*.
One who possesses an equal (*sama*) ripening is *samavepākinī*; [the stomach] is so called because of that.

Precisely because of that state of having an equal ripening, it correctly receives and retains everything, hence it is called the *gahaṇī* (the receiver). For through the excellence of the *gahaṇī*, the food consumed as it was eaten—
When it decays properly, the food remains in the body, not otherwise; that is, the food consumed is digested through the sharpness of the digestive fire (*gahaṇī*).
"It remains just so" means it remains in the very form in which it was eaten, due to the dullness of the digestive fire.
A desire for food arises precisely because the food consumed has undergone proper transformation. "For that very reason" means precisely because of the state of being equally heated.
When wealth and possessions are being exhausted, they do not go to exhaustion all at once suddenly, but rather gradually;
likewise with kinsmen—thus he said, "by degrees. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "fear of famine, etc.," he includes the fear of disease and so forth.
305. He said, "The expositions on the teachings have been announced," because the exposition is grasped by means of the headings of the announcements.

Alternatively, those teachings which are called "announcements" (uddesa) in the sense of being things to be announced are themselves called "expositions" (niddesa) in the sense of being things to be explained;
thus the meaning stated is "the expositions on the teachings have been announced. Or else, those teachings which, by way of clarifying impermanence and so forth, [are presented] higher and higher...

They will teach; those teachings they will teach exactly as they are, in their entirety—thus should the lack of difference in meaning between the summary (uddesa) and the detailed exposition (niddesa) be understood.
Therein means in the proximity of aging and death. "Inconstant" (addhuva) means devoid of constancy, not stable; the meaning is "impermanent.
Therefore he said, "devoid of the state of constancy," which means it is separated from the causes of the constant state that is unarisen, unbecome, and unconditioned.
Or, "it is led away" (*upanīyyati*) means that the world is completely led by aging and death; therefore, it should be understood here as "unstable.
"By one who protects" means being deprived of a Lord capable of protecting [beings] from calamities such as birth and so forth. [The Lord thinks:
"I shall liberate this world from the suffering of this cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*); I shall not allow them to overcome aging, sickness, and death."
"Abhisaraṇa" means "one who rushes toward"; it refers to some Lord (issara) who is the giver of the world's happiness and the provider of its welfare.

Because such a being does not exist, it is said: "Without a lord (anabhissara), without a refuge (asaraṇa). It is "without a protector" (nissaka) because of the absence of any object to be cherished as "mine.
Therefore, it says: "Deprived of one's own goods," and so forth. It is called "the slave of craving" because he has come under the power of craving and is conquered by craving.
306. Because it is within the domain of elephants or because it is dependent upon elephants, the elephant-lore (*hatthisippa*) is understood by the word “elephant”;
thus he said, “In elephant-lore (*hatthismiṃ*); in the science of elephants. The same method applies to the remaining terms as well.
He said, “Possessing thigh-strength (*ūrubalī*),” meaning one who has preeminent strength in the thighs; and in order to demonstrate that very meaning clearly, he said, “Of whom...”
The passage beginning with "hī" has been stated. [It refers to one] who splits an enemy army that was united, and who maintains and supports his own army which had been split.
Regarding the term "bāhubalī" (one possessed of arm-strength), here too the meaning should be explained by the passage beginning with "for he, having taken a shield and a weapon," and so forth;

however, in this context, the construction is "arm-strength [is used] to bring back a kingdom that has fallen into the hands of an enemy. For just as in the case of the term "ūrubalī" (one possessed of thigh-strength) [the meaning is understood through the context].

In this case as well, the meaning should be understood without referring to the strength of the arms; likewise, in the term "bāhubalī" (possessing arm-strength), the meaning should be understood without referring to the strength of the thighs.
That in which the conceit of "I" (ahaṃmāna) is placed is the self (attā); it is the personal existence (attabhāva). Because the self is capable (alaṃ samattho) therein, it is called "alamatta";
thus he said, "one whose personal existence is capable."
"Pariyodhāya" means either "having polished" or "having established protection all around. "There exist, Master Raṭṭhapāla, in this royal family even a body of elephants...
[and so on]... they will continue to exist"—this too the king said while bringing forward a reason for the subsequent exposition of the Dhamma.
Speaking by way of singing after what has already been stated is "anugīti. Those verses, however, are [for the purpose of] the expositions of the Dhamma.

It is called "the recapitulation" (*anugīti*) because it summarizes [the teaching] as appropriate, even without following the exact sequence of the exposition; thus he says, "the recapitulation of the four summaries of the Dhamma.

(307) "One" means of a single kind. It should be understood that the sensual pleasures of objects (*vatthukāma*) and the sensual pleasures of defilements (*kilesakāma*) are spoken of in that way after being distinguished by way of their respective spheres.
"By the ocean's edge" means bounded by the ocean.

*Aho vata* is a particle used for lamentation, as in such expressions as, “Alas, what an evil deed has been done by me! In phrases such as *amarā*, they say it means “they speak. When one ought to say “for us” (*amha*) with reference to the deceased, it is called “immortal” (*amara*) due to the influence of grief.

*Vosānaṃ* means an end; the meaning is “conclusion. *Sāvā* is wisdom itself. “Than wealth” means than all forms of wealth. It is “more excellent,” the best; therefore he said, “They call the life of one who lives by wisdom the best life.
Among those beings who are committing evil, this locative case is used in the sense of selection. “By succession” means by the succession of individual existences (*attabhāva*).
"Having entered into saṃsāra": by way of entering into saṃsāra within the realms of existence (*bhava*) and so forth, one goes to the next world;
and while going to the next world, one enters the womb, which consists of manifold suffering. "Of such a person":
of one who is of that nature—namely, one of little wisdom who has become a basis for the sufferings of dwelling in the womb and so on—and another of little wisdom who places his faith in him.
Thinking with conviction that these bring about welfare and happiness;

because it was said, "one of evil nature," he stated, "in the next world, the world of the states of misery (apāya)," meaning that for such a person, the so-called other world is indeed a state of suffering.
"In manifold forms" means in many various ways, by way of visible forms, sounds, and so forth, and even therein, by way of being more refined and so on.
"Sāmaññameva" means that the state of being a recluse (*samaṇabhāva*) alone is better. Here, the fourth discourse on the Dhamma is chanted in the first two verses;
the third [discourse] in the fourth verse; the second [discourse] in the fifth verse; the second and third [discourses] in the sixth verse;
and the first discourse on the Dhamma is chanted in the seventh verse, while the eighth and subsequent verses concern the engagement with and withdrawal from sensual pleasures and renunciation.

And having clarified, as appropriate, the dangers and benefits [of household life], he concludes the aforementioned summary of the Dhamma by showing his own reason for going forth from the perspective of another.

Therefore it is said: "But those verses were recited as a summary, gathering [the topics] as appropriate, even without following the sequence of the teaching of the summaries of the Dhamma. The rest is easy to understand.
The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning of the Raṭṭhapāla Sutta is completed.
3. Commentary on the Maghadeva Sutta: 308.
"In the past, there was a king named Maghadeva" refers to a time in this very eon when the lifespan was many thousands of years.

Among humans, the first king to appear in succession among the eighty-four thousand wheel-turning monarchs was a king named Maghadeva. Regarding this, worldly people say that "Dhamma" refers to the duties of a king (*rājadhamma*).
However, [in the ultimate sense], "Dhamma" refers to that which is comprised of the perfections (*pāramitā*) and the treasure-store of Great Enlightenment (*mahābodhi-nidhāna*).
“Righteous” (*dhammika*) means existing according to the Dhamma. “In accordance with the Dhamma” (*dhammena*) means by way of the proper method.

At that time, because the King had not yet attained the Dhamma consisting in the cultivation of the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*), or because he shared a common capacity for application through non-covetousness and other such qualities, it is said that he was “established in the ten courses of wholesome action.
“In accordance with the Dhamma” (*dhammam*) means not departing from the Dhamma; for likewise, due to his lack of partiality, he is called “impartial” (*samo*).
He said, "He walks evenly. "By the natural order" means precisely by the order handed down through tradition.
Since the majority of householders are gathered in towns and districts, for that reason it is stated in the commentary as "of householders" (*gahapatikānaṃ*).
However, in the Canon, the conduct of city-dwellers is one thing and the conduct of those in towns and districts is another; thus, they are taken separately.
“Both in the villages and in the countryside. *Pāṭihāriya* means the warding off of the Uposatha by way of going forth to meet it and coming back;
that itself is the *pāṭihārika*, the fortnight. “These days” refers to these four days. 309.
*Deva* (the god) is so called in the sense of overcoming death (*maccu*). For just as a god overcomes ordinary beings, so too—

Death overcomes beings. They are called "messengers" because they are like the messengers of the god of Death who carry out his commands, saying: "I have come to crush so-and-so; you must seize him by the hair and not let him go.
The phrase "adorned and prepared" is stated to show that she stood there having manifested her own divine power. It is exactly like a prophecy by a deity.
It does not take long because death is imminent. "The pure devas" refers to Brahmās whose taints are exhausted;
for they manifest aging and other such signs to Bodhisattvas in their final existence.
"Afflicted and diseased" means having arisen into suffering by way of illness. [This refers to] Bodhisattvas in their final existence.

Because the state of being attended upon by the *visuddhidevas* (pure deities) applies, even for other wise persons who are not so attended, the usage [of the term] is established by way of figurative expression (*pariyāya*);
thus he said, "by this figurative expression. *Disampati*:
this is a designation formed by the elision of a case ending; since regions are spoken of by means of their cardinal points, it means "the sovereign king of those regions."
The meaning is as follows: they grow on the head, which is the supreme limb, thus they are "hair of the head" (*uttamaṅgaruhā*).
Since these, by virtue of their graying, unconditionally indicate the final stage of life, they are therefore called "the harriers of age.
A "pair of men" (*purisayuga*) is so called because it is defined by the stability of the men born within that lineage; therefore, he said: "in the origin of the lineage."
"Men. By the phrase "subsisting on alms brought from the royal palace," he shows that [the boy] had entered upon the life of a novice monk.

"Being carried about" means that, as if being carried here and there, he was attended at every moment by that great retinue and played the games of children. Some, however, take it with emphasis: "being carried about indeed."
If they say [he was] "attha" (meaning), then it would follow that for eighty-four thousand years he was a young child still nursing; therefore, that is incorrect.
Furthermore, this is contradictory because, after mentioning his childhood, it immediately follows with the mention of his being viceroy (*oparājja*).
[The following list includes: *pañcamaṅgala-vacana*, *unnaṅgala-maṅgala*, *ukkanta-namaṅgalakamma*, *mahāmaṅgala*, and *dussamaṅgala*.
It should be understood that they have indeed come together.
(311) "Puttapaputtakā" refers to the lineage consisting of sons and grandsons—those such as sons and nephews who have arrived by way of successive generations (*savaṃsava*).
"Nihataṃ" means placed or established; the meaning is that it has been set in motion. Alternatively, "nihataṃ" [means] by virtue of its state of being constantly established.
The meaning is "to be employed. Therefore he said, "the virtuous conduct" (*kalyāṇavatta*). Regarding "two qualities exceeding [those of others]":

from the time of the Great Being as Maghadeva, there were two qualities exceeding those of other kings; moreover, his qualities were of many hundreds of thousands of varieties, exceeding even those. 312.
"Thirty-three together with those who perform meritorious deeds are reborn here"—the place associated with that is the "Thirty-three" (*tettimsa*); that very [place]...
The Thirty-three (Tāvatiṃsa): those who have that as their abode are the Tāvatiṃsas. And since their state of residing there was preceded by their having been reborn there, he said:
"Of the gods of the Thirty-three" means "of the gods reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa realm. "Of the king" refers to King Nimi.
"Abiding by his advice" refers both to the manner of restraining him, saying, "Do not come into my presence unless you guard your virtue," and so forth.
"By dwelling entirely within my realm, you must guard your virtue"—having thus established him in the instruction by means of this advice delivered.
Then [he addressed] King Nimi, who was of great luster, great radiance, and great majesty.
Having made known his own status as Sakka, saying, "I am Sakka, the lord of the gods, come into your presence," he added, "I shall dispel your doubt."
He said: Therefore he says, "The lords of all beings," and so forth.
He speaks while disparaging [the Buddha] with the word "what? because of his own inferiority compared to the Buddha's virtue.

"By way of distinguished qualities" means by way of the state of supreme excellence, being the cause for gains, fame, and so on, as well as for being dear and agreeable, culminating in the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhaya*). At that time...
The Elder Anuruddha, the Sakyan, spoke the words beginning with "For I" while elucidating how, through his own previous birth, he had realized for himself that virtue is greater than giving.
In this context, the phrase "from the realm of hungry ghosts" (*pettivisayato*) refers to the sense-sphere world of the devas (*kāmāvacara-devaloka*) over which he presided.

For it was there that, during a period of one hundred thousand eons, his aspiration for the turning of the wheel of Dharma (*vivaṭṭajjhāsaya*) had been fulfilled and his perfections (*pāramī*) completed.
The world of the gods appeared like the world of the *petas*. For this very reason, he said: "Resounding with throngs of celestial nymphs, frequented by hosts of *pisācas*.

Regarding "a noble" (*khattiya*), it means one of the noble caste. "He is purified" refers to rebirth in the Brahma-world, because of being purified from the defilement of sensual desire. And by "body," he means the Brahma-body.
Having seen this form never seen before, and thinking, "Great indeed is my fear," he said: "Without wavering."
For one who is afraid indeed trembles because of the alteration of the mind and the trembling of the body; therefore he said, "fearless.
"It is easy to speak" means it is easy to speak of the fruit of merit.
"They become truly fit by relying on the mind" means that having understood the mind of Mātali the Sakka, they became as if already prepared.
The sons of the gods perform the function of noble steeds yoked to chariots. Thus, at such a time, they act in such a way as the son of the gods Erāvaṇa performs the function of an elephant.
"From the binding onwards" means from the point where the axle is connected by means of the circumference of the chariot-fender;
that is the "binding. It is called "axle-bound" (*akkhabaddha*) because the axle is bound there.

The place where the axle is fastened to the chariot. Just as he sent the chariot downward by his own power from the world of the gods as far as the path of the moon’s orbit, so too did he send it from the path of the moon’s orbit as far as the king’s palace.
"Having shown two paths" means [pointing] toward the sky with the goad-stick.
As if painting with his own supernatural power, he showed two paths—one leading to hell and one leading to the heavenly world—and said, "By which [path]?

and so forth. This is merely a pedagogical device; what is intended is the actual performance of that act by which, for one traveling in that chariot, both hell and the heavenly world become manifest.
Referring specifically to the reason already stated, the Great Being said, “Mātali, lead me by both paths. “Difficult” means hard to traverse.
“Vettaraṇī” is the name of a particular hell. “Boiling” means seething, with a surface resembling boiling oil.
“Filled with alkaline matter” means like alkaline water.
"Having turned back the chariot" means having turned it away from facing toward hell.
"To the divine daughter Bīraṇī" refers to the celestial maiden (accharā) named Bīraṇī. "To the divine son Soṇadinna" refers to the divine son named Soṇadinna.
"Of the divine sons belonging to a group" refers to those divine sons who were reborn as a group because they had performed merit as a group.
"At the time of the meal" means at the approaching hour. "The guest" refers to the Paccekabuddha;
some also say he was a certain elder whose taints were destroyed during the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa.
"As a mother rejoices in her son once" means that just as a mother rejoices once—at the time of his arrival—when her son returns from abroad, so too did she rejoice at all times.
He served [the meal] with due care. "Self-restraint and sharing" refers to the virtue of self-restraint and the virtue of sharing. Regarding the "Jātaka," it is the Nimijātaka.

"Cittakūṭa" is the gate-tower in the southern direction of the city of the gods. "Sakka being unable to restrain his mind" means that, on account of the honor and hospitality shown by the deities toward the Great Being, he was unable to control the state of his own mind that had arisen.
