Unable to conceal his envious mind within himself and failing to keep it from being revealed externally, he demonstrated his service to Sakka out of a desire to provoke the Great Being, saying, "Dwell under the power of others' merit.
Because the former Sakka was long-lived, he was made to appear as if aged and decrepit; thus he is called "Jarasakka" (the Old Sakka).
315. "The rest of all" refers to the royal conduct of the ancient kings of his own lineage, remaining [unpracticed] after he had gone forth into homelessness.

"Returned to its natural state" means that it once again became exactly as it was by nature. By the very statement that he did not remain in the state of a householder, the absence of the qualities of renunciation—such as the cultivation of the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*) and so forth—is indicated.
316. One who does not exert effort cuts it off, yet it is not yet severed.
When the necessary conditions—such as association with virtuous friends—are present, one is able to carry out the virtuous conduct of those possessing moral discipline.

For one who is immoral, it is said to be "severed," because practice itself becomes impossible due to their lack of aspiration for that [virtue]. The seven types of trainees (sekha) maintain this virtuous conduct.
Because its task was not yet completed. That which was uttered by one whose taints were destroyed is called "completed," because its task had been finished. The rest is easy to understand.
The elucidation of the hidden meaning in the commentary on the Maghadeva Sutta is complete.
4. Commentary on the Madhura Sutta.
317. They speak of Madhurāyanti as Uttaramadhurāyaṃ. Gundāvana is the forest of black sippali trees;
they also call it the atimuttaka forest. Among the four castes, the brahmin alone is the most excellent caste.

"Pale" means pure; "black" means impure. "In places where birth, lineage, and so forth are designated" refers to those who, by way of birth, lineage, and so on, consider themselves pure—namely, the brahmins.

The intended meaning is that they alone are of pure birth, and not others. Alternatively, the intention is that through pure reflection regarding *saṃsāra*, only Brahmins are purified, because the purification prescribed by the Vedas is not within the domain of others.

However, this contradicts their own [scriptures], since the study of mantras is permitted for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas as well, and there is no purification from *saṃsāra* through the procedure of studying mantras.
Sons may indeed be those who are not born from the breast (*anorasa*), but these are not like that; thus he said, "born from the breast" (*orasa*).
Even a son reared on the breast is called "born from the breast. However, to show that these [sons] emerge from the mouth and are then reared on the breast, it is said:
"born from the breast, born from the mouth. For that very reason, they are "born of Brahmā" (*brahmajā*); even those produced from Brahmā are called "born of Brahmā."
They are not called so in that way; rather, these [brahmins] are "created by Brahmā" (brahmanimmitā) because they were directly fashioned by Brahmā,

and for that very reason, they are "heirs of Brahmā" (brahmadāyādā), being heirs to the inheritance of knowledge and so forth obtainable from Brahmā— all of this is like the boastful pretexts of the brahmins,
a mere verbal fabrication that is unauthoritative and incapable of withstanding scrutiny by the wise, serving only to uphold the doctrine of Brahmā.
Because of its non-existence. Whatever else needs to be said here has already been stated in the *Visuddhimagga-vaṇṇanā*. Therefore, he said:
“It is merely a sound,” and so forth. “Merely conventional usage” means that this is merely the verbal expression, such as “The brahmin caste alone is the best caste”;
there is no actual referent for it of the kind intended by those [who speak thus].
318. *Samijjheyya* means that one’s own aspiration would be fulfilled by way of illuminating one’s right view.

Therefore he said, “one’s desire would be fulfilled. *Khattiyo pi* means even a kshatriya of another lineage. *Assa* refers to one who has attained wealth and so forth that have been successfully accomplished.
Therefore he said, “of one endowed with sovereignty. *Nesam*—among these four castes, by virtue of being the first to rise, etc.

The construction is: "There is no difference [in function] because they must be attended to by others. 322. The construction is: "I am your attendant with robes and other requisites; you should tell me whenever you desire anything, whatever you need.
Protection (*rakkhāgutti*) is the warding off of dangers such as thieves; guarding (*āvaraṇagutti*) is the warding off of dangers caused by [the lack of] giving and so forth.
Protection through guarding consists in the prevention of present harm; protection through warding consists in the prevention of future harm.

And herein, regarding the duty of those such as Khattiyas and others to obey whoever among them is their lord, and regarding the consequences to be obtained for them in the future life through their performance of wholesome or unwholesome deeds, as well as the respectful service to be rendered by those who have gone forth—even the slightest [violation of these]...
There is no distinction; therefore, that absence of distinction has been elucidated in various places in the Canon by means of the phrase "this being so," and so forth.
The rest is easily understood.
The *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Hidden Meaning) for the commentary on the *Madhurasutta* is completed.
5. Commentary on the Bodhirājakumāra Sutta 324.
"Olokanaka-paduma" refers to a play-lotus. Because it has the shape of a *kokanada* (red lotus), it receives the designation "kokanada.
325. From "as far as the western... down to "the plank," [it is so called] because it was spread out last of all. For that which is on the uppermost plank...

The top of the staircase. "For the sake of looking" means not only for the sake of looking at the Blessed One’s arrival, but also for the sake of stepping upon the cloth mat that had been spread out according to his own aspiration.
"Young birds" refers to the offspring of ducks and lapwings. "He might be someone else" means [he might have been] other than a woman in that particular existence.
"Now there might be another woman who becomes his wife. 'May he obtain a son'—[this refers to] a son by virtue of his own karma, not [the son] of the other [woman].

By both of these" means by these very two. "For these reasons" refers to that prince’s false apprehension concerning the Buddha, the complaints of the sectarians (titthiyā), and [the fact that] in the future, people will [act] on account of the monks.
"Remorse" refers to these three reasons. "Laid out" means spread out as a cloth-covering. "Desiring good fortune" means those who seek auspiciousness (*maṅgalikā*). 326.
By the phrase "the third reason," he speaks of the non-arising of remorse among the monks.
Thinking with the intention that "any pleasure in enjoyment is devotion to the pursuit of sensual pleasure," and perceiving it as such... [as before] ...thinking thus, he spoke.
327. Then the Blessed One, desiring to detach him from that wrong adherence, began to demonstrate his own difficult ascetic practices by means of the passage beginning with “So kho ahaṃ.
This should be understood in the same manner as explained in the *Mahāsaccaka Sutta*, because the reading beginning with “So kho ahaṃ” follows the very same sequence as it appears there.
The phrase “in the manner stated in the *Pāsarāsi Sutta*” follows this same principle here as well.
343. *Aṅkusagahaṇasippaṃ*: "They seize with this; one becomes skillful in seizing by means of it," thus it is the art of seizing with a hook (*aṅkusa*).
*Meghautuṃ*: the cold season that arises dependent upon the clouds (*megha*). *Pabbatautuṃ*: the hot season that arises dependent upon the mountains (*pabbata*).
And because his cold and hot seasons came (*āgato*) in that manner due to both [the clouds and the mountains], they changed the letter *t* to *d* and gave him the name *Udena*.
The ascetic, through his deepened knowledge, learned of the king’s death. "From the beginning" means from the time she became the chief queen of King Parantapa in the city of Kosambī.
"Formerly" refers to the period when he was possessed of virtue. "Elephant-taming science" (*hatthigantha*) is the manual for bringing elephants under one's own control;
by means of that very science, he trained him, and thus his task was accomplished.
344. "The state of striving" (*padhānabhāvo*) means devotion to meditation (*bhāvanānuyogo*). Or, one who is engaged in striving is "striving" (*padhāniyo*);
for a striving bhikkhu, the factors that are the causes of that very state of striving are the "factors of striving" (*padhāniyaṅgāni*). One who possesses faith is "faithful" (*saddho*).
Although the faith of even the *paccekabodhisattas* is indeed faith that has come from the time of their initial resolve (*abhinīhāra*), [it is not so] for the *mahābodhisattas*.
However, because faith (*saddhā*) is more predominant, it alone is taken [as the primary factor].

"Fixing by way of immovability" (*okappana*) means the settling (*kappana*) after having plunged into the qualities of the Triple Gem with a state that cannot be shaken by anything, thinking: "The Blessed One is the Perfectly Enlightened One; the Dhamma is well-expounded; the Saṅgha has practiced well.
The arising of clarity (*pasāda*) is simply the act of being confident (*pasīdana*) in the Triple Gem. "Enlightenment" (*bodhi*) is stated to be the knowledge of the four paths (*catumagga-ñāṇa*).
Because it is the cause of omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*), it is called "enlightenment" (*bodhi*) or "perfect enlightenment" (*sammāsambodhi*).

For path-knowledge (*maggañāṇa*) has omniscient knowledge as its proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*), and omniscient knowledge has path-knowledge as its proximate cause; thus, it is called "perfect enlightenment.

Because the Dhamma is well-understood through its definitive realization, the excellence of the Dhamma (*sudhammatā*) and the right practice of the Saṅgha (*suppaṭipatti*) are indeed determined. Therefore, he said: "It is precisely the basis of the teaching..."

"Mindful," and so forth. His striving—his energy—succeeds because, through faith in the Triple Gem, he is not averse to the application of effort, thinking, "By this practice I shall be liberated from aging and death.
"Free from illness," and so forth, has already been explained above. One who confesses a fault and undertakes restraint for the future [is established] in right practice.

For the purpose of purification. "In order to understand both arising and passing away" means to know the arising and the passing away of the five aggregates of clinging by means of the formula beginning with "with the arising of ignorance.
Therefore he said, "By this," and so forth. "Completely purified" means free from defilements.
"To break through" means to abandon by way of partial eradication (*tadaṅga*), thereby becoming a condition for abandonment by complete cutting off (*samuccheda*). That which...
"Suffering is exhausted" refers to the suffering that would arise dependent upon that [defilement] and its supporting karma, provided the defilements have not been abandoned. 345.
"On the remaining days" means from the seventh day onwards until two nights and days have passed.
346. The embryo residing in the womb is called "the womb" by way of a metaphorical designation for its support;
since she possesses that [embryo], she is "pregnant. Therefore, it is said: "one who has conceived a being. Furthermore, protection is established for her:
the refuge taken by the mother is called a "wholesome refuge" for that being once he has emerged from the womb and has proclaimed his going for refuge; thus, the mother provides protection.
"Even for a son, it is established": this means at the time of being an elder, that is, at the time of understanding the meaning of the words.

"They cause him to recollect" means they cause him to recollect by way of establishing the qualities of the Triple Gem according to what has been seen and according to his own strength. "Having observed" means having reflected upon the meaning already stated.
It is called "the going for refuge is accomplished" precisely because of the state of a mind previously directed toward that [refuge] through the observation of the Triple Gem's nature as a refuge.
The remainder is easy to understand.
The elucidation of the hidden meaning (*līnatthappakāsanā*) of the commentary on the *Bodhirājakumārasutta* is complete.
6. Commentary on the *Aṅgulimālasutta*.
347. By the phrase "he wears a garland of fingers," it is shown that his name is appropriate to his function. "Therein" means: in that wearing of the finger-garland according to the teacher’s word.
The intention is that he becomes like a single ear of rice in a field of a thousand measures of chaff—his own specific purpose being no longer discernible.
They sent him to Takkasilā, [saying]: "By means of the proper application for mastering a craft in the presence of such a teacher..."
“Knowing the welfare pertaining both to this life and the life to come, one should not commit what is burdensome.
Thus they became outsiders [regarding the teacher Ahiṃsaka], due to the state of being produced from the nature of the teacher’s mind through his perfection in conduct.
“Speaking as if out of affection” means speaking as if with affection.
"He does not even learn counting" means he does not even perceive the method of counting. Regarding this, he states the reason with the words "by nature," and so forth.
"In the place where it was set down" refers to a place such as between trees or shrubs where the fingers are lost due to birds and jackals.
"Bhaggava" is said by way of the family name of the chaplain to the King of Kosala. "A thief" means one who is untrustworthy because of his reckless nature.
A branch that has long been established is not to be trusted, for it is susceptible to the entry of scorpions and other such creatures.

A king is not to be trusted because of his intoxication with power and greed for wealth, as there is sometimes even suspicion regarding his life. A woman is not to be trusted because of her fickle character and state of mind.
He will not be lifted up from the mire of saṃsāra.
348. "Having gathered together" means having made a collective agreement, thinking: "Having assembled in one place, we shall kill or drive away the thief.
"Exertion of psychic power" (iddhābhisaṅkhāra) refers to the mental formation or resolution (adhiṭṭhāna).
"He exerted" means he resolved. "Having withdrawn" means having contracted. "In the vicinity" means in the area near the thief.
349. *Daṇḍa* refers to punishment, such as the cutting off of hands and other limbs, which is designated as "punishment. *Pavattayitabbo* means it should be brought [into effect].
*Apanetvā* means having abandoned by way of complete eradication from one’s own mental continuum. *Paṭisaṅkhāya* means by means of reflective contemplation (*paṭisaṅkhāna*).

*Avihiṃsāya* means by means of compassion (*karuṇā*). *Sāraṇīyadhammesu* means among all six qualities that lead to remembrance; [the phrase] "standing" refers to those who have not yet stood [firmly] in them.

Because evil qualities were utterly eradicated even at the foot of the Bodhi tree. Showing that just as he has wandered through immeasurable time in the past, so too will he wander in the future by means of this practice, he said, "Now," and so forth.

*Itveva* means *iti eva*; the word *iti* has the sense of indication. Therefore he said, "having spoken thus. *Akiri* means he scattered; he threw away all five weapons. Hence it is said, "he hurled and cast them away."
350. "From there" means she went to Sāvatthī by the very same path she had come.
"He will consent" means that when it is said, "I shall go to restrain the robber," he will remain silent. "A name arisen from a cruel deed" refers to this name, "Aṅgulimāla."
351. Elephants become "wild forest elephants" because humans are unable to go there; the same applies to horses.
The reason for the breaking of the thousand peaks was that, out of fear of the Elder’s arrival, they abandoned their water-jars and fled.
"With a miscarriage" means with a difficult labor. It is said, "by the power of his renunciation," meaning by the majesty of the Teacher’s teaching.
But it must be said: for that [truth] is also the cause of this. "Noble ones" (ariyā) refers to birth and renunciation, because they are born for the sake of the noble state (ariyabhāva).
"This is called a great protection" (mahāparittaṃ nāmetaṃ) means this is a protection of great power.

For the Elder performed it with the full nature of a noble one through the resolution of truth (saccādhiṭṭhāna). Therefore he said: "In the place where the act of truth was performed. "Conceived in the womb" (gabbhamūḷhaṃ).

Regarding "mūḷhagabbhaṃ" (obstructed birth): for when the fetus has matured and the process of birth is proceeding correctly, at the time of delivery it is moved and turned by the winds born of karma (*kammaja-vāta*);
with its feet upward and its head downward, it faces the opening of the womb.
Thus, being unattached to anything, it emerges safely outside. However, when the process goes wrong due to a failure in turning, it blocks the path of the womb.
It lies crosswise; thus, when the birth canal is blocked, she who is there, being turned back and forth by the winds born of karma, is called "confused in womb" (*byākulā mūḷhagabbhā*);
it is with reference to her that it is said, "confused in the womb.
What is called a "truth-act" (*saccakiriyā*) is performed after reflecting upon one's own virtue in accordance with the Buddha’s intention; therefore, it is a truth-act.
"It should be understood that there is no medical treatment. By the words "And for the Elder too," etc., he states the reason why [the Blessed One] should approach him.
Relying on these two causes, the Blessed One caused the Elder to perform an act of truth (*saccakiriya*). "Birth" (*jāti*) means the root-birth.
"With his head split, having been struck and exhausted" refers to a corresponding kamma to be experienced in the present life (*diṭṭhadhammavedanīya-kamma*) in hell.
It is kamma to be experienced in the present life (*diṭṭhadhammavedanīya-kamma*) that is of the same nature as the specific kamma that produced [the rebirth].
And "likeness" (*sabhāgatā*) consists in complete similarity by way of having a common basis, a common object, and being included within the same cognitive process (*vīthi*), and so forth;
for even that which is similar is indeed called "that very thing," as in the expressions, "the fruition of that very kamma," and "that very partridge, those very medicinal herbs."
Now, in order to demonstrate that very similarity, the passage beginning with “Kammaṃ hi” is commenced.

“Only while being performed” means only while being produced in succession through the convergence of conditions. It fulfills three portions; it fulfills the three parts known as *dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya* (to be experienced in the present life), *aparāpariyāyavedanīya* (to be experienced in subsequent lives), and *upapajjavedanīya* (to be experienced upon rebirth);
it proceeds by way of those three portions.
"Visible here and now" (diṭṭhadhamma) refers to the present personal existence that has become manifest;

karma whose fruit is to be experienced therein is "to be experienced in this very life" (diṭṭhadhammavedanīya). Karma whose fruit is to be experienced immediately after the present existence is "to be experienced upon rebirth" (upapajjavedanīya).
[Karma whose fruit is to be experienced] in another turn of personal existence or change of personal existence subsequent to the one immediately following the present existence...
Kamma whose fruit is to be experienced is "to-be-experienced-in-a-subsequent-becoming" (aparāpariyāyavedanīya).

However, when a first impulsion consciousness (paṭhamajavana-cetanā) has attained a state of strength through not being overcome by opposing factors and through having acquired excellence via specific conditions, it becomes preeminent due to such prior formative volitions (pubbābhisaṅkhāra) and, proceeding with such intensity, yields its fruit in that very same individual existence;
this is "to-be-experienced-in-the-present-life" (diṭṭhadhammavedanīya).

It is called "name" (nāma). For, in the manner described, because it is powerful within the stream of impulsion (javana), because it proceeds by way of providing benefit or non-benefit toward those endowed with specific qualities, and because it lacks the attainment of repetition (āsevana) and has only a slight result (appavipāka), it does not—like the other two types of karma—depend on the cessation of the active stream or depend on the acquisition of a new location.
Thus, it yields its fruit right here, like a mere flower, consisting merely of the result of its own occurrence.
"Unable to do so" means that the giving of the fruit of karma occurs only through the convergence of other conditions such as the physical basis (*upadhi*) and the application (*payoga*);

thus, due to the absence of those, it is "unable to give its result in that very same existence. "Lapsed karma" (*ahosikamma*) refers to karma that has simply "been" (*ahosi*), but whose result has not "been," nor will it "be," nor is it "present"—it is karma that must be described in this way. "Productive of benefit" (*atthasādhikā*)...
It is that which accomplishes the purpose of giving and so forth, as well as killing and so forth. But what is it? He says: "The seventh impulsion-consciousness (javana-cetanā).

For that is the decisive volition (*sanniṭṭhāpaka-cetanā*); having acquired distinction through the aforementioned method and having been cultivated by the preceding impulsions, it yields its result in the immediately following existence.
It is called "kamma to be experienced upon rebirth" (*upapajjavedanīya-kamma*). Therefore he said: "In the next [existence]..."

"It gives its result within the present selfhood. By the phrase "as long as the process of saṃsāra continues," it is meant that in the absence of the process of saṃsāra, the action remains on the side of the "ineffective" (*ahosikamma*), because there is no opportunity for it to ripen.
They are eradicated by bringing about the state of non-arising for the opportunity of ripening. [This refers to] karma to be experienced in the present life (*diṭṭhadhammavedanīya*).
It exists because the state of being capable of ripening has not yet been brought about, and because the opportunity for ripening has not been cut off.
For when karma that has been performed and accumulated has not yet given its fruit, as long as there is an opportunity for ripening, it indeed continues to exist by virtue of its capacity to ripen.
The phrase "for one who" (*yassa kho*) is an indefinite expression used by the Blessed One in a general sense, according to the similarity of karmic types.
He said, "Of whatever kind," because it was so stated.
"Freed from the defilements of negligence" means freed from all defilements rooted in negligence.
"The covering over of evil" means bringing about its state of being subject to non-rebirth; thus he said, "it is made such that there is no further rebirth-linking."
"In the Buddha's teaching" (*buddhasāsane*) means in the dispensation of the Blessed Buddha, which comprises the three trainings.
"He dwells engaged in what is fitting" means he proceeds by way of not doing what should not be done and by way of fulfilling what should be done.

"Those who see and those who are angry" are called *disā*; he says "rivals" (*sapattā*) to mean adversaries. "In the manner of praising that" refers to the mode of proclaiming the benefits of loving-kindness (*mettā*).
"Kālena" (at the right time) is a designation by means of eliding the repetition [of the word]; thus he says "khaṇe khaṇe" (at every moment). "Anukarontu" (let them emulate):
let them emulate those spiritual friends in whose presence they hear the Dhamma, and let them follow their example according to what they have heard;
he expects that even his own enemies will come to listen to the Dhamma in the presence of the Blessed One and practice correctly.
“They tremble” means they long for a destination; they are called *tasa* because of their state of wandering through various existences and so forth.

Therefore it was said: “Those with craving are called *tasa*. They lead water to the place where it is to be led, thus they are *nettika*. “Having bound” means having bound firmly. “With sour gruel mixed with oil” means with sour gruel mixed with oil.

One who is the same toward the unattractive as toward the attractive is *tādi*, being without partiality toward the pleasant and the unpleasant. But for those [beings] who [crave] the bait of sensual pleasures and so forth...

Because of having vomited out, abandoned, and crossed over lust and the other [defilements], as well as the flood of sensual desire and the rest, there would be the state of being "such-like" (*tādibhāva*).

These have been entirely vomited out, abandoned, and crossed over by the Blessed One; therefore, the Blessed One is "such-like" because he has vomited them out, is "such-like" because he has abandoned them, and is "such-like" because he has crossed over them.
It is through being endowed with those unique qualities such as virtue (*sīla*) that the Blessed One has reached the highest perfection in the state of being "such-like."
It is a designation for that; it is "such" (tādī) because it is to be designated according to its true nature by means of those qualities.

Just as a machine is moved by a machine-rope, so too, the craving by which existence (bhava) is led is called "the lead to existence" (bhavanetti) or "the rope of existence" (bhavarajjū). Therefore he said, "By that," and so forth.
It is "kamma-vipāka" because wholesome and other kamma ripen (vipaccanti) or do not ripen (apaccanti) by means of this.
He said, "of path-intention," because the state of being free from debt refers to the volition of the noble path.
He said, "born debtless and stainless," because as long as the defilements are not abandoned, these beings remain indeed in debt due to their state of not living without servitude.
What is called "enjoyment by theft" is so called because of the absence of enjoyment [as if] belonging to an owner; for even in the Blessed One’s own teaching, [he spoke of] one who is virtuous...
The use [of requisites] is permitted for one who is virtuous, not for one who is immoral;
the relinquishment by donors is intended only for those possessing virtue, not for one who is immoral, because the latter expects a great fruit for his own services.

Thus, because it was not permitted by the Teacher and because it was not relinquished by the donors, it is said that "the use of what belongs to an immoral person is called 'use by theft'. This is on account of its being like a debt.
"Enjoyment as a debt" means enjoyment after having taken on a debt because there is no purification of the offering through the recipient.
Since those in training (sekkhā) are the legitimate sons of the Blessed One, they enjoy those requisites as heirs to the requisites belonging to their father;
thus, their enjoyment is called "enjoyment as an inheritance. Why?
But do they enjoy those requisites belonging to the Blessed One, or are they given by householders?

Even when given by householders, they belong to the Blessed One because they have been authorized by him; for there is no enjoyment whatsoever of what has not been authorized, while enjoyment is possible only in the case of what has been authorized.
In this regard, the *Dhammadāyāda-sutta* is the supporting proof.
For those who have not yet abandoned lust, there is no state of mastery over the enjoyment of requisites due to their subjection to craving;
because that [mastery] is absent, for those who have abandoned lust, there is mastery therein, since they can enjoy the requisites according to their own preference.
For in this way, they enjoy the requisites by perceiving even the repulsive as non-repulsive, the non-repulsive as repulsive, or by avoiding both and perceiving them with equanimity.
And they fulfill the aspirations of the donors. Whatever else needs to be said here should be understood according to the method already stated in the *Visuddhimagga* and its commentaries.
It is with reference to the absence of the "debts" (*aṇa*) of the defilements that he is called "debtless" (*anaṇo*), not merely because of his mindful enjoyment [of requisites].
Thus the Venerable Bākula said: "For seven days indeed..."
"Friends, I ate the country alms-food while being a refuge-seeker.

He said, "In both kinds of sensual pleasures, there is intimacy with craving and delight," because the conventional expression "delight" (ramaṇa) exists in dependence upon the mode of occurrence of craving through both sensual objects (vatthukāma) and sensual defilements (kilesakāma). "Mantita" means spoken. [It refers to] those who have arisen as those claiming to be teachers. "Saṃvibhattā" means...
It is analyzed by way of the aggregates and so forth, according to categories such as the wholesome (*kusala*) and others. "Welcome" (*svāgata*) means a beautiful arrival;
for that very reason, it is not an ignoble arrival. Because the sixteenfold function has been completed, he says, "All that has been done by me.

He says, "By the three knowledges (*vijjā*) and the nine supramundane states (*lokuttara-dhamma*)," because the designation "third knowledge" applies specifically to the wisdom of the path (*magga-paññā*).
The Elucidation of the Meaning Obscured in the Commentary on the Aṅgulimāla Sutta is completed.
7. Commentary on the Piyajātika Sutta 353.
"In the natural order" means that, prior to the arising of sorrow, the mind—by way of non-delusion regarding those things that ought to be done—[remains focused].
It leaps forward, and these [objects] appear to him; this is not so for sorrow, because its nature is the contraction of the mind.
Therefore it is said: "But they do not appear according to their natural order. Some, however, say: "A few neighbors do not support the family.
That is why he said: 'They do not appear in their entirety. "Here" refers to the second phrase.
Because verbal roots have multiple meanings, he explains the meaning of the phrase "it does not occur to me" (*na paṭibhāti*) as "it is not pleasing to me.
Alternatively, "it does not occur to me" means that the mind desiring to eat has not arisen. He says that "a place where there is standing room" refers to a location entered by the sense faculties.
Because they are to be loved, they are "dear" (*piya*); those for whom birth—that is, the source of origin—is dear are "of a dear nature" (*piyajātika*). [The word] *piya* is the beginning.
Where it should have been said *piyappabhutikā*, the letter *u* was changed to *va* and the letter *ta* was elided, resulting in the form *piyappabhāvikā*.
Therefore, he said: "They originate from what is dear.
(355) He stated the word *pire* because it has the same meaning as the word *para* and serves to exclude internal cultivation (*ajjhattika-bhāva*).
“*Amhākaṃ pare*” means “others than us. Or, since *pire* is a particle (*nipātapada*) having the same meaning as “*parato*” (from elsewhere), he says:
“*Cara pire* means ‘go elsewhere.
356. Regarding “having cut in two”: if the woman is dear to that man, how does she cut her in two? To this he says: “If indeed,” and so forth.
357. "How should one speak? means: just as the Blessed One spoke to this brahmin, and as he spoke to me, so too should I speak.
Change by way of death occurs because of the transformation and turning over of the personal existence (*attabhāva*).
Change by way of fleeing and departing occurs because of the alteration of friendship and association due to their having become otherwise.

"By way of being discarded" means by way of being turned over. "The state of becoming otherwise through coming into one's hands" refers to the fact that those who were previously under one's own control are now no longer subject to one's will.

"Ācamehi" means "cause [him] to rinse," that is, cause him to wash his mouth. Since people wash their mouths by first washing their hands and feet, therefore, having said "having rinsed," he subsequently shows its meaning: "the mouth..."
"Having rinsed it," he said. The rest is easy to understand.
The elucidation of the hidden meaning of the commentary on the *Piyajātika-sutta* is completed.
8. Commentary on the *Bāhitika-sutta*.
359. Because it is worthy of censure due to its blameworthiness, it is called *opārambho*. Therefore he said, "one who is liable to have faults attributed to him.
Fools shout out, attributing even groundless grounds for censure to another;

therefore, without taking those fools into account, one should take up this word "by the wise" and, by means of the question, fulfill the answer regarding the matters intended to be known, such as the grounds for censure and so forth.
"We were not able. "That reason" means that cause of its arising. For if I had spoken by inserting the word "by the wise," my question would have been complete; however, it was not so stated.
Now, that reason has been fulfilled by the Venerable Ānanda providing the answer, namely, "by the wise."

360. Ignorance (*avijjā*) is called "unskillfulness" (*akosalla*) because it is the opposite of skill (*kosalla*); [the phrase] "born of unskillfulness" means born from that which originates from it. "Blameworthy" (*sāvajja*) refers to what is censurable;

"with blame" (*sāvajja*) means together with what is blameworthy—that is, censurable. "With fault" (*sadosa*) means having faults such as lust (*rāga*) and so forth. By those very same [faults], it is "with affliction" (*sabyābajjha*);
for that very reason, it is "accompanied by suffering" (*sadukkha*) both now and in the future. "With affliction" and so forth refer to the outflow-result (*nissanda-vipāka*).

“Thus the meaning might be stated”: the meaning might be stated even in accordance with the nature of the question, yet it does not yet satisfy the mind of the questioner. Therefore he said: “But such an answer is not burdensome”;
the intention is that there is no sense of weightiness and no hesitation. Therefore he said: “For even one who has not abandoned the unwholesome would praise its abandonment.”
But one who acts in such a way does not necessarily speak accordingly; therefore, he said, "The Blessed One," and so forth, to show that it is not so.
"He answered thus" means he answered: "Great King, the Tathāgata has indeed abandoned all unwholesome states.
By the phrase "the same method applies to the white side as well," it is meant that when it is stated, "He praises the attainment of all wholesome states," the same principle holds.
If the answer had been stated exactly as the question was asked, such an explanation would not have been significant;

even one who has not fully accomplished the wholesome qualities (*kusaladhamma*) might describe the higher ordination (*upasampadā*). However, because the Blessed One has perfectly accomplished the wholesome qualities, he says "he explained it thus" to show that he is "one who acts as he speaks. The rest is easily understood.
The Elucidation of the Meaning of the Commentary on the Bāhitika Sutta is completed.
9. Commentary on the Dhammacetiya Sutta: 364.
Because stones with the color of fat and the color of ulupa-mushrooms were abundant here and there, [it was called] Medāḷupa, the name of the village.
A conventional designation has arisen. Some say that "stones with the color of fat" (*medapāsāṇā*) are so called because their color is similar to that of the moon;
however, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated: "It is said that stones with the color of fat were abundant there. "His" refers to the general (*senāpati*).
"For the purpose of initiating a discourse" means for the purpose of initiating a Dhamma talk to dispel Mallikā’s grief.
"Of the king" means of King Pasenadi of Kosala. "Greatly" means with great [splendor]. This is stated by way of an inversion of the word order (*padavipallāsa*).

They are called "graceful" (*pāsādikāni*) because they merit confidence (*pasāda*). Therefore he said, "possessing qualities that cause delight. Furthermore, those things which are graceful are worthy to be seen.
Alternatively, "graceful" means accompanied by faith (*saddhā*). Therefore he said, "producing confidence. Regarding the terms "free from illness" (*appābādha*) and so forth:
Since the sense of "absence" (abhāva) implies being "without sound," he says "soundless.
Because the particle *ya* expresses an unrestricted sense and can also denote an unrestricted manner, he explains the word *yattha* with the phrase "in such [places]" (*yādisesu*), and so forth.
For instance, in the Aṅgulimāla Sutta, the meaning of the phrase *yassa kho* is stated as "of whatever kind" (*yādisassa kho*).

366. *Paṭicchadanti* means that which conceals. *Rājakakudhabhaṇḍānīti* means those things that constitute the royal insignia. *Rahāyatīti* means he makes it secret; the meaning is that he requests me in private. 367.

It is called *dhamma* because it bears and maintains what is to be known according to its true nature; thus he says, "of the *dhamma* consisting of direct knowledge (*paccakkha-ñāṇa*). *Anunayo* means that which follows after.
For from what is seen, there is inference (*anumāna*) of what is not seen. Therefore he says, "inference."

"Anubuddhī" means "fully understood. "Āpāṇakoṭikaṃ" means until the end of life, as far as the limit of one's lifespan. "Etaṃ" refers to the inference known as the "conformity of the Dhamma" (dhammanvaya).
"Evaṃ" refers to the manner stated in the passage beginning with "But here, I...
(369). "As if not binding the eye" means that because of its lack of beauty, it does not bind the eyes of those looking at it to itself.
A disease that follows along with the lineage of a family is a "family disease" (*kularoga*). "Exalted" (*uḷāra*) means possessing majesty;

for one who is endowed with majesty, they call him "of great influence" (*mahesakkha*). "Attaining arahantship" is a description of the highest case, though it includes those attaining the lower fruits as well.
"Livelihood" (*jīvikā*) is the mode of living.
374. They are called *dhammacetiyāni* because one intends (*ceteti*) and experiences (*saṃvedeti*) [reverence] through them; they are terms for the worship of the Dhamma.
But are these not also illuminations of the qualities of the Buddha and the Saṅgha? How then is it said that "they are terms for the honoring (*cittīkāra*) of the Dhamma"?
To this he says: "For in the three... and so forth. Therein, because the remaining Jewels are rooted in the Jewel of the Buddha, [the latter is primary].
Because it is to be obtained by means of them. And herein, out of reverence for the Buddha, the King of Kosala manifested reverence for the Dhamma and the Saṅgha;
therefore it is said: "When honor is paid to the Blessed One, honor is also paid to the Dhamma. And because right practice in the Dispensation is preceded by confidence in the Triple Gem, it is said:
"They are the foundations of the holy life," meaning they are the foundations of the holy life of the Path.
"Are the primary elements. The remainder is indeed easy to understand.
The elucidation of the hidden meaning in the commentary on the *Dhammacetiyasutta* is complete.
10. Commentary on the *Kaṇṇakatthalasutta*.

375. "By the very same means stated in the *Anantara-sutta*" refers to the course of action described as: "Failing to find delight for his mind in either palaces or theatrical performances, he began to wander here and there.

For it is those who are not yet corrupted by malice who act in this way. 376. "He was asked" means he was asked, "Did you not find another messenger? "He" refers to the king. "Their salutation"—if performed at a later time—will cause him to explain the reason for his own arrival.

378. "By a single adverting" (*ekāvajjana*) means by a single cognitive process of impulsion (*javana*). Let a single consciousness remain for a moment; even within a single cognitive series (*cittavīthi*), [this occurs].

This shows that it is not possible to know everything. By saying, "I shall know this particular past thing," one who adverts without making a specific determination knows whatever past thing happens to come before him;
however, when a determination has been made, he knows only that which was determined. Thus he says: "For by one [moment of consciousness]... one knows only a single part.
"By that mind" means by the mind that has proceeded with the thought, "I shall know all the past. "In the others" means...
Regarding the future and the present: "of the nature of cause" means having a logical essence; the meaning is that it is consistent with logic.
"Quality pertaining to the future life" means the excellence resulting from karma performed in the future life.
379. Those mixed with the supramundane have been explained, as in the *Bodhirājakumāra-sutta*, as both mundane and supramundane.
And here, the inclusion of the factors of striving (*padhāniyaṅga*) as supramundane should be understood by way of whatever is obtained.
Their status as factors of striving should be seen individually, just as it is said: "The eight liberations are seen mixed with the supramundane.
As for what must be said regarding their being exclusively supramundane, that will become clear later. "The diversity of striving" (*padhānanānatta*)...
The meaning is: the diversity of footprints and the distinction in the application of development.

For one who has thoroughly rubbed away the formations (*saṅkhāra*) and abandoned the opposing states (*paṭipakkhadhamma*) to some extent, the application of development is subtle and clear compared to the application of development for one who has not thoroughly rubbed away the formations and has not abandoned the opposing states;
[this occurs] through the realization of the truths (*saccābhisamaya*) within the continuum.

He said, "Because a distinction has been established," meaning: "For the striving of an ordinary person (puthujjana) is of one kind, while that of a stream-enterer (sotāpanna) is of another kind," and so forth.

Furthermore, showing that this distinction is not found only between the non-noble (anariya) and noble (ariya) persons, but is also obtained among the noble ones themselves through the distinctions of those in training (sekkha) and so on—due to the excellence of their volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra) and the success of their directed application (abhinīhāra)—he said, "That of a once-returner (sakadāgāmin) is of another kind," and so forth.
"He does not reach" means that because a worldling, even while exerting effort in every way, attains the path of stream-entry,
and a stream-enterer attains the path of once-returning— since one cannot abandon the lower [defilements] by means of the higher,

which are grosser than them, nor the higher by means of the other, which are subtler than them— it is thus, by virtue of the distinction between what is to be attained and the practice leading to attainment.
It is said—“The striving of an ordinary person does not reach the striving of a stream-enterer,” and so forth—in order to indicate its smooth subtlety and its sharp clarity.
“Not acting deceptively” means an act free from trickery. “Not cutting off” means over-driving. “Not prodding” means not pulling [the reins] too hard.
Having untied the fastening and turned it all around, one discards it with an even edge. Its cause is "taṃkāraṇaṃ";
or rather, "taṃ kāraṇaṃ" means that action or that undertaking. "The ground to be traversed by the tusks" means the place to be reached by the tusks, or the object to be attained.
All four are called "lacking faith" (assaddhā) in comparison to the progressively higher degrees of faith.

Because of non-existence. For whatever has not been attained by someone, that does not exist for them. In the case of the noble disciple... [etc. ...it does not exist because deceit and hypocrisy are to be abandoned by the first path itself.
"By that very same [reason]" means because faith and the other qualities intended here are precisely those opposed [to their opposites].
If this is so, how can there be a mixed discourse? He says: "But in the *Assakhaḷuṅka Sutta*," and so forth. There are only four types, according to the categories of worldlings and so on.

In the *Opammasaṃsandana*, it was stated collectively and generally by combining both sides— on the dark side (the *kaṇhapakkha*) with the phrase "like untamed elephants and so forth," and on the bright side (the *sukkapakkha*) with the phrase "like tamed elephants and so forth. To show this by distinguishing them individually rather than generally,
the passage beginning with "This is what is meant" (*idaṃ vuttaṃ hotī*) and so forth was stated.
380. "They possess right exertion and have exerted their energy. Therefore he said: "I do not say there is any difference whatsoever between one liberation and another liberation.

For indeed, there is no difference in the liberation of those who possess dry-insight (sukkha-vipassaka) and those who possess the threefold higher knowledge and the six direct knowledges (tevijja-chaḷabhiñña).
That is why it was said: "That which belongs to one," and so forth. The connection is: "Do you not know? ... "They come."
They come by way of arising. "They do not come"—here too the same principle applies.

"Asking this" means showing that one asks this question. "Those whose mental suffering has not been abandoned" means those who have not attained the state of a non-returner (*anāgāmitā*). Therefore he said, "those who come by way of rebirth.
"Those whose suffering is utterly destroyed" means those whose mental suffering has been eradicated.

381. "From that place" means from that state of sovereignty as it was attained. "Again, from that place" means from there, having fallen into a miserable rebirth (*duggata*). "Endowed with excellent sense-pleasures" means possessed of sublime qualities of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*).

"There" refers to the world of the devas of the sense-sphere (*kāmadevaloka*). "Because of the nature of the place": if arahantship has been attained, then at that very moment one attains final nibbāna (*parinibbāna*).
"And the higher devas" refers to the devas dwelling in progressively higher planes; the construction is that even by means of visual consciousness, they are unable to see [the lower ones].
"By the very method already stated" means by the very method stated in the Devaputta’s question. "That discourse" refers to the discourse beginning with:
"There is no ascetic or brahmin who can know everything all at once. "Those two" refers to Viṭaṭūbha and Sañjaya.
"In this very place" means in this very Migadāya. The rest is easy to understand.
The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning of the Commentary on the Kaṇṇakatthala Sutta is completed.
And the commentary on the Rājavagga is finished.
5. The Brāhmaṇavagga.
1. Commentary on the Brahmāyu Sutta. 383.

In such passages as “the Great Being was of great psychic power (mahiddhika) and great majesty (mahānubhāva),” the meaning is that of excellence; in such passages as “a great body of people assembled,” the meaning is that of a large number.
But here, both of these meanings apply, thus it says “great” (mahatā) by way of greatness of virtue as well.

The passage beginning with "By means of the great" has been stated. Regarding "fewness of wishes and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) includes contentment, effacement, seclusion, non-association, the arousal of energy, and so on.

In the phrase "by way of what is termed the community consisting of the commonality of view and virtue," it is said: "He is fixed upon enlightenment as his ultimate goal"—"Monks, it is impossible, it is out of the question, that a person endowed with right view should intentionally deprive a living being of life..."

Because of such statements as, "There is no possibility that he would transgress [the precepts]," stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*) are also united with one another through the commonality of their view and virtue (*diṭṭhi-sīla-sāmañña*), owing to the fixed nature of these qualities; how much more so for once-returners (*sakadāgāmin*) and those beyond.
This is because of the statement: "He dwells having attained a commonality of view through such a view, and he dwells having attained a commonality of virtue through such virtues."

Even among worldlings (*puthujjana*), a state of being bound together by the commonality of view and virtue is indeed obtainable—by way of the manner of striking with the lips and by way of the analysis of meaning. Regarding the phrase "together with the *Nighaṇḍu* and *Keṭubha*":

here, *nighaṇḍu* means that which "divides and shows" (*khaṇḍati*) both the meaning and the word by way of the relationship between the signified and the signifier; thus it is *nikhaṇḍu*. That very same [term]...

Here, by changing the letter *kha* to *gha*, it is called "Nighaṇḍu. It is called *keṭubha* because it moves (*kiṭati*) or causes one to go through the classification of grammatical operations and so forth;
or, because it goes through (*gamanto*) and fulfills that [classification] by exhausting it without remainder. "Exhibiting synonyms" means illuminating synonymous terms;
the meaning is that it reveals many synonymous expressions for each single meaning. And this is merely an illustration, as it applies to many others as well.
This is because that treatise was composed even for the purpose of elucidating how multiple things can be expressed by a single word.
Since it is by means of this work that action—characterized by vocal expression and so forth—is conceptualized (*kappīyati*), it is called *kiriyākappa* (the conceptualization of action).

Furthermore, because it contains many conceptualizations (*vikappa*) through its descriptions, phrases, connections, and analysis of word-meanings, it is referred to as the *kiriyākappavikappa*. This [term] refers to the root treatise, the *Mūlakiriyākappa*.
It has been stated. For that work, consisting of one hundred thousand [verses], is the *Nalacariya* and other such treatises.

They are called *akkharappabhedā* (the divisions of syllables) because by means of them syllables are analyzed according to their places of articulation (*ṭhāna*), their modes of formation (*karaṇa*), and so forth, as well as according to their etymological analysis (*nibbacana*). "Of these" refers to the Vedas.
One who recites those very Vedas word by word (*padaso*) is a *padaka*. One who explains—that is, analyzes—the various sounds and their meanings is a *byākaraṇika*.

*Etena-ati-byākaraṇaṃ* refers to the science of grammar (*saddasattha*). It is called *lokāyata* because by means of it, the world does not strive (*yatati*) nor exert itself (*īhati*) for its welfare in the future.
For, relying on that treatise, sentient beings do not even give rise to the thought of performing meritorious deeds. *Vaya* means "decay";
*na vaya* is *avaya*; *na avaya* is *anavaya*, meaning that which does not perish or diminish at any point—beginning, middle, or end—and which neither falters nor expands.

The meaning is that he retains and fulfills those books. Showing that two negations lead back to the original affirmative state, it says, "There is no decline (*avaya*)," and then, in order to demonstrate what that decline is, it says, "He is unable to... [etc.]... decline.
(384) It is difficult to depart after having freed oneself from a heavy burden; moreover, misfortune arises.

"Censure, accusation, reproach, and so forth. Regarding the term *abbhuggato*, because of its connection with the prefix *abhi-*, the accusative case is used in the sense of expressing a particular state (*itthambhūta-ākhyāna*).
"Characteristics" (*lakkhaṇāni*) refers to the mantra-words that illuminate characteristics.
"They disappear" means that not only the characteristic-mantras, but other [mantras] as well, gradually disappear due to the absence of the power of knowledge among the brahmins. For thus they say:
“*Ekasataṃ addhariyaṃ dipaññāsamattato sāmā*,” and so forth. The word *maha-* (great) should be applied individually to each term, as in “*paṇidhimahato samādānamahato*,” etc.
His greatness of aspiration and so forth is to be understood through the *Buddhavaṃsa*, the *Cariyāpiṭaka-vaṇṇanā*, and other such works. *Niṭṭhā* means accomplishments.

*Jātisāmaññato* means because of the state of equality through the commonality of the class (*jāti*) of characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*), that is, by virtue of possessing the nature of the [thirty-two] marks.
For just as the marks of the Buddhas are perfectly pure, clearly manifest, and complete, they are not so for the wheel-turning monarchs (cakkavattins).
Therefore it was said: "One does not become a Buddha by those [marks] alone.
[The Buddha is distinguished] by four wonderful qualities: physical beauty, long life, freedom from illness, and being dear and pleasing to brahmins and others.
By means of these four bases of sympathy—generosity, pleasant speech, beneficial conduct, and impartiality—and by way of "delighting" (rañjanato), that is, by generating joy;
he is a *cakkavattī* because he causes the wheel, the Wheel-Treasure, to turn and proceed.
He himself turns the wheels of prosperity, and through them, he turns and causes the multitude of beings to proceed; thus he is a *cakkavattī*, one who brings about the welfare of others.
One is a *cakkavattī* because he possesses the turning (*vatta*) or the act of turning the wheels of the modes of deportment (*iriyāpatha*).
Alternatively, one is a *cakkavattī* because he turns the wheel known as his unimpeded command (*appaṭihata-āṇā*). Or, one is a *cakkavattī* because he turns the wheel known as his unimpeded command.
Or, one is a *cakkavattī* because he turns—that is, brings under his own control—the wheel or assembly known as the circle of khattiyas and so forth. [The same applies to] the Dhamma...

He acts according to the Dhamma, thus he is "Dhammika. Because he does not deviate from the Dhamma, he is the Dhamma; and because he is a king in the sense of "coloring" (rañjana), he is a "Dhammarāja.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in "anger, etc.," one includes sensual greed, conceit, pride, and so forth. "Victorious" (*vijitāvī*) means one who has conquered.
He has attained stability of the realm in the sense of being unshakable by anyone. Alternatively, it is where the people have attained stability due to their state of firm devotion.
He has attained sovereignty over the realm. The status of the Wheel as a treasure (ratana) is to be understood through its being treated with honor and so forth.

This same method applies to the remaining [treasures] as well. Alternatively, because the state of being treated with honor and so forth is the cause of delight, it is not mentioned separately since it is subsumed under the sense of "producing delight.
Now, in order to show whatever specific benefit the Wheel-turning Monarch (cakkavatti-rāja) experiences by means of these treasures:
The passage beginning with “But among these... has been stated. [The Wheel-Treasure] conquers Ajita because it is the natural outflow (*nissanda*) of kamma conducive to great majesty.

Having mounted the Elephant-Treasure and the Horse-Treasure, it traverses the entire earth at its own pleasure within the time it takes to eat a morning meal by means of their power, and returns to the royal capital. By means of the Counsellor-Treasure...

He protects his conquest because, by means of that, he provides for the duties to be performed here and there. "By the remaining [treasures]" refers to the jewel-treasure (*maṇiratana*), the woman-treasure (*itthiratana*), and the householder-treasure (*gahapatiratana*).
Among these, by means of the jewel-treasure, he experiences happiness by dispelling darkness over an area of one *yojana* and providing light and vision;

by means of the woman-treasure, through the sight of her physical perfection which surpasses that of ordinary humans; and by means of the householder-treasure, through the acquisition of whatever wealth he desires, such as gems, gold, and silver.
The "application of energy and courage" (*ussāha-satti-yoga*) is mentioned because it achieves the state of a wheel of command unopposed by anyone.

Because elephants, horses, jewels, and so forth possess great majesty, the attainment of power is also achieved through the perfection of the treasury; thus, it is said: "the application of elephants...
[and so on]... and the treasury. For indeed, when there is the perfection of energy—[characterized by] high-spiritedness, delicate prowess, and a serene countenance—the treasury [becomes effective].
“He attains [them] in person. “By the last” means by the *pariṇāyaka-ratana* (the counselor-jewel). For that is skilled in all royal duties and possesses unfailing application;
thus he said, “the employment of the power of counsel (*mantasatti-yoga*)”. The connection is: “The fruit of the threefold employment of power becomes complete.
“By the rest” means by the remaining five jewels. “By the power of karma produced from the wholesome root of non-hatred (*adosa-kusalamūla*): [end of fragment].

The [first] three succeed by virtue of the power of karma produced through the condition of co-nascence and others, based on the wholesome root known as non-hatred (*adosa*), because they are of a nature like gentle jewels.

The middle ones—the jewel-treasure (*maṇiratana*), woman-treasure (*itthiratana*), and householder-treasure (*gahapatiratana*)—succeed by virtue of the power of karma, because they are caused by the perfection of renunciation, which is the cause for obtaining vast wealth and the means for acquiring such vast wealth, rooted in non-greed (*alobha*). … [and so on] … by virtue of the power of karma.
"Last" refers to the Jewel of the General. For that [Jewel] arises through the power of non-delusion... and by the force of karma;
it is accomplished because the duties of a Wheel-Turning Monarch must be executed by one of great wisdom alone.
They are "brave" (sūra) because they dispel adversaries through their refuge [in virtue]. Therefore he said, "of a nature that is fearless. Because they stand having conquered the asuras...

The hero is Sakka, the lord of the devas; his son Aṅga is called a "limb" because he is a member of the army. Thus it is said: “Having the form of a hero’s limb” means having bodies like those of the sons of the devas.
“Sabhāva” (nature) means that which has become one’s own nature. “Vīrakāraṇa” (cause of heroism) means the cause of the state of being a hero.
“As if their bodies were made of energy” means they resemble embodied energy; for if energy were to have a physical form, they would be like it.

The meaning [of the compound] is as follows. One might object: "Since a universal monarch (cakravartin) has no opposing army that his sons could crush, why was it said that they are 'crushers of enemy armies'?

Addressing this objection, he says "If," and so forth. By this he shows: whether there actually be an enemy army or not, they possess such great power. "By the Dhamma" means by their own [merit] accumulated through past deeds.

By means of that meritorious dhamma. Urged on by it, all the kings on earth go out to meet him, say such things as, "Welcome to you, Great King," and hand over their own kingdoms to the Wheel-turning Monarch (Cakkavatti). Therefore it is said: "He...
dwells in sovereignty. In the Commentary, however, it is stated that for that aforementioned dhamma to ripen for a longer duration—
In order to show the Dhamma that serves as a condition—consisting of the perfection of practice arising from the conduct of a wheel-turning monarch (cakkavatti)—it is said:
"by means of the Dhamma of the five precepts, beginning with 'no living being shall be killed.
For in this way, the statement "without stick or sword" is more thoroughly supported; because when evil states such as lust and the like arise...
They remain covering and enveloping the continuum of beings (sattasantāna), obstructing the occurrence of wholesome states; therefore, they are called "coverings" (chadana) and "shelters" (chada).
Having turned away from the cycle and having overturned it.
Their worthiness for worship is expressed by the phrase, "one who is worthy (arhati) is an arahant. "Tassa" refers to that worthiness for worship.

Because he is a Perfectly Enlightened One (sammāsambuddha), therefore he is an Arahant. The state of having the covering removed (vivaṭṭacchadatā)—which serves as the cause for his Buddhahood—is mentioned because the attainment of the state of a Buddha is preceded by the abandonment of all defilements together with their latent tendencies (savāsana).

"An Arahant by virtue of the absence of the round [of existence]" (vaṭṭābhāvena) is a demonstration of the inference of the cause from the fruit. "A Perfectly Enlightened One by virtue of the absence of the covering" (chadanābhāvena) is a demonstration of the inference of the fruit from the cause.
Two causes have been stated: "the round has been turned away from" (vivaṭṭo) and "the covering has been removed" (vicchado).
And so it is said. "By the second intrepidity" means by the intrepidity presented in the passage beginning, "When you claim, 'The taints are destroyed in me,'" and so forth.

"The accomplishment of the former" means the establishment of the meaning of the preceding term. "By the first" means by the intrepidity presented in the passage beginning, "When you claim, 'I am a perfectly enlightened Buddha,'" and so forth.
"The accomplishment of the second" means the accomplishment of Buddhahood. "By the third and fourth" refers to [the passage beginning], "But as for those... and so forth.

By means of the third and fourth grounds of self-confidence (*vesārajjāni*) as they have been handed down in the passages beginning with "those are obstructive states" and "but for whatever purpose you [have declared them]," there is the "accomplishment of the third," which is the accomplishment of having the veil removed (*vivaṭṭacchadanatā*).

For, by way of correctly describing obstructive and emancipating states, the Teacher’s state of having the veil removed became manifest to the world. "The former eye of Dhamma" refers to the first phrase.
The first term establishes the *dhammacakkhu* (the eye of Dhamma), because it illustrates the state of having destroyed the spokes of the wheel of defilements and the wheel of saṃsāra.

The second term establishes the *buddhacakkhu* (the eye of a Buddha), because that [eye] is possible only for a Perfectly Enlightened One (*sammāsambuddha*). The third term establishes the *samantacakkhu* (the all-encompassing eye), because it illustrates the abandonment of all defilements along with their latent tendencies (*vāsana*). For it is said: "A Perfectly Enlightened One..."

Having spoken thus, he explains that the phrase "one who has removed the veil" (*vivaṭṭacchada*) reveals the abandonment of all defilements (*sabbakilesappahāna*), which alone brings about the state of Buddhahood.
"The state of being brave" (*sūrabhāva*) refers to the clarity of knowledge (*visadañāṇatā*) through the manifestation of its characteristics.
"He sought" (*gavesī*) means he performed a search by means of knowledge. "He brought together" (*samānayī*) means, while comparing [things] with knowledge, he brought them into harmony.
He withdrew [his mind]. He is not able [to do so] because, for the most part, those [states] are difficult to develop while the modes of conduct are contracted.
Regarding the word *kaṅkhati*, he says its meaning is “he desires,” explaining: “‘Oh, may I see!’—thus he arouses a longing.
*Kicchatī* means “he is weary. Having previously stated that the word *kaṅkhati* has the sense of aspiration, he now [explains] its...
Showing that very state of being a matter of doubt through another conceptualization, it is said: “Or, by means of doubt, weak perplexity is expressed,” and so forth.
By three factors—that is, by three kinds of doubtful states. The state of turbidity is the condition of being clouded, which serves as the cause for lack of confidence.
Because the Blessed One’s sheath-covered private organ—the unique possession of all Buddhas—is like a perfectly pure golden disk.

By its own beauty of form and configuration, it shines forth, surpassing with its own splendor the excellence of the noble limbs of a well-bred scent-elephant, the graceful play of the whorls of filaments in a blooming golden lotus,
and the luster of the full orb of the moon distinguished by the surrounding forest of waters colored by the twilight glow; for it has long remained unstained by external or internal impurities.
Because of his mastery over the holy life well-cultivated and because of the perfection of his well-proportioned physical form, even though he had a loincloth, it was as if he had none;
therefore it is said, "Of the Blessed One," and so forth. "Abundance" means breadth.
For his doubt concerned only this [breadth], whereas regarding his other qualities such as thinness, softness, and delicacy, he did not even entertain an investigation.
“Hiri-karaṇa-okāsa” means the basis for feeling shame. “Chāyā” means a reflection. To the question “Of what kind? he says, “By psychic power,” and so forth.

“Chāyārūpa” is the reflected form of the Blessed One. Moreover, that is merely a physical form dissociated from the Buddha’s own mental continuum—a mere image made of psychic power, possessing the color, shape, and limbs of the Blessed One’s body. And while displaying that, [he said...]
The Blessed One displays his own form as a Buddha by making it invisible to others. "Having brought forth" means having pervaded [the area].
Because the ears have fine, thin, and golden-brown hairs growing upon them, they are said to resemble tubes of polished silver. "At the edge of the mouth" refers to the ends of the hair.
"Performing the action" refers to the practice of physical and verbal deeds. "Therein" refers to among those duties.
The suppression of seeds was performed in order to demonstrate the proper conduct (*vatta*) of those who discourse on the Dhamma;
for otherwise, the moon-like orb of the Buddhas' faces—which is the ornament of the entire world and has reached the highest excellence through training and self-restraint—would be obscured.

[This was done] in a fragrant circular pavilion (*gandhamaṇḍalamāḷa*) where canopies were spread out and garlands of perfumes and flowers were suspended. Having demarcated the area by means of the eastern section...

Having delimited the time by means of a preliminary resolve such as, “I will spend this much time in meditative attainment,” he either exalts or encourages the assembly out of favoritism toward those who provide requisites,
or disparages or discourages the assembly out of resentment toward those who do not provide them.
"Security from bondage" (*yogakkhema*) means the absence of obstacles. "By its very intrinsic quality" means by the very qualities already described.
Because the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*), together with its physical form, was unable to sustain the quality of the Blessed Gotama in its full extent, being too narrow;
and because the summit of existence (*bhavagga*) was unable to sustain it, being too low, as it could not support it layer upon layer.
386. One whose feet are well-placed on the ground when standing, walking, and so forth, is called *suppatiṭṭhitapāda*.
To clarify this quality of the Blessed One’s well-placed feet by way of contrast, the passage beginning with “*yathā hi*” was stated.
Therein, *aggatalaṃ* means the surface of the forefoot; *paṇhī* means the surface of the heel; and *passaṃ* refers to the side of the foot.
One sees one limit at each of the two sides, or one sees both limits together. It is placed straight down like the sole of a golden sandal.
"All at once" means in a single moment. The construction is: "The entire sole of the foot touches the ground when it is placed down;
all at once, the entire sole of the foot rises from the ground."
In that context, "therefore" means because of those well-placed feet; this wonderful and marvelous thing being described is the outflow-result (*nissandaphala*).

To make this very point clearly evident through the Teacher’s journey to the Heaven of the Thirty-three (*Tidiva*), he says "for thus," and so forth, and then supports it with "not indeed," and so forth.
By this, it is shown that the second characteristic is of greater power even than the first characteristic.
He shows this; for he will say: “Even including the assembly of a wheel-turning monarch, all is merely the retinue of the mark of the wheels.

That the natural placement of footprints upon Mount Yugandhara and in the realm of the Thirty-three Gods occurs during the approach [of the Buddha] is due neither to the power of the Buddhas nor to the power of the deities, but rather to the power of the marks of the Buddhas—this is the meaning [he intends to show].

It has been demonstrated. Regarding the phrases "by the power of the heat of virtue" and so forth, up to "by the majesty of the ten perfections," this too should be understood as a mere description of the specific kamma that produced the characteristic marks.
"By all sides" means by all locations. "Circumscribed by the navel" means situated with a boundary defined at the navel. "The band encircling the face of the navel" means...
The rim-band is the strip that should be placed facing the hub for the purpose of protecting the axle-end of the natural wheel.
"Jewel-designs on the rim" refers to the lines of jewels situated on the rim in the form of a border.
"A multitude of instances" refers to the section illustrating various types of line-patterns. "Spear" refers to a weapon-spear. "Śrīvatsa" refers to...
*Sirimukha*: a face of glory. *Nandī*: a right-turning [swastika]. *Sovattika*: marked with a *sovattika*. *Vaṭaṃsaka*: a garland for the head. *Vaḍḍhamānaka*:
a man-carrying [figure], a male attendant. *Morahatthaka*: a bundle of peacock feathers, or a specific type of fan woven from peacock feathers.
*Vālabījanī*: a yak-tail fan. *Siddhattha*, etc.: full jars and full bowls.
Having stated "the world-system" (*cakkavāḷa*), in order to show its primary constituent parts, it was said: "Himavā, Sineru... [and so on] ... thousands.
Regarding the phrase "long-tailed" (*āyatapaṇhī*), this was said with reference to the length from the tail of others, but not because of being excessively long;
thus he said "full-tailed" (*paripuṇṇapaṇhī*). As for how the characteristic of a tail is called "complete," that is shown by way of contrast:
To demonstrate this, the passage beginning with “Just as” was spoken. “With the tip” means with the point of the circle.
“Having rounded it” means having rounded it so that it becomes well-rounded. “Resembling a ball made of red wool” means resembling a ball made of red woolen cloth.
“Just like a monkey’s” means like that of a monkey; this was said with reference to the similarity in length. “With resin-oil” means with oil mixed with resins such as *chadika* resin and others.
"Talunā" means delicate.
"Cammena" means by the skin wrapped around the space between the fingers. "Paṭibaddha-aṅgulantaro" means having the spaces between the fingers joined together on one side.
"Ekappamāṇā" means equal in length. "Yavalakkhaṇaṃ" refers to that which is situated within the joints of the fingers.
"Having penetrated the characteristic mark": because those respective bones occupy the same location, when the fingers are extended, they remain touching as if pierced through one another.
"Saṅkha" refers to the ankles; "ussaṅkha" means those which have the ankles above them—namely, the feet. "Near the back of the foot" means in the vicinity of the heel.
The feet turn over easily during the lifting and placing of the feet; for that very reason, the soles of the feet of those walking are visible from below.
"By that" means because the ankles are established above the back of the foot.
For they are established after rising four finger-breadths upward, and thus they remain concealed, not being visible as they are in other people.
The term "nābhi" (navel) is not included for the purpose of showing that mindfulness remains steady even when moving to another place.
Because the hind legs of the enī deer have flesh of a uniform thickness all around and gradually become thicker toward the top, it is said:
"legs like those of the enī deer. "Full-thighed" means having thighs that are full due to a complete accumulation of flesh all around.
Therefore he said, "Not on one side," and so forth.
By this—meaning by the statement beginning with "not bending," which illustrates the fitness of the knees—it is shown.
By the phrase "the rest of people," he refers to those individuals who lack these characteristics; they may be hunchbacked because the upper body is shorter than the lower body.

Or they are dwarfs (*vāmanā*) because their lower bodies are short compared to their upper bodies. By this, he shows that—with the exception of the Perfectly Enlightened One (*sammāsambuddha*) and the Wheel-turning Monarch (*cakkavatti*)—all other beings are hunchbacked or dwarfs.
"Deposited" (*ohita*) means placed within or included; since such a thing is covered by that [upper body], he says "concealed" (*paṭicchanna*).
"Suvaṇṇavaṇṇo" means "one whose color is the color of gold"; this is the meaning here, as he says, "by means of natural vermilion," and so forth.
This meaning should also be understood through the principle of repetition (āvutti).

Having stated the first alternative with the intention that the word *vaṇṇa* here refers to the body (*sarīra*), he then considers the absence of such conventional usage (*ruḷhi*) and [proceeds] by way of the element of color (*vaṇṇadhātu*) alone.
Having taken up the word *vaṇṇa* (color/appearance), the second alternative was stated.

*Raja* means fine dust. *Jalla* is a collection of particles that brings about a state of being soiled; thus he said, "or dirt. If it turns away [from the body], how can there be bathing and so forth? To this he said, "washing the hands," and so on.
"At the end of the turning" means at the conclusion of the clockwise circumambulation.

Because the body of Brahmā rises straight up without leaning forward or backward, it is said: "He is straight-limbed like Brahmā. "Crooked on one side" means crooked toward either the right or the left side.
"Seven protuberances" (sattussada) means that he has seven protuberances by way of the backs of the hands and so forth.
"The lion’s forequarters" (sīhapubbaddha) refers to the front part of a lion; because all his limbs are complete, his entire [upper body] is like the lion’s forequarters.
"Having a body" means having a body like that of a lion's forequarters. "Of a lion indeed" means like that of a lion. "Are formed" means they are well-proportioned.

"By various minds" means by diverse states of mind. "By a virtuous mind" means by way of a mind characterized by the merit of the perfections (pāramitā). "Variegated" means having the quality of consciousness produced.
"The space between two shoulders" means the middle of the two hind-limbs, the upper portion of the back.
“Citta is full”: it is *cita* by way of its non-sunken state; it is *paripuṇṇa* (full) because of its levelness across both sides. “Uggamma” means having risen up.
“Nigrodhaparimaṇḍala” means being as circular as a banyan tree (*nigrodha*); this is formed by eliding one of the two instances of the word *parimaṇḍala*.
For not every banyan tree is circular. Therefore he said: “A banyan tree with symmetrical trunk and branches.”
Alternatively, by the proximity of the word *parimaṇḍala*, the meaning "round like a banyan tree" is obtained even without the elision of the word *parimaṇḍala*;
thus he said, "round like a banyan tree. The expression *yāvataka-v-assa* is stated by substituting the letter *va* for the vowel *o*.

“With a symmetrical trunk” means a trunk that is evenly rounded. The construction is as follows: like cranes, with long necks; like herons, with curved necks; like boars, with broad necks. “Resembling a golden liṅga” means resembling a small golden *mudiṅga* drum. “The foremost of those who taste flavors” (*rasaggasaggī*):
they are called “taste-takers” (*rasagga-sā*) because they take (*gasanti*) or swallow flavors such as the sweet and so forth into their insides;

the “foremost” (*agga*) among these taste-takers are the “foremost of those who taste flavors,” and he possesses these, thus he is “the foremost of those who taste flavors. “By that” refers to the non-pervasion by nutritive essence (*ojā*), due to having inferior physical constituents (*dhātu*).
They are subject to many ailments.
"Jaws" (*hanu*) is a designation for the support upon which the teeth rest; that of the Blessed One is like the jaw of a lion, therefore the Blessed One is "Lion-Jawed" (*sīhahanu*).
In this regard, because any comparison for the physical body (*rūpakāya*) and the Dhamma-body (*dhammakāya*) of the Buddhas is necessarily an inferior comparison, [it is called thus].
There is no equal simile, much less a superior one; therefore, in order to show that this too is an inferior simile, the words beginning with “tattha” were spoken.
By way of three parts, due to their circularity, they resemble the moon in the twelfth day of the lunar fortnight.
The unevenness of the teeth—some being high and some low—should be understood by reference to both the inner and outer surfaces, not merely by the tips alone. Thus he said:
“Like a section of a conch shell cut by an iron band. Here, “iron band” refers to a saw. “Irregular” means having an uneven shape.
They are also “broken-sounding” because they produce sound as they repeatedly break apart; they are also “split-sounding” due to their manifold forms;
and they are also “crow-sounding” because they have a harsh sound like that of a crow. “Unobstructed” means because their physical basis is not impaired.
"Vatthu" refers to the locus where the syllables arise. Regarding "endowed with eight factors," those eight factors will be explained later.
"Mañjughosa" means having a sweet voice.
When the song of the karavīka bird reaches the range of hearing of certain beings, it [causes] their own nature [to manifest] through the excellence of its tone.
Just as one who has subdued others brings them under his own control, he spoke the words beginning with "In this regard" (*tatridam*) to show that [the teaching] is likewise sweet.

"That rapture" (*taṃ pītiṃ*) refers to the rapture directed toward the Buddha. By that very method, proceeding again and again without abandoning it, the elders—having suppressed their defilements and having obtained the favorable conditions for hearing the Dharma in the presence of the Theras through the perfection of their supporting causes (*upanissaya*)—[attained realization].

Because his knowledge was fully matured, it is said: “With seven... he stood firm. Because he approached the presence of the elders on foot together with a retinue of about seven hundred women of the harem, it is stated: “Together with seven hundred legged ones (jaṅghāsata).
