“Abhinīlanetta” means having eyes that are intensely blue. And this intense blueness should be understood as an exceeding degree of blueness.
He said, “nor with eyes that are entirely blue,” and so forth, because it is not the case that there is an excess of only the blue color in the eyes.

The yellow and red colors are to be understood by way of the lines situated within the white circle (the sclera), while the blue, white, and black colors are to be understood by way of their respective circles.

“The eye-ornament” (*cakkhubhaṇḍa*)—some say this refers to the eyelids; others say it refers to the eyelashes. However, it should be understood as the eyeball together with the eyelids; for in this way, the description of its deep, protruding luster is also appropriate.
In common worldly usage, the word *uṇṇā* generally signifies hair; however, here it refers to a specific kind of hair, as indicated by the phrase "woolly hair" (*uṇṇaloma*).
"Born in the middle of the forehead" means situated in the center of the forehead. This is a comparison based on its whiteness, not its softness.
"Silver bubbles" refers to silver stars. It is said that this was spoken for two reasons: because both Buddhas and Wheel-turning Monarchs possess a full forehead and a full cranial image.
And because they are called "having a turban-like head" (*uṇhīsasīsa*), it was said that he has a "turban-like head" (*uṇhīsasīso*) for two reasons.
Now, in order to show that these two meanings are well-established in the Blessed One, the passage beginning with "of the Tathāgata" was spoken.
Due to its extreme smoothness and its golden color, it shines like the bound turban-cloth of a king. [This is] *kappasīsa*.

*“Two-headed” (dvidhābhūtasīsā): “Fruit-headed” (phalasīsā) means having a head resembling a fruit. “Bone-headed” (aṭṭhisīsā): because of the absence of flesh, it is a head consisting of nothing but bone covered over by skin.

“Gourd-headed” (tumbasīsā): a head resembling a gourd (*lābu*). “Overhanging-headed” (pabbhārasīsā): a head that hangs down over the back portion. “By the former method” (purimanayena): by way of the side [of the head] where the forehead is full.
“Like a head wrapped in a turban” (uṇhīsaveṭhitasīso viya): a region of the head wrapped with a turban-band (*uṇhīsapaṭṭa*).*"
"Like a turban" means like a turban-circle fashioned by a skilled craftsman.

"Kamma" refers to whichever specific deed produced whichever specific mark; that is the deed. "Correspondence with the deed" (kamma-sarikkhaka) is the conformity of each respective mark to its corresponding deed.
"Mark" (lakkhaṇa) refers to that mark of a Great Man.

"Of unerring nature" means that its characteristic is such that it is not subject to change. "The benefit of the characteristic" refers to the qualities obtainable through the acquisition of that characteristic.
Having shown these factors—namely, action, what is similar to action, and so forth—which were just mentioned, the commentator should explain them by revealing their true nature.
It is said that at that time there was no golden archway adorned with jewels in the human world; therefore, it is called "in the city of the devas.
A *sāla* tree in full bloom, possessing such extraordinary beauty, cannot be found within the reach of humans; thus, he says "between the rocks.
"Conduct" (*kiriya-ācāra*) refers to the manifestation of physical and verbal actions.

387. *Satatapāṭihāriyaṃ* means the perpetual miracle, which is the unique miracle of the Buddhas caused by the power of the karma that produces the [major] marks throughout all time in their final existence.
Because even for those wishing to place their feet too far from the Buddhas, the placement occurs not too far away, it is said:
"He lifts [the foot], thinking, 'I will not set it down too far. This is said with reference to the manner of ordinary walking.
It has been said: "I shall place [the foot] many leagues away with such a step"—thus there is indeed even the lifting [of the foot].

"Because it is too far," and so forth, is the demonstration of the fault in exceeding the proper measure. "When this is so" means when the right and left feet are situated in their intended places of placement.
"The breaking of the steps" refers to the interruption of the sequence of the steps. Just as one extends [the leg], so too is the lifting and placing of the left foot.
The same applies to the right foot; thus, because their positions for lifting and placing are identical, being neither deficient nor excessive in their mutual relationship, it is said:
"The function of the right foot is determined by the left foot, and the function of the left foot is determined by the right foot."
“Divā” means at the time when [the day] has drawn near [to its end]. “For the sake of a monastery meal” means for the sake of the meal that is to be received in the monastery according to seniority.
“Coming from behind” means coming from behind by his usual way of walking. “Does not find space” means he does not find a place to set down his foot.
He says, “He does not lift up the thigh,” because here the word *satthi* (thigh) is used as a synonym for the *ūru* (thigh). “The staff-hook.”

It is called a long-handled hook; just as when a man cuts a tree branch with it, his feet tend to slip backward, so too the Blessed One’s feet do not slip. Thus he said: "As if cutting a tree branch...
causes [the feet] to slip. It is as if he were striking the foot at both the bound and unbound places—that is, by means of both the bound place and the unbound place.
And as if crushing a foot into pieces while making it stiff, one does not move it here and there; that is, one does not move it back and forth.
Because the feet turn over with ease due to the quality of having the heels turned upward (*ussaṅkhapādatā*), the upper body from the navel upwards does not stir;
thus, only the lower body stirs. Therefore he said: "The upper... [is] motionless. One does not know.

"Because of immovability. "By bodily strength" means by the specific strength residing in the body, which is characterized by the exertion of walking; or, by the bodily strength that serves as the cause for swift movement.
Therefore he said, "throwing out his arms," and so forth. For one who walks with speed throws out his arms, and sweat is released from the body.
"In the manner of a dragon’s backward glance" means in the manner of looking back by turning the entire body around, just like the backward glance of a dragon (nāga).

"Of unobstructed knowledge" means by means of the vision provided by the power of unobstructed knowledge. The section on "unobstructed" was stated for the purpose of showing that even the seeing of forms established within the body is indeed unobstructed.
"Starting from the city gate pillar" means starting from the city gate pillar at the entrance to the city.
"In his natural posture" means simply by walking upright, without performing such actions as bowing down. If this is so...
Regarding the question of how one enters a house through the gate of a fortification, he said: "Of poor people," and so forth.
"Turning over" means turning the body over for the purpose of lying down.
"Grasping with the hands" means grasping both sides of the waist with both hands. He falls at the place where he was sitting.
It falls by way of reclining. "Sitting leaning against the near side" means:
having folded the legs crosswise (pallaṅka), while establishing the upper body upon the lower body in a squatting posture, one sits leaning against the near side by way of making it heavy.
"Rubbing" means rubbing the seat area with the buttocks. "The far side" refers to the region of the spine.
The place for the sitting mat (*ānisada-padesa*). “In the same way” means while rubbing [the cloth]. “As if holding a hanging ornament” means as if lowering a hanging thread;
by this, he refers to the sitting mat being perfectly straight. Because the causes for the body’s heaviness have been removed from afar, it is very light, like placing a tuft of cotton down.
When entering the homes of those of little authority, there may be trepidation, agitation of the mind,
various kinds of imaginings due to distress, and trembling through fear or craving; to show that none of this exists for the Blessed One,
the phrase "he does not tremble" and so forth was spoken in the Pāḷi— thus he said, "he does not tremble," and so on.
"Water-giving" (*udakadāna*) means that by which water is given; it refers to a water vessel such as a ladle (*bhiṅkāra*).
"Having made bound" means having brought [the mind] under one's own control, like clay held in the hand. "Having turned back" means having become angry.
"While scattering" means while casting away by way of dispersing the water.
In that way he does not take [it], taking it merely for the sake of the sauce (*byañjana*). Or, the construction is: "having brought [it] and considering the food unpalatable.

Regarding these two—namely, covering the morsel with sauce and covering the sauce with the morsel—it should be understood that the first alone is rejected in the Canon because it is improper and undesirable. "In all cases" means...
In all things that are to be consumed, the flavor becomes manifest as being well-prepared because it has been fully understood through knowledge.
Yet, there is no craving for flavor because the bridge [to rebirth] has been destroyed.
"Assā" refers to the phrase beginning with "not for sport," and so forth. It has already been stated that "the detailed exposition is found in the *Visuddhimagga*."
This was stated by way of commentary in the *Sabbāsavasutta*; therefore, the intention is that it need not be discussed here.

Consequently, whatever specific explanation is desired for each respective determination should be understood according to the method already set forth in the *Visuddhimagga-vaṇṇanā* (the Sub-commentary to the Path of Purification) within the *Paramatthamañjūsā*.
"The place of grasping the bowl" refers to the spot on the hand where the bowl is held.
"Having turned back" means that having turned back with all the food and provisions in his bowl along with the meal, he goes away.

"Exceeding the proper measure" means that out of a sense of possessiveness, he establishes a guard that exceeds the proper measure. "Between the layers of robes" means between the folds of the robe-cloth.
"Having stepped upon with the belly" means having pressed down with the belly itself.

To bend forward toward that which has not yet reached its time is to bring it near; thus, he "over-bends" (atināmeti). To bend away from that which has reached its time by letting it pass is to remove it;
thus, he "over-bends. Showing that both meanings are taken together in the Pāḷi as "he does not over-bend the time for the expression of appreciation," he says "For whoever... and so forth.
Having wrapped it with a swift motion, he runs along. "Too high" means it is drawn up and worn excessively high;
therefore he said, "For one who [wears it] as far as the jawbone... [etc.]... "Too low" means it is drawn down and worn excessively low;
therefore he said, "having lowered it as far as the ankles. "Lifting it up on both sides" means...
"From right to left" means having lifted up the upper robe (uttarāsaṅga) on both sides. "The breast" refers to the right breast.
"Relaxed" means released. Therefore he said: "And it is to be understood precisely because of its being relaxed.

Since the speech of one who does not speak with release does not become smooth due to a lack of relaxation, whereas that of one who speaks with release is so, he said: "Glossy. "To be understood" means...
Because it is well-defined, it is capable of being understood both in terms of the syllables (*akkhara*) and the phonemes (*byañjana*). Therefore, he said "manifest" (*pākaṭa*).
"Communicable" (*viññāpaniya*) means that which is to be known. And here, the state of being communicable should be understood as being through the phonemes alone, because the sound is intended.
"Sweet" (*madhura*) means dear, lovely, and unobstructed. It is worthy of hearing; for hearing is [the function] of the ear.

Or, "beneficial" (*hita*) means it is worthy of being honored. "Coherent" (*sampiṇḍita*) means joined together. For the Blessed One’s sound reaches the range of perception in a unified manner, because it is produced at its source and accumulated;
it is not scattered like a bronze bowl struck by an iron rod. Therefore he said, "non-dispersing. "Profound" (*gambhīra*):
just as knowledge receives the designation "profound" through its discernment of a profound object, [so too is his voice].
Because such a sound arises from a profound source, it receives the designation "profound"; thus he said: "Profound means arisen from what is profound. It resounds with distinction;
this distinction is established by its profundity, hence he said: "And because of its very profundity, it resounds.
In this way, the four factors here should be understood as being produced by these four factors. Without cause.

The statement that the stream's boundaries receded on all sides "as if through the power of the Buddha" (*buddhānubhāvena*) should be understood as occurring solely by way of natural law (*dhammatā*), because its primary cause was established in such a manner.
"Having retreated" (*paccosakkitvā*) means having turned back. [It was] like a towering mountain of gold, with a summit spread over with sapphires (*indanīla-ratana*).
Adorned with streaks of lightning. The great earth and so forth are illustrations because they correspond to the qualities of the Teacher;
they are cited merely by way of their vastness. "Unannounced" means not having been informed.

And here, since it is "announced" by way of the arrival [of the guest], he says "one whose arrival is unperceived. "State of loftiness" refers to a state of excellence due to lineage, wealth, knowledge, and so on. "Endowed with compassion" means merciful.
391. By suddenly making way [for her], her high birth is revealed; thus he said, "Rising up with speed and splitting in two," and so forth.
"A name identical with that of a woman" means a name indicating the female state. Therefore he said, "The feminine gender. "Should be addressed" means they should be spoken to. 394.
While answering the eight questions with a single effort, [the verse] beginning with "Former births... pe ... is proclaimed" [explains] the knowledge of former births.

Since it was stated that the cause is known, he said, “His past lives are manifest. The knowledge of the divine eye is mentioned because it serves as a preliminary adjunct to the knowledge of the destiny according to karma.

And because it is stated, “He has reached the destruction of birth; he is perfected in direct knowledge,” the term “muni” here refers to the Asekha-muni (the one beyond training); thus he said, “endowed with the munificence of the knowledge of arahantship.”
By means of the stains of passion and the stains of disfigurement. Because he has reached the destruction of birth, it is said: "And thus he has reached the destruction of birth.
"Having fully known" (*abhijānitvā*) means having known by means of the supreme wisdom of the final path (*aggamagga-paññā*) due to its pre-eminence.

Now, according to the method presented in the *Paṭisambhidā*, the meaning here is that he is "one who has gone beyond" (*pāragū*) because of his reaching the further shore through full understanding, abandoning, developing, realizing, and attaining.
To demonstrate this, the passage beginning with “pāragūti vā” was stated. One who has reached the further shore by way of knowing the phenomena that are to be directly known is an “abhiññāpāragū.
“Such as that” means such as he who was described by the two phrases beginning with “pāragū sabbadhammānaṃ.
“By six modes” means by the six modes already mentioned, namely, thorough understanding (pajānana) and so forth.

In this context, although there are only two verses of questions and two verses of answers, the answer proceeds without confusion according to the sequence of the questions; therefore, the passage beginning with "But why...
was stated in order to determine that. "Because they have gone by means of the Vedas" means because they have gone beyond by means of the Vedas, which are the knowledges of the Path (*magga-ñāṇa*).
"Because of the manifestation of the true nature of the clear knowledges" refers to the existence of the true knowledges (*vijjā*) through such terms as "past lives" and so forth.
"Of evil states" means that it is so called because the thirty-six evil states have been completely purified by being brought to their safe emergence upon the path. 395.
"Dhamma" refers to the path to arahantship, according to the supreme designation based on its attainment of the highest excellence among wholesome states.
Because they are states corresponding to that [path], the lower paths and fruits are called "anudhamma. That which was [taught] in the presence of the Teacher...
One who, having heard the Dhamma, does not practice according to the instruction, is said to harass the Tathāgata regarding the Dhamma.
However, one who practices but, due to sluggish direct knowledge (*dandhābhiññatā*),

approaches the Blessed One from time to time to discuss the matter many times for the sake of purifying the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*)— to that extent, he [does not harass] the Tathāgata regarding the Dhamma.
One should not say that he "harassed" [the Blessed One]. For there is no weariness in the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma;
and this point can be illustrated by such discourses as the Mahāsudassana Sutta.

Therefore, although it should have been said, "in accordance with the true Dhamma," the phrase "and you did not harass me regarding the Dhamma" was stated specifically to clarify the matter by way of its opposite (vyatireka).
It should be seen. In this context, "one who attains final nibbāna" (*parinibbāyī*) includes both the time of another and the act of final nibbāna itself;
however, since that is already included here, he said: "The peak [of the teaching] is grasped by means of arahantship alone.
The *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Hidden Meaning) on the commentary to the *Brahmāyu Sutta* is completed.
2. Commentary on the Sela Sutta 396.
"Keṇiya" is his name; they say it was given because he had previously made his living as a hunter. "Jaṭila" means one who wears matted hair.
Because he was of brahmin birth and possessed great wealth, he was a "brahmin mahāsāla. He lived there having provided support and acting as a patron.
Or, the construction may be: "He experiences the fulfillment of sensual pleasures at night.
"Well-prepared" means thoroughly prepared with ghee, honey, sugar, and so forth, as well as black pepper, ginger, and so forth.
"Because of the clarity [arising] from rejection" refers to one who is being invited, thinking: "Oh, how this person is of few desires, since he does not consent even when being invited!"
"Regarding the rejection [of the claim] that it was out of faith in the sectarians (tīrthikas): how so? He rejects it by saying, 'This is contradictory;
this is without reason. (398) 'Even in a thousand eons... it did not happen': this refers to an inference based on tradition (anussava).

He says 'in the measure of a word' because it is a designation using the elision of the latter member (*uttarapadalopa*). It is called a 'word' (*pada*) because one places or deposits [the meaning] therein."
Or "pada" means the place where the foot is set down by nature; [he falls into negligence] at that spot. He falls into negligence through such things as playing or sleeping.
He says "the conduct of a Bodhisatta" with reference to the practice of difficult austerities (dukkaracariyā).

399. "By way of perfection" means by way of being complete. "By way of having no deficiency in limbs" means because of the state of being without lack. "Rocati" means radiance; it is the bodily luster.
“Suruci” means one whose taste (or inclination) for beauty is excellent. “Perfection of height” is the body’s appropriate stature.

“Perfection of circumference” is a girth that avoids being either too thin or too thick. “Perfection of configuration” is the well-proportioned arrangement of the limbs. Because he was lovely to behold—meaning his appearance was dear—one said, “Even after a very long time,” and so forth.
“A complexion like gold” refers to [a color] produced by rubbing together natural vermilion...
Having performed the preparatory work as if with the polishing of stone, he possesses the luster of a solid golden image that has been set in place.
They are called *byañjanāni* because they manifest and reveal the state of a Great Man; thus he says, “the very same marks (*byañjanāni*) mentioned first.

What was mentioned previously is what was said before as “of beautiful radiance” (*suruci*); it is stated again as “you shine like the sun” (*ādiccova virocasī*). “Of lovely appearance” (*cārudassano*).

He said, "The same principle applies to the subsequent verse as well," with reference to the fact that what was previously stated as "you are golden-colored" is stated again as "the bhikkhu is beautiful to behold, his skin like refined gold.

He said, "of one endowed with supreme beauty," because after describing the supreme beauty in an exceptional manner, he makes it known as existing through the phrase "possessing supreme beauty. [And] "supreme charioteer":
The charioteer of the best of men. Because it is adorned here and there with groves of *jambu* trees, Jambudīpa is called "Jambusaṇḍa.
"Sovereignty" refers to the sovereignty of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti*).

"Kṣatriyas by birth" means kṣatriyas who possess noble lineage. Regarding the term "king of kings," he states that the prefix *abhi-* here has the sense of worship, thus: "one worthy of worship by kings."
“Immeasurable” means immeasurable world-systems; for it is said, “as far as he might wish.

Regarding the phrase “the unsurpassed King of Dhamma,” the state of being unsurpassed mentioned there is made more explicit by the words beginning with “as far as,” in order to clarify his status as the King of Dhamma.
“By the Dhamma” means by the Dhamma of penetration (*paṭivedhadhamma*). Therefore, he said, “by the unsurpassed [Dhamma] itself.”
"Anuttarena" means by that which is distinguished and supreme. In this interpretation, "dhammena" is also included as meaning "by the dhamma of practice.
The construction is: "I set in motion the wheel of authority (āṇācakkam) by means of the dhamma of the scriptures (pariyattidhammo), that is, the dhamma of the teaching.

Alternatively, it may refer simply to the Wheel of Dhamma (dhammacakkam) itself, distinguished by the knowledge of teaching (desanāñāṇa) and the knowledge of penetration (paṭivedhañāṇa). "Appaṭivattiyan" means incapable of being turned back.
"Born by the Tathāgata" means born through the cause that is the Tathāgata, namely, through noble birth. The instrumental case is used here in the sense of a cause (*hetu*).
Furthermore, when the term *anujāta* (born after) is used, by virtue of the prefix *anu*, the word "Tathāgata" takes the accusative case;
and since that prefix *anu* indicates the sense of a cause, it is said: "He was born after the Tathāgata as his cause. This is because [he is one] whose state is not to be disparaged.
“Born” means born base, because of his wrong practice; therefore he is called “immoral. For it was said concerning Kokālika: “A man, a wretch, born base.
He is not truly a son because he does not abide by his father’s exhortations and instructions.
Thus he spoke: “He is born after the likeness of the Tathāgata”—thus he spoke.
Knowledge (*vijjā*) here refers to the knowledge of the path (*magga-vijjā*). By way of the highest description, "liberation" (*vimutti*) refers to the liberation of the fruit (*phala-vimutti*).

But is it not the case that the path is already included among those things to be developed? True, it is included; however, since all seven factors [of enlightenment] are to be directly known (*abhiññeyya*), their status as objects to be directly known is stated by means of "knowledge.
Or rather, it should be understood that by this method, the status of all [seven factors] as objects to be directly known is likewise stated. [This is] by way of the fruit.
Because the state of being a cause does not exist apart from the very fact of its non-existence, the fruit is established by the statement of the cause;

and the state of the Path as a cause is established by bringing about cessation. The fact that craving is the origin of suffering is included in this very meaning, since it is implied by the sense [of the preceding].
"By a logical reason" means: he establishes the state of Buddhahood by means of a reason endowed with logical consistency (*yutti*), [which is] distinct from the [four noble] truths.

Because there is nothing further to be awakened to, and because he has awakened to that [truth] in its entirety through his perfect awakening to the truths. This is a statement of meaning; as for the functional expressions, they are:
"O Brahmin, I am the Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha), the teacher of the Dhamma entirely without error.
Because I am the Perfectly Enlightened One, I declare everything without error, just as I am the teacher of the entire path. What [is this]?
But does the Blessed One proclaim his own state of being a perfectly enlightened Buddha (sammāsambuddha) of his own accord?
It is because of his great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and for the sake of others' vast benefit. In this regard, such suttanta passages as "I am the one who is perfectly enlightened;
I am the conqueror of all, the knower of all," and this very sutta passage, establish this meaning.

“Sallakantano” means one who has completely eradicated the arrows [of defilement]. “Of disease” means of the disease of the defilements (*kilesa*). “Therefore” means because of curing by ensuring that there is no further arising [of suffering].
“Brahma-bhūto” means having attained the sublime (*brahma*), the supreme, Perfect Enlightenment (*sammāsambodhi*). By the phrase “Thus come,” it is said:
“Sensual desires are your first army; the second is called discontent;”
The third is hunger and thirst for you; the fourth is called craving.
Sloth and torpor are the fifth for you; the sixth is called fear.
The seventh is doubt for you; the eighth is flattery and obstinacy.
“Gain, fame, and honor, and that reputation acquired through wrong means;
whoever exalts himself and disparages others—
this, O Namuci, is your army, the assault of Kaṇha.”

Thus, the ninefold army is comprised. "Having brought under control" means having brought under control by means of eradication and the prevention of future arising. "Fearless from any quarter" means free from dread.

"To be seen by oneself" means that whatever has been attained must not be traversed through the faith of others; rather, it must be seen personally through the knowledge of reflective contemplation (*paccavekkhaṇā-ñāṇa*) without delusion. Therefore he said, "directly perceived" (*paccakkha*). It is praised.
*Diṭṭhi* means "visible. Just as one who wins by means of a chariot is called a "charioteer," so too this holy life of the path is called *sandiṭṭhika* because it wins by means of what is visible.
Alternatively, *diṭṭha* refers to seeing; that which is seen is itself *sandiṭṭha*, meaning "that which is shown.
That which is worthy of being seen is *sandiṭṭhika*, just as a pair of garments is said to be "worthy" [of wearing].
"Consisting of a pair of robes. With reference to the giving of its fruit here and now (*sandidṛśika*), there is no "wrong time" for it; thus it is "timeless" (*akālika*).
It does not give its fruit after wasting away an interval of time; rather, the meaning is that it gives its fruit immediately upon its own occurrence.
Alternatively, it is "timely" (*kālika*)—meaning mundane wholesome states (*kusaladhamma*)—because they reach a distinguished time for the giving of their own fruit.
However, this [offering] is not "timely" (kālika) because its fruit follows immediately.

Regarding such passages as "He performed a great sacrifice," it is stated that "there is no sacrifice for Brahmins" because the term "sacrifice" (yañña) applies exclusively to acts of giving, dharma, and so forth;
for the Brahmins hold that "the gods have fire as their mouth," and thus [a true sacrifice] must be preceded by the offering into the fire.

They perform the sacrifice. Therefore he said: "The meaning is 'those for whom the offering of fire is the primary thing. Regarding the words "Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ," the *Sāvitrī* is the "mouth" because it is the precursor;

that is, the forerunner. Just as in expressions such as "the mouth is like a face," here too he says, "The king is called the 'mouth' because he is the best among men," demonstrating that the word "mouth" (*mukha*) is used here in the sense of "primary" (*padhāna*). [The phrase] "by way of being the support" (*ādhāratoti*)...
Because it serves as the support for rivers that descend into it, because it is their refuge, and because it is the place they must reach.

"As a sign" means because it is made known today as being under such-and-such a constellation by way of its conjunction with the moon. "As a maker of light" means because it outshines the constellations and produces light.
"As a state of coolness" means because it possesses the quality of coldness and is protected from the biting winds of the Himalayas. "Of those burning" refers to the flames of a lamp.
"Flaming tongues of fire, thunderbolts, wheels," and so forth—referring to those things that are crackling. "The gateway" is by virtue of being the foremost object of offerings (*aggadakkhiṇeyya*).

"By these five eyes"—namely, the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*), the Dhamma-eye (*dhammacakkhu*), the wisdom-eye (*paññācakkhu*), the Buddha-eye (*buddhacakkhu*), and the universal eye (*samantacakkhu*)—"to them who have gone for refuge":
this means both "to those who have gone for refuge" and [the refuge] itself, because the other two [aspects] are rooted in the state of having gone for refuge (*saraṇabhāva*), as has been stated.
The meaning of "of another" (*parassa*) is [to be understood] from what was stated by the word *te*. This is what is meant:
"O, the power of refuge—both yours (*te* = *tuyhaṃ*) and that of the other! Alternatively, by way of repetition (*āvutti*), the meaning here in the phrase *te saraṇassa* should be clarified as:
"the power of you who have become the refuge, and of the other refuge. The rest is easily understood.
The explanation of the *Selasutta*, the elucidation of its hidden meaning, is completed.
3. Commentary on the *Assalāyana Sutta* 401.

Because they are distinguished from one another, their respective kingdoms are dissimilar (*visadisa*). "From the dissimilar" (*virajjato*) means having come from there; "born therein" (*tattha jātā*) means born in those [kingdoms].

Or "from various kingdoms" (*nānāverajjakā*); since they are born in such a way that they are of diverse kinds through the distinction of garments, ornaments, and so forth, it is therefore said, "from those of various kingdoms.
In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, however, their diversity is stated by way of the kingdom itself.
"By means of witnessing sacrifices and so forth" means by means of experiencing sacrifices, incantations, seeking sacrificial fees, and so on. "Common to the four castes" (*catuvaṇṇasādhāraṇaṃ*).
It is a common means for the four castes, beginning with the Khattiyas, for purifying the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) and for crossing over evil.

"By purification through bathing" means by the purification of bathing consisting of descending into water three times in the evening and so forth, preceded by the chanting of mantras at bathing places, oceans, and reservoirs.
"By purification through cultivation" means by the purification known as the cultivation of the person, which is the supreme light. "A ploughed field" means...
"Having shaved his hair"—for it is that very head which is said to be "shorn.
"A speaker of reality" means one who speaks according to things as they truly are. "Those going forth" refers to those entering the brahminical renunciation;
therefore, by you who are training in the rules for the renunciation of brahmins, [the claim] must not be made that "only brahmins are purified, not non-brahmins."
"This method was learned thoroughly, with its causes and its basis; therefore, there is no defeat for you... so they said. 402.
"For the purpose of breaking a tenet" means for the purpose of overturning the tenet that has arisen thus: "Only Brahmins are the legitimate sons of Brahmā, born from his mouth, born of Brahmā.
"For the purpose of obtaining a son" means: "In this way, we [shall obtain] a son from our father..."
"Standing upon this doctrine, we shall purify our debt for the sake of obtaining a son"—this was the intention of those unrighteous brahmins.
"Of them" refers to the brahmins. "The word might be true" means that if the statement beginning with "sons of Brahmā" were true, it would apply to the brahmin women...
[and so on] ...it would be so; but this is not the case. [They claim he was] born from the mouth of Mahābrahmā.
The "debater who cuts off speech" is one who utters clever words directly from his mouth.

Although Assalāyana was wise by nature and knew that what had been spoken by the ascetic Gotama was irrefutable, he nevertheless said, "Even though the venerable Gotama... and so forth, for the sake of protecting the feelings of the Brahmins who were present with him.
403. Now, in order to refute the claim that "the brahmin alone is the highest caste," the passage beginning with "Have you heard [of the Yonakas and Kambojas]?
is commenced. If the brahmin alone were the highest caste, then the brahmin would have to be the highest everywhere;
why then is there no status as the highest for brahmins in countries such as those of the Yonakas and Kambojas? For in those places, the castes are as follows: [text continues].
Therefore, the notion that "the brahmin alone is the best" is merely a matter of opinion. For in those regions, people gathered together, deliberated, and made an agreement;
having established one as a master and the rest as slaves, they honored him and remained under his authority.
He who was their lord became the master, while all the others became his slaves. After the lapse of several years, they...
Having seen some fault in him, they remove him from that position and appoint another;
thus, one who was a master becomes a slave, and the other, having been a slave, becomes a master. In this way, some explain the meaning here as: "Having been a master, he becomes a slave;
having been a slave, he becomes a master. However, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, that meaning is [explained] according to the former method alone.
To demonstrate this, it was said: "The brahmin together with his wife," and so forth.

The phrase "when the sons have reached maturity and are absent" is first an illustration of the child who is about to be mentioned as the owner of the inheritance. Regarding the expression "pure on the mother's side":

herein, one who is a nobleman (ayya) by virtue of being pure on the mother's side, yet becomes a slave because of impurity on the father's side—that very person, having become a slave due to impurity on the father's side, [remains] a nobleman on the mother's side.
"He becomes" means he undergoes birth; thus, he breaks through the cycle of existence. Others say that it is impossible to state that "he becomes entirely and in every way" [the same].
"What is the basis?"—in this great world-system, throughout the beginningless past, since the minds of women are unstable, slaves remain slaves and masters remain masters;
what here is the certain, causal support for that, and what is its proof?
The meaning is: "What is the illustration of the established doctrine (siddhanta)?
404. "The doctrine of the cutter of the white" means: that which is spoken thus, "Only the brahmin is the white caste," is called the section on the cutter of the white.
408. "While performing the function of fire in all [cases]"—by this it is shown that fire, having arisen from any source whatsoever, is provided with its fuel.

"He performs the function of fire"—this shows that whoever is born into any servant family whatsoever, if endowed with the necessary support (*upanissaya*) and practicing rightly, is purified from *saṃsāra*. 409.
"The color of a foot-soldier" means an intermediate color. "Of these" refers to the son born of a Kṣatriya youth and a Brāhmaṇa maiden.
"The son born of a Brāhmaṇa youth and a Kṣatriya girl"—this refers to these two young men.
"At a funeral meal" means at a meal prepared in honor of the deceased. "At a *thālipāka*" means at a meal prepared for an auspicious occasion.
(410) He says "you" (*tumhe*), addressing the young man together with the Brāhmaṇas as one group on account of their common birth. Who?

Now, thinking, "This is the ascetic's claim that one is 'head-downwards' [inferior]," he approached them in the guise of a village boy in order to demonstrate the insignificance of birth by showing the incapacity of those Brahmin women.
Therefore it is said: "Like a village gambler. *Koṇḍadamaka* means a tamer of the untamed. 411. *Janetīti janikā janetti*:
she who gives birth is the mother (*janikā*, *janetti*). The same rule applies here for the father (*janako pitā*). *Gandhabbapañhaṃ*: a question concerning the Gandhabba.
This is a question concerning whether a being arising in the mother’s womb as a *gandhabba* is a kṣatriya or otherwise.
The craft of preparing medicinal extracts (*dabbigahaṇasippa*) should also be understood as one branch of knowledge (*vijjā*).

It is said that one skilled in this, having taken any edible leaf, flower, fruit, or seed—even as small as an *elālu*—and having prepared it by mixing it with medicines and cooking it, makes it have a flavor identical to ghee, honey, and molasses.
If one is able to accomplish [the task] after having undertaken it, Puṇṇa is also like that; therefore, the connection is that by this it is known:

"You do not know even the mere craft of handling a ladle. "Faithful" means faithful through faith in the fruit of kamma, being confident through the confidence in the Triple Gem characteristic of an ordinary person.
For this very reason he said: "May the venerable one accept me as a lay follower... who has gone for refuge."
The *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Hidden Meaning) for the commentary on the *Assalāyanasutta* is completed.
4. Commentary on the *Ghoṭamukhasutta* 412.
Because it was planted by the queen of the king named Khemiya, that mango grove is called the "Khemiya Mango Grove."
They say: "Dhammika" means one who is endowed with the Dhamma, having entirely abandoned non-Dhamma and being established in the Dhamma.
"Paribbaja" (the wandering life) is that by which one wanders forth; it is the undertaking of virtue through the assumption of the [ascetic] marks, preceded by departing from the household life.
"In this" means in this wandering life. "The true nature" refers to that state of being a wanderer, [defined] by those various wanderers.
The intrinsic nature (sabhāva), which consists of the practice of the Dhamma, is not to be disregarded.

By the statement "the Dhamma alone is the authority," we speak according to how it appears to our own minds without shame; therefore, that [subjective impression] is not the authority. However, whatever herein is the Dhamma that is non-erroneous—that alone is the authority.
There exists the intrinsic nature consisting of the practice already attained; of that, each of you must take more [as the standard].
The intention is that one must cultivate here various acts such as showing [the way], for much remains to be said in this regard.

414. *Sārattarattā* means "colored by passion" (*sārajjanavasena rattā*); the meaning is "delighted" (*abhirattā*) due to an abundance of lust. *Anuggaha* means that which causes one to grasp or understand the matter that is to be made known by oneself;
it is the cause of making it known. *Sahanuggahena* means "together with that cause of making it known."
It is accompanied by a motive. Therefore he said, "with a reason. But what is that reason? His intention was this: "I have said there is no righteous wandering life;
surely the Venerable Udena will explain to me the righteous wandering life as it truly is.
Therefore he said, "For this has been said," and so forth.

421. "All this, both the stationary and the moving, is made by man; therefore, having done whatever [is necessary], one must nourish and protect oneself"—this is the path of policy based on Lokāyata, beloved by Ghoṭamukha. Therefore he said, "In his art of knowledge," and so forth.
There is no such thing as being reborn in heaven, because it results from doing what ought not to be done. The wealth included within the heavenly realms belongs to humans.
Because his merit was exhausted, he departed after first pointing out the wealth he had previously deposited, saying, "It is with such-and-such," and then went away. The rest is easy to understand.
The *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Hidden Meaning) for the commentary on the *Ghoṭamukha-sutta* is completed.
5. Commentary on the *Caṅkī-sutta*.
422. "In that Sāla grove": *opāsādaṃ* means in the northern direction from the village of Opāsāda.
Regarding the word *uttarena*, because it is joined with the pronoun *ena*, it takes the accusative case.

As for the phrase "he dwells" (*ajjhāvasati*), the commentator says "he dwells" (*vasati*) while taking into account that the prefixes *adhi-* and *ā-* have no distinct meaning here. Now, he shows how their specific meanings are developed:
He says, “‘Having overcome [them], he dwells,’ and so forth. Regarding the word *opāsāda* (palace), he asks, “How is it in cases such as *sattussada*?
He replies: “Because that [word] has no further application, the same applies to the remaining words.
Grammarians maintain that when the action of dwelling (*vasana*) is preceded by the prefixes *upa*, *anu*, *adhi*, or *iti*, the accusative case alone is reached; thus he says, “the rule...”

"It should be sought from the treatise on grammar (saddasattha). For it has been stated: "In this context, however, the accusative case should be understood as having the sense of the locative by virtue of the prefix.
Here, 'profusion' (ussadatā) means abundance; to demonstrate that abundance, the words "many people" (bahujana), etc., were spoken.
"Having brought to mind" (āvajjitvā) means having surrounded [them].

It is called *rājabhogga* because it is to be enjoyed by the king, as if it were his own. It is that which has become the king’s inheritance (*dāyabhūta*) by virtue of being enjoyed through the lineage of the family;

hence he said, "the meaning is 'inheritance' (*dāyajja*). Because there is no better gift than the acquisition of enjoyment after one has raised the royal parasol and enjoys [it] under the designation of "king," he said: "having raised the parasol, by way of the title of king..."
"It should be used. "At river fords, mountains, and so forth" means at river fords, the foot of mountains, village gates, forest entrances, and the like.
"Relinquished and abandoned" means having made it abandoned by way of a liberated generosity. "Of these brahmins and householders. 423. "Assembled": whoever among the wise is desired;

one who is capable of answering correctly whatever question is asked, capable of explaining the questions asked. "A high official" (*mahāmatta*): one who possesses great measure (*mattā*) by virtue of his family, lineage, and so forth.

424. By "those from various kingdoms," the aforementioned brahmins are meant. When only "well-born on both sides" was stated, it might have been understood as being well-born by virtue of any two parts whatsoever;

furthermore, since the word *sujāta* (well-born) is used in such phrases as "well-born and handsome" (*sujāto cārudassano*) as a synonym for excellence of stature and proportion, the phrase "from the mother’s side and from the father’s side" (*mātito ca pitito ca*) was stated specifically to clarify that the state of being well-born is by way of lineage (*jāti*). This is also [the case] with respect to sons other than those born of the breast (*anorasa-putta*).

The designation "mother" and "father" is seen in the world; however, to show that here it is intended specifically in the sense of one's own biological children, the phrase "one with a pure digestive tract" (*saṃsuddhagahaṇīko*) is stated.
"Father and mother" is *pitaro*; "the fathers of the fathers" are the grandfathers (*pitāmahā*);
their pair is the "grandfather-pair" (*pitāmahayugo*). Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as "down to the seventh grandfather-pair. The word *yuga* [is used here].

And here it should be understood by way of the method of single remainder (*ekasesanaya*): "the yoke and the yoke are 'yokes'. For in this way, two [terms] are indeed included in each instance. Therefore he said:
"Beyond that, all ancestors are included by the mention of the grandfather alone.

And here, the mention of "man" (*purisa*) should be understood as being made by way of an inclusive designation (*ukkaṭṭhaniddesa*). For in this way, [the phrase] "from the mother's side" (*mātito*)...

The Pāli expression is thus established. "Unreviled" (akkhitta) means one who has not been subjected to a throw [of abuse]. "Uncensured" (anavakkhitta) means one who has not been disparaged in matters such as faith or the offering of cooked rice.
To show that the instrumental case is used here in the sense of a cause (*hetu*), the phrase beginning with "by what reason" (*kena kāraṇena*) was stated.
And herein, by the expression "on both sides... through ten generations of ancestors," the absence of any defect in the Brahmin’s lineage (*yoni-dosa*) is demonstrated.
This is because it describes the state of having a completely pure disposition. By the term "uncensured" (*akkhitta*), the absence of any fault in action is indicated;
for it is through faults in action that sentient beings incur censure. By the term "unreviled" (*anupakuṭṭha*), the absence of improper association is indicated;
for it is also in dependence upon improper association that sentient beings receive abuse.
"Lord" (*issara*) means one whose nature is to rule as a result of karma conducive to sovereignty.
Since that lordship of his becomes manifest through the condition of the attainment of wealth, he says, "The wealthy is the lord," speaking by way of its synonym for being rich.
He is "of great wealth" (*mahaddhana*) because he possesses great riches both buried in the earth and stored in the air. "His" refers to each respective [person]. They say, "By way of sequence..."
"And let us describe the reason for not approaching from the perspective of contrast.
"Adhikarūpa" means having a distinguished form or an excellent body. "Dassanīya" means worthy of being seen; therefore he said, "fit for seeing.
"Pāsādika" means bringing about serenity; therefore he said, "because it generates mental serenity. "Vaṇṇassa" refers to the element of color (the physical appearance).
The "body" (*sarīra*) is the collection of parts—such as hands, feet, neck, and head—distinguished by their arrangement;
and since it is apprehended by way of its configuration, it is said: "with supreme beauty of complexion" (*paramāya vaṇṇapokkharatāya*), meaning "with supreme...
excellence. Among all complexions, the golden complexion is the most excellent; thus it is said: "endowed with the most excellent golden complexion. For indeed:
Buddhas and wheel-turning monarchs are indeed golden-colored. "Brahmavacchasī" means having a supreme bodily luster, a golden luster;
for it is with reference to this very meaning that it is said: "endowed with a body similar to the body of Mahābrahmā. It does not mean being straight-limbed like Brahmā.
"Of no small presence for seeing" refers to the perfection of height and girth, and the complete fulfillment of all limbs.
And the opportunity for seeing [the Buddha] is not insignificant. Therefore he said, "all indeed," and so forth.
One who possesses virtue (*sīla*) characterized by restraint and non-restraint is "virtuous" (*sīlavā*).

Furthermore, because that virtue of his has been long-practiced, matured, and increased, he is "one whose virtue is matured" (*vuddhasīlī*); and because he is always endowed with it, he is "possessed of matured virtue."
They say this refers only to the five precepts (*pañcasīla*), because beyond that there is no further virtue (*sīla*) therein, and because those [beings] do not understand it.

It is called "having complete words and phrasing" (*parimaṇḍalapadabyañjanā*) because its words, phrases, and syllables are perfectly rounded, with no deficiency whatsoever in the perfection of the vocal organs (*ṭhānakaraṇa*) or the perfection of the training (*sikkhā*).
Alternatively, it is so called because meaning (*attha*) is understood (*pajjati*) by means of it.

A *pada* (word) consists of names and so forth. That which manifests the intended meaning is the *byañjana* (expression), namely the sentence. Because these are complete, it is "possessing full and perfect words and expressions.
Alternatively, speech itself is the instrument because it is the means for making the meaning known; thus it is the "instrument of speech" (*vākkaraṇa*), which is the sound of utterance.
By virtue of its being complete in excellence, that Brahmin—or the meaning to be spoken by him—is "full" (*pūre*), in the sense of being complete.
In the first sense, the locative case is used for the *ādhāra* (locus); in the second sense, it is used for the *visaya* (object).
By the phrase "by its delicacy," he expresses the softness and smoothness of that speech. "Unobstructed" means not blocked by bile, phlegm, and so forth.

"Partial statement" (*ekadesakathana*) is like showing everything as if it were already directly perceived (*sandidṛṣṭa*). "Drawn-out" (*vilambita*) means speaking slowly after a long delay. [The compound] is "unclear, drawn-out, and so forth. (*Sandiddhavilambitādīti*)
Or this is another reading. In that context, "doubtful" means that which generates doubt. By the word "etcetera," it includes such things as stammering and trailing off.
By the phrase "having made the beginning, middle, and end clear," they state that there is a fulfillment of the meaning through his speech.
425. "Similar" means similar in some respect; for there are no qualities whatsoever that are similar in every way to the qualities of the Buddhas.
"These others are found elsewhere. "The others" refers to those whose qualities are incomparable to one's own. "This" refers to this collection of matters.
"Like water in a cow’s footprint" means water standing in the footprint of a cow. "By way of family succession" means by the order of families. "Therein" means upon the couch.
"He assumed the lion’s posture" means [in the manner] that Rāhu, lord of the asuras, [assumes it] in length, width, and height.
And being unable to grasp the limits of the Blessed One’s physical body (rūpakāya), he performed such a feat of supernormal power (iddhābhisaṅkhāra) and lay down in the lion’s posture.
He said, “Noble (ariya)” in the sense of being utterly pure; “supreme and pure” means noble. It is wholesome (kusala) in the sense of being blameless.

Not in the sense of having a pleasant ripening (*sukhavipāka*). For in some places eighty-four thousand beings, and in others even immeasurable gods and humans, drink the nectar of the path and its fruits (*maggaphalāmata*) in twenty-four locations—countless and immeasurable. Even by a measure of hundreds of thousands of millions and so forth, they are indeed many.
Therefore, the Blessed One is the teacher of the many solely by way of training them in the unsurpassed conduct. "Them" refers to those [beings] from sensual lust (*kāmarāga*).
Others [refer] to the defilements abandoned by the Blessed One.
Regarding the phrase *apāpapurekkhāro*: it is so called because one is honored (*purakkharīyati*) by those who are sinless, or alternatively, because one does not place sin before oneself;
in order to show this meaning, it is said, "the nine supramundane states which are sinless," and so forth. In that context, "sinless" (*apāpe*) means the opposites of sin.

And "in one free from evil. *Brahmaññā* means: existing in the state of a Brahmin (*brahman*), or beneficial to a Brahmin through such acts as showing reverence, or that which knows the path of a Brahmin;
[it belongs] to that people who possess such *brahmaññā*.
Regarding the terms *tiroraṭṭhā* and *tirojanapadā*: here, "kingdom" (*raṭṭha*) is so called because kings (*rājāno*) rule by means of it (*rājanti*). These [terms] refer to parts of that [kingdom].
"Districts," however, are so called because people (*jana*) go there (*pajjanti*) and attain a comfortable livelihood.

"Having observed the fault in the question" is the syntactical connection. "The Blessed One answers, having considered their perfection of supporting conditions (*upanissaya-sampatti*)" is the intended meaning.
"Newcomers" means we are fresh [to this] by virtue of being visitors.

426. *Opāteti* means he causes to fall out or expels. Being thus disposed, he is sent there; hence it is said, "he causes to enter. *Saṃpurakkharonti* means they respectfully act as forerunners. Therefore he says, "moving about having placed [him] in front. 427.
Having placed the *suddas* outside, in the sense that they are to be instructed in secret, the *mantas* themselves—because they are the cause for the practice of various goals—are the *padāni*;
thus it is "the *mantapada*," namely the Veda. Therefore he says, "the Veda. *Evaṃ kira* means "thus, indeed," as handed down by way of oral tradition.

It has been handed down through the lineage of teachers (*ācariyaparamparā*). Regarding "the excellence known as the *pāvacana*": this refers to the excellence of the *udātta* (high-pitched) and other accents in the principal words.

By "with the metrical compositions such as the *Sāvitti*, etc., and with the groupings," it means both the metrical compositions such as the *gāyattī*, etc., consisting of the *ajjhāyas* and *anuvākas*, and the groupings [of verses].
"Having accomplished" means without losing the perfection of the words. Or, "those who cause it to proceed" refers to them by way of the *pāvacana*.
"Reciters. "Chanted" means chanted by way of singing; however, since that is intended only in terms of the *pada* (word/verse), he says "by way of the perfection of the *pada*.
"Stated for others" means stated for others by way of their own respective scriptures (*pāvacana*). "Collected" means collected by way of the *Ṛgveda*, *Yajurveda*, *Sāmaveda*, and so forth;
and within those as well, individually by way of the *mantras*, the *brahmans*, and so forth, or by way of the *adhyāyas*, *anuvākas*, and so forth.

"Delightful. "Having observed with the divine eye" means: having observed, by means of the knowledge of the destination according to karma—which is an adjunct to the divine eye—the ownership of karma by sentient beings;
and having observed, by means of the knowledge of past lives—which is similar to the divine eye in the sense of direct vision—the manner of the Brahmins' mastery of the mantras in past eons.
"Having compared it with the current teaching" means: [having compared it] with the word of the Buddha.
Having made it non-contradictory with whatever teaching of the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa was dependent upon the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*).
For the meaning dependent upon the turning away from the cycle (*vivaṭṭa*) was not directly evident to them. "Successively" means by Aṭṭhaka and others;
"subsequent" means those who arose later, during the time of King Okkāka and so forth. "Having inserted" means into the sections of the mantras composed by Aṭṭhaka and others.
Having inserted the words dependent on defilement (*kilesa*) here and there into the respective places.
"They made them contradictory" means they made them into opposites by illustrating the meaning of defilement according to the method found in such suttas as the *Brāhmaṇadhammika-sutta*.
428. "Arranged in sequence" means connected in order. "Mutually intertwined" [refers to] the handle of the *ādāniyā* (the water-strainer).
They are closely joined. Therefore he said: “by a sighted man holding a staff. “Of the first one” means:
having had the hand of the very first person in a blind procession standing in a circular formation grasp the hem of the garment of the very last person. “Even for a day” means: even for many days.
Having known the future state of the eye, one follows it by stepping exactly where it has already stepped, as if it were a path already trodden.
Having observed, he lamented: "Where is the one with vision? Where is the path?
Regarding the two mentioned in the text: these are the two, namely, faith (*saddhā*) and hearsay (*anussava*).

"Of such a kind" means that they are precisely those who accept things based on faith and hearsay; this is the meaning. "Three" refers to preference (*ruci*), mental mode (*ākāra*), discursive thought (*parivitakka*), view (*diṭṭhi*), contemplation (*nijjhāna*), and acceptance (*khanti*).

"Having the actual as their fruition" (*bhūta-vipākā*) means those things which lead to the conclusion of what is real and accomplish the intended meaning; by the opposite of what was stated, those having the non-real as their fruition (*abhūta-vipākā*) are to be understood.

"In this regard" (*ettha*) means in these bases such as being trustworthy and so forth. One is not able to reach a conclusion with absolute certainty because the grasping of faith and the other qualities is not one-sided (*anekantikattā*).
Having opened the way for the subsequent question, he established [the matter] out of a desire to know while protecting the truth.
Because it has been produced. For the Blessed One saw: "When I have said, 'By one who guards the truth...
[and so on] ...one should reach the goal,' that young man, desiring to know the guarding of truth, will ask, 'To what extent? and so forth.

Having answered him thus, and having given him the opportunity to ask about the awakening to truth, I shall explain the supporting conditions that are helpful for his spiritual potential (*upanissaya*)."
Therefore it was said: “Having opened up the path for the subsequent question, he established it.
(430) He speaks referring to himself alone, since it is stated in the Pāḷi:

“But as for this Dhamma which this venerable one teaches, that Dhamma is deep, hard to see, and hard to understand,” and so forth. They are “alluring” (*lubbhantīti lobhanīyā*) in the sense of being objects of lust.
Regarding the phrase “leading to states of deprivation,” he says: “among things that incite greed” means “among greedy states.

Or, just as visible forms and other phenomena are things that incite greed, so too is greed itself; thus he says: “among things that incite greed” means “among greedy states. For this very reason he said:
“Whatever in the world is lovely and pleasing, therein this craving arises when it arises, and therein it settles when it settles.”
"...it settles. This same method applies to the other two phrases as well.
"He establishes" means he places or sets forth. "He attends upon" means he approaches and sits down by way of waiting upon.
He says "the ear of clarity" because it is heard by means of this; for that [ear] must be directed toward hearing. It bears [the sound].
"Retains" means he fixes the mind right there. "In terms of meaning" (*atthato*) means in terms of the meaning of the Dhamma as it has been stated.

"In terms of reason" (*kāraṇato*) means by way of logic, through causes and examples, and through demonstration. "Observation" (*olokanaṃ*) means they endure being seen by the eye of wisdom according to their true nature as "it is thus";
and that [nature] is revealed like a great, blazing jewel. Of the meaning...
"Establishment in the mind" is what is meant by the words "here," and so forth. "Desire for action" (*kattukamyatā-chanda*) is wholesome desire characterized by the wish to act.
"Exerts effort" means that he performs exertion and striving by means of all four kinds of energy from the very beginning.
"He exerts the right effort of the path" means that he exerts the right effort (*sammappadhāna*) which brings about the path and is included within the path; this is by way of such exertion.

He fulfills that. "Supreme truth" (paramasacca) means the ultimate truth (paramatthasacca) because its nature is unfailing. "By the co-nascent body of name" means by the body of name co-nascent with the wisdom of the Path.
"That very same" refers to that very same supreme truth, Nibbāna. For this reason it was said:
"He sees, making manifest—that is, making clear—by means of the realization through direct experience."
433–4. *Maggānubodho* means the awakening and the act of waking up according to the sequence of the path.
It refers to the fruit of recluseship (*sāmaññaphala*) that occurs by way of the subsiding of those defilements for which penetration of the path has occurred through their total eradication;

or it refers to the truths penetrated by the path, or rather, the intention is that it is the awakening to the ultimate truth (*paramatthasacca*) itself in accordance with its nature. “*Saccānuppatti* means... [the rest of the passage follows].

"...the realization of the fruit. For this being so, the twelve factors mentioned below—beginning with the acquisition of faith—are aids to the attainment of the truths; therefore it was said, "of those very same," meaning "of the twelve mentioned below.

This is not the meaning of the phrase "of those very same"; for although there is a difference in terms of being wholesome, resultant, and so forth, [they are the same] by way of their basis, object, plane, function, and so on.

However, because the path-factors, when cultivated and repeatedly practiced by way of the means (upāya), deserve to be called "fruits," the expression "of those path-associated factors" is used by applying that designation to what is similar to them.

For it is only in this way that the inclusion of "cultivation" (āsevana) is justified, and not otherwise; for there can be no cultivation or repeated practice of path-factors that exist for only a single moment of consciousness.
"Or 'it exists'": weighing (*tulanā*) is insight (*vipassanā*). For that [insight], being the means of emergence (*vuṭṭhānagāminī*), is of great service to the path as the primary factor;

for in its absence, there would be an absence of the path itself as the primary factor. Thus, by the sequence beginning with "effort is of great service to weighing, zeal is of great service to effort," it is very easy to understand how each preceding factor assists each subsequent one.
Therefore, he said: "By this method, the meaning in all the terms [is to be understood]."
"It is to be understood. The remainder is indeed easy to understand.
The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning (*Līnatthappakāsanā*) for the commentary on the *Caṅkīsutta* is completed.
6. Commentary on the *Esukārīsutta*.
437. *Koṭṭhāsaṃ* means a portion of flesh. *Laggāpeyyuṃ* means they would tie it with sinew or with thread and hang it from a man’s hand or from his garment as a suspension.
*Satthadhammaṃ* means the legal procedure to be administered by the caravan leader among the caravan traders.
*Tassa nikkhamanatthaṃ* means for the purpose of clearing that debt from the caravan traders.
“Pāpaṃ assa” means that for one who serves, the service would be harmful; therefore he said, “not better.

Noble birth and so forth are spoken of by the second section and so on, whereas here the meaning is that the failure and success regarding the substrata (upadhi) are expressed by the terms “worse” and so forth.
Therefore he said: “‘Worse’ (pāpiyo) means his personal existence (attabhāva) would be evil, base, and miserable. “Seyyaṃso” means a portion of welfare, or having the nature of welfare.
The meaning is as follows. Regarding "being of high birth," he says "by reason of being of high birth" because the nominative case is used in the sense of the instrumental.
As in such passages as "The complexion of the Tathāgata does not fade," the word *vaṇṇa* here is a synonym for praise;
thus he says, "For even a Vessa may possess a noble complexion."
440. Because it is said, “He should wander without a sound, without the noise of footsteps, with a bowl full of clay from the Soḷāra clan, moving without attachment,” alms must indeed be sought;
the intention is that this is their family custom. *Haritvā* means having removed. A *sattajīvo* is a dealer in living beings.
One who guards (*gopeti*) or protects is a *gopo*, appointed to the duty of guarding. *Asanti* means they reap.

*Tena* means "by that," which is to say, by what has been carried and cut. *Byābhaṅgī* refers to a carrying-pole (*kāja*), so called because various loads (*vividhaṃ bhāraṃ*) are broken against it or suspended from it.
441. *Anussarato* means "due to recollecting"; at the moment of recollecting one's family lineage, one comes to be designated by such terms as "a noble" (*khattiya*) and so forth.
Therefore he said: "When the ancient... is being recollected. And the definition of family is for the purpose of knowing high and low status.
"It is said": the brahmins prescribe the wealth and livelihood of those four castes through the occupations of the khattiya and other families;
the Tathāgata, however, prescribes only the supramundane Dhamma as a person’s wealth, because by means of that, a being achieves the state of supremacy in the world. The rest is easy to understand.
The commentary on the *Esukārīsutta*, the Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning, is completed.
7. Commentary on the *Dhanañjānisutta* 445.
"Of the mountain standing encircling Rājagaha" refers to Mount Paṇḍava. [This was said] regarding the city of Rājagaha.
The country situated near the mountain in the southern direction is Dakkhiṇāgiri.

Because there is a row (*pāli*) of bags of rice (*taṇḍula*) there, it is called Taṇḍulapāli. It is said that near its gate, rice merchants would sit down after opening their bundles of rice and arranging them in a row; therefore, it acquired the common name "Taṇḍulapāli Gate. All of this...
"He takes the crop" means that after paying only the daily wage to poor farmers, he takes all the grain produced from the field. "Poor crops" means crops with a meager yield. 446.
"In this manner" refers to the providing of clothing, food, and wages for the slaves and laborers on auspicious days.

And he should support them by providing wealth, dwellings, ornaments, and so forth. He should perform what is to be done for friends and companions, such as speaking kindly to them, acting for their welfare, and treating them with equality;
likewise for kinsmen and blood relations. In this context, they are called "kinsmen" (*ñāti*) because they are known as "these are ours" through their connection via marriage;
they are called "blood relations" (*sālohita*) because they share the same blood through their connection to parents and other ancestors.

Because they do not cling even when gifts are properly given, they have no fixed abode (*tithi*); thus they are called *atithi*. One should perform what is to be done for them by sharing one’s own provisions;

this is the meaning of "offering to guests" (*atithibali*). Those who were formerly kinsmen but have now entered the realm of the hungry ghosts (*pettivisaya*) are the "deceased ancestors" (*pubbapeta*).
Having given gifts from time to time to those worthy of offerings, dedicating them to these [ancestors] is "what is to be done for the deceased ancestors" (*pubbapetakaraṇīya*).

The meaning is "an offering to spirits. Worshiping the deities from time to time with perfumes, flowers, ointments, incense, and food is "what is to be done for the deities" (*devatākaraṇīya*); the meaning is "an offering to the deities" (*devatābalī*).
Performing the duties of a king and attending upon him is "what is to be done for the king" (*rājakaraṇīya*).
"This body too" refers to one's own body. It is with reference to this meaning that he said: "The meaning should be understood by this method."

447. "The five acts of immorality" refers to those states that are the opposites of constant virtue (*sīla*). The ten unwholesome courses of action (*akusala-kammapatha*) are the ten acts of immorality.

The meaning of the term "one of uneven conduct" (*visamacārī*)—namely, one who practices what is contrary to the Dhamma because of engaging in bodily impropriety and so forth—is not stated separately.
448–453. *Osaranti* means they depart; the sense is that they are perishing. Therefore he said, "they decline. *Abhisaranti* means they proceed by way of increasing.
Therefore he said, "they increase. *Tatra* means in the Brahma-world. *Assa* refers to Dhanañjāni who had arisen in the Brahma-world.
*Tato paṭṭhāya* (from then on) refers to when the Blessed One said, "Bhikkhus, this is Sāriputta," and so forth.
It was stated from that point onward. "Free from the Four Truths" means being devoid of the truths as they are defined and analyzed.
But in terms of actual meaning, why was it not said that even prior to that [the path] was free from the truths? Because there is no deliverance (niyyāna) that is free from the truths.
The Elucidation of the Meaning Obscured in the Commentary on the Dhanañjāni Sutta is completed.
8. Commentary on the Vāseṭṭha Sutta 454.
“They desire to purify their birth” means that this is due to the influence of the actions of the brahmins with whom they live, or because of their own lack of suitability.
Or, they desire to purify that [text] because of an impurity regarding its origin or out of apprehension.

"They desire to purify the *manta*" means that when a doubt arises—either through a challenge to the teacher’s reasoning regarding the recitation of the *manta* or for some other reason—they desire to purify it.
"In between" (*antara*) means in the middle; however, since the word *antara* can have other meanings, it should be understood as the phrase "another statement" (*aññā kathā*).
"One endowed with qualities such as patience, loving-kindness, and compassion is indeed 'virtuous' (sīlavā)";

thus he says, "virtuous means possessing qualities. Even at the time of relinquishing those [qualities], one is called "virtuous" because of that virtue. Or, because of being perfected in virtue, one is indeed possessed of them; thus he says, "virtuous means possessing qualities.
"Endowed with conduct" means one who practices good conduct.

455. "Trained" means you have been trained in the threefold knowledge (*tevijjā*); the meaning is that there is nothing further for you to do now. "Recognized" means they stand having made a formal acknowledgment.
They are called "those of the threefold knowledge" (*tevijjā*) because they study the three knowledges comprised within the three Vedas. Therefore he said, "of those who know the three Vedas.

They are called "brāhmaṇas" because they recite and study the three Vedas; [the text refers to] them. Whatever single word has been declared, that [should be understood] in terms of its meaning and its phrasing.

And for those who possess complete knowledge (*kevalin*), it is accomplished with little effort. "We have reached the goal" means we have attained perfection in the exposition of the threefold knowledge (*tevijjā*) and our own tradition.
For this meaning was stated by way of the metaphorical usage of the excellence of conduct as being caused by mental action; thus he said: "One endowed with that is one perfected in conduct."

"Beyond waning" (*khayātīta*) means situated on the side of increase; for it is said that from the first day of the bright fortnight (*pāṭipada*) onwards, the moon increases, not wanes. "People who pay homage" means they offer salutation.
"By the seeing of the goal" (*atthadassana*) means having arisen as the eye of the world in the sense of being a guide through vision by means of exposition. 456.
"Let the brahmin’s pondering rest for now"—namely, whether one becomes a brahmin by birth or by action.
"Let this discussion regarding brahmins stand for now.

'I shall explain in detail the classification of births in the world, starting from grass, trees, insects, and moths, for the purpose of demonstrating birth'—with these words, he promises the subject to be taught in order to gladden their minds.
In that regard, the phrase 'for these births are mutually distinct' is a statement of reason, because these things called births..."
They are distinct from one another; therefore, I shall explain the analysis of birth (*jātivibhaṅga*).
Since here it is *upādinnaka-jāti* (clung-to birth) that has come down as the subject to be explained, while the other [types of birth] serve as its illustration, it is stated in the Pāḷi:
"The analysis of birth of living beings. The meaning is: the birth of those various living beings.
Having thus spoken this illustration while explaining that which is to be illustrated: "Tassa" means of Vāseṭṭha.

Granted that the teaching arrived at by way of both young men—beginning with "I shall explain them to you"—nevertheless, the Blessed One, addressing Vāseṭṭha alone in various places with such words as "Know thus, Vāseṭṭha," placed him foremost according to this method.
He did so. Therefore it was said: “Of him, that is, of Vāseṭṭha. A distinction of birth (*jātibheda*) is a specific difference of birth;
the distinction of birth will become manifest through the illustration brought to clarity, because the meaning already admitted attains a state of clarity through that illustration.

“Yes, it is not allowable”—this is a statement of refusal based precisely on the diversity of actions (*kamma*), which implies a diversity of what is acquired (*upādinnāna*), and not on the diversity of seeds (*bīja*).
In order to show that it is a statement of negation by way of non-appropriation (*anupādāna*), the passage beginning with “Kamma, however” was stated. Its meaning is as follows:

the efficacy of kamma consists merely in the casting [of a being] into this or that womb; however, those specific qualities (*vaṇṇa*) which are determined for each respective womb are established only through the actual accomplishment of that particular womb.
Thus, that kamma which casts one into a particular womb is [the cause] of that which is overcome by the specific distinctions characteristic of that particular womb.

Because there is no distinction in the fruit without a specific distinction in the condition— namely, that it is conditioned by the aspiration for existence (bhavapatthanā) which serves as a condition either through the accomplishment of application or by being itself uninfatuated— it follows that this intended kamma,
having attained a distinct capacity or a specific power differentiated from mere aspiration and so forth, produces specific fruits such as the eye-faculty and the rest.
Thus, by being cast into a womb, there occurs the bringing about of specific distinctions determined by that womb. For the Elder,
having rejected the objection that the diversity of karma might be a condition for the diversity of what is acquired— just as the diversity of seeds [is a condition for the diversity of sprouts]—
it should be understood that he has determined that the diversity of karma, as distinguished by specific conditions, is indeed the condition.

"Of various colors" means of diverse kinds of color. Because they are well-known species of grass in the world—such as the *tāla* and *nāḷikera* palms—they are specifically understood according to the method of what is well-known (*abhiññāta*).
In the phrase "one who is a brahmin by birth," the word "only" (*eva*) is used in the sense of impossibility;

the construction is: "One could only be a brahmin by birth. And it is not accepted [that this is the case], because among brahmins—as with grasses, trees, and so forth—there is no such thing as being fixed by birth.

Because the characteristic mark (*liṅga*) is not perceived; because activities such as drinking, eating, speaking, laughing, and so forth—which are invariably restricted to the specific characteristic mark of being a Brahmin—are not perceived even in the absence of Vedic recitation (*mantajjhena*) and the like;
and because [the text] says "only by a distinction of speech," meaning only by a direct statement.
In cases such as "insects (*kīṭa*)" and "moths (*paṭaṅga*)," a diversity of species is obtained through the observation of their mutual distinction of characteristics. "Kunthas" are insects.
*Khajjakhādakā* are ants. *Uppatitvā* means having flown up again and again. They are called *paṭaṅgā* because they go to the state of a winged insect (*paṭa-bhāva*);
they are not small creatures or insects (*kīṭā*) per se. "Of those insects" refers to the *kāḷaka*-ants and so forth, such as the *kalandaka*-ants and others.
Their feet are indeed their bellies, because they move along by means of their bellies.
Showing that the grammatical formation is preceded by the noun *saññā* (perception), he said “in water,” just as one says “the state of a hero is heroism.
The word *pakkha* (wing) refers to the collection of wings; thus it is said, “they go by means of wings,” for there is no whole apart from its constituent parts.

It was stated in brief by the phrase, "Diverse according to birth," and so forth. Since there is nothing here in the meaning of the words that is difficult to understand, the passage beginning with "In this regard, the construction is as follows" was stated merely to show the connection.

This very sentence—"For there is no fixed rule such as 'brahmins have such a head' or 'khattiyas have such a head,' in the way that [there is for] elephants, horses, deer, and so on"—should be applied everywhere.
Showing this in brief, he said: "In this manner, everything should be applied.
Regarding the word *tassa* (of that), the application of the aforementioned concluding statement is as follows; the application now being stated should be understood.
457. *Vokāraṃ* means "removal" (*vokaraṇaṃ*); the meaning is that by which no distinction of genus is removed due to its excellence. Therefore, he said: "diversity" (*nānattaṃ*).
One who lives by means such as cattle-herding is failed in livelihood; one who engages in violence and so forth is failed in virtue;
and one who has abandoned the observances and so forth is failed in conduct. Since a general designation is applied to specific instances, he said:
“Cattle-herding means guarding fields. For it is said: “‘Go’ is a name for the earth. Craft (*sippa*) is that which is to be learned by various means; it is skill therein.
One who rules over others (*īsana*) or harms them (*hiṃsana*) is an *issa*; one who possesses such a person is an *issa*, namely a professional warrior (*yodhājīvika*).
The work of an *issa* is striking; a livelihood carried out by means of arrows and spears is *issatta*. Therefore he said, "one who lives by weapons.
To demonstrate precisely that which serves as the basis for his livelihood, it was stated: "arrows and spears."
The *Veda* is called *Brahma*; one who "goes by" (*aṇati*) or knows that is a *brāhmaṇa*.
