And this knowing consists precisely in practicing according to the method established by the ancient *brāhmaṇas*, through the tranquility performed by *brāhmaṇas*, and through the austerity of practice such that it is accepted by both those learned in worldly affairs who follow the *brāhmaṇa*-dharma and by the wise, thinking: "There is no one who has failed in livelihood, virtue, or conduct."
He said: "Having thus accomplished [the task] according to the Brahmin convention...

When this is so—that is, when one whose livelihood, virtue, and conduct are corrupted lacks the status of a Brahmin—it is not by birth that one is a Brahmin; rather, it is by means of qualities, namely the perfection of livelihood, virtue, and conduct, that one is a Brahmin.
Therefore, since it is qualities alone that constitute the state of being a Brahmin, in whatever context the division of the four castes occurs...

One born into a noble family who, by being endowed with qualities such as virtue (*sīla*), is possessed of merit—that person, by virtue of having expelled evil in the literal sense according to the stated definition, is a *brāhmaṇa*.
This is the method for understanding the state of being a *brāhmaṇa* here; thus, having established that this method is attained through its actual meaning.
"That" refers to that very method already described. "By way of the praise of a *brāhmaṇa*" means by way of the family's reputation, such as being well-born on both sides from the mother’s side.
He was born of a mother who was of such a kind as to be praiseworthy and commended, worthy to be the mother of a brahmin;
by this, a specific distinction has been made among the four modes of birth (yoni). Therefore he said: "Even there, by way of distinction.
Thus, by way of a specific distinction within the general [category], it is called "born of a womb, produced from a mother" (*yonijaṃ mātisambhavam*).

Having explained the meaning of the word (*pada*), he now states the meaning by way of indicating its specific distinction (*visesa-jotana*) without resorting to its general indication (*sāmañña-jotana*).
Thus, the words beginning with "by means of supplication" (*yācāya*) were spoken. Since "womb" (*yoni*) is defined as the path of pure birth, the connection is:
"this womb which has been described as the path of pure birth by virtue of being irreproachable. Furthermore, [the phrase] "born and produced from that" (*tatopi jātasaṃbhūtattā*) follows.
"Because of being born from a womb" means because of being produced through the attainment of a mother and father.

"Distinguished" means that human beings, as a collective whole, are distinguished by passion (*rāga*) and so forth. "Possessing something" (*sakiñcana*) means possessing something along with passion and so forth.
Likewise, "possessing impediments" (*sapalibodha*) means possessing impediments in the sense of obstacles, namely those designated as passion and so forth.
"By the relinquishing of all grasping" means by the renunciation of all grasping, which is designated as clinging (*upādāna*).
Since he has banished evil—that is, removed evil from his own continuum—therefore, "him I call a brahmin"; this is the meaning that should be stated.
Such is the instruction of this discourse, analyzed in its various aspects; therefore, in those respective places...
It should be understood in the manner already stated.
458. "Among those who have taken up a staff" means among those who have grasped a staff for the purpose of harming others, setting aside mere possession.
459. "Any kind of grasping" refers to any form of grasping, such as the grasping of craving (*taṇhā-gāha*) and so forth.
That sensual existence by which one is bound to the five strands of human sensual pleasure is "human bondage" (*mānusaka-yoga*).
In the phrase "human bondage," this is stated by taking a single part [of the whole]; the same principle applies to the term "divine bondage" (*dibba-yoga*).
"Dissociated from all bondages" means dissociated from all bondages of the defilements (*kilesa-yoga*) mentioned by the two preceding terms.

*Raṭiṃ*: attachment, delight, and clinging. *Kusalabhāvanāya*: weary of the cultivation of wholesome states, such as the cultivation of the body and so forth. *Vīriyavantaṃ*: he designates one as "heroic" (*vīra*) by virtue of possessing energy (*vīriya*);
for heroism is indeed energy. *Sundaraṃ ṭhānaṃ*: Nibbāna. *Sundarāya paṭipattiyā*: by means of the beautiful practice, that is, the noble practice.
*Nibbattiṃ*: the culmination. *Atīte*: in the past section. *Kiñcanakārako*: one who creates an obstacle, being a cause of impediment.

In the great qualities such as the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha) of those beyond training (asekkha), and because of having conquered the five Māras, he is the Conqueror of Victors (vijitavijaya).
460. "Not knowing this" means not knowing that what is called "a brahmin by birth" is merely a worldly convention.
That which produces a third kind of dogmatic adherence (diṭṭhābhinivesa) regarding the name and clan among brahmins—that indeed is their view. "Made" (kataṃ) means conditioned (abhisaṅkhataṃ).
It is merely constructed and established by way of conceptualization (*parikappa*), and thus accumulated; it does not arise through the conjunction of causes and conditions (*hetu-paccaya*).

"Convention" (*sammuti*) means by way of designation (*sammuti*). To the question, "What is that designation? he says, "by way of common usage" (*samaññāya*); the meaning is "by way of worldly common usage.

However, for those who do not know [reality] correctly from the perspective of the ultimate truth (*paramattha*), it is name and clan that are thus conceptualized; therefore he says, "If not," and so forth. But that...
They adhere even to what is non-existent as if it were truly existent; in order to show that this is their fault, it was said:
"Thus fashioned," and so forth. Therefore the Blessed One said: "One should not adhere to local dialects.
In the phrase "those who do not know" (*ajānantāno*), the word *no* has the sense of emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*), as in such expressions as "There is nothing equal to the Tathāgata."
He said, "They speak thus simply because they do not know.

*Nippariyāya* is an expression in the neuter gender; its meaning is "in a non-figurative sense," that is, directly and straightforwardly, and not by way of a figurative approach as in the previous [verse] beginning with "Whoever...
By the first half of the verse beginning with "Not by birth," he rejects the doctrine of birth.
Establishing the doctrine of action (*kammavāda*) by means of the latter half [of the verse].
"Therein" (*tattha*) means in this verse. For the purpose of expanding upon the meaning of the half-verse, it is said: "The farmer [is known] by his work.
Therein, the meaning common to both the former four lines and the latter two lines has been expanded. Therein...
Regarding the phrase "agriculture and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) includes crafts, trade, and the like.

Since the meaning of the term *paṭiccasamuppāda* (dependent origination) as a condition—understood primarily through its verbal expression—is dependent upon that which arises from the condition, it is said:
"By means of this condition, this comes to be. Whatever else needs to be said on this matter has been explained in the *Visuddhimagga*.
And this should be understood according to the method stated in its commentary. Regarding "families worthy of honor or contempt":
rebirth occurs through karma in families worthy of honor, such as those of the kṣatriyas and so forth, and in families worthy of contempt, such as those of the caṇḍālas and so forth;

for there is no production in such high or low families without karma acting as the cause that provides the occasion for its ripening. Wealth, poverty, and so forth—these are other forms of inferiority and excellence.
And here, just as the words *loka*, *pajā*, and *satta* express one and the same meaning, so too do the remaining terms;
however, it is said, "In this case, by the first phrase," etc., to show that there is indeed a distinction in their intended meaning (*adhippāya*).
This world was not created by Brahmā, because it arises through kamma; for no effects produced by proximate causes can be brought about by another.
The view of [the world's] arising is logical. Therefore he said: "The negation of that view is to be understood.

Furthermore, what ought to be said here should be understood according to the method explained in the *Visuddhimagga-ṭīkā* and other such works. Likewise, regarding the claim that the first arising of the world was not from Brahmā, it is stated:
"For by karma indeed, in those various [worlds]," and so forth. By the third [verse], [it is shown that] "from the very beginning, this world..."
This concludes the meaning already stated: "It proceeds by means of productive kamma. For a conclusion (*nigamana*) is the indication of that very meaning already expressed;
moreover, it serves to restrict the sense, which is why he said: "Having been bound by kamma alone, they proceed, and not otherwise.
By the fourth phrase: *yāyato* means "of one going"; *nibbattato* means "of one being reborn"; *pavattato* means "of one proceeding."
The ascetic practices (dhutadhammā) function specifically by way of burning away craving; thus he said, "By austerity" means "by the austerity of the ascetic practices.

Abstinence from sexual intercourse is specifically the holy life (brahmacariya) of the brahmins; since that is intended here by the term "holy life," he said, "By the holy life" means "by abstinence from sexual intercourse.
By these—namely, by these four terms beginning with "by austerity"—...
"By what has been spoken": by that which is supreme. "Purified through defilement and purification. "Brahma": the state of being Brahmā, the state of excellence.
Since its meaning here is the state of being a brahmin (*brāhmaṇabhāva*), he says, "it brings about the state of a brahmin.
"Both Brahmā and Sakka": because it is to be honored even by Sakka for those who revere Sakka, and because it is to be honored by Brahmā for those who revere Brahmā.
“Brahmā,” because he is to be honored even by Brahmā. “By those who know” means by the wise who understand the distinction of the ultimate (paramattha) brāhmaṇa;
for it is immeasurable for the ignorant. Therefore he said, “by the wise. The rest is easy to understand.
The *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Hidden Meaning) of the commentary on the *Vāseṭṭha-sutta* is completed.
9. Subhasuttavaṇṇanā 462.

He is called Todeyya because his village or market town is named Tudi; thus he is "born of him" (attaja), meaning the son of Todeyya. Therefore, [the Buddha] said, "From the village of Tudi," and so forth.
An *ārādhaka* is one who propitiates or wins over. Since the settling in the Dhamma (*dhammanisanti*) is desired through its accomplishment and fulfillment, therefore—
It is said: "the accomplisher, the fulfiller. It is a *ñāya* because it leads with certainty to Nibbāna, or because Nibbāna is reached and penetrated by means of it;
thus, because it is the cause for accomplishing this, the Dhamma is a *ñāya*, namely the Noble Path.
Therefore he says: "the causal Dhamma" (*kāraṇadhamma*). "Blameless" (*anavajja*) is the opposite of what is blameworthy (*avajja*).
463. It is called "leading out" (*niyyānika*) because it leads out from the round of existence (*vaṭṭa-cāraka*); this is formed by shortening the vowel *ī* and changing the letter *y* to *k*.
Alternatively, it is "leading out" because it is connected with leading out, or because its nature is leading out; that which is the opposite of this is "not leading out.
Since that [state] is, in terms of meaning, unwholesome activity, he says: "the course of the unwholesome" (*akusala-paṭipadā*).
The word *mahā* here signifies "many," as in expressions such as *mahājano* ("the great multitude"); thus he says, "by many who are great.
*Attha* means purpose (*payojana*). *Mahantāni* means numerous. *Kiccāni* means duties (*kātabbāni*). *Adhikaraṇāni* means matters of business or forms of livelihood.

The work of the household life itself is so called because it consists of the five offerings, the ten duties, and the eight stations, and because it is the basis for the maintenance of worldly existence.
Or it is the "home-life meditation subject" (gharāvāsakammaṭṭhāna) because it is the cause for the maintenance of life:
"Even with a small load, a wise and discerning man raises himself up, like a tiny fire that is well-tended."
Just as in the manner described in the verse regarding the junior pupil (Cūḷantevāsika).

464. Having set aside agricultural work—which is a state of misery like trade conducted through improper means—as an illustration, he spoke with reference to the duties of household life that proceed by way of unwise attention: "Just as farming... [etc.]..."
"In this way, the household life is also a subject for meditation (kammaṭṭhāna). Regarding the phrase "he was a supporter of brahmins":
it is said that he performed sacrifices after giving wealth to many brahmins. Regarding the word "above" (*upari*):

although he was made to explain his own doctrine by the brahmins with the words, "Tell us how it stands above," he spoke exactly as it stood [in truth] and passed away; having died, he was reborn in hell. Then the brahmins...
Thinking, “He has brought a fault upon our sacrifice,” they became angry and refused to take his corpse to the charnel ground.
Then, when his relatives offered a thousand [pieces of money], they accepted that thousand and allowed him to be removed from the house.
During the time of the Sammasambuddha Kassapa, thirty-six women gave various offerings, such as one giving cloth, another perfume, and another a jasmine garland.
Having performed merit consisting of giving, at the end of their lives they were reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven as attendants of Sakka,
the king of the gods, accompanied by a retinue of a thousand nymphs. When they were summoned after the Great Bodhisatta— who had become the teacher Guttila—
had sent the Vejayanta chariot of Sakka, the king of the gods, they each related to him the various deeds they themselves had performed.
They proclaimed it as merit. It was with reference to this that it was said: "It should be illustrated by the entire account of the *Guttila-vimāna*.
Regarding the phrase "the business of trade failing," the manner in which that fails has been explained below.
The connection is made by bringing in the point that likewise, when the subject of the practice for going forth fails, it becomes fruitless. "One who is incomplete in the precepts," and so forth.
This is the demonstration of the manner of its failure. Regarding the phrase "the happiness of jhāna, etc.," here the word "etc.

(ādi) should be understood as including the happiness of the perfection of virtue (sīlasampadā) and so forth together with one's fellow celibates, just as it includes the happiness of the higher knowledges (abhiññā) and insight (vipassanā).
The intention is that one attains even Arahantship, let alone the attainments of those still in training (sekkha) or worldlings (puthujjana).
"By means of a head of generosity" means having made that refuge through generosity—that is, giving—as the primary factor. "In this there is no discomfort for you":
the meaning is that he has made it straight, made it free from conflict, and brought it into harmony. "The practice of austerity" refers to the tending of the sacred fire;
and the practice of austerity is mentioned because the practice of the holy life (*brahmacariya*) is inherently incompatible with such conduct.

"State of not knowing" means the state of not being omniscient. However, the Blessed One’s omniscience stands spread out like oil poured upon the surface of water throughout the world with its devas; [thinking] "This is not fitting for me;
therefore, I shall turn back," he said, "O Gotama, you are a brahmin," and so forth. "To counter-respond" means to strike back by means of an opposing argument. "Resembling a white lotus."
“Having a color like the petal of a white lotus. “Well-rounded” means well-rounded in those places where roundness is appropriate.
“Merely a name” means merely a name, merely a word. Because even the state of being such [a thing] is absent, it is called “lowly”;
the word *nāma* is a synonym for “lowly. Therefore he said: “merely base.”
467. "Which speech is better for them? means: among the various types of speech being described for those wealthy brahmins such as Caṅkī and others, which speech is better?
The word "better" (*seyyā*) is stated with a change of grammatical gender. "By convention" (*sammutiyā*) means by worldly convention that does not transgress the boundaries of what is good;
thus he said, "by worldly usage. "By counsel" (*mantā*) means having deliberated by means of wisdom (*paññā*), which is designated as "counsel."

Having understood this, he said, "having weighed it. "Connected with the goal" means connected with the cause. Since that is, moreover, unilaterally endowed with logical consistency, he said, "dependent on reason.
Regarding the terms "obstructed" (āvuta) and so forth: first, it is "obstructed" (āvuta) by the blocking of the course of knowledge;
it is "shrouded" (nivuta) by the specific binding of the course of knowledge through concealment; and thus it is "covered over" (ophuṭa) or "wrapped around" (paliguṇṭhita).
“Enveloped” (*pariyoṇaddho*) means covered all over, concealed. Therefore he said, “wrapped around. 468.

“If this condition exists”: if this condition—namely, that “the fire burns by taking grass and wood as its fuel”—exists, or if it should be the case, then that other fire which takes grass and wood as its fuel would exist.
[Such a fire] would be possessed of defilement (*sadoso*) and accompanied by danger (*sādīnavo*).

"With defilement" means accompanied by afflictions. "Pure" means completely purified due to the absence of adventitious defilements (*upakkilesa*). "By the absence of birth and so forth" means by the removal of the karma and afflictions that are the conditions for birth. 469.

"They do not stand motionless" means that because there is something remaining to be added to them, they do not remain motionless or unshakable as they were originally established. "That fault" refers to the fault of deficiency.
"In the absence of another" means in the absence of false speech that destroys welfare (*atthabhañjakamusāvāda*).

For here, "another" is intended as the opposite of that false speech which, arising from a lack of desire to give away what belongs to oneself and so forth, has reached the status of a course of action (*akammapatha*);
thus, the other [type] is called "conventional false speech" (*vaḷañjakamusāvāda*) because it is for the most part used in common transactions and spoken in ordinary dealings. It is never...
"Deceitful" means they do not speak two kinds of talk. Because one might say that even those among outsiders who are esteemed for blameless austerity are dependent [on such talk], he said:

"The virtuous person is dependent on austerity. Because those with open mouths, adorned with the secrets of mantras, are entirely devoted to recitation, whereas others are not, he said: "Those gone forth recite constantly."
470. "Having gone out for a long time" means having departed for a long duration. They do not become entirely forgotten due to confusion of mindfulness and because the paths have been altered.
"Delaying" refers to the procrastination in saying, "This is the path.
"Procrastinating" means being without eloquence. To illustrate this with a simile, he said "Just as," and so forth.
“Endowed with strength” means being possessed of bodily strength. Regarding “kamma of limited measure”:
because the defilements such as lust (*rāga*) and so forth that produce limits have not been suppressed, it is said, “Kamma of limited measure is that of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*);

but because those [defilements] have been suppressed, it is stated, “Kamma of immeasurable measure is that of the fine-material and immaterial spheres (*rūpārūpāvacara*). Within that [immeasurable category], specifically, there is the cultivation of the immeasurables (*appamaññā*).
He says "in these too" and so forth because it is possible [that they might obstruct]. To show how the designation "measureless" (appamāṇa) is obtained due to their lack of activity, he says:
"The measure... is said. It does not linger and does not remain;

thus, even though sensual-sphere karma has been performed and accumulated, when the attained sublime jhāna is not lost, that [karma] is overcome, surpassed, and left behind on the path like something cast aside.
It does not remain because it lacks the capacity to grant rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). "To seize" means to obstruct. "To stand" means to establish itself.
"Having struck back" means having counter-attacked. "Having exhausted" means having spent its efficacy.
He said, "having warded off its result," because the exhaustion of kamma consists precisely in the prevention of the arising of its ripening (*vipāka*). The rest is easily understood.
The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning (*Līnatthappakāsanā*) of the Commentary on the *Subhasutta* is completed.
10. Commentary on the *Saṅgāravasutta* 473.
"Fully confident" (*abhippasannā*) means having become confident through direct realization. Therefore, he said: "Confident by way of unwavering confidence" (*aveccappasādavasena*).
The brahmin woman, being free from the stain of stinginess, said, "Give your gift to whoever you find pleasing.

Because her stinginess had been abandoned through the very path [of practice], she was one who belonged to both sides—both the side of the Buddhas and the side of the brahmins. *Kiṃsu* is a question-word meaning "what" or "how.
*Chetvā* means having cut off, not grasping, and destroying. *Sukhaṃ seti* means "he lies down in happiness" due to the absence of mental distress.
"He sleeps happily": from that very state he destroys what is called sorrow (*soka*).

"Anger" (*kodha*): anger characterized by the nature of being angry. "Having cut"—that is, having completely severed—it. "He lies down happily": because he is not scorched by the fever of anger, he sleeps happily.
Because his mental distress (*domanassa*) has been destroyed through the destruction of anger, he does not grieve. "Of the poison-rooted": of that which has the ripening of suffering.
"Of sweet-tipped" (*madhuragga*) refers to the pleasure that arises from retaliating against one who reviles, or from striking back at one who strikes;
it is with reference to this that he is called "sweet-tipped. In this context, the conclusion is designated as the "tip" (*agga*).
"Noble ones" (*ariya*) refers to the Buddhas and others who are noble.
"He spoke a question," it is said, because the brahmin thought: "The ascetic Gotama is honored by the world;
it is not possible to intimidate him by saying just anything or that. I shall ask a subtle question. Having composed a verse of inquiry, he thought:
"If he says, 'I would approve of the execution of such-and-such a person,' then those whom you do not approve of—"
"I shall refute him by asking: 'Do you wish to kill them? You have arisen for the destruction of the world; what is the use of your being a recluse?
If he says, 'I do not approve of the killing of anyone,' then I shall refute him by saying, 'If so, you do not even desire the killing of passion and the other defilements;
therefore, you wander about merely as a recluse. Thus questioned with this dilemma involving both sides, the recluse—"
Thinking, "Gotama will be unable to either swallow it or spit it out," he asked this question.
The Blessed One spoke to him in accordance with his disposition. His mind being satisfied by the answer to his question, he requested the going-forth (*pabbajjā*).
The Teacher ordained him, and he brought the duties of the going-forth to their ultimate completion. Therefore it is said: "Having gone forth, he attained *arahantship*."
“*Avabhūtā*” means fallen low (*adhobhūtā*). Since falling low for beings is non-prosperity and an ill omen, he said:

“become non-prosperous, become an ill omen. “*Paribhūtā*” means having come to be despised. Regarding the word “*vijjamānānan*,” it is a genitive used in the sense of disregard (*anādare*) in the Pāḷi;
showing this meaning, he said “*vijjamānesu*. Knowledge that is pre-eminent or increased—
"Paññāṇa" is said to distinguish the knowledge (ñāṇa) of the Blessed One.
"Abhijānitvā" means having known by means of highly distinguished knowledge.

"Vositavosānā" means that which has reached complete exhaustion and finality due to the completion of what was to be done. "Pāramisaṅkhātaṃ" means reckoned as a perfection (pāramī) because of its state of supreme excellence.
Therefore he said, "the far shore of all phenomena. "Of the holy life" means it is the beginning of the holy life of the Dispensation.
Therefore he said, "the originators, the producers. "Reasoning" (*takka*) is the conjecture that "this will be thus" or "this will be exactly so";
one who possesses such [reasoning] is a "reasoner" (*takkī*). Because he grasps various objects after having reasoned about them in such and such ways, therefore it was said:
“Takkagāhī” means one who has the habit of investigating, an investigator, who— due to the mere act of investigating by means of wisdom that functions as investigation—
speaks thus after having caused the course of wisdom to proceed. Having said, “It is so,” he expresses his own inspired thought,
which is refined by reasoning and accompanied by investigation, through the state of being an investigator of the aforementioned type of reasoning.
485. "Possessing a firm exertion": elsewhere, in the case of any other person, there was no such firm exertion;
the exertion of Master Gotama was unique, not shared by others. It was the exertion of a true person (*sappurisa*);
it was the exclusive exertion of such wonderful individuals as the Arahants who have attained the state of possessing the exertion of a true person. [He spoke] while being unaware.
"He proclaims" means that, not knowing the matter asked about through his own direct perception, he spoke with the notion that he had proclaimed it merely by producing a sound.
"While there is non-knowing" means while there is an absence of direct knowledge that "these are the presiding deities.
"By a wise person" means by a human being skilled in worldly convention; you, however, are unskilled even in worldly convention.
For one who does not understand the meaning of words says whatever comes to mind. "Highly esteemed" means highly manifest and approved by everyone, even by young children.
This is known from the phrase, "that there are gods. Therefore he said, "even by little children," and so forth. "Gods" refers to gods by birth (*upapatti-devā*).
They are called "super-gods" (*adhidevā*) because they are superior gods compared to conventional gods (*sammuti-devā*); and as for others, [they are so called] in comparison to humans.
What more need be said regarding the state of abundance? The remainder is indeed easy to understand.
Thus ends the Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning in the Commentary on the *Saṅgāravasutta* of the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*.
The commentary on the Brāhmaṇa-vagga is finished.
The sub-commentary to the Majjhima-paṇṇāsa is completed.
